topics.description: Share experiences with the languages spoken in the class and family (Herkunftssprachen), foreign languages and German Sign Language (Deutsche Gebärdensprache), and compare sounds, scripts, words and greetings across languages.
evidence: Say a greeting or number in another language and compare it
Find a similarity and a difference between German and another language
Describe that Deutsche Gebärdensprache is a language of its own
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know which languages their classmates speak — and can they tell you one way another language works differently from German?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Misunderstandings and Nonverbal Signals
topics.description: Notice and name misunderstandings in communication, interpret facial expression and gesture, and see how verbal and nonverbal signals together shape what is understood.
evidence: Describe a misunderstanding and its cause
Interpret facial expressions and gestures in a scene
Show how body language can contradict words
topics.assessmentPrompt: When there's a misunderstanding between {{name}} and a friend, can they explain afterwards what went wrong — words, tone or body language?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Telling About Own Experiences
topics.description: Tell others about a personal experience so that listeners can follow: in a sensible order, with who, where and when, and with some detail. Practised in the classic Erzählkreis (e.g. after weekends or holidays).
evidence: Tell about an experience in chronological order
Give the listener the who, where and when
Answer listeners' follow-up questions
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} tells you about their day, can you follow the order of events and know who was there and where it happened?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Expressing Feelings and Resolving Conflicts by Talking
topics.nameDe: Gefühle äußern und Konflikte im Gespräch klären
topics.description: Name own feelings (using symbols at first), voice a concern with an 'I' statement and take part in ritualised conflict talks such as Streitschlichtung or the Klassenrat, increasingly considering the other side's view.
evidence: Describe own feelings in a situation (I felt angry when …)
Follow the steps of a guided conflict talk
Restate the other person's point of view before replying
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} has an argument with a friend, can they say how they feel without shouting — and listen to the other side to find a solution together?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Conversation Rules
topics.description: Follow jointly agreed class conversation rules: raise a hand or use a talking stone, let others finish, listen, and stay on topic — also in video calls. German classrooms typically display these rules and practise them in the Morgenkreis or Sitzkreis.
evidence: Wait for a turn and let the speaker finish without interrupting
Remind others of a rule in a friendly way
Keep to rules in a video call (mute, wait, use the hand sign)
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a family conversation or a game with friends, does {{name}} wait until others have finished before speaking — and listen to what they said?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Retelling and Continuing Stories
topics.description: Retell a story heard or read in one's own words, keeping the main events in order, and invent a continuation or a different ending, supported by pictures or objects.
evidence: Retell a familiar story with beginning, middle and end
Use picture cards to retell events in the right order
Invent a plausible continuation of a story
topics.assessmentPrompt: After hearing a story, can {{name}} retell it in their own words in the right order — and make up what might happen next?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Speaking Clearly in Standard German
topics.description: Speak audibly, with clear articulation and in complete sentences oriented towards spoken Standard German (Standardsprache), switching from dialect or family language where the situation requires it.
evidence: Speak loudly and clearly enough for the class to understand
Use complete sentences when explaining something
Switch to Standard German forms in class discussions
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} explains something to an adult they don't know, do they speak clearly, in full sentences and in a way that anyone in Germany would understand?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Role Play and Drama
topics.description: Act out scenes from stories or everyday situations in role play, freeze frames (Standbild), improvisation or short performances, using voice, facial expression and gesture to fit the role.
evidence: Speak and move in a way that fits a given role
Create a freeze frame that shows a key moment of a story
Perform a short scene for an audience with partners
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} plays out a scene from a story, do they change their voice and body to show who the character is and how they feel?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Listening for Understanding
topics.description: Listen attentively to a speaker or a read-aloud text, retain key information, pass it on and ask a question when something is not understood.
evidence: Repeat the main information of a short message or instruction
Answer questions about a story listened to
Ask a clarifying question when something was not understood
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you give {{name}} a short message to pass on to someone else, do they get the important details right — and do they ask if something wasn't clear?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Choosing Books and Using the Library
topics.nameDe: Bücher auswählen und sich in der Bücherei orientieren
topics.description: Find one's way in a school or public library (Bücherei) — sections, shelf labels, borrowing — and choose books and media by interest and reading level, giving reasons for the choice.
evidence: Find the section for a type of book in the library
Choose a book using cover, blurb and a first look inside
Explain why a book was chosen
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a library, can {{name}} find the shelf with books they like and choose one that suits them — and tell you why they picked it?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Characters, Plot and Setting
topics.nameDe: Figuren, Handlung, Ort und Zeit erfassen
topics.description: Identify the characters, the sequence of events, and where and when a story takes place, and describe them using the terms Figur and Handlung.
evidence: Name the main characters and describe them briefly
Put the main events of a story in order
Say where and when the story happens
topics.assessmentPrompt: After a story, can {{name}} tell you who was in it, what happened in what order, and where it took place?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Rhyme, Line and Stanza
topics.description: Recognise poems and describe their form with the terms Reim, Vers (line), Strophe and speaker, and notice rhythm and sound effects.
evidence: Count the lines and stanzas of a poem
Mark rhyming words at the line ends
Describe the mood or sound of a poem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} a poem, can they point out the rhyming words and tell you how many stanzas (Strophen) it has?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Reciting Poems by Heart
topics.description: Learn short poems by heart using memorisation techniques and recite them expressively — a long-standing practice in German schools (e.g. seasonal poems, class celebrations).
evidence: Recite a learned poem without notes
Use voice, pauses and stress to bring out the meaning
Apply a memorisation technique such as line-by-line building
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} recite a short poem by heart — not just rattle it off, but with expression and pauses?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Audio Plays, Audiobooks and Explainer Videos
topics.description: Use audio and audiovisual media for enjoyment and learning — Hörspiele, audiobooks, podcasts, children's news and explainer videos — follow their content and describe how sound effects and music create atmosphere.
evidence: Retell the plot of an audio play
Describe how noises or music create mood
Take information from a children's explainer video
topics.assessmentPrompt: After listening to a Hörspiel, can {{name}} tell you what happened and how the sounds and music made it exciting?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Fairy Tales and the Brothers Grimm
topics.description: Know classic fairy tales, especially the Kinder- und Hausmärchen of the Brothers Grimm (Rotkäppchen, Hänsel und Gretel, Frau Holle), and recognise typical features: 'Es war einmal', good vs. evil, magic, numbers three and seven, happy ending.
evidence: Retell at least two Grimm fairy tales
Identify typical fairy-tale features in a text
Write or tell a short fairy tale using these features
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know stories like 'Hänsel und Gretel' — and can they tell you what makes a story a Märchen?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Writing a Picture Story
topics.description: Write a coherent story to a sequence of pictures (Bildergeschichte): one or more sentences per picture, joined with time words (zuerst, dann, plötzlich, am Ende), and a fitting title.
evidence: Write at least one sentence for each picture in order
Link sentences with varied time words instead of always 'und dann'
Add a title and an ending that fits the pictures
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you give {{name}} three or four pictures showing a little story, can they write what happens in order and connect the sentences with words like 'dann' or 'plötzlich'?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Letters and E-Mails
topics.description: Write personal letters, cards and e-mails with place and date, salutation followed by a comma and lower-case continuation (Liebe Oma, / wie geht es dir?), a closing and signature; capitalise the polite Sie/Ihr forms in formal letters.
evidence: Include date, salutation, main text, closing and name
Continue in lower case after the comma of the salutation
Choose du/Sie and the closing to suit the addressee
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes a thank-you letter to their grandmother, does it have a greeting like 'Liebe Oma,', a closing like 'Viele Grüße' and their name — in the right places?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: First Free Writing
topics.description: Write own short messages and texts from the first weeks of school — labels, a wish list, a sentence about a picture, a short note — using sound-based spelling, and read them to others. Free writing (freies Schreiben) is a strong tradition in German Anfangsunterricht.
evidence: Write a short sentence about a self-chosen topic or picture
Write a wish list or note for a real reader
Read own text aloud to others
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} sometimes write little notes, lists or sentences of their own — and can they read them back to you?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Writing Short Poems (Elfchen, Rondell)
topics.description: Write poems following simple forms common in German primary schools: the Elfchen (eleven words in five lines), acrostics, Rondell and rhyming couplets, playing with words and sounds.
evidence: Write an Elfchen following the word count per line
Write an acrostic on a given word
Use rhyme or repetition deliberately in a short poem
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write an 'Elfchen' — a poem of exactly eleven words in five lines — about a topic like autumn?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Fact File
topics.description: Present key facts about a person, animal or object in the fixed format of a Steckbrief (name, appearance, habitat, food, special features) using short notes rather than full sentences.
evidence: Fill in the standard headings of a Steckbrief
Write concise notes instead of full sentences
Add a fitting picture or drawing
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} makes a fact file about their pet or favourite animal, do they organise the information under clear headings with short notes?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Infinitive and Personal Verb Forms
topics.description: Distinguish the infinitive (Grundform: spielen) from the conjugated personal form (ich spiele, du spielst, er spielt, wir spielen …) and match verb endings to the subject.
evidence: Give the infinitive of a conjugated verb (läuft → laufen)
Conjugate a regular verb in the present for all persons
Match the verb ending to the subject in own sentences
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} 'What's the Grundform of du liest?', can they say 'lesen' — and conjugate 'spielen' for ich, du and wir?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Personal Pronouns
topics.description: Use personal pronouns (ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie) to replace nouns and avoid repetition, choosing er/sie/es by grammatical gender (der Löffel → er).
evidence: Replace a repeated noun with the fitting pronoun
Choose er, sie or es according to the noun's gender
Identify what a pronoun refers to in a text
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes 'Der Hund bellt. Der Hund rennt.', can they improve it with 'er' — and would they say 'es' for 'das Pferd'?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Comparing with Adjectives
topics.description: Form and use the comparative and superlative of adjectives (groß – größer – am größten, gut – besser – am besten) and compare with als and wie.
evidence: Form comparative and superlative of regular adjectives
Use irregular forms (gut, viel, gern)
Use als for inequality and so … wie for equality
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} say 'größer als' (not 'größer wie') and know that the forms of 'gut' are 'besser' and 'am besten'?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Past, Present and Future
topics.description: Understand that verbs can locate events in the present, past or future (Zeitstufen) and identify time words that support this (gestern, heute, morgen).
evidence: Say whether a sentence tells about the past, present or future
Change a sentence from today to yesterday orally
Match time words to the right time level
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you say 'Gestern spielte ich Fußball', can {{name}} tell you whether that happened in the past, is happening now or will happen?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Reading Fluently
topics.description: Read age-appropriate texts accurately, automatically and at an appropriate pace, respecting sentence boundaries and reading across line breaks. Reading fluency (Leseflüssigkeit) is an explicit KMK standard and a focus of German reading-promotion programmes.
evidence: Read a known-level text aloud with few errors at a steady pace
Read across line ends without pausing mid-sentence
Read silently faster than aloud while keeping track of content
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads a page of a children's book aloud, does it flow at a natural pace — not word by word — with pauses at full stops?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Reading Digital Texts and Hyperlinks
topics.description: Read digital texts on child-friendly websites and apps: follow hyperlinks purposefully, use menus and back buttons, and keep the reading goal in mind instead of getting lost.
evidence: Follow a link to find specific information and return
Distinguish links, menus and adverts on a children's website
Explain how a hypertext differs from a printed text
topics.assessmentPrompt: On a children's website, can {{name}} click through to the information they are looking for — and find their way back — without getting lost?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Paired Repeated Reading
topics.description: Practise fluency in a reading pair (Lautlese-Tandem): a stronger and a weaker reader read a text aloud in sync, the weaker one signals to continue alone, and the pair rereads until it flows.
evidence: Read in sync with a partner and follow the agreed signals
Reread the same passage until it is fluent
Help a partner by quietly correcting errors as agreed
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads a passage together with you several times in a row, does their reading get noticeably smoother each round?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Finding Your Way in Texts and Books
topics.nameDe: Sich in Texten und Büchern orientieren
topics.description: Use text features to get an overview and find things: title, table of contents, chapters, headings, subheadings, paragraphs, line numbers, columns, captions and glossary.
evidence: Find a chapter using the table of contents
Use headings to locate a section on a subtopic
Refer to a passage by page and line number
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to find the chapter about dinosaur teeth in a non-fiction book, do they use the table of contents and headings rather than flicking through every page?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Linking Information and Making Inferences
topics.description: Connect information across sentences (local coherence), resolve what pronouns refer to and draw simple conclusions that are not stated explicitly, using prior knowledge.
evidence: Say who or what a pronoun refers to
Combine two pieces of information to answer a question
Infer feelings or reasons not stated directly
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a story says 'Tom put on his boots and took an umbrella', can {{name}} work out that it was probably raining, even though it isn't written?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Before-Reading Strategies
topics.description: Prepare reading: set a reading goal, activate prior knowledge, look at title, headings and pictures, clarify the text type and formulate expectations about the content.
evidence: Make a prediction from title and pictures
State what one already knows about the topic
Name a goal for reading (e.g. find out how bees communicate)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before {{name}} reads a new non-fiction text, do they look at the title and pictures and guess what it will be about?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Reading Aloud with Expression
topics.description: Read a prepared text aloud to others with expression (sinngestaltend): suitable volume, emphasis, pauses and different voices for characters, using reading-aloud techniques such as marking pauses in the text.
evidence: Prepare a text by marking pauses and stressed words
Use voice to distinguish narrator and characters
Read so that listeners can follow and enjoy the text
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads a story aloud to a younger sibling, do they use different voices and pauses so that it sounds exciting?
topics.laenderNotes: Many schools take part in the national Vorlesewettbewerb of the Börsenverein, aimed at Klasse 6.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Decoding Long Words via Syllables and Morphemes
topics.nameDe: Unbekannte Wörter über Silben und Wortbausteine erlesen
topics.description: Read long, unfamiliar words — including the long compounds typical of German (Fußballweltmeisterschaft) — by breaking them into syllables, frequent letter clusters and morphemes such as ver-, vor-, -ung.
evidence: Split a long compound into its parts to read it
Recognise frequent prefixes and suffixes at a glance
Read an unknown multi-syllable word correctly on the first or second try
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} meets a long word like 'Geburtstagsüberraschung', do they break it into parts they know to read it?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Deriving ä and äu from Related Words
topics.nameDe: Ableiten: ä und äu von a und au
topics.description: Decide between ä/e and äu/eu by looking for a related word with a or au (Bäume – Baum, Hände – Hand, läuft – laufen); words without such a relative are normally written with e or eu.
evidence: Find the related word with a/au for words with ä/äu
Write plural forms with Umlaut correctly (Häuser, Wälder)
Explain why Eltern is written with E but Ältere with Ä
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes 'Bäume', can they tell you it has ä because it comes from 'Baum'?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Double Consonants, ck and tz
topics.nameDe: Doppelkonsonant, ck und tz nach kurzem Vokal
topics.description: After a short stressed vowel followed by a single consonant sound, double the consonant (kom-men, Mut-ter); write ck instead of kk and tz instead of zz (Decke, Katze). The syllable-joint (Silbengelenk) model explains this Schärfung.
evidence: Write two-syllable words with double consonants correctly (Sonne, Teller)
Use ck and tz instead of kk and zz
Explain the double consonant with the short vowel or the syllable joint
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes 'Mutter', 'Decke' or 'Katze', do they double the consonant or use ck/tz — and can they tell you it's because the vowel before is short?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Proofreading for Spelling
topics.description: Develop alertness to likely errors, proofread own texts deliberately (e.g. reading backwards word by word), mark doubtful spellings and clarify them with strategies or the dictionary; know one's personal error hotspots.
evidence: Mark words one is unsure about while writing
Find and correct a good share of own spelling errors when proofreading
Name own typical error types and a strategy against each
topics.assessmentPrompt: After {{name}} writes something, do they read it through to catch spelling mistakes — and do they know which kinds of mistakes they typically make?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Spelling Long i as ie
topics.description: Write a long, stressed i in native German words as ie (Biene, Spiel, fliegen), the regular case, while recognising short i (Kind) and a few exceptions (Igel, mir, Maschine).
evidence: Write words with long i using ie
Distinguish long and short i in word pairs (bieten – bitten)
Name a few common exceptions as Merkwörter
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes words like 'Spiel' or 'Brief', do they write ie for the long i sound?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Memorising Exception Words
topics.description: Memorise words whose spelling cannot be derived from rules (Vater, Vogel, Hexe, Fuchs, Saal, Igel) using practice routines such as card boxes, colour-marking the tricky spot and regular review.
evidence: Mark the tricky part of a Merkwort
Practise Merkwörter with a card box until spelled correctly
Spell common Merkwörter correctly in free writing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know which words they simply have to remember — like 'Vater' with V — and spell them correctly when writing freely?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Talking About Spellings
topics.description: Compare spellings (Wal/Wahl, Raum/Saum, Hund/Hunde) and discuss in a Rechtschreibgespräch why a word is written as it is, naming the strategy used (schwingen, verlängern, ableiten, merken).
evidence: Explain the spelling of a word by naming a strategy
Compare word pairs and describe similarities and differences
Discuss a doubtful spelling with a partner and agree on a solution
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} why 'Hund' is written with d, can they explain it with a strategy — like 'because you say Hunde'?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Hyphenating at the End of a Line
topics.description: Divide words at the end of a line according to spoken syllables (Ta-fel, Kat-ze), keeping ck and ch/sch together (Zu-cker, la-chen) and never leaving a single vowel alone.
evidence: Divide words correctly between syllables
Keep ck, ch and sch together when dividing
Split double consonants between syllables (Son-ne)
topics.assessmentPrompt: When a word doesn't fit at the end of the line, does {{name}} split it at a syllable boundary — like 'Zu-cker', not 'Zuc-ker'?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Lengthening Words to Hear Final Consonants
topics.description: Find the right letter at the end of a word where German final-obstruent devoicing (Auslautverhärtung) makes d sound like t, g like k and b like p, by lengthening the word (Hund – Hunde, Berg – Berge, gelb – gelber, er lebt – leben).
evidence: Lengthen nouns with the plural to check the final letter
Lengthen adjectives and verbs (gelb – gelber, lebt – leben)
Use lengthening to decide between d/t, g/k, b/p in new words
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} isn't sure whether 'Hund' ends in d or t, do they say 'Hunde' to hear the answer?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Using a Dictionary
topics.description: Look up spellings in a children's dictionary (Wörterbuch) using alphabetical order to the second or third letter, and turn inflected forms into the base form first (lief → laufen, Bäume → Baum).
evidence: Find a word quickly using alphabetical order beyond the first letter
Convert a verb or plural form to its base form before searching
Check and correct a doubtful spelling with the dictionary
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is unsure how to spell 'fährt', do they know to look up 'fahren' in the dictionary — and can they find it quickly?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Typing on a Keyboard
topics.description: Find letters on a German QWERTZ keyboard, type words and short sentences with capitals (Shift), Umlaute, ß, spaces and punctuation, and correct typing errors.
evidence: Type a short sentence including capitals and an Umlaut
Use the space bar, Shift and Backspace keys purposefully
Find ß and the punctuation keys on a German keyboard
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} types a short message on a computer or tablet, can they find the letters, make capitals, type ä, ö, ü and fix their typos?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Joined Handwriting
topics.description: Learn a joined script developed from print — depending on the Land or school the Lateinische Ausgangsschrift (LA), Vereinfachte Ausgangsschrift (VA), Schulausgangsschrift (SAS) or the partly joined Grundschrift — including letter joins and writing whole words in one flow.
evidence: Write all letters of the school's joined script in the correct form
Join letters within a word with the correct connecting strokes
Write short words in one flow without lifting the pen unnecessarily
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write their name and a short sentence in the joined handwriting they learned at school, with the letters properly connected?
topics.laenderNotes: The script is a Land or school decision: Bayern allows VA or SAS; NRW lets schools develop a joined hand from print without prescribing a model; Hamburg and several other Länder permit the Grundschrift; the eastern Länder traditionally use the SAS. Timing ranges from end of Klasse 1 to Klasse 3.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Giving and Receiving Feedback
topics.description: Give specific, kind and criteria-based feedback on others' talks or contributions (e.g. two stars and a wish) and accept feedback on one's own without taking it personally.
evidence: Name one strength and one specific improvement using agreed criteria
Phrase criticism respectfully
Use received feedback to improve a second attempt
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a sibling shows {{name}} a drawing or performance, can they say what was good and give one helpful, kind tip — and take tips themselves without sulking?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Stating and Justifying an Opinion Orally
topics.nameDe: Eigene Meinung mündlich vertreten und begründen
topics.description: Put forward one's own wish or position and back it with at least one reason (weil …), e.g. when the class decides on a trip destination or in the Klassenrat.
evidence: State an opinion clearly (Ich finde …, weil …)
Give at least one relevant reason for a position
Respond to a counter-argument with a further reason
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} wants something, can they explain why with a real reason — not just 'because I want it' — and answer if you disagree?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Voice and Body Language
topics.nameDe: Sprechweise bewusst gestalten (Lautstärke, Betonung, Tempo, Körpersprache)
topics.description: Deliberately vary volume, stress, speed, pauses, gesture, facial expression and posture to suit the situation and listeners, and notice their effect, e.g. by recording one's own voice.
evidence: Adapt volume and speed to the room and audience
Use pauses and stress to highlight important points
Describe the effect of a recorded talk and improve it
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} tells a joke or presents something, do they change their voice, pause and use gestures to make it work for the listeners?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Talking About One's Learning
topics.description: Describe how one solved a task, explain observations and reasons, present learning results using subject terms and reflect on what worked — e.g. in a closing circle or learning conference.
evidence: Explain step by step how a task was solved
Use subject terms (e.g. Nomen, Silbe) when describing results
Say what one would do differently next time
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} how they worked out a tricky homework task, can they explain their steps and say what helped them?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Understanding Characters' Feelings and Motives
topics.description: Take the perspective of a literary character, infer feelings and motives from what they say and do, take a stance on their behaviour and compare it with one's own experience.
evidence: Explain why a character acts as they do
Describe a character's feelings at a key moment with evidence
Say whether one agrees with a character's decision and why
topics.assessmentPrompt: When a character in a book does something surprising, can {{name}} explain why they might have done it and how they were feeling?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Presenting a Children's Book
topics.description: Present a self-chosen children's book to the class (Buchvorstellung): title, author, main characters, a teaser of the plot, a read-aloud passage and a reasoned personal judgement.
evidence: Give title, author and main characters
Read a well-chosen passage aloud
Give reasons for recommending or not recommending the book
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} presents their favourite book to the class, do they say what it's about without spoiling the end, read a good part and explain why they like it?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Reading Journal
topics.description: Record reading experiences in a reading journal (Lesetagebuch) or reading box: summaries of chapters, drawings, questions, favourite quotes and personal reactions.
evidence: Write a short entry after reading a chapter
Record a question or personal reaction to the text
Collect quotes or drawings that capture the book
topics.assessmentPrompt: While reading a book, does {{name}} keep notes, drawings or thoughts about it — and can they show you how their view of the book developed?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Literary Conversation
topics.description: Take part in a structured conversation about a literary text (literarisches Gespräch), sharing impressions, questions and interpretations and responding to others' views.
evidence: Share a personal impression or question about a text
Respond to another reader's interpretation
Refer to the text when explaining a view
topics.assessmentPrompt: When you talk with {{name}} about a book you both read, do they share their own ideas and respond to yours — referring back to the story?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Kinds of Texts
topics.nameDe: Erzählende, lyrische und szenische Texte sowie Sachtexte unterscheiden
topics.description: Distinguish narrative, poetic and dramatic texts as well as literary texts and factual texts (Sachtexte) by simple features, in print and other media.
evidence: Sort texts into story, poem, play and factual text
Name a feature that identifies each kind
Say whether a text tells an invented story or informs about facts
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} a poem, a short play and a factual text about frogs, can they tell you which is which and how they know?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Instructions and Recipes
topics.description: Write instructions, game rules or recipes: list materials, give steps in the correct order, use precise verbs and a consistent form of address (imperative or 'man').
evidence: List all materials or ingredients needed
Write numbered steps in a logical order
Use imperative or man-forms consistently
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes down how to make their favourite sandwich, could someone else follow the steps exactly without asking?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Personal Narrative
topics.description: Write about a real experience as a structured narrative with introduction (who, where, when), a main part building to a climax (Höhepunkt) and a conclusion, usually in the Präteritum and with thoughts, feelings and some direct speech.
evidence: Structure the story into introduction, main part with climax and ending
Keep the past tense consistent
Include feelings and at least one piece of direct speech
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes about something exciting they experienced, does the story have a clear beginning, an exciting high point and an ending — told in the past tense?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Imaginative Story
topics.description: Invent a story from a prompt — a story starter, a picture, music or three given 'trigger words' (Reizwortgeschichte) — with a plausible plot, a problem and a resolution.
evidence: Use all given trigger words meaningfully in the plot
Build a story around a problem and its resolution
Give the story an original title
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you give {{name}} three random words like 'Schlüssel, Gewitter, Hund', can they invent a story that uses all three in a way that makes sense?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Varied and Precise Wording
topics.description: Make texts readable and lively by varying sentence openings, choosing precise verbs and adjectives from word fields (instead of always sagen, gehen, schön) and linking sentences coherently.
evidence: Vary sentence openings in a text
Replace general words with precise ones from a word field
Use linking words so that sentences connect logically
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes a story, do the sentences start in different ways and do they use precise words like 'flüstern' or 'rennen' instead of always 'sagen' and 'gehen'?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Planning a Text
topics.nameDe: Ideen sammeln und Text planen (Cluster, Mindmap, Schreibplan)
topics.description: Collect ideas with a cluster or mind map, select and order them, and draft a simple writing plan (Stichpunkte, numbered outline) before writing; in Klasse 5–6 plan to a time limit and text type.
evidence: Create a cluster or mind map on a topic
Number the ideas in the order they will appear
Use the plan while writing and tick off covered points
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before writing a story or report, does {{name}} jot down ideas and put them in order first — and then actually use that plan?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Rewriting and Continuing Literary Texts
topics.nameDe: Produktiv zu Texten schreiben (umschreiben, weiterschreiben, Paralleltext)
topics.description: Write creatively based on a literary model: continue a story, change the ending or perspective, write a letter to a character or a parallel text to a poem or fairy tale.
evidence: Write a continuation that fits characters and plot
Retell a scene from another character's perspective
Write a parallel text keeping the model's structure
topics.assessmentPrompt: After reading a story, can {{name}} write a new ending or tell part of it from another character's point of view in a way that fits the original?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Writing Conference and Peer Feedback
topics.description: Discuss drafts in a small group (Schreibkonferenz) or give written peer comments with a Textlupe sheet: say what works, ask questions and suggest concrete improvements; the author decides which to use.
evidence: Read a partner's text and note strengths and suggestions on a Textlupe
Ask the author a clarifying question about the text
Decide which feedback to use and revise accordingly
topics.assessmentPrompt: When a classmate reads {{name}}'s story, can {{name}} use their suggestions to improve it — and give helpful comments on the classmate's text in return?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Purpose and Audience
topics.description: Before writing, clarify why one is writing (inform, entertain, persuade, ask), who will read the text and what they already know, and which text type fits.
evidence: State the purpose and the reader of a planned text
Choose a text type that fits the purpose
Adapt content and wording to a known reader
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before {{name}} writes something, can they tell you who it is for and what it should achieve — and does the text fit that reader?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Revising with Criteria
topics.description: Treat a text as a draft and revise it using a checklist of text-type criteria (content, structure, wording, spelling), e.g. by reading it aloud, inserting, deleting and rearranging, before producing a final copy.
evidence: Check a draft against a criteria checklist
Make content revisions, not just spelling corrections
Produce an improved final version
topics.assessmentPrompt: After {{name}} finishes a first draft, do they go back and improve it — adding, cutting or reordering — rather than only fixing spelling?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Compound Nouns
topics.description: Form and analyse German compounds written as one word (Haus + Tür = Haustür), identify the head word (Grundwort) that determines meaning and article and the modifier (Bestimmungswort), including linking elements (Geburtstag-s-kuchen).
evidence: Form compound nouns from two or more words
Identify the Grundwort and take its article (die Tür → die Haustür)
Explain the meaning of a compound from its parts
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that a 'Hundehütte' is a kind of Hütte, not a kind of Hund — and say which article it takes?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Words with Several Meanings
topics.description: Recognise words with several meanings (Bank, Schloss, Maus) — played as the classic German guessing game Teekesselchen — and use context to decide which meaning is meant.
evidence: Explain two meanings of a homonym
Use context to choose the intended meaning
Invent a Teekesselchen riddle for others
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain two different meanings of 'Schloss' — and play Teekesselchen with you?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Prefixes and Suffixes
topics.description: Identify prefixes (ver-, vor-, be-, ent-, un-) and suffixes (-ung, -heit, -keit, -lich, -ig, -bar) as word-building blocks, describe how they change meaning, and use suffixes to change word class (frei → Freiheit, Freund → freundlich).
evidence: Split words into prefix, stem and suffix
Form new words with given prefixes and explain the change in meaning
Turn adjectives into nouns and nouns into adjectives with suffixes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} make new words from 'fahren' with prefixes like 'ab-', 'ver-' or 'weg-' — and turn 'Freund' into 'freundlich'?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Word Families and Word Stems
topics.description: Group words that share a common stem into a word family (fahren, Fahrer, Fahrrad, Abfahrt, gefährlich) and identify the stem as the shared meaning-bearing part.
evidence: Collect words belonging to one word family
Mark the shared stem in each word
Explain how family members are related in meaning
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} find several words that belong to the family of 'spielen' — like 'Spieler', 'Spielplatz' or 'verspielt' — and show the part they all share?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Word Fields, Synonyms and Opposites
topics.description: Collect words of similar meaning in a word field (Wortfeld 'sagen': flüstern, rufen, antworten), distinguish their nuances, find opposites (Gegensatzwörter) and build up personal word collections for writing.
evidence: Collect at least five words for a word field
Choose the most precise word from a field for a context
Name opposites for common adjectives and verbs
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} list different ways to say 'gehen' — like 'schleichen', 'rennen', 'schlendern' — and explain when each fits?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Future Tense (Futur I)
topics.description: Form the Futur I with werden plus infinitive (ich werde reisen) and know that German often expresses the future with the present tense plus a time word (Morgen fahre ich).
evidence: Form the Futur I correctly for different persons
Change sentences from present to future
Recognise present tense with a time word as future reference
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} turn 'Ich spiele' into the future — 'Ich werde spielen' — and notice that 'Morgen spiele ich' also talks about the future?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: The Four Cases
topics.description: Identify the four German cases (Nominativ, Genitiv, Dativ, Akkusativ) of nouns with their articles using the case questions Wer/Was?, Wessen?, Wem?, Wen/Was?, and notice how the article changes (der Hund – des Hundes – dem Hund – den Hund).
evidence: Ask the case question to determine the case of a noun group
Name the four cases and their questions
Decline a noun with definite article through all four cases
topics.assessmentPrompt: In 'Der Junge gibt dem Hund den Ball', can {{name}} work out which case each noun is in by asking Wer?, Wem? and Wen?
topics.laenderNotes: KMK lists 'Fall' among the Primarstufe terms and Bayern expects case changes to be described in Jgst. 3/4; other Länder introduce the case questions in Klasse 4 and consolidate the Genitiv in Klasse 5.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Conjunctions
topics.nameDe: Konjunktionen (und, oder, aber, weil, dass, wenn)
topics.description: Use conjunctions to link words and clauses and express relations: addition (und), alternative (oder), contrast (aber), cause (weil, denn), condition (wenn), time (als, nachdem).
evidence: Join two sentences with a fitting conjunction
Explain the meaning relation a conjunction expresses
Use weil and denn with the correct verb position
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} join 'Ich bleibe drinnen' and 'Es regnet' with 'weil' — and say 'weil es regnet' with the verb at the end?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Place and Time Phrases
topics.description: Identify sentence parts that tell where (Ortsangabe: Wo? Wohin? Woher?) and when (Zeitangabe: Wann? Wie lange?) and use them to make texts more precise.
evidence: Find place and time phrases with the matching questions
Add a place or time phrase to a sentence
Move a time phrase to the start of a sentence
topics.assessmentPrompt: In 'Am Montag gehen wir in den Zoo', can {{name}} find the part that says when and the part that says where?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Perfect Tense (Perfekt)
topics.description: Form the Perfekt with haben or sein plus the past participle (ich habe gespielt, wir sind gelaufen) and know it is the usual past tense of spoken German, in contrast to the written Präteritum.
evidence: Form the Perfekt of regular and common irregular verbs
Choose sein for verbs of movement and change (ist gefahren)
Explain that people mostly use the Perfekt when talking about the past
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} talks about the weekend, do they say 'Wir sind geschwommen' and 'Ich habe gegessen' — choosing haben or sein correctly?
topics.laenderNotes: The KMK Primarstufe appendix only lists Präsens, Präteritum and Futur; most Länder curricula and textbooks nevertheless introduce the Perfekt in Klasse 3–4 (Bayern: 'verschiedene Zeitformen'), with systematic treatment in Klasse 5.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Prepositions and the Cases They Require
topics.description: Recognise prepositions as words expressing relations of place, time and cause, and use the case they govern: mit/bei/nach + Dativ, für/durch/ohne + Akkusativ, and two-way prepositions (in, auf, an) with Dativ for location (Wo?) and Akkusativ for direction (Wohin?).
evidence: Find prepositions in a sentence
Use mit and für with the correct case
Choose Dativ or Akkusativ after in/auf by asking Wo? or Wohin?
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} say 'Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch' but 'Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch' — and can they explain the difference?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Present and Simple Past
topics.description: Form and name the Präsens and the Präteritum, including frequent strong verbs with vowel change (gehen – ging, singen – sang), and know that written stories are usually told in the Präteritum.
evidence: Convert a short text from present to Präteritum
Form the Präteritum of common strong verbs
Use the Präteritum consistently when writing a story
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes a story, do they use forms like 'ging', 'sah' and 'rief' consistently — and can they tell you the tense is called Präteritum?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Substitution, Deletion and Expansion Tests
topics.description: Use the operational tests of German school grammar to analyse and improve sentences: replace a word or group (Ersatzprobe), delete what is unnecessary (Weglassprobe) and add precise information (Erweiterungsprobe).
evidence: Replace a repeated word using the Ersatzprobe
Shorten a sentence with the Weglassprobe without losing key information
Add detail to a sentence with the Erweiterungsprobe
topics.assessmentPrompt: When revising a text, can {{name}} replace boring repeated words, cut what isn't needed and add useful details — and name these steps?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Subject and Predicate
topics.description: Identify the predicate (Prädikat, the verb part, also called Satzkern) and the subject (Wer oder was …?) of a sentence and the agreement between them; know that the predicate can have two parts (hat … gespielt).
evidence: Underline the predicate in a sentence
Find the subject with the question Wer oder was?
Correct subject–verb agreement errors
topics.assessmentPrompt: In 'Die Kinder spielen auf dem Hof', can {{name}} find the predicate and use 'Wer spielt?' to find the subject?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Moving Sentence Parts (Umstellprobe)
topics.description: Identify the constituents (Satzglieder) of a sentence by moving word groups around while keeping the meaning (Heute spielt Tim im Garten. / Im Garten spielt Tim heute.) — groups that move together form a Satzglied, and the conjugated verb stays in second position.
evidence: Rearrange a sentence in several correct ways
Mark word groups that always move together as one Satzglied
Notice that the conjugated verb stays in second position
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you give {{name}} the sentence 'Oma backt heute einen Kuchen', can they rearrange it in different ways and tell you which words always stay together?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Grasping the Whole Text
topics.description: Build an overall understanding of a text (global coherence): state its topic or central message, summarise it in a few sentences and give it a fitting title.
evidence: State the main topic or message of a text in one sentence
Summarise a text in a few sentences
Choose or invent a fitting title
topics.assessmentPrompt: After reading a chapter or article, can {{name}} tell you in one or two sentences what it was mainly about?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: After-Reading Strategies
topics.description: After reading, summarise central statements, visualise the content (sketch, table), check earlier expectations and give a reasoned evaluation of the text.
evidence: Summarise the central statements orally or in writing
Turn text information into a sketch or table
Compare initial predictions with what the text actually said
topics.assessmentPrompt: After finishing a text, can {{name}} sum it up, say whether their first guess was right and tell you what they thought of it?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Reading Tables, Charts and Plans
topics.description: Extract information from non-continuous texts (diskontinuierliche Texte) such as tables, timetables, bar charts, maps and plans, and relate it to accompanying text.
evidence: Read a value from a table or timetable
Compare two bars or entries in a diagram
Use a simple plan or map to answer a question
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} a bus timetable or a simple chart, can they find the information you ask for — like when the next bus leaves?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Monitoring Comprehension
topics.description: Check one's understanding while reading, notice and describe where understanding breaks down (Nichtverstehen begründen) and choose a fix-up strategy such as rereading, asking or looking up.
evidence: Point to the place in a text where understanding broke down
Explain why it was difficult (unknown word, long sentence)
Choose and apply a suitable fix-up strategy
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} doesn't understand part of a text, can they show you where exactly it got confusing and what they could do about it?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: During-Reading Strategies
topics.description: While reading, mark key information, underline and clarify unknown words, divide the text into sections with headings and take notes.
evidence: Underline key words relevant to the reading goal
Clarify unknown words by context, asking or looking up
Divide a text into sections and give each a heading
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} works through a school text, do they mark important parts and figure out unknown words instead of just reading on?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Capitalising Abstract Nouns
topics.description: Capitalise nouns that name feelings, ideas and events (Angst, Freude, Glück) and recognise suffixes that always form nouns (-ung, -heit, -keit, -nis, -schaft) as capitalisation signals.
evidence: Capitalise abstract nouns in own texts
Use noun suffixes as a test for capitalisation (Freiheit, Erlebnis)
Apply the article test to abstract words (die Angst)
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes about feelings, do they capitalise words like 'Freude' or 'Angst' — and words ending in -ung or -heit?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Silent h and Double Vowels
topics.description: Learn the long-vowel markings that cannot be derived from rules: the silent h (mostly before l, m, n, r: Zahl, nehmen, Uhr) and double vowels (Meer, Boot, Saal), treated as Merkwörter and word families.
evidence: Spell frequent words with Dehnungs-h correctly (fahren, Zahl, wohnen)
Spell the common words with aa, ee, oo correctly
Keep the h or double vowel across the word family (fahren – Fahrt)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} spell words like 'fahren', 'Uhr' or 'Boot' correctly — knowing these are words to remember rather than rules?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Spelling Common Loanwords
topics.description: Distinguish native core words (Kernwörter) from loanwords (Fremdwörter) and spell frequent loanwords correctly (Maschine, Melone, Computer, Pizza, Rhythmus), noticing that they follow other patterns, e.g. no Dehnungs-h, i instead of ie.
evidence: Identify words that look or sound foreign
Spell frequent loanwords from school and everyday life correctly
Use the dictionary to check loanword spellings
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes words like 'Maschine' or 'Computer', do they spell them correctly — and notice that these words follow different rules?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Commas in Lists
topics.description: Separate the items of a list with commas, with no comma before the final und/oder (Äpfel, Birnen und Bananen) — unlike the optional serial comma in English.
evidence: Insert commas between listed words or word groups
Leave out the comma before und or oder in a list
Punctuate a list of adjectives correctly (ein großer, alter Baum)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes a shopping list as a sentence, do they put commas between the items but not before the last 'und'?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: s, ss or ß
topics.description: Choose between s, ss and ß: voiced s is written s (Rose); a voiceless s after a long vowel or diphthong is ß (Straße, heißen); after a short vowel it is ss (Wasser, Kuss); lengthening helps at the word end (Gras – Gräser, Fuß – Füße).
evidence: Write ß after long vowels and diphthongs in common words
Write ss after short vowels (Klasse, muss)
Lengthen words to decide on s or ß at the end (Haus – Häuser, Gruß – grüßen)
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes 'Straße', 'Wasser' and 'Haus', do they choose ß, ss and s correctly — and can they say why?
topics.laenderNotes: Uniform across Germany since the 1996/2006 orthography reform (dass instead of daß); Switzerland does not use ß.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Punctuating Direct Speech
topics.nameDe: Zeichen der wörtlichen Rede und Redebegleitsatz
topics.description: Mark direct speech with German quotation marks („…“) and punctuate the reporting clause (Redebegleitsatz) before, after or inside the speech: colon before, comma after the closing quote (Sie rief: „Komm!“ / „Komm!“, rief sie.).
evidence: Put speech in German quotation marks with low opening and high closing marks
Use a colon after a preceding Redebegleitsatz
Use the comma correctly when the Redebegleitsatz follows the speech
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes a story with dialogue, do they write 'Mama sagte: „Komm her!“' with the colon and the low-high quotation marks?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Keeping the Word Stem
topics.description: Split words into prefix, stem and suffix and keep the stem spelling constant across the word family (fahren – Fahrt – Fahrer, kommen – kommt), so that difficult spots are inherited from the stem (Stammprinzip).
evidence: Divide words into building blocks (ver-fahr-en, Kind-heit)
Explain a spelling by pointing to the stem (kommt with mm from kommen)
Spell unfamiliar derived words correctly using a known stem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes 'er kommt', can they explain the double m by thinking of 'kommen' — keeping the stem the same?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Fluent, Legible Personal Handwriting
topics.description: Write quickly, automatically and legibly in a personal handwriting developed from the school script, adjusting speed and neatness to the purpose (quick notes vs. a fair copy or handwritten letter).
evidence: Copy or write a paragraph at an age-appropriate speed while remaining legible
Keep letter size, slant and spacing consistent
Choose between quick note-writing and careful fair copy depending on purpose
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes a page of homework, can someone else read it easily — and do they write fast enough to keep up when taking notes?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Word Processing
topics.nameDe: Texte am Computer gestalten und überarbeiten
topics.description: Use a word processor to format text (font, size, headings), insert images, and revise by inserting, deleting and moving words and sentences; in Klasse 5–6 also comment functions and simple tables.
evidence: Format a heading and body text differently
Move a sentence by cut and paste while revising
Insert a picture with a caption into a document
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes something on the computer, can they move sentences around, format a heading and add a picture without help?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Everyday vs. Academic Register
topics.description: Distinguish everyday language from the more precise school and academic language (Bildungssprache, Fachsprache) and switch register depending on situation, e.g. 'das Ding da' vs. 'das Thermometer'.
evidence: Rephrase an everyday statement in school language
Use subject terms instead of vague words
Explain which register suits a situation
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} explains a science experiment, do they use the proper terms rather than 'das Ding' — and know when casual language is fine?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Dialects and Standard German
topics.description: Explore regional varieties of German (e.g. Bairisch, Schwäbisch, Sächsisch, Plattdeutsch/Niederdeutsch) alongside Standard German: compare words and pronunciation and discuss when each is used.
evidence: Give examples of regional words for the same thing (Brötchen – Semmel – Schrippe)
Describe differences between a dialect and Standard German
Explain where dialect and where Standard German are expected
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that people in different parts of Germany say 'Brötchen', 'Semmel' or 'Schrippe' — and when it's better to use Standard German?
topics.laenderNotes: Weight differs regionally: Niederdeutsch is a school subject option in northern Länder (e.g. Hamburg, Schleswig-Holstein); Bayern and Baden-Württemberg integrate dialect awareness.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Spoken vs. Written Language
topics.description: Compare spoken and written language (and in-between forms such as chat or voice messages): incomplete sentences, fillers and immediacy versus planned, complete and permanent text; reflect on roles of speaker/writer and listener/reader.
evidence: Name differences between a told and a written version of the same event
Turn a chat message into a written text and explain the changes
Explain why a written text needs more context than speech
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why a text message to a friend looks different from a letter to the teacher about the same thing?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: How Wording Affects Others
topics.description: Investigate how word choice, tone and politeness forms affect others, and phrase things respectfully and objectively, also with regard to gender-fair language and roles, offline and online.
evidence: Compare two formulations of the same request and their effect
Rephrase a hurtful statement in a respectful way
Explain when du or Sie is appropriate
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} notice when the way something was said hurt someone — and can they say the same thing more kindly?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Discussing and Building on Others' Ideas
topics.description: Take part in discussions with topic-related contributions that refer to what others have said (Ich stimme zu, aber …), take roles such as discussion leader, and work towards a result. In Klasse 5–6 this extends to moderated class debates.
evidence: Refer explicitly to a previous speaker's contribution
Take on a role such as Gesprächsleitung or timekeeper
Summarise the result or open points at the end of a discussion
topics.assessmentPrompt: When your family discusses something, does {{name}} pick up what others said — agreeing or disagreeing with reasons — rather than just repeating their own point?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Short Talk with Notes and Poster
topics.description: Prepare and give a short structured talk (Kurzreferat, e.g. on an animal) using a cue card with key words and a poster or board picture, speaking freely rather than reading aloud.
evidence: Prepare a cue card with key words in a sensible order
Speak for two to three minutes mostly freely
Use a poster or picture to support the talk and answer questions
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has to present their favourite animal, can they prepare a few key words, talk freely for a couple of minutes and answer a question afterwards?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Listening Strategies
topics.description: Use strategies before, during and after listening: build expectations, keep the listening task in mind, take short notes or sketches, listen again to a recording and summarise afterwards. In Klasse 5–6 notes are extended towards simple minutes.
evidence: Activate prior knowledge and set a listening goal before a recording
Take key-word notes while listening
Summarise what was heard using the notes
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} watches an explainer video for school, do they jot down key words or replay parts they missed — and can they then explain what it was about?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Comparing Book and Film
topics.description: Compare a story in different media (e.g. a fairy tale or children's novel and its film adaptation): what was changed, left out or added, and how camera, music and images tell the story.
evidence: Name differences in plot or characters between book and film
Describe how the film shows something the book describes in words
Give a reasoned preference for one version
topics.assessmentPrompt: After reading a book and seeing the film, can {{name}} tell you what was different and which version they preferred — and why?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Forming and Justifying an Interpretation
topics.nameDe: Eigene Deutung formulieren und am Text belegen
topics.description: Formulate one's own reading of a text (Lesart), support it with text passages (page/line) and compare it with classmates' interpretations, accepting that different readings can be justified.
evidence: State a personal interpretation of a text
Support it with a quoted or referenced passage
Compare own reading with another and explain differences
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} says what a story is really about, can they point to a passage in the book that supports their view?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Fables
topics.description: Read fables (Aesop, La Fontaine, Lessing) and recognise their features: animals with human traits, a short conflict and a lesson (Lehre/Moral) that can be applied to human behaviour.
evidence: Name the human traits the animals stand for
State the lesson of a fable in own words
Write a simple fable with a lesson
topics.assessmentPrompt: After reading 'Der Fuchs und der Rabe', can {{name}} explain what lesson the story teaches people?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Reflecting on Media Use
topics.nameDe: Eigene Mediennutzung und digitale Angebote reflektieren
topics.description: Describe and reflect on one's own use of digital formats (games, videos, chats, apps), recognise that internet communication is potentially public and judge the intentions behind digital offers (entertainment, advertising, information).
evidence: Describe own media habits and their effects
Explain why posts and messages online can become public
Identify whether a digital offer mainly entertains, informs or advertises
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} talk about how much and what kind of media they use — and explain why you should think before posting something online?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Creating Media Products
topics.description: Create own media products — poster, digital presentation, audio play, photo story or short video — choosing tools and design means that fit the content and audience.
evidence: Plan a media product with content and audience in mind
Choose suitable analogue or digital tools
Explain design choices such as layout, images or sound
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} makes a short presentation or audio recording for school, do they choose the tools and design so that it suits the topic and audience?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Simple Research with Child-Friendly Sources
topics.description: Research a question using children's encyclopedias, non-fiction books and child-friendly search engines (e.g. fragFINN, Blinde Kuh), choose search terms and note the source.
evidence: Choose suitable search terms for a question
Find relevant information in a book or on a children's search engine
Note where the information came from
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to find out how long elephants live, do they know how to search a children's search engine or book and tell you where they found the answer?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Purposes of Non-Fiction Texts
topics.description: Distinguish pragmatic text types by purpose: informing (encyclopedia article), instructing (game rules), regulating (class rules) and advertising/persuading (advert, flyer).
evidence: Name the purpose of a given factual text
Sort texts into informing, instructing, regulating and advertising
Point out features that reveal an advert's purpose
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} a recipe, an advert and a page from a children's encyclopedia, can they say what each text wants from the reader?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Describing People, Animals, Objects and Routes
topics.description: Write a factual description in a sensible order (e.g. from overall impression to details, top to bottom), in the present tense, with precise adjectives — person, animal, object or route descriptions.
evidence: Describe in a consistent spatial or logical order
Use precise adjectives and the present tense
Describe so that a reader can identify the person, object or route
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} describes their lost cuddly toy in writing, could a stranger recognise it from the description?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Writing a Book Recommendation
topics.description: Write a short recommendation for a book, film or game (Buchtipp): title and author, a teaser of the content without spoiling the ending, and a reasoned judgement for a specific audience.
evidence: Give title, author and a short teaser
Avoid giving away the ending
Justify the recommendation and name who would enjoy it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes a book tip for classmates, does it make others curious without revealing the ending — and explain why the book is worth reading?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Writing an Opinion with Reasons
topics.description: State a wish or opinion in writing — e.g. a letter asking the head teacher for a new playground rule — and support it with reasons and examples.
evidence: State the opinion or request clearly at the start
Give at least two reasons with an example
End with a polite request or conclusion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes to ask for something — say, more time for break — do they give convincing reasons, not just repeat what they want?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Informative Texts and Encyclopedia Entries
topics.description: Write short informative texts on a factual topic — an encyclopedia entry, a poster text or a fact page — in own words, organised in paragraphs with subheadings.
evidence: Present researched facts in own words
Organise the text with paragraphs or subheadings
Write factually without personal storytelling
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes a short article about hedgehogs for a class booklet, is it factual, in their own words and organised into sections?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Using the Right Case Forms
topics.description: Use correct case endings on articles, adjectives and nouns in own speech and writing (mit dem großen Hund, wegen des Regens), including the Genitiv in written language.
evidence: Use correct article and adjective endings in Dativ and Akkusativ
Form the Genitiv of common nouns (des Vaters, der Mutter)
Correct case errors in own texts
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} say and write 'mit dem neuen Fahrrad' and 'für den kleinen Bruder' with the right endings?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Dative and Accusative Objects
topics.description: Identify objects as Satzglieder required by the verb and determine them by case question: Akkusativobjekt (Wen oder was?) and Dativobjekt (Wem?), e.g. Ich schenke [meiner Schwester] [ein Buch].
evidence: Find the Akkusativobjekt with Wen oder was?
Find the Dativobjekt with Wem?
Explain that some verbs require one or both objects
topics.assessmentPrompt: In 'Paul gibt seinem Freund einen Apfel', can {{name}} name the Dativobjekt and the Akkusativobjekt?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Verb Position and the Sentence Bracket
topics.description: Understand that in German statements the conjugated verb is in second position (Verbzweitstellung), in yes/no questions and commands in first position, and that multi-part predicates form a bracket around the middle field (Ich [habe] gestern Fußball [gespielt]; Er [ruft] seine Oma [an]).
evidence: Identify the verb in second position in statements
Mark both parts of a sentence bracket (Perfekt, separable verbs, modal verbs)
Form correct sentences with separable verbs (anrufen: Ich rufe dich an)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} build sentences like 'Morgen rufe ich dich an' with the verb second and the 'an' at the end — and can they show you the two parts of the verb?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Using Digital Spellcheckers Critically
topics.description: Use the spellchecker of a word processor or an online dictionary to check texts, understanding its limits (it misses wrong-but-real words such as das/dass or Wahl/Wal and capitalisation errors).
evidence: Use the spellchecker's suggestions selectively
Identify an error the spellchecker did not catch
Look up a doubtful word in an online dictionary
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} types a text, do they check the red underlines sensibly — and know that the computer won't catch every mistake?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Word Origins and Language Change
topics.description: Investigate where words come from (loanwords from French, Latin, English; Anglicisms such as chillen, Handy), how meanings change over time and how digital communication influences language.
evidence: Trace the origin of a few everyday words
Give examples of Anglicisms and German alternatives
Describe a word whose meaning has changed
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you that words like 'Computer' or 'cool' come from English — and find a German word that came from French?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Judging Information Sources
topics.description: Judge whether information is reliable and relevant: who wrote it, is it advertising, is it up to date, do other sources confirm it?
evidence: Identify the author or publisher of a web page
Recognise advertising and sponsored content
Check a fact against a second source
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} finds something surprising online, do they check who published it and whether another source says the same?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Legends and Myths (Sagen)
topics.description: Read local legends (e.g. Rattenfänger von Hameln, Loreley), hero legends and Greek myths, and distinguish the Sage from the Märchen: real places, persons or events form a historical core.
evidence: Name the real place or event behind a Sage
Compare a Sage and a Märchen by their features
Retell a local or ancient legend
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know a legend like the Pied Piper of Hamelin — and can they explain how it differs from a fairy tale?
topics.laenderNotes: Regional legends of the child's own Land are often used; Greek myths are typical in Klasse 5–6 (Gymnasium).

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Imagery, Comparisons and Personification
topics.nameDe: Sprachliche Bilder und Vergleiche in Texten
topics.description: Recognise and explain language devices in poems and stories — repetition, comparison (wie), personification and simple metaphors — and describe their effect.
evidence: Find comparisons with wie in a poem
Explain what a personification or image means
Describe the effect of a repetition
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a poem says 'der Wind heult wie ein Wolf', can {{name}} explain what the comparison tells us about the wind?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Writing a Report
topics.description: Report an event (accident, class trip, sports day) factually and in chronological order, answering the W-questions (wer, was, wann, wo, wie, warum, welche Folgen), in the Präteritum and without personal feelings or suspense.
evidence: Answer all relevant W-questions
Keep a factual tone without suspense or feelings
Use the past tense and chronological order
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes a report about a school sports day for the school newspaper, does it answer who, what, when, where and why — factually and without making it into an adventure story?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Idioms and Proverbs
topics.description: Understand and use common German idioms and proverbs (jemandem einen Bären aufbinden, Tomaten auf den Augen haben, Übung macht den Meister) by distinguishing literal and figurative meaning.
evidence: Explain the figurative meaning of common idioms
Use an idiom appropriately in a sentence
Distinguish literal and figurative meaning
topics.assessmentPrompt: If someone says {{name}} 'hat Tomaten auf den Augen', do they understand what is meant — and can they use such a phrase themselves?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Adverbs
topics.description: Recognise adverbs as non-inflecting words that specify time, place, manner or reason (gestern, dort, gern, deshalb) and distinguish them from adjectives, which can be declined (der schnelle Läufer) even when they describe a verb (Er läuft schnell).
evidence: Find adverbs of time, place, manner and reason in a text
Show by declension that 'schnell' is an adjective but 'gern' an adverb
Use adverbs such as deshalb or trotzdem to link sentences
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 'Sie singt gern und laut', can they explain why 'gern' is an adverb but 'laut' counts as an adjective in German grammar?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Adverbials of Time, Place, Manner and Reason
topics.description: Identify adverbials (adverbiale Bestimmungen) of time, place, manner and reason by their questions (Wann? Wo? Wie? Warum?), including single adverbs (gestern, gern), and use them for precise writing.
evidence: Classify adverbials by their questions
Distinguish adverbials from objects
Use adverbials of reason to explain in own texts
topics.assessmentPrompt: In 'Wegen des Regens spielten wir gestern drinnen', can {{name}} name the adverbials of reason, time and place?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Latin Grammar Terminology
topics.description: Use the Latin-based grammar terms of secondary school (Nomen/Substantiv, Verb, Adverb, Nominativ to Akkusativ, Präsens, Präteritum, Subjekt, Prädikat, Objekt) instead of primary-school German terms (Namenwort, Tuwort, Wer-Fall) and use them to talk precisely about language.
evidence: Match primary-school terms to their Latin equivalents
Describe a sentence using only the Latin terms
Use the terms when comparing German with English or Latin
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears 'Bestimme das Prädikat und das Akkusativobjekt', do they know what is meant without asking for the German terms?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern requires the Latin terms from Jgst. 5; elsewhere they are introduced gradually, often in step with Latin as a second foreign language.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Future Perfect (Futur II)
topics.description: Form the Futur II with werden + Partizip II + haben/sein (Morgen werde ich den Aufsatz geschrieben haben) and use it for actions completed by a point in the future or for assumptions about the past (Er wird den Bus verpasst haben), completing the system of six German tenses.
evidence: Form the Futur II of verbs with haben and with sein
Explain its two uses: completed future and assumption
Name all six tenses of a given verb
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears 'Sie wird schon nach Hause gegangen sein', can they name the tense and explain that it expresses an assumption?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Main and Subordinate Clauses
topics.description: Distinguish main clauses (verb second) from subordinate clauses introduced by a conjunction such as weil, dass, wenn, als, ob, where the conjugated verb goes to the end (Verbletztstellung), and combine them into a Satzgefüge.
evidence: Identify the subordinate clause and its introducing word
Show that the conjugated verb is last in the subordinate clause
Combine two clauses into a Satzgefüge in different orders
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why it's 'weil ich müde bin' and not 'weil ich bin müde' — and find the main clause in a longer sentence?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Past Perfect (Plusquamperfekt)
topics.description: Form the Plusquamperfekt (hatte/war + participle) and use it to show that something happened before another past event (Nachdem er gegessen hatte, ging er los).
evidence: Form the Plusquamperfekt of common verbs
Use it with nachdem for an earlier past event
Order events correctly in a narrative using tense
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} complete 'Nachdem wir … (essen), gingen wir spazieren' with 'gegessen hatten'?
topics.laenderNotes: Some textbooks touch it in Klasse 4; systematic introduction is typical in Klasse 5 (Gymnasium, Realschule).

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Kinds of Pronouns
topics.nameDe: Pronomenarten: Possessiv-, Demonstrativ-, Reflexiv- und Indefinitpronomen
topics.description: Distinguish the main kinds of pronouns beyond the personal pronoun — possessive (mein, sein), demonstrative (dieser, jener), reflexive (sich), indefinite (jemand, man, etwas) and interrogative (wer, welcher) — and decline them correctly with the noun they accompany or replace.
evidence: Name the kind of each pronoun in a short text
Use sein/ihr correctly according to the possessor
Use pronouns to avoid repetition without creating unclear references
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes 'Lisa und Tom holen ihre Fahrräder. Er findet ihres nicht.', can they say which pronouns are possessive and explain why the reference is unclear?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Strong and Weak Verbs
topics.description: Distinguish weak verbs (spielen – spielte – gespielt) from strong verbs with a vowel change (singen – sang – gesungen) and mixed verbs (bringen – brachte – gebracht), and form the three principal parts (Infinitiv, Präteritum, Partizip II) needed to build all tenses.
evidence: Give the three principal parts of common strong and weak verbs
Sort verbs into strong, weak and mixed
Look up unknown principal parts in a verb table or dictionary
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked for the Präteritum and Partizip of 'schwimmen', 'denken' and 'lachen', can they give 'schwamm – geschwommen', 'dachte – gedacht' and 'lachte – gelacht'?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Using Tenses Consistently
topics.description: Choose tenses deliberately in own texts: keep the Präteritum as the narrative tense, mark earlier events with the Plusquamperfekt, use the Präsens for summaries and descriptions, and avoid unmotivated switches of tense.
evidence: Keep one narrative tense throughout a story
Mark earlier events with the Plusquamperfekt (Nachdem er gegessen hatte, …)
Find and correct tense switches in a text
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes a story in the past, do they stay in the Präteritum and use 'hatte … gegessen' for things that happened even earlier?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Word Classes Overview
topics.nameDe: Wortarten im Überblick: flektierbar und nicht flektierbar
topics.description: Sort all word classes into one system: inflecting words (the verb is conjugated; noun, article, adjective and pronoun are declined) and non-inflecting words (adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection), using the Wortartenbaum as the reference model for grammar in secondary school.
evidence: Classify every word of a sentence by word class
Test whether a word can be conjugated, declined or not changed at all
Complete a word-class tree (Wortartenbaum)
