Weigh the textual evidence for each reading
Explain why literary texts allow several readings
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads an open text by Kafka, can they develop two different readings and argue which one the text supports better?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Text-Based Argumentative Essay
topics.description: Write a text-based Erörterung: reproduce the thesis and arguments of a non-fiction text, then discuss them critically — agreeing, refuting or modifying with own arguments and examples — and develop a reasoned position on the issue.
evidence: Summarise the author's position accurately
Assess the author's arguments one by one
Develop an own position with additional arguments
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets a commentary on school uniforms, can they first present its argument fairly and then discuss it critically with their own arguments?
topics.laenderNotes: Baden-Württemberg introduces the textgebundene Erörterung in Kl. 9/10; Niedersachsen makes it an obligatory test form in the Einführungsphase.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Writing an Essay
topics.description: Write an essay as an open, reflective form of argument: approach a question from several angles in a personal, associative but thoughtful way, use examples, quotations and stylistic devices, and favour reflection over a closed result.
evidence: Explore a question from several perspectives
Use examples, anecdotes and quotations reflectively
Distinguish the essay from the Erörterung in structure and style
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes an essay on 'Was ist Heimat?', does it explore the question from different angles in a personal style rather than just listing pros and cons?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern and Baden-Württemberg introduce essayistic writing already in Kl. 10.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Creative Writing with Reflection
topics.nameDe: Gestaltendes Schreiben zu literarischen Vorlagen mit Reflexion
topics.description: Write a creative text that continues, rewrites or responds to a literary model (a missing scene, a letter between characters, a modern adaptation) with aesthetic awareness, and reflect in a commentary on how it corresponds to the original's language, period and meaning.
evidence: Imitate the style and period language of a model
Stay consistent with the original's characters and themes
Explain the interpretive decisions in a reflection
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes a missing letter in 'Die Leiden des jungen Werthers', does it sound like Werther and can they explain how it reflects their reading of the novel?
topics.laenderNotes: According to the KMK, purely creative writing is not an Abitur task type but may follow an analysis as a further task.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Interpretation Essay (Abitur)
topics.description: Write a complete interpretation of a literary text or excerpt under exam conditions: develop an interpretation thesis, analyse content, structure and language in their interplay, include genre and period knowledge as the task requires, and reach a well-founded overall interpretation.
evidence: Develop and justify an interpretation thesis
Link analysis findings to an overall interpretation with quotations
Integrate period or genre knowledge where the task requires it
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} interprets a poem in an exam, does the essay move from a thesis via analysis with quotations to a well-founded overall reading?
topics.laenderNotes: Most Länder set obligatory texts or focus topics for the Zentralabitur that change every few years (e.g. Baden-Württemberg's 'Sternchenthemen', NRW's and Niedersachsen's Vorgaben); they are not separate topics here.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Non-Fiction Analysis (Abitur)
topics.description: Analyse a complex non-fiction text (essay, speech, commentary, scholarly text) in exam form: reconstruct the line of argument, determine intention and communicative situation, analyse argumentative and stylistic means and their effect, possibly in comparison with a second text.
evidence: Reconstruct the argument structure of a complex text
Relate the devices to intention and audience
Compare two texts on the same topic methodically
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} analyses a political essay in an exam, can they show how the argument unfolds and how the language serves the author's intention?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Formulating a Research Question
topics.description: Turn a topic into a focused research question, justify the aspects to be examined, plan the investigation and search for literature systematically in library catalogues and academic databases, evaluating sources for scholarly quality.
evidence: Narrow a broad topic into a researchable question
Search a library catalogue and a database with suitable terms
Judge whether a source is scholarly
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to write about Kafka, can they narrow it to a concrete question and find two scholarly sources on it?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Expressionism
topics.description: Interpret Expressionist poetry and prose (c. 1910–1925): the city as threat, the dissolution of the self, apocalyptic visions and war, the Reihungsstil and drastic imagery, e.g. Jakob van Hoddis' 'Weltende', Georg Heym, Gottfried Benn, Else Lasker-Schüler or Georg Trakl.
evidence: Explain typical Expressionist themes
Analyse the Reihungsstil and imagery in 'Weltende'
Compare an Expressionist city poem with an earlier one
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads 'Weltende', can they explain how the list of unconnected images creates a sense of catastrophe?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Literature Around 1900
topics.nameDe: Literatur um 1900: Moderne, Ästhetizismus und Sprachkrise
topics.description: Understand the plural currents of the early Moderne around 1900 — Impressionism, Symbolism, Décadence, Jugendstil — and their shared experience of crisis: the loss of a unified self, the Sprachkrise (Hofmannsthal's 'Chandos-Brief') and new narrative forms such as Schnitzler's interior monologue.
evidence: Name currents of the Moderne around 1900 and their features
Explain the Sprachkrise using the Chandos-Brief
Analyse the interior monologue in Schnitzler's 'Leutnant Gustl' or 'Fräulein Else'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads an excerpt from the Chandos-Brief, can they explain why the writer feels he can no longer trust words?
topics.laenderNotes: Niedersachsen: compulsory module 'Krise und Erneuerung des Erzählens' (Literatur um 1900).

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Weimar Classicism
topics.description: Understand Weimar Classicism (c. 1786–1805) around Goethe and Schiller: the ideal of humanity, the harmony of reason and feeling, the orientation to antiquity and aesthetic education, in works such as Goethe's 'Iphigenie auf Tauris' and 'Faust I' or Schiller's ballads and dramas.
evidence: Explain the ideal of humanity using a key text
Show the classical ideal of form in a drama or poem
Distinguish Klassik from Sturm und Drang
topics.assessmentPrompt: After reading 'Iphigenie auf Tauris', can {{name}} explain how Iphigenie's truthfulness reflects the humanity ideal of the Klassik?
topics.laenderNotes: Goethe's 'Faust I' is a frequent set text for the Zentralabitur; the lists of obligatory texts differ by Land and change every few years.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Naturalism
topics.description: Understand Naturalism (c. 1880–1900) as an attempt to depict reality scientifically: determination by milieu and heredity, the social question of industrialisation, the Sekundenstil and dialect, in works such as Gerhart Hauptmann's 'Die Weber' or 'Bahnwärter Thiel'.
evidence: Explain Arno Holz's formula Kunst = Natur – x
Show milieu determination in a naturalist text
Identify the Sekundenstil and its effect
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads 'Bahnwärter Thiel', can they explain how environment and inner drives determine Thiel's fate?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Poetic Realism
topics.description: Understand Poetic Realism (c. 1848–1890) as a depiction of everyday bourgeois reality transfigured by art ('Verklärung'), with the Novelle and the novel as typical genres and authors such as Fontane ('Effi Briest'), Storm and Keller.
evidence: Explain the realist programme of 'Verklärung'
Analyse the depiction of society in a realist novel or Novelle
Distinguish Realismus from Naturalismus
topics.assessmentPrompt: After reading 'Effi Briest', can {{name}} explain how Fontane shows the pressure of social conventions without open protest?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Romanticism
topics.description: Understand German Romanticism (c. 1795–1835): longing (the blue flower), night, nature and the unconscious, the turn to the Middle Ages and folk poetry, Romantic irony and the idea of a 'progressive Universalpoesie', with texts by Novalis, Eichendorff, E. T. A. Hoffmann and the Brothers Grimm.
evidence: Explain central Romantic motifs with examples
Interpret an Eichendorff poem as typically Romantic
Compare Romantic and Enlightenment views of reason
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads Eichendorff's 'Mondnacht', can they show which Romantic motifs appear and what longing the poem expresses?
topics.laenderNotes: Niedersachsen's compulsory module asks 'Romantik als Gegenbewegung zur Aufklärung?'.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Vormärz and Political Literature
topics.nameDe: Vormärz und Junges Deutschland: politische Literatur
topics.description: Understand the Vormärz (c. 1830–1848) as a politically engaged literature against censorship and restoration: political poetry and satire (Heine, Herwegh), Büchner's 'Der Hessische Landbote' and 'Woyzeck', and the debate about the writer's role in society.
evidence: Explain the political situation and censorship after 1815
Analyse a political poem by Heine
Explain Büchner's social criticism in 'Woyzeck' or the 'Landbote'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads Heine's 'Die schlesischen Weber', can they explain its political message and connect it to the Vormärz?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Literature of the Weimar Republic
topics.nameDe: Literatur der Weimarer Republik und Neue Sachlichkeit
topics.description: Understand the literature of the Weimar Republic (1918–1933): the Neue Sachlichkeit with its sober, reportage-like style and Gebrauchslyrik (Kästner), the big-city novel (Döblin's 'Berlin Alexanderplatz', Keun's 'Das kunstseidene Mädchen') and the montage technique.
evidence: Explain the style of the Neue Sachlichkeit
Analyse montage in a passage of 'Berlin Alexanderplatz'
Relate a text to the social situation of the Weimar Republic
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads a poem by Kästner, can they explain what is 'sachlich' about its tone and what it criticises?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Trends in Present-Day German
topics.description: Describe and evaluate current developments of German — Anglicisms, digital writing, simplification, gender-fair language, Kiezdeutsch — on the basis of language-critical texts, distinguishing descriptive linguistics from normative complaints about 'language decline'.
evidence: Describe a current trend with examples
Analyse the argument of a language-critical text
Distinguish descriptive and normative views of language change
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads an article claiming that German is 'in decline', can they analyse its arguments and respond from a linguistic point of view?
topics.laenderNotes: Niedersachsen: compulsory module 'Tendenzen in der deutschen Gegenwartssprache'.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Conversation Analysis and Power
topics.description: Analyse transcripts of conversations and literary dialogues — turn-taking, interruptions, question–answer patterns, register, verbal, paraverbal and nonverbal signals — and show how they reveal symmetrical or asymmetrical relationships and power.
evidence: Analyse turn-taking and interruptions in a transcript
Identify verbal and nonverbal signals of dominance
Explain the power relation in a dialogue
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads a transcript of a job interview or a doctor's visit, can they show how the conversation reveals who holds power?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Multilingualism and Language Contact
topics.description: Analyse individual and societal multilingualism in Germany: code-switching, ethnolects such as Kiezdeutsch, heritage languages and their status, and the effects of language contact on German.
evidence: Describe code-switching in a transcript
Explain features of Kiezdeutsch
Discuss the status of heritage languages in school and society
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain whether Kiezdeutsch is 'bad German' or a variety with its own rules?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Analysing Political Speeches
topics.description: Analyse political and public speeches with rhetorical categories — situation, speaker and audience, ethos, pathos and logos, structure, rhetorical figures and persuasive strategies — and evaluate their effect and legitimacy, e.g. Richard von Weizsäcker's speech of 8 May 1985 or historical speeches.
evidence: Describe the speech situation and the audience
Analyse ethos, pathos and logos in a speech
Evaluate the speech's persuasive strategies critically
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} analyses Weizsäcker's speech of 8 May 1985, can they explain how he persuades his audience and why the speech was so influential?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Language, Thought and Reality
topics.description: Discuss the relationship between language, thought and reality: Humboldt's idea of language as a world view, the strong and weak Sapir–Whorf hypothesis (linguistic relativity) and universalist counter-positions, tested against examples such as colour terms or grammatical gender.
evidence: Explain the strong and the weak version of linguistic relativity
Evaluate an empirical example
Take a reasoned position in the debate
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain whether speakers of a language with many words for snow actually perceive snow differently?
topics.laenderNotes: NRW: Grundkurs in the new plan (from 2027), before only Leistungskurs; Niedersachsen: elective module; KMK names positions from the philosophy of language for eA.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: First Language Acquisition
topics.description: Describe the phases of first language acquisition (babbling, one-word and two-word stage, telegraphic speech, overgeneralisation such as 'gegeht') and the conditions that support it, using transcripts of child language.
evidence: Order the phases of language acquisition with examples
Explain overgeneralisation errors
Analyse a transcript of child language
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears a three-year-old say 'Ich habe gegeht', can they explain why this 'mistake' shows learning?
topics.laenderNotes: Placement differs: Grundkurs in NRW (2014 plan) and as an elective module in Niedersachsen; Leistungskurs only in the new NRW plan (from 2027) and theory-based only for eA in the KMK standards.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Steering Thought Through Language
topics.nameDe: Sprachlenkung: Framing, Schlagwörter und Sprache im Nationalsozialismus
topics.description: Analyse how word choice steers thinking in public discourse — framing (e.g. 'Steuerlast'), political slogans and euphemisms — with the language of National Socialism (Victor Klemperer's 'LTI') as a historical example of systematic language manipulation.
evidence: Explain framing with current examples
Analyse features of Nazi language with Klemperer
Evaluate the power and limits of steering through language
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why 'Steuerlast' and 'Steuerbeitrag' frame the same thing differently and compare this with Klemperer's observations?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Steered and Natural Language Change
topics.description: Distinguish natural (ungesteuert) language change from deliberate intervention (gesteuert): standardisation (Luther, Duden, spelling reforms), language societies and purism, language policy and guidelines — and assess how effective such steering is.
evidence: Give examples of natural and steered change
Explain the role of the Duden and the spelling reform
Assess arguments for and against regulating language
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain the difference between how 'Handy' entered German and how the 1996 spelling reform changed 'daß' to 'dass'?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Speech Act Theory
topics.description: Describe utterances as actions with speech act theory — locution, illocution and perlocution (Austin), Searle's classes of speech acts and indirect speech acts — and use these categories to analyse authentic and literary communication.
evidence: Classify utterances by Searle's classes of speech acts
Explain an indirect speech act
Analyse a dialogue with speech act categories
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why 'Es zieht' can be a request to close the window and name the speech act involved?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Varieties and Social Meaning
topics.nameDe: Sprachvarietäten und ihre gesellschaftliche Bedeutung (Soziolekt, Dialekt)
topics.description: Compare varieties of German — dialects and regional languages (including Niederdeutsch), sociolects, youth language, technical languages — describe their features and functions and judge their social prestige and their role for identity.
evidence: Describe features of a dialect or sociolect
Explain the identity function of a variety
Discuss attitudes towards dialect speakers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why a strong regional accent may be valued at home but judged negatively in a job interview elsewhere?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Oral Exam: Talk and Discussion
topics.description: Prepare and deliver a structured talk on a task within a fixed preparation time, then defend and extend it in an examination conversation on wider subject connections — the format of the oral Abitur exam.
evidence: Structure a talk from notes within the preparation time
Answer follow-up questions precisely and link them to wider topics
Use subject terminology confidently in free speech
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a mock oral exam, can {{name}} present a poem analysis from notes and then answer questions linking it to the period?
topics.laenderNotes: Several Länder offer a presentation-based exam (Präsentationsprüfung or Besondere Lernleistung) as the fifth Abitur component.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Theory-Based Argument Analysis
topics.description: Analyse the structure of argumentative texts with a theoretical model such as Toulmin's scheme (claim, data, warrant, backing, rebuttal), reconstruct implicit premises and judge the validity of an argument and its fallacies.
evidence: Reconstruct an argument with the Toulmin scheme
Make an implicit premise explicit
Identify a fallacy and explain it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads an op-ed, can they reconstruct its main argument as claim, data and warrant and show a hidden premise?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Brecht's Epic Theatre
topics.description: Understand Brecht's epic theatre as a counter-model to Aristotelian drama: instead of empathy and catharsis, the Verfremdungseffekt (songs, direct address, projections, narrator figures) should make the audience think critically about changeable social conditions, e.g. in 'Der gute Mensch von Sezuan' or 'Mutter Courage und ihre Kinder'.
evidence: Contrast Aristotelian and epic theatre
Identify Verfremdungseffekte in a scene
Explain the intended effect on the audience
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a scene where an actor steps out of the role and sings to the audience, can they explain it as a Verfremdungseffekt and say what it is for?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Comparative Poetry Interpretation
topics.description: Interpret two poems on the same motif from different periods (e.g. love, nature or city poems), comparing speaker, form, imagery and worldview, and explain the differences with the respective period and its poetics.
evidence: Interpret each poem against its period background
Compare the poems along explicit aspects
Explain differences by the change of period and worldview
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares a Romantic and an Expressionist poem on night or the city, can they explain the differences in view of the two periods?
topics.laenderNotes: Niedersachsen reads motif-related poems from several periods already in the Einführungsphase; NRW sets the vergleichende Interpretation as an Abitur task type.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Analysing a Stage Production
topics.description: Analyse a theatre production (live or recorded) of a play studied in class — stage design, costumes, acting, cuts and updating (Regietheater) — and explain and judge it as one interpretation of the dramatic text.
evidence: Describe the staging choices of a production
Relate staging choices to the text
Judge whether the production's interpretation convinces
topics.assessmentPrompt: After watching a modern production of 'Faust', can {{name}} explain why the director set it in the present and whether that works?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Approaches to Interpretation
topics.nameDe: Literaturtheoretische Zugänge: werkimmanent, biografisch, historisch, rezeptionsästhetisch
topics.description: Distinguish basic approaches of literary theory — text-immanent, biographical, historical-sociological, psychoanalytical, reception-aesthetic and gender-oriented — and apply at least two of them to the same text to see what each reveals.
evidence: Describe the focus of four approaches
Apply two approaches to the same text
Reflect on the limits of an approach
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} interpret a short story once text-immanently and once biographically, and explain what each reading shows and misses?
topics.laenderNotes: The KMK standards name literary-theory approaches for all courses; Leistungskurse work with them in more depth and with secondary literature.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Intertextuality and Motif History
topics.description: Trace how literary works take up, transform and comment on earlier texts, materials and motifs — e.g. the Faust material, the Medea or Prometheus myth, the Doppelgänger motif — from antiquity to the present, and explain what the reworking adds.
evidence: Identify references to an earlier text or myth
Compare two treatments of the same material
Explain the meaning of a modern rewriting
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares Goethe's 'Prometheus' with the Greek myth, can they explain how Goethe changes the material and why?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Film Adaptations as Interpretations
topics.description: Analyse a film adaptation of a literary work as an interpretation: compare plot, characters and focus with the original, explain changes through film-specific means and the director's intention, and judge the adaptation by reasoned criteria.
evidence: Compare a key scene in book and film
Explain changes with film-specific means
Judge the adaptation with explicit criteria
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how a film version of a novel changes a key scene and what interpretation of the book this reveals?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Multimodal and Serial Storytelling
topics.nameDe: Multimodales Erzählen: Serie, Graphic Novel, Computerspiel
topics.description: Analyse narratives that combine text, image and sound — TV series, graphic novels, video games, audio plays — with categories of narrative analysis (characters, plot, perspective) and media-specific aesthetics.
evidence: Apply narrative categories to a graphic novel or series episode
Explain the interplay of text and image
Compare a multimodal narrative with a printed one
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} analyses a page of a graphic novel, can they explain how panel layout and text create perspective and time?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Poetics and Drama Theory
topics.nameDe: Poetologische Konzepte: Aristoteles, Lessing, Schiller, Brecht
topics.description: Relate literary works to poetological programmes — Aristotle's catharsis, Lessing's drama of compassion (Mitleidsdramaturgie), Schiller's theatre as a moral institution, Brecht's epic theatre, Romantic and naturalist programmes — and use them to explain the aesthetic quality of texts.
evidence: Summarise the core of two poetological concepts
Apply a concept to explain how a drama is designed
Compare how two programmes define the effect of art
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how Lessing's idea of Mitleid shapes 'Emilia Galotti' and how Brecht would criticise it?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Using Secondary Literature
topics.description: Include scholarly secondary texts, philosophical writings and historical documents in the interpretation of a literary work: summarise the critic's thesis, relate it to own findings and take a reasoned position.
evidence: Summarise the thesis of a scholarly interpretation
Confirm or challenge it with own textual evidence
Integrate secondary sources with correct references
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads a scholar's interpretation of 'Faust', can they test it against the text and say where they agree or disagree?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Argumentative Essay on Literature
topics.description: Discuss a thesis or question about a literary work (e.g. whether a character is responsible for the tragic outcome): analyse relevant passages, weigh interpretations and arguments drawn from text and context, and reach a reasoned judgement.
evidence: Clarify the thesis and its implications
Support arguments with analysis of text passages
Weigh alternative interpretations and conclude
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked whether a character is more victim or perpetrator, can they argue both sides with evidence from the play and reach a judgement?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Writing a Research Paper
topics.description: Write an academic-style paper (Facharbeit, Seminararbeit) of roughly 10–20 pages: introduction with question and method, a structured main part, a conclusion that answers the question, consistent citations, bibliography and formal layout, and document the work process.
evidence: Structure the paper with a numbered outline and table of contents
Cite and reference sources consistently in one citation style
Answer the research question in the conclusion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} hand in a Facharbeit whose conclusion clearly answers the question raised in the introduction, with consistent citations and bibliography?
topics.laenderNotes: NRW: Facharbeit in Q1, replacing a Klausur; Bayern: Seminararbeit in the W-Seminar; other Länder use a project paper or Besondere Lernleistung; it can be written in any subject.

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Material-Based Argumentative Writing (Abitur)
topics.description: Write an argumentative text (commentary, essay, speech) for a given communicative situation on the basis of a dossier of materials: evaluate the materials critically, use them selectively as evidence and develop an independent, well-structured argument.
evidence: Evaluate the materials for reliability and perspective
Integrate evidence from the materials with references
Develop an independent position suited to the target text type
topics.assessmentPrompt: Given a dossier on AI in school, can {{name}} write a newspaper commentary that uses the materials selectively and argues independently?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Material-Based Informative Writing (Abitur)
topics.description: Write an informative text for a defined purpose and audience (e.g. an encyclopedia article or a feature for a website) from a dossier of texts, graphics and data: select and synthesise the relevant information, structure it independently and present it in a suitable form with sources.
evidence: Select the relevant information from a dossier for a given purpose
Synthesise the information in a self-chosen structure
Adapt register and form to the target text type and audience
topics.assessmentPrompt: Given a dossier on language change, can {{name}} write a coherent encyclopedia article that synthesises the materials in their own structure?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Writing a Review
topics.description: Write a review of a book, film or theatre production for a public audience: inform briefly about content and context, analyse selected aspects and give a reasoned evaluation by explicit criteria in an engaging journalistic style.
evidence: Balance information, analysis and evaluation
Justify the evaluation with explicit criteria
Write for a non-specialist audience
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reviews a novel for the school website, do readers learn enough to decide whether to read it, with a reasoned judgement?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Exile Literature
topics.description: Understand the literature of authors who fled National Socialism (Brecht, Thomas Mann, Anna Seghers, Mascha Kaléko, Klaus Mann): experiences of exile, loss of language and home, resistance and warning, e.g. in Seghers' 'Transit' or Brecht's exile poems.
evidence: Explain why and where German authors went into exile
Analyse the experience of exile in a poem or novel excerpt
Relate exile literature to the book burnings and censorship of 1933
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads Brecht's 'Gedanken über die Dauer des Exils', can they explain the speaker's situation and hopes?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Contemporary Literature
topics.description: Explore trends in contemporary German-language literature: pop literature, intercultural and migrant literature (Saša Stanišić, Emine Sevgi Özdamar), autofiction, literature about climate and digital life, and new forms such as poetry slam and digital literature.
evidence: Name and illustrate three current trends
Analyse a contemporary text with suitable categories
Compare a contemporary text with a traditional treatment of the same theme
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads an excerpt from Stanišić's 'Herkunft', can they explain how it deals with identity and migration and why it is typical of current literature?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Post-War Literature
topics.description: Understand German literature after 1945: the 'Kahlschlag' and Trümmerliteratur with reduced language (Eich's 'Inventur', Borchert), the Gruppe 47, coming to terms with the Nazi past (Böll, Celan's 'Todesfuge') and Adorno's question about poetry after Auschwitz.
evidence: Explain the idea of the Kahlschlag using 'Inventur'
Interpret 'Todesfuge' in its historical context
Name aims of the Gruppe 47
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads Eich's 'Inventur', can they explain why the speaker only lists his few possessions and what that says about 1945?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Literature in Divided Germany
topics.nameDe: Literatur in BRD und DDR (1949–1990) und Wendeliteratur
topics.description: Compare literature in the two German states — socialist realism and its critics in the GDR (Christa Wolf, Wolf Biermann, Reiner Kunze), engaged and later postmodern literature in the Federal Republic — and literature about the fall of the Wall and reunification (Wendeliteratur).
evidence: Explain the conditions of writing under GDR censorship
Analyse a critical GDR text such as a poem by Kunze or Biermann
Describe how the Wende is reflected in a literary text
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads a poem by Reiner Kunze, can they explain how it criticises the GDR and why it was risky to publish?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Literary Value and the Canon
topics.description: Reflect on how literary value is attributed — by criteria such as aesthetic quality, innovation, relevance and reception history — and on how and why a canon of 'classics' forms, changes and is contested, e.g. from gender or postcolonial perspectives.
evidence: Justify a literary judgement with explicit criteria
Explain how a work entered or left the school canon
Discuss arguments for and against a fixed canon
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why a book counts as a 'classic' and argue whether a contemporary novel should be added to the school canon?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Theories of Language Acquisition
topics.description: Compare theories of language acquisition — behaviourism (Skinner), nativism (Chomsky's language acquisition device), cognitivism (Piaget) and interactionism (Bruner) — and test them against evidence such as overgeneralisation or cases of language deprivation.
evidence: Summarise the core assumptions of three theories
Test a theory against a piece of evidence
Evaluate which theory explains acquisition best
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why children's overgeneralisations are a problem for behaviourism but support Chomsky's view?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Language Scepticism
topics.description: Analyse philosophical and literary expressions of scepticism about language — Nietzsche's 'Über Wahrheit und Lüge im außermoralischen Sinne', Hofmannsthal's Chandos-Brief, Wittgenstein's limits of language — and relate them to literary works of the Moderne.
evidence: Summarise Nietzsche's critique of concepts
Relate the Chandos-Brief to a philosophical position
Discuss the limits of language with reference to Wittgenstein
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain Nietzsche's claim that truths are 'worn-out metaphors' and connect it to the language crisis around 1900?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Explaining Language Change
topics.description: Explain language change with linguistic theories — e.g. Rudi Keller's 'invisible hand', economy and expressiveness, language contact, grammaticalisation — and apply them to examples such as the decline of the genitive or the spread of Anglicisms.
evidence: Explain the invisible-hand theory
Apply a theory to a concrete change
Compare two explanations of the same change
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use Keller's theory to explain why 'wegen dem' spreads although many people criticise it?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Film Criticism and Theory
topics.description: Engage with film criticism and basic film theory — e.g. auteur theory, genre theory, film as art or entertainment, the relation of image and reality — and write or evaluate a film review in the light of these positions.
evidence: Analyse the criteria used in a professional film review
Explain one position of film theory
Write a reasoned film review
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read a professional film review, identify its criteria and write their own review that uses similar arguments?

topics.subject: Deutsch
topics.name: Media Change and Media Theory
topics.description: Reflect on media change (print, television, internet, AI-generated content) with positions of media theory — e.g. McLuhan's 'the medium is the message', Postman's critique of entertainment, theories of the digital public sphere — and assess their explanatory power today.
evidence: Summarise two positions of media theory
Apply a position to a current media phenomenon
Evaluate how relevant the position is today
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain Postman's thesis about entertainment and judge whether it applies to short-video platforms?
topics.laenderNotes: NRW Leistungskurs 'Medientheorie: mediale Umbrüche'; Niedersachsen compulsory module 'Medien im Wandel' with depth by course level.

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Letters, Sounds and the English Alphabet
topics.description: Understand that English letters and letter groups stand for different sounds than in German, learn common spelling patterns, and spell aloud with English letter names. German learners typically mix up the letter names e/i and a/r.
evidence: Explain that the same letters sound different in English and German (e.g. "i" in "like", "u" in "bus")
Say the English alphabet and spell their name aloud without confusing e/i or a/r
Read familiar spelling patterns aloud (ee, ea, oo, -ight, silent e)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} spell their name aloud with English letter names, and say "e" and "i" the English way?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: English Sounds German Lacks
topics.nameDe: Typische englische Laute (th, w, r, æ)
topics.description: Hear and produce English sounds that do not exist in German or that German speakers typically replace: the two th-sounds, w versus v, the English r, and vowels such as /æ/.
evidence: Produce the two th-sounds /θ/ and /ð/ (three, mother) instead of s/z or d
Distinguish /w/ (water) from /v/ (very) in listening and speaking
Imitate the English /r/ and the vowel /æ/ (black, cat) in known words
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} says "three" or "water" in English, do they use a real "th" and "w", rather than "sree" or "vater"?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Comparing English and German
topics.description: Notice similarities and differences between English and German in familiar words. English nouns are written in lower case, many words look alike (Haus–house), and most plurals simply add -s.
evidence: Notice and explain that English nouns are written with a small letter (except names and "I")
Find English–German word pairs that look or sound similar (Haus–house, Maus–mouse)
Notice that most English plurals add -s, unlike the many German plural endings
topics.assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} noticed that English nouns don't start with a capital letter like German ones, and can they find English words that look like German words?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Classroom Phrases and Instructions
topics.description: Understand the English classroom phrases and short instructions the teacher uses all the time (Total Physical Response), and respond with actions or words. Early English lessons in German primary schools are taught almost entirely in English, so this is the entry point.
evidence: Respond correctly with actions to at least 10 routine instructions (e.g. "Open your books", "Stand up", "Listen and point")
Follow a two-step spoken instruction in a game (e.g. "Take a red pencil and colour the cat")
Use gestures, pictures and the situation to work out an unfamiliar instruction instead of asking for a German translation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If the teacher says "Take out your blue pencil and draw a circle" in English, can {{name}} do it without a German translation?
topics.laenderNotes: English starts in Kl. 3 in most Länder (2 lessons/week). Hamburg and Rheinland-Pfalz start in Kl. 1, and Brandenburg reportedly does too. NRW moved the start from Kl. 1 to Kl. 3 (cohorts from 2021/22) and Baden-Württemberg did the same from 2018/19. Since 2024/25 Bayern may teach English in Kl. 3/4 for 1 or 2 lessons. In Saarland, and in BW schools along the Rhine (Rheinschiene), the first foreign language in primary school is French.

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Listening to Stories and Short Texts
topics.description: Follow a picture-book story read aloud (storytelling) or a short, clearly spoken text with known words, grasping the storyline and picking out specific details. Facial expression, pictures and props support understanding.
evidence: Retell the main events of an English picture-book story read aloud, in German or with pictures
Pick out specific details (who, where, what colour, how many) from a short, clearly spoken text with known words
Put 4–5 story pictures in the right order after listening
topics.assessmentPrompt: After hearing a short English picture-book story, can {{name}} tell you what happened and who was in it?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Songs, Rhymes and Chants
topics.description: Listen to and join in with English songs, action rhymes, chants and raps. The repetition and rhythm build up chunks of language, sound patterns and confidence before children read or write English.
evidence: Join in with the words and actions of at least five familiar English songs or chants
Recite a short rhyme or tongue twister from memory with recognisable rhythm
Point to or act out the matching picture when a key word of a song is heard
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} sing along to a few English songs or rhymes from school, with the actions, and say a short rhyme by heart?
topics.laenderNotes: In Länder that start English in Kl. 1 (e.g. Hamburg, Rheinland-Pfalz), songs and rhymes are the main activity in Kl. 1–2.

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Festivals and Customs
topics.nameDe: Feste und Bräuche im englischsprachigen Raum
topics.description: Know how festivals and customs such as Halloween, Christmas, Bonfire Night, Easter or Thanksgiving are celebrated in English-speaking countries, use typical phrases, and compare them with German traditions.
evidence: Describe how Halloween, Christmas (stockings, crackers) or Bonfire Night are celebrated
Use typical festival phrases ("Happy Halloween!", "Merry Christmas!", "Trick or treat!")
Compare a festival with how it is celebrated in Germany (e.g. presents on 24 vs 25 December)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain one difference between Christmas in Britain and in Germany, like when the presents are opened?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Politeness Conventions
topics.description: Use English politeness conventions: please, thank you, sorry and excuse me, indirect requests, and softened refusals. Direct translations of German requests ("Give me…") can sound rude in English.
evidence: Use please, thank you, sorry and excuse me appropriately in role plays
Make polite requests ("Could I have…?", "Can you help me, please?") instead of direct German-style imperatives
Explain that a direct translation can sound rude and choose a softer phrasing
topics.assessmentPrompt: In an English shop role play, does {{name}} say "Could I have…, please?" rather than "I want…" or "Give me…"?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: English-Speaking Countries
topics.description: Know where English is spoken (Great Britain, Ireland, the USA, Australia and others), know a few symbols and sights, and compare aspects of children's daily life there with your own.
evidence: Find Great Britain, Ireland, the USA and Australia on a world map
Name some sights or symbols of the UK (London, Big Ben, double-decker bus, flag)
Compare one aspect of children's daily life (e.g. school uniform, school day) with their own
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} show you on a map where English is spoken and tell you one way school is different in Britain?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Languages Around Us
topics.nameDe: Sprachen um uns herum: Englisch im Alltag und Mehrsprachigkeit
topics.description: Discover English in German everyday life (loanwords, packaging, games, songs) and the many languages spoken by classmates, and understand why English is learnt worldwide.
evidence: Collect English words used in German everyday life (e.g. on packaging, in games, in songs)
Name languages spoken by classmates and say "hello" in some of them
Explain why many people around the world learn English
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} find English words in everyday German life, like on packaging or in games, and name some languages their classmates speak?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Reading Short Picture-Supported Texts
topics.nameDe: Kurze bildgestützte Texte und Anweisungen lesen
topics.description: Understand very short written texts with known words and picture support, such as illustrated instructions, invitations, birthday cards, posters and picture-book pages, and act on them.
evidence: Carry out a short illustrated written instruction (e.g. "Colour the dog brown")
Answer simple questions about an invitation, birthday card or poster
Find the sentence that matches a picture on a short picture-book page
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read a short English birthday invitation and tell you when and where the party is?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Reading Familiar Words
topics.description: Recognise the written form of words already known orally and connect the written word to its English sound and meaning, even in new contexts. In primary English, the written form is introduced after children have heard and used the words.
evidence: Match at least 30 known word cards to pictures
Read known words aloud with English rather than German pronunciation (e.g. "blue", "house")
Recognise known words in a new context (poster, label, menu)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees English words they know from lessons written on a poster, can they read them and say what they mean?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Copying Words Accurately
topics.description: Copy English words and short sentences without mistakes, using focused techniques such as "read, look up, write down" to memorise whole word shapes. English spelling differs a lot from pronunciation, so careful copying matters.
evidence: Copy five short English sentences without spelling mistakes
Use the "read, look up, write down" technique instead of copying letter by letter
Spot differences between the English and German spelling of similar words when copying (e.g. "house" / "Haus")
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} copy a few English sentences from the board into their exercise book without any spelling mistakes?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Writing with Model Texts
topics.description: Write short personal texts such as a profile (Steckbrief), greeting card, invitation or wish list by completing and adapting model texts and choosing words from word banks.
evidence: Write a personal profile (name, age, likes, pets) by completing a model
Write a birthday card, invitation or wish list by adapting a template
Change words in a model sentence to express their own information
topics.assessmentPrompt: Using a model, can {{name}} write a short English profile of themselves or a birthday card to a friend?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Self-Assessment and Language Portfolio
topics.description: Assess your own English skills with "I can…" statements, set learning goals, and collect work in a language portfolio. Many Länder use the European Language Portfolio or adapted versions in primary school.
evidence: Assess their own skills with "I can…" statements (e.g. "I can introduce myself")
Set a concrete learning goal for the next unit and choose a strategy for it
Collect their best work in a portfolio and explain their progress
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you what they can already do in English and what they want to get better at next?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Vocabulary Learning Strategies
topics.description: Organise and remember new words with suitable strategies: word webs and picture cards in primary school, and from Kl. 5 a vocabulary notebook or card box, spaced repetition, learning in phrases and apps.
evidence: Organise words in word webs or on picture cards by topic
Learn new words with a vocabulary notebook or card box, testing themselves regularly (spaced repetition)
Learn words in phrases and with their pronunciation, not as isolated German–English pairs
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} has English words to learn, do they have a method, e.g. a card box or testing themselves over several days, rather than reading the list once?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Explaining English in German
topics.nameDe: Sprachmittlung: Englisches sinngemäß auf Deutsch wiedergeben
topics.description: Pass on the meaning of simple English utterances, instructions or very short texts and videos in German, to help others understand or to show you have understood. The aim is the gist, not a word-for-word translation.
evidence: Tell a classmate in German what an English instruction or announcement means
Explain in German what a very short English video, song or text is about
Give the meaning rather than a word-for-word translation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a younger sibling hears a short English message or song, can {{name}} explain to them in German what it means?
topics.laenderNotes: Sprachmittlung is an explicit Kl. 3/4 competence area in Bayern (LehrplanPLUS). In other Länder it is often formally introduced only from Kl. 5.

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Describing Yourself and Pictures
topics.nameDe: Zusammenhängend sprechen: sich und Bilder beschreiben
topics.description: Speak a few connected sentences about yourself, your family and favourite things, or describe what you see in a picture, using simple, list-like sentences and familiar sentence patterns.
evidence: Say 4–5 connected sentences about themselves (name, age, family, pet, favourite things)
Describe a picture or person using colours, numbers, clothes and "There is / There are"
Ask for a word they need ("What's … in English?")
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} talk in English for half a minute about themselves, e.g. age, family, pet and favourite food?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Greetings and Introductions
topics.description: Greet people, say goodbye, introduce yourself and others, and ask how someone is, using fixed English phrases. This is usually the very first unit of primary English.
evidence: Greet, say goodbye and introduce themselves (name, age, where they live) to a partner
Ask and answer "How are you?" with several different answers
Introduce a friend or family member ("This is my sister Mia")
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} met an English-speaking child, could they say hello, give their name and age, and ask how the other child is?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Mini-Dialogues and Role Plays
topics.nameDe: Einfache Fragen stellen und beantworten, Rollenspiele
topics.description: Take part in short dialogues by asking and answering very simple questions with memorised patterns. Act out everyday situations such as shopping or a café, using gestures and props to support what you say.
evidence: Ask and answer questions with familiar patterns ("Have you got…?", "Do you like…?", "What's your favourite…?") in a pair interview
Act out a shopping role play: ask for an item, give the quantity and price, say thank you
Express likes, dislikes, agreement and disagreement with memorised chunks ("I like…", "I don't like…", "Me too")
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a pretend shop, can {{name}} ask for three apples in English, understand the price and say thank you?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Keeping a Conversation Going
topics.description: Use communication strategies when language runs out: ask for repetition or clarification, explain a missing word with gestures or other words, and use routine phrases to open, continue and close a conversation.
evidence: Ask for repetition or clarification in English ("Sorry, can you say that again, please?", "What does … mean?")
Get around a missing word with gestures, a drawing or a paraphrase ("It's an animal, it's big and grey")
Open, continue and close a short conversation with routine phrases
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} doesn't know a word in English, do they find another way to explain it, or ask politely for help in English, instead of switching to German?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Food and Drink
topics.description: Know and use words for common food and drink, say what you like to eat, and ask for food politely in a shop or café.
evidence: Name at least 15 food and drink items, including fruit and vegetables
Say what they like / don't like to eat and order food politely ("Can I have…, please?")
Sort food words into categories (fruit, vegetables, drinks, breakfast)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} name lots of foods in English and politely ask for something to eat, e.g. "Can I have an apple, please?"

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Family, Friends and Pets
topics.description: Know and use words for family members, friends and animals, especially pets, and talk about your own family and pets.
evidence: Name family members (mum, dad, brother, sister, grandma…) and introduce their own family
Name at least 12 animals, including common pets
Ask and answer "Have you got a pet / a brother…?"
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} name their family members and some animals in English, and say whether they have a pet?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Hobbies and Free Time
topics.description: Know and use words for hobbies, sports and free-time activities, and say what you can do and like doing.
evidence: Name at least 10 hobbies and sports (play football, ride a bike, go swimming)
Say what they can / can't do and what they like doing
Ask a partner about free-time activities and report back
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you in English what they like doing in their free time and ask a friend about theirs?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Days, Months, Seasons and Weather
topics.description: Know the days of the week, months and seasons, say your birthday, and describe the weather. These words are usually practised daily in a morning routine.
evidence: Say the days of the week and the months in order and give their birthday ("My birthday is in May")
Describe today's weather ("It's sunny / rainy / windy…")
Link seasons with typical weather, clothes and festivals
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} say in English what day it is today, when their birthday is and what the weather is like?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Body and Clothes
topics.description: Know and use words for parts of the body and everyday clothes, and describe what someone looks like or is wearing.
evidence: Name and point to at least 10 body parts (head, shoulders, knees and toes…)
Name everyday clothes and describe what someone is wearing, using colours
Use plural forms for paired items (trousers, shoes, eyes)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} name parts of the body and describe in English what someone is wearing, e.g. "a red T-shirt and blue jeans"?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: School and Classroom
topics.description: Know and use words for classroom objects, school subjects and places, and describe where things are using basic prepositions.
evidence: Name classroom objects (pencil case, rubber, ruler…) and ask to borrow one
Name school subjects and say which ones they like
Describe where things are using in, on, under, next to
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} name the things in their pencil case in English and say where something is, like "The ruler is under the book"?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Numbers and Colours
topics.description: Know and use English number words (first to 20, later to 100) and colour words, the first vocabulary fields of primary English. They are also used for prices, ages, phone numbers and describing things.
evidence: Count and say numbers to 20 (later to 100) in English, telling teens from tens (thirteen / thirty)
Name at least 10 colours and use them to describe objects
Understand numbers in dictation games, phone numbers and prices
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count to 20 in English and name the colours of things around them?
topics.laenderNotes: English starts in Kl. 3 in most Länder (2 lessons/week). Hamburg and Rheinland-Pfalz start in Kl. 1, and Brandenburg reportedly does too. NRW moved the start from Kl. 1 to Kl. 3 (cohorts from 2021/22) and Baden-Württemberg did the same from 2018/19. Since 2024/25 Bayern may teach English in Kl. 3/4 for 1 or 2 lessons. In Saarland, and in BW schools along the Rhine (Rheinschiene), the first foreign language in primary school is French.

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Using a Dictionary
topics.description: Look up words in a picture dictionary, the textbook word list and later a bilingual print or online dictionary: find the entry, choose the right meaning and use the information on word class and pronunciation.
evidence: Find words quickly in a picture dictionary or the textbook word list using alphabetical order
Use a bilingual dictionary entry: choose the right meaning and read word class and pronunciation
Look up a word in an online dictionary and listen to the audio pronunciation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} look up an English word in a dictionary, or an online one, and pick the right German meaning for the sentence?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Telling the Time and Daily Routine
topics.description: Tell and ask the time in English and describe a daily routine with times. German "halb drei" means 2:30, but English "half past two" names the previous hour, which is a well-known trap for German learners.
evidence: Tell and ask the time on the hour, half past, quarter past / to
Say 2:30 as "half past two" and avoid the "halb drei" trap
Describe a daily routine with times ("I get up at seven o'clock")
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a clock showing 2:30, do they say "half past two" in English, not "half three"?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Final Voiced Consonants
topics.description: Pronounce voiced consonants at the end of English words (dog, bed, eyes) without the German final devoicing that turns them into "dock", "bet" or "ice", which can change meaning.
evidence: Pronounce final voiced consonants without devoicing ("dog" not "dock", "bed" not "bet", "his" not "hiss")
Hear and produce minimal pairs (bag / back, eyes / ice)
Pronounce plural / 3rd-person -s as /z/ after voiced sounds (dogs, plays)
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} says "dog" or "bag" in English, can you hear a soft g at the end, or does it sound like "dock" and "back"?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Intonation and Sentence Stress
topics.description: Use English intonation patterns for questions and statements, contractions and weak forms, and stress key words so that speech sounds natural and meaning is clear.
evidence: Use rising intonation for yes/no questions and falling intonation for wh-questions and statements
Use contractions and weak forms in fluent speech (I'm, can't, "to" as /tə/)
Stress key words to show meaning or emotion when reading a dialogue aloud
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads an English dialogue aloud, does it sound like real speech, with questions going up and short forms like "I'm" and "can't"?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Reading Phonetic Symbols
topics.description: Read the phonetic transcription (IPA) given in textbook vocabulary lists and dictionaries, so you can pronounce new words correctly on your own.
evidence: Read the phonetic transcription in the textbook vocabulary list to pronounce a new word
Identify key symbols that differ from letters (θ, ð, æ, ə, ʃ, ː)
Use the transcription or audio in a dictionary to check stress and pronunciation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use the funny symbols next to a word in their English vocabulary list to work out how to say it?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Spelling Common Words
topics.nameDe: Rechtschreibung: Grundwortschatz und Großschreibung im Englischen
topics.description: Spell high-frequency English words and follow basic spelling and capitalisation rules. English capitalises "I", days, months and nationalities, but not ordinary nouns, which is the reverse of German habits.
evidence: Spell high-frequency words from the textbook vocabulary correctly in a dictation
Use capitals correctly in English: "I", names, days, months, nationalities and languages, but not ordinary nouns
Apply spelling rules for -ing, -ed and plural -ies
topics.assessmentPrompt: In an English text, does {{name}} write "I" and "Monday" with capitals but "dog" and "school" in lower case?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Questions and Negatives with do/does
topics.description: Form simple present questions, short answers and negatives with do / does / don't / doesn't, including wh-questions. German has no auxiliary "do", so learners often produce "I like not…" or "Like you…?".
evidence: Form yes/no questions and short answers with do / does ("Do you like…?" – "Yes, I do.")
Form wh-questions with question words ("Where do you live?", "What does she like?")
Form negatives with don't / doesn't and avoid German-style "I like not…"
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} ask "Do you like pizza?" and say "I don't like it", rather than "Like you pizza?" or "I like it not"?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: False Friends and Pseudo-Anglicisms
topics.description: Recognise English–German false friends (become ≠ bekommen, gift ≠ Gift) and German pseudo-anglicisms that English speakers do not use (Handy, Beamer). Use real cognates as a help while checking that the meaning really matches.
evidence: Explain at least 8 false friends (become ≠ bekommen, gift ≠ Gift, also ≠ also, chef ≠ Chef)
Recognise pseudo-anglicisms that are not used in English (Handy → mobile phone, Beamer → projector)
Use cognates as a strategy while checking whether the meaning really matches
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that "I become a present" doesn't mean "Ich bekomme ein Geschenk", and that a "Handy" is a "mobile phone" in English?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: "Have got" and "can"
topics.description: Use "have got / has got" for possession and family, and "can / can't" for ability and permission. Both form questions and negatives without do (Have you got…? Can you…?).
evidence: Use have got / has got and haven't / hasn't got to talk about possessions and family
Use can / can't for ability and permission
Form questions by putting "have" or "can" first ("Have you got…?", "Can you…?") and give short answers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} say in English what they have got and what they can or can't do, e.g. "I've got a bike, but I can't swim"?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Plural Nouns and Possessive 's
topics.description: Form regular and common irregular plurals, and show possession with 's / s' and possessive determiners (my, his, her, their), keeping plural -s and possessive 's apart in writing.
evidence: Form regular plurals including -es and -ies, and know common irregular ones (children, men, feet, mice)
Use possessive 's and s' (my sister's room, my parents' car) and possessive determiners (my, his, her, their)
Tell plural -s from possessive 's, and its from it's, in writing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} write "my brother's bike" with an apostrophe but "two bikes" without one?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Present Progressive
topics.description: Use the present progressive (am/is/are + -ing) for actions happening now, and choose between it and the simple present. German has no grammatical progressive, so the contrast must be learnt explicitly.
evidence: Form the present progressive (am/is/are + -ing), including spelling changes (sitting, making)
Describe what people are doing in a picture right now
Choose correctly between simple present (routine) and present progressive (now) using signal words
topics.assessmentPrompt: Looking at a busy picture, can {{name}} say in English what the people are doing right now, e.g. "The boy is reading", and know when to say "He reads every day" instead?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Simple Present
topics.description: Use the simple present for habits, routines and facts, including the 3rd-person -s (he plays, she watches) and the position of frequency adverbs. The 3rd-person -s is the best-known persistent error in German classrooms.
evidence: Use the simple present for habits and routines with signal words (always, often, never, every day)
Add -s / -es in the 3rd person singular (he plays, she watches) consistently in writing
Place frequency adverbs correctly ("She often plays…", not "She plays often…")
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes about someone else's routine in English, do they remember the -s, as in "My sister gets up at seven"?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: The Verb "to be" and Pronouns
topics.description: Use the forms of "to be" (am, is, are) with personal pronouns, including short forms, questions and negatives. This is usually the first explicit grammar of Kl. 5, after the chunks learnt in primary school.
evidence: Use am / is / are correctly with all personal pronouns, including short forms (I'm, she's, they're)
Form questions and short answers with be ("Are you…?" – "Yes, I am.")
Form negatives with "not" ("He isn't…")
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} reliably say "she is" and "they are" in English, and answer "Are you hungry?" with "Yes, I am" or "No, I'm not"?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: English Word Order
topics.description: Understand and apply English subject–verb–object word order. Unlike German, the verb does not move to second position after a fronted phrase or to the end of a subordinate clause. Place comes before time at the end of a sentence.
evidence: Keep subject–verb–object order after a time phrase ("Yesterday I played football", not "Yesterday played I")
Keep the verb right after the subject in because/that clauses ("…because I like it", not "because I it like")
Put place before time at the end of a sentence ("I go to school every day")
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} write "On Sundays I play football" in English, not "On Sundays play I football" as in German?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Understanding Short Videos
topics.description: Understand short film sequences (textbook films, children's videos) by combining what is said with images, tone of voice and body language, and use replay or subtitles purposefully.
evidence: Summarise in a few words what happens in a short film sequence, using both picture and sound
Answer questions about characters' feelings or intentions shown through images, tone and words
Use subtitles, replay or slowed playback deliberately to understand a difficult passage
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} watches a short English video for school, can they explain what happened and how the people felt?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Listening for Gist and Detail
topics.description: Understand textbook dialogues, announcements and phone messages by choosing a listening purpose: gist (what is it about?), selective (find one piece of information) or detailed. Use clues before listening to predict content.
evidence: State the topic and situation of a short textbook dialogue after one listening
Note specific information (times, prices, names, numbers) from an announcement or phone message
Use pre-listening clues (title, pictures) to predict content and check the predictions while listening
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears a short English announcement at a station, can they pick out the time and platform of their train?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Everyday Life in Britain
topics.description: Know about everyday life in Britain as presented in Kl. 5–6 textbooks (school life, homes and families, London and other regions, pounds and pence) and reflect on similarities and differences with your own life.
evidence: Describe a typical British school day and compare it with their own (uniform, houses, assembly)
Use pounds and pence when shopping in a role play
Name key places in London and facts about at least one other part of the UK
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe what a school day is like for a child in Britain and say what is different from their own school?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Reading Everyday Texts
topics.description: Read short everyday and factual texts (messages, emails, signs, timetables, menus, simple websites and textbook texts) by skimming for the main idea or scanning for specific information.
evidence: Scan a timetable, menu, sign or website for specific information (time, price, place)
Skim a short factual text and give its topic and main points
Understand a short email or chat message from a peer and identify what is being asked
topics.assessmentPrompt: Given an English menu or bus timetable, can {{name}} quickly find the price of a dish or the time of the next bus?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Working Out Unknown Words
topics.description: Work out the meaning of unknown words from context, pictures, word parts and similar words in German or other languages (cognates), and judge when a dictionary is really needed.
evidence: Guess the meaning of unknown words using context, pictures and similar German words (e.g. "garden", "finger", "kindergarten")
Use known parts of a word to infer its meaning (e.g. "unhappy", "footballer")
Check a guess against the context and decide whether a dictionary is needed
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} meets a new word in an English text, do they try to work it out from the sentence or from a similar German word before looking it up?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Reading Simple Stories
topics.description: Read short stories, comics and graded readers with familiar vocabulary, following the plot, understanding characters and their feelings, and responding personally to the text.
evidence: Identify the main characters, setting and key events in a short story or graded reader
Describe how a character feels and give a reason from the text
Give their own reaction to a story ("I liked / didn't like it because…")
topics.assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} read a short English story or comic on their own, and can they tell you what it was about and which character they liked?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Writing Short Messages
topics.nameDe: Kurze Nachrichten, E-Mails und Postkarten schreiben
topics.description: Write short messages, notes, postcards, emails and chat posts to exchange information with others, answering their questions and using the usual opening and closing phrases.
evidence: Write a short email or chat message to a pen friend that answers their questions and asks one back
Use suitable opening and closing phrases (Hi / Dear…, Love / Best wishes…)
Write a short note giving essential information (where, when, what to bring)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} write a short English email to a pen friend, answering their questions and asking one of their own?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Writing Connected Texts
topics.nameDe: Zusammenhängende Texte schreiben (my day, a story)
topics.description: Write short connected texts on familiar topics, such as your daily routine, family or a simple story or diary entry, linking sentences with basic connectives and organising them into a beginning, middle and end.
evidence: Write a text of 60–100 words about their daily routine or family, linking sentences with and, but, because, then
Write a simple story or diary entry in the past from picture prompts
Organise a text into beginning, middle and end
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write a short English text of about ten sentences about their day or a little story, with linking words like "and", "but" and "then"?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Checking and Revising Own Writing
topics.description: Check and improve your own English texts: look for typical errors with a checklist, fix spelling with the vocabulary list, dictionary or spell-checker, and revise after peer feedback.
evidence: Use a checklist to check their text for known error types (3rd-person -s, capital "I", word order)
Correct spellings using the vocabulary list, a dictionary or a spell-checker
Improve a text after peer feedback by adding detail or linking words
topics.assessmentPrompt: After writing something in English, does {{name}} check it for typical mistakes like a missing -s after he/she/it, and correct them?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Digital Tools for Learning English
topics.description: Use digital tools for learning English (online dictionaries with audio, vocabulary apps, textbook apps, machine translation) on purpose and critically, knowing their limits and the class rules.
evidence: Use an online dictionary or vocabulary app to practise and check words
Check a machine translation critically (e.g. translate it back, spot word-for-word errors)
Explain when using a translator is helpful and when it prevents learning or breaks class rules
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} uses an online translator for English homework, do they check the result and know when they shouldn't use it?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Mediating in Everyday Situations
topics.description: Act as a language mediator between German and English speakers in everyday situations, in both directions. Pass on the key information from a sign, menu, flyer or conversation, and explain culture-specific terms.
evidence: Help a German-speaking family member on holiday by explaining the key information on an English sign, menu or announcement
Give an English-speaking visitor the main points of a German text (e.g. school timetable, flyer) in simple English
Leave out unnecessary details and explain culture-specific words (e.g. "Hausaufgabenheft")
topics.assessmentPrompt: On holiday, could {{name}} explain to a family member in German what an English sign or menu says, or help an English-speaking visitor understand a German notice?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Everyday Conversations and Arrangements
topics.nameDe: An Gesprächen teilnehmen: Verabredungen, Auskünfte, Meinungen
topics.description: Take part in short everyday conversations about familiar topics: make plans and arrangements, ask for and give information or directions, and give a simple opinion with a reason.
evidence: Make an arrangement with a partner (activity, time, place) and confirm it
Ask for and give simple directions or information in a role play (station, shop, café)
State an opinion with a simple reason ("I think … because …") and react to a partner's opinion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} arrange in English to meet a friend: suggest an activity, agree on a time and place, and confirm?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Giving a Short Presentation
topics.nameDe: Kurzvortrag halten (z. B. My pet, My hobby)
topics.description: Give a short, prepared talk on a familiar topic (my pet, my hobby, my favourite place), using notes, a poster or slides rather than reading out a text, and answer simple questions.
evidence: Give a rehearsed 1–2 minute talk on a familiar topic using a poster, slides or cue cards rather than a read-out text
Structure the talk with a beginning, middle and end ("Today I want to tell you about…")
Answer one or two simple questions from the audience
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} give a two-minute talk in English about their hobby using only a few keywords on a card?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Home, Town and Directions
topics.description: Know and use words for rooms and furniture, places in town and directions, so you can describe your home and find your way.
evidence: Name rooms and furniture and describe their own room
Name places in town (station, library, supermarket) and say where they are
Understand and give simple directions ("go straight on", "turn left", "it's on the right")
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} describe their room in English and give a tourist simple directions to the station?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Future with "going to"
topics.description: Talk about plans, intentions and predictions based on present evidence with "be going to + verb", including questions and negatives.
evidence: Talk about plans and intentions with going to ("I'm going to visit my aunt")
Make predictions from present evidence ("Look at the clouds – it's going to rain")
Form questions and negatives with going to
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you in English what they are going to do in the holidays?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Simple Past: Irregular Verbs and "did"
topics.nameDe: Simple Past: unregelmäßige Verben, Fragen und Verneinung mit did
topics.description: Use common irregular past forms and form past questions and negatives with did / didn't. Germans often say "I have seen him yesterday", copying the spoken German Perfekt, so this has to be unlearnt.
evidence: Use the simple past of at least 30 common irregular verbs (went, saw, had, bought)
Form questions and negatives with did / didn't + infinitive ("Did you go…?", "I didn't see…")
Use the simple past, not the present perfect, with yesterday, last week and ago
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} say "I saw him yesterday" in English, rather than "I have seen him yesterday"?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Simple Past: Regular Verbs
topics.nameDe: Simple Past: regelmäßige Verben und was/were
topics.description: Form and use the simple past of regular verbs (-ed, with its spelling and three pronunciations) and was/were to talk about finished past events.
evidence: Form the simple past of regular verbs with -ed, including spelling changes (stopped, tried)
Pronounce -ed endings correctly as /t/, /d/ or /ɪd/ (walked, played, wanted)
Use was / were to talk about the past ("I was at home yesterday")
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you in English about yesterday using verbs like "played", "watched" and "was"?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Comparing with Adjectives
topics.description: Compare people and things with comparatives and superlatives (-er/-est, more/most, irregular forms) and with "than" and "as … as". German "als" leads learners to say "taller as" instead of "taller than".
evidence: Form comparatives and superlatives with -er/-est and more/most (bigger, most exciting)
Use the irregular forms good–better–best and bad–worse–worst
Compare with "than" and "as … as" ("Tom is taller than Ben", not "taller as")
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} compare two animals in English, e.g. "An elephant is bigger than a horse", using "than" and not "as"?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Talking about Past Events
topics.description: Talk briefly about past events and experiences (the weekend, a holiday, a school trip) in the simple past, putting events in order and asking others about their experiences.
evidence: Tell a partner in 4–6 sentences what they did at the weekend, using simple past forms
Use sequencing words (first, then, after that, in the end) to put events in order
Ask a partner about their holiday with "Did you…? / Where did you…?" and react
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you in English what they did last weekend, in a few sentences, in the right order?

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Weak Forms and Connected Speech
topics.description: Understand and use features of natural spoken English: weak forms of small words (/ə/ in to, of, can), linking between words (linking r, an apple), contractions and unstressed syllables. Their speech sounds more fluent and fast speech becomes easier to follow.
evidence: Pronounce the weak form in "I can swim" /kən/ and the strong form in "Yes, I can" /kæn/
Link words smoothly ("far away" with linking r, "an orange")
Write down a short fast-spoken sentence and identify the reduced words
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads an English sentence aloud, does it sound connected and natural rather than word by word?
topics.laenderNotes: NRW lists vowels in unstressed syllables and linking r for Kl. 7–8.

topics.subject: Englisch
topics.name: Conditional Sentences Type I
topics.description: Talk about real, possible conditions and their likely results with if + simple present and will, can, must or an imperative in the main clause, and use when and unless correctly.
evidence: Form type I sentences with the simple present in the if-clause (no will after if)
