evidence: Puts the steps of Nazi foreign policy 1933–1939 in order
Explains the policy of appeasement
Judges the role of foreign-policy successes for consent to the regime
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked why Britain and France gave in to Hitler in Munich in 1938, could they explain the policy of appeasement?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.domainEn: National Socialism and the Second World War
topics.name: Persecution and Exclusion 1933–1939
topics.description: Pupils describe the step-by-step persecution of Jews (boycott 1933, Nuremberg Laws 1935, November Pogrom 1938) and of other groups (political opponents, Sinti and Roma, homosexuals, Jehovah's Witnesses, people with disabilities) before the war.
evidence: Puts anti-Jewish measures of 1933–1939 in chronological order
Explains the Nuremberg Laws and their consequences
Describes the November Pogrom using a local example
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learned that the synagogue in their town was destroyed on 9/10 November 1938, could they place this in the persecution of Jews since 1933?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.domainEn: National Socialism and the Second World War
topics.name: Flight and Expulsion 1944–1950
topics.nameDe: Flucht und Vertreibung im europäischen Kontext
topics.description: Pupils explain the flight and expulsion of Germans from the eastern territories and Eastern Europe at the end of the war and after, place it in the context of Nazi expansion and population policy, and assess its consequences for the victims and post-war society.
evidence: Explains causes of flight and expulsion in the context of Nazi crimes and war
Describes the experience of refugees using eyewitness accounts
Assesses the integration of expellees in post-war Germany
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learned that a great-grandparent came from Silesia after 1945, could they explain why millions of Germans had to leave their homes?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.domainEn: National Socialism and the Second World War
topics.name: The Holocaust
topics.description: Pupils describe the systematic murder of six million European Jews: ghettos, mass shootings by Einsatzgruppen, the Wannsee Conference and the extermination camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau, as well as the genocide of Sinti and Roma (Porajmos) and the "euthanasia" murders.
evidence: Describes the stages from persecution to systematic mass murder
Explains the role of the Wannsee Conference
Explains with a biography or testimony what the Holocaust meant for victims
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read the diary of Anne Frank or a survivor's testimony, could they place it in the history of the Holocaust?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.domainEn: National Socialism and the Second World War
topics.name: Nazi Ideology
topics.description: Pupils explain the core elements of Nazi ideology – racism and antisemitism, "Volksgemeinschaft", leader principle, "Lebensraum" in the East, anti-democratic and anti-communist thinking – and where these ideas came from.
evidence: Explains the Nazi "racial doctrine" and why it is pseudo-scientific
Explains the terms Volksgemeinschaft and Führerprinzip
Traces antisemitism back to older roots
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read a passage from a Nazi schoolbook, could they identify the ideological ideas in it and explain why they are false and dangerous?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.domainEn: National Socialism and the Second World War
topics.name: The Nazi Seizure of Power 1933/34
topics.description: Pupils describe how the Nazis destroyed the constitutional state within months: Reichstag Fire Decree, Enabling Act, ban of parties and unions, Gleichschaltung of the Länder and society, the "Röhm Putsch" and Hitler as "Führer" in 1934.
evidence: Puts the steps from January 1933 to August 1934 in order
Explains the significance of the Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act
Explains the term Gleichschaltung with examples
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked how Hitler could become dictator "legally", could they explain the steps of 1933/34?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.domainEn: National Socialism and the Second World War
topics.name: The War of Annihilation in the East
topics.nameDe: Vernichtungskrieg und Verbrechen an der Zivilbevölkerung
topics.description: Pupils explain why the war against Poland and the Soviet Union was a racist war of annihilation: occupation crimes, starvation of prisoners of war, forced labour and the Wehrmacht's involvement in crimes.
evidence: Explains the difference between a conventional war and a war of annihilation
Describes crimes against civilians and prisoners of war
Explains the system of forced labour in Germany
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard someone claim that the Wehrmacht only fought a normal war, could they explain with evidence why historians disagree?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.domainEn: National Socialism and the Second World War
topics.name: Everyday Life in the Nazi State
topics.nameDe: Alltag zwischen Zustimmung, Propaganda und Terror
topics.description: Pupils describe life in the Nazi state between consent and repression: propaganda, Hitler Youth and BDM, the "Volksgemeinschaft" and its exclusions, terror by SS and Gestapo, and discuss the room for action of ordinary people.
evidence: Analyses a Nazi propaganda poster
Describes the aims of the Hitler Youth
Discusses the room for action of ordinary people in the dictatorship
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard a grandparent say that "not everything was bad" under Hitler, could they explain how propaganda and terror worked together?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.domainEn: National Socialism and the Second World War
topics.name: Resistance against National Socialism
topics.description: Pupils describe forms of resistance – from non-conformity and help for persecuted people to the White Rose, Georg Elser, communist and church resistance and the attempt of 20 July 1944 – and judge motives and room for action.
evidence: Distinguishes forms of resistance from non-conformity to assassination attempts
Describes the White Rose or 20 July 1944 using sources
Judges motives and risks of resistance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read a leaflet of the White Rose, could they explain the students' motives and the risk they took?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.domainEn: National Socialism and the Second World War
topics.name: The Second World War
topics.nameDe: Der Zweite Weltkrieg in Europa und Asien
topics.description: Pupils outline the course of the Second World War: Blitzkrieg, war against the Soviet Union, the war in the Pacific after Pearl Harbor, the turning points (Stalingrad, D-Day), bombing war and the end in May and August 1945.
evidence: Places the main phases of the war on a timeline and map
Explains the global dimension including the Pacific war
Describes the end of the war in Europe and Asia
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a world map of 1942, could they explain how the war had become a world war?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Great Depression and the End of Weimar
topics.description: Pupils explain the effects of the Great Depression (unemployment, radicalisation), the presidential cabinets from 1930, the rise of the NSDAP and the appointment of Hitler on 30 January 1933, and judge the responsibility of actors.
evidence: Relates unemployment figures to election results of 1928–1933
Explains how the presidential cabinets hollowed out parliamentary democracy
Judges the roles of Hindenburg, conservative elites and voters
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared a chart of unemployment with NSDAP election results from 1928 to 1932, could they explain the connection and its limits?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Crisis and Stabilisation 1919–1929
topics.description: Pupils describe the crisis years up to 1923 (Kapp Putsch, political murders, occupation of the Ruhr, hyperinflation, Hitler Putsch), the stabilisation under Stresemann (Rentenmark, Dawes Plan, Locarno) and the cultural boom of mass media, consumer society and modern art.
evidence: Explains causes and consequences of the 1923 hyperinflation
Names elements of stabilisation under Stresemann
Describes new mass media and culture of the 1920s
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a banknote for one billion marks from 1923, could they explain how this happened and how the currency was stabilised?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The November Revolution 1918/19
topics.description: Pupils explain how the monarchy ended in November 1918 and the choice between a council system and a parliamentary democracy, the Spartacist uprising and the elections to the National Assembly in January 1919 (first vote for women).
evidence: Describes the events from the sailors' revolt to the proclamation of the republic
Compares council democracy and parliamentary democracy
Explains the significance of women's suffrage in 1919
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learned that the republic was proclaimed twice on 9 November 1918, could they explain the two different visions behind this?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Weimar Constitution
topics.description: Pupils analyse the Weimar Constitution – Reichstag elected by pure proportional representation, strong Reich President with emergency powers (Art. 48), basic rights, referendums – and explain its strengths and weaknesses.
evidence: Draws and explains a diagram of the Weimar Constitution
Explains the role of Article 48
Compares the constitution with that of 1871
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a diagram of the Weimar Constitution, could they point to the features that later helped to undermine democracy?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: West Germany in the Adenauer Era
topics.nameDe: Die Bundesrepublik in der Ära Adenauer
topics.description: Pupils describe the early Federal Republic: integration into the West and reconciliation with France (Élysée Treaty 1963), the "economic miracle" and the social market economy, integration of expellees, recruitment of guest workers and the (often silent) handling of the Nazi past.
evidence: Explains Adenauer's policy of Western integration
Explains causes of the economic miracle
Describes how the Nazi past was dealt with in the 1950s
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watched a 1950s newsreel about the economic miracle, could they explain why West Germany grew so quickly and what was left out?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The GDR as SED Dictatorship
topics.description: Pupils describe state and society in the GDR: the SED's claim to leadership, the Stasi, planned economy, youth organisations (FDJ), the uprising of 17 June 1953, everyday life, opposition and church groups.
evidence: Explains the SED's claim to power and the role of the Stasi
Describes the uprising of 17 June 1953
Compares everyday life in the GDR with life in the FRG
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} visited the former Stasi prison in Berlin-Hohenschönhausen, could they explain how the SED kept control over society?
topics.laenderNotes: Taught in more depth in the eastern Länder; Berlin/Brandenburg and Sachsen add regional studies of everyday life in the GDR.

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Peaceful Revolution of 1989
topics.description: Pupils explain the causes of the collapse of the GDR – economic crisis, Gorbachev's reforms, opening of the Hungarian border, mass flight, the Monday demonstrations in Leipzig – and the fall of the Wall on 9 November 1989.
evidence: Distinguishes long-term causes from immediate triggers of 1989
Explains the role of Gorbachev and of the Eastern European reform movements
Describes the Monday demonstrations and the fall of the Wall
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard the chant "Wir sind das Volk", could they explain where and why it was shouted in autumn 1989?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Berlin Wall and Ostpolitik
topics.description: Pupils explain why the GDR built the Berlin Wall in 1961, what it meant for people, and how relations between the two states changed through Brandt's new Ostpolitik (Basic Treaty 1972) and détente.
evidence: Explains the reasons for building the Wall from the GDR's point of view and its consequences
Explains the idea of "Wandel durch Annäherung"
Judges the room for action of politicians in both states
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} stood at the Berlin Wall memorial on Bernauer Straße, could they explain why the Wall was built and how relations changed in the 1970s?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: German Reunification 1990
topics.description: Pupils describe the steps to unity in 1990 – free Volkskammer election, monetary union, Two-plus-Four Treaty, unification on 3 October – and judge the economic and social transformation in the east (Treuhand, unemployment).
evidence: Places the steps to unity in 1990 in order
Explains why the Two-plus-Four Treaty was needed
Judges economic and social consequences of unification
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked why 3 October is a public holiday, could they explain the steps that led to German unity in 1990?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Participation and Freedom: A Longitudinal Study
topics.nameDe: Politische Partizipation und Freiheitsstreben im Längsschnitt
topics.description: Students compare struggles for participation and freedom across epochs – Athenian democracy, conflicts in late-medieval towns, the American and French revolutions with their debates on slavery, and 1848/49 – asking who could take part and where the limits lay.
evidence: Compares participation in Athens and in a late-medieval town
Explains the contemporary debates about slavery and abolitionism
Discusses the aims and options of the groups in 1848/49
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked who could take part in politics in Athens, in a medieval town and in 1848, could they compare the three and name the excluded?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: China and Russia as Empires
topics.description: Students characterise the imperial foundations of China and Russia around 1900, explain the revolutionary upheavals (China 1911 and 1949, Russia 1917), judge Maoism and Stalinism, and assess the reforms of Deng Xiaoping and Gorbachev and imperial self-images ("Middle Kingdom", "russkij mir").
evidence: Describes the imperial structures of China and Russia around 1900
Explains the consequences of the revolutions of 1917 and 1949
Judges the reform policies of Deng Xiaoping and Gorbachev
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard Russian politicians speak of the "Russian world", could they explain the imperial history behind this idea?
topics.laenderNotes: NRW (from 2027) makes China and Russia obligatory in the Einführungsphase; BW offers Russia and China as electives in Kl. 9/10.

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Source Criticism
topics.description: Students interpret sources of different genres in exam form: external and internal source criticism, analysis of argument and language, contextualisation and judgement of the source's value for a question, including digital and AI-generated material.
evidence: Writes a full source interpretation with description, analysis, context and judgement
Judges the value of a source genre for a given question
Checks a digital or AI-generated text for authenticity and plausibility
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were given an unknown speech from 1933 in an exam, could they write a structured interpretation that judges its reliability and value?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Forming a Historical Judgement
topics.description: Students form reasoned judgements on historical questions, weighting several categories (e.g. continuity and change, freedom, power) and time levels, check whether their information is sufficient, and revise hypotheses in the light of evidence.
evidence: Uses explicit criteria and categories in a written judgement
Distinguishes judging by the standards of the time and by present-day norms
Checks and revises a hypothesis against new evidence
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked "Was the revolution of 1848 a failure?", could they write a judgement that names its criteria and weighs arguments on both sides?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Nation, Nationalism and Empire
topics.nameDe: Nation, Nationalismus und Imperium als Begriffe
topics.description: Students define and distinguish key concepts – nation (state nation, cultural nation, "imagined community"), nationalism (liberal and integral) and empire – and apply them to examples from the 19th and 20th centuries.
evidence: Distinguishes state nation and cultural nation with examples
Distinguishes liberal-emancipatory from integral nationalism
Names characteristics of an empire and applies them to one case
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard Germany described as a "Kulturnation" before 1871, could they explain what this means and how it differs from France?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Explaining National Socialism
topics.description: Students discuss different explanations of National Socialism – intentionalist and structuralist views, polycracy, "Sonderweg", totalitarianism and fascism theories, consent and "Volksgemeinschaft" – and judge their explanatory power.
evidence: Explains two contrasting explanations of the Nazi dictatorship
Explains the intentionalism–functionalism debate on the Holocaust
Judges the explanatory power and limits of one approach
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked whether the Nazi regime was run by Hitler alone, could they compare explanations that stress Hitler and those that stress structures?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Comparing Twentieth-Century Dictatorships
topics.description: Students compare National Socialism and Stalinism (and optionally the SED state) using totalitarianism theory (Arendt, Friedrich/Brzezinski), discuss its strengths and the criticism of it, and reflect on comparing without equating.
evidence: Names criteria of totalitarian rule according to a theory
Compares Nazi and Stalinist rule using these criteria
Discusses criticism of the totalitarianism concept
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard the claim "Hitler and Stalin were the same", could they compare the two regimes carefully and show where the comparison works and where it fails?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Colonialism and Its Legacies
topics.nameDe: Kolonialismus und seine Folgen für die globalisierte Welt
topics.description: Students explain motives and forms of European colonialism and its effects on today's world – borders, economic structures, racism, migration – and evaluate how Germany remembers its colonial history (restitution of artefacts, recognition of genocide).
evidence: Explains forms of colonial rule (settler, trade and exploitation colonies)
Traces present-day problems of a post-colonial region back to colonial rule
Evaluates a current debate on colonial remembrance in Germany
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard about the return of the Benin Bronzes to Nigeria, could they explain the colonial history behind the debate?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Coming to Terms with the Nazi Past
topics.nameDe: Vergangenheitsbewältigung und Erinnerungskultur in Ost und West
topics.description: Students evaluate how both German states and united Germany dealt with Nazi crimes: denazification, Nuremberg and Auschwitz trials, antifascism as state doctrine in the GDR, debates (Historikerstreit) and memorials such as the Holocaust Memorial in Berlin.
evidence: Compares the handling of the Nazi past in the FRG and the GDR
Explains the significance of the Frankfurt Auschwitz trials
Evaluates a current memorial or debate on remembrance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} visited the Holocaust Memorial in Berlin, could they explain how German remembrance of the Nazi past developed after 1945?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Discussing Historians' Interpretations
topics.description: Students analyse and discuss interpretations from historiography – e.g. the Fischer controversy on war guilt, the "Sonderweg" thesis or debates on the end of Weimar – identifying the thesis, arguments and position of the historian.
evidence: Identifies thesis, arguments and evidence in a historian's text
Compares two conflicting interpretations of the same event
Discusses the plausibility of an interpretation with own knowledge
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read two historians disagreeing about who caused the First World War, could they lay out both positions and argue which is more convincing?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: How Historical Knowledge Is Made
topics.description: Students reflect on the nature of historical knowledge: history as a reconstruction from sources, the perspective and present-day questions of historians, objectivity and plausibility, and the meaning of historical concepts and narrative.
evidence: Explains why history is a reconstruction rather than the past itself
Explains criteria of plausibility (empirical, normative, narrative)
Reflects on how present-day questions shape historical research
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked whether history can ever be objective, could they give a reasoned answer that explains how historians work?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: German Jews and Modern Antisemitism
topics.description: Students describe emancipation and social integration of German Jews in the 19th century, the rise of racial antisemitism in the Kaiserreich and Weimar, and how Jewish families reacted to exclusion.
evidence: Describes steps of Jewish emancipation in the 19th century
Explains the difference between religious anti-Judaism and racial antisemitism
Describes reactions of German-Jewish families to exclusion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read about a Jewish family that fought for Germany in 1914 and was persecuted after 1933, could they explain this history of integration and exclusion?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Modernisation Processes
topics.description: Students explain indicators of social, economic and technological modernisation around 1900 (urbanisation, industry, science, mass society, democratisation) and judge the effects of industrialisation on living conditions under social and ecological aspects, including ambivalent reactions to modernity.
evidence: Names and explains indicators of modernisation
Judges social and ecological effects of industrialisation
Explains ambivalent reactions to modernity (e.g. life reform, cultural pessimism)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared Berlin in 1850 and 1910, could they explain what "modernisation" means using concrete indicators?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Decolonisation: Case Study Namibia
topics.description: Students evaluate a decolonisation process in depth – e.g. Namibia's path from German colony to South African rule, apartheid and independence in 1990 – and the role of non-aligned states and the UN.
evidence: Describes the stages of Namibia's path to independence
Explains the role of the UN and the non-aligned movement
Evaluates the results of decolonisation and the German–Namibian reconciliation process
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} followed the German–Namibian negotiations about the genocide, could they explain Namibia's long road to independence?

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: After the Boom: 1973 and Structural Change
topics.nameDe: Nach dem Boom: Ölkrise 1973 und Strukturwandel
topics.description: Students explain the end of the post-war boom with the oil crisis of 1973, the "limits to growth" debate, structural change and unemployment in the West, the economic crisis in the GDR, and new social movements (environmental and peace movements).
evidence: Explains the causes and effects of the 1973 oil crisis
Compares economic developments in East and West Germany after 1973
Explains the rise of the environmental movement in the context of the growth debate
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard about the car-free Sundays of 1973, could they explain why the oil crisis marked the end of the post-war boom?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Automata in Everyday Life
topics.description: Recognise automata in everyday life (vending machines, traffic lights, automatic doors, bottle-return machines) as machines that work by themselves according to fixed rules, reacting to inputs.
evidence: Name automatic machines in their environment (vending machine, traffic light, automatic door)
Describe what input an automaton needs and what it does in response
Explain that an automaton follows fixed rules and does not think
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain what a drinks machine needs from you and what it does, step by step, and that it just follows rules?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Algorithms in Everyday Life
topics.description: Recognise and follow step-by-step instructions in everyday life (game rules such as "Mensch ärgere Dich nicht", recipes, routines), describe them in your own words, and see that the order and completeness of the steps matter.
evidence: Carry out an everyday algorithm step by step (e.g. game rules, recipe, hand-washing routine)
Describe a familiar routine as a precise sequence of steps in everyday language
Find what goes wrong when a step is missing or in the wrong order
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain step by step, in the right order, how to brush their teeth or play a simple board game, without leaving anything out?
topics.laenderNotes: In Kl. 1–4 informatics is not a separate subject. It is integrated into Sachunterricht (technical perspective) and Mathematik and follows the GI 2019 recommendations, which are non-binding. Länder frameworks such as the NRW Medienkompetenzrahmen and Lehrpläne 2021 make parts of it binding.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Arrow Programs and Floor Robots
topics.description: Give precise movement commands as a sequence of arrows to guide a classmate or a floor robot (Bee-Bot, Blue-Bot) across a grid. Predict where it will end up, and correct wrong commands.
evidence: Guide a classmate or a Bee-Bot across a grid with a sequence of arrow commands (forward, turn left / right)
Write down an arrow program for a given path and predict where the robot will end up
Find and correct one wrong arrow in a program that misses the target
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} plan a sequence of arrow commands that gets a toy robot from start to goal on a grid, and fix it if it goes wrong?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: My Media World
topics.description: Describe and reflect on your own media use (which media, when, why, how long), for example with a media diary, and say what you like and what bothers you about it.
evidence: Keep a short media diary and describe which media they use, when and why
Distinguish media used for learning, playing, information and communication
Say what they like about their media use and what bothers them
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you which media they use in a normal week, what for, and whether anything about it bothers them?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Reality and Fiction in Media
topics.description: Distinguish real reports from invented stories, cartoons and staged videos, and understand that photos can be edited (filters, cut-outs) and videos staged.
evidence: Distinguish real reports from invented stories and animated films
Explain how photos can be edited (filters, cut-outs) and videos staged
Spot clues that a picture or clip has been changed
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell whether a video shows something real or made up, and explain that photos can be changed with filters?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Signs, Symbols and Codes
topics.nameDe: Zeichen, Symbole und Codes im Alltag
topics.description: Understand that symbols and codes (traffic signs, pictograms, emojis, secret signs) carry information only because people agreed on what they mean. Sender and receiver must share the agreement for a message to be understood.
evidence: Explain what everyday symbols mean (traffic signs, pictograms, emojis) and that people agreed on their meaning
Invent a secret sign code with a partner and use it to send a message
Explain why a message cannot be read if sender and receiver did not agree on the code
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} and a friend invent their own secret signs, can they send each other a message and explain why someone else couldn't read it?
topics.laenderNotes: In Kl. 1–4 informatics is not a separate subject. It is integrated into Sachunterricht (technical perspective) and Mathematik and follows the GI 2019 recommendations, which are non-binding. Länder frameworks such as the NRW Medienkompetenzrahmen and Lehrpläne 2021 make parts of it binding.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Using a Tablet or Computer
topics.description: Operate school devices purposefully: switch on, log in, open and close apps, use touch gestures, mouse or trackpad, and try simple fixes before asking for help.
evidence: Switch on, log in, open an app and close it properly
Use touch gestures, a mouse or a trackpad to select, drag and scroll
Try simple fixes when something does not work (check the volume, restart the app) and ask for help
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} switch on a school tablet, open the right app and close it again on their own, and check the volume when nothing can be heard?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Digital Devices Around Us
topics.description: Recognise computers and other informatics systems in everyday life, including hidden ones (washing machines, cars, toys, supermarket checkouts), and understand that people design and program them.
evidence: Name devices that contain computers, including hidden ones (washing machine, car, toys)
Explain that computers are designed and programmed by people
Sort devices by what they are used for (communicating, playing, learning, household)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} find things at home that have a computer inside, even ones that don't look like a computer, like the washing machine?
topics.laenderNotes: In Kl. 1–4 informatics is not a separate subject. It is integrated into Sachunterricht (technical perspective) and Mathematik and follows the GI 2019 recommendations, which are non-binding. Länder frameworks such as the NRW Medienkompetenzrahmen and Lehrpläne 2021 make parts of it binding.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Photos and Audio Recordings
topics.nameDe: Fotos und Audioaufnahmen erstellen (z. B. Hörspiel)
topics.description: Take photos and make audio recordings with a tablet on purpose, choosing distance and angle or re-recording until it sounds right, and combine pictures and sound into simple products such as a talking picture or a radio play.
evidence: Take a photo with a tablet, choosing distance and angle deliberately
Record, listen to and re-record a short audio message or part of a radio play
Combine pictures and sound into a simple product (e.g. talking picture, audio book page)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} take a good photo with a tablet and record a short audio message, listening back and re-doing it if needed?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Personal Data
topics.description: Know which data are personal (name, address, birthday, photos, location, school) and why they should not be shared online without an adult, and use nicknames and avatars that do not reveal who you are.
evidence: Sort information into personal data (name, address, birthday, photo, location) and non-personal data
Explain why they should not share personal data in games, chats or forms without asking an adult
Choose a nickname or avatar that does not reveal their identity
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a game asks {{name}} for their full name, address and a photo, do they know to stop and ask an adult first?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Repeats and Decisions in Instructions
topics.description: Identify and use the basic building blocks of algorithms without a computer: sequence, repetition ("3 × step forward") and decisions ("if the card is red, … otherwise …").
evidence: Shorten a long instruction by using a repeat ("3 × step forward")
Follow and write an instruction with a decision ("If the card is red, …, otherwise …")
Identify sequence, repeat and decision in a familiar routine or game
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a game like "If I clap, jump; if I stamp, sit down – do it five times", can {{name}} follow the rules and point out the "if" part and the "repeat" part?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Advertising and Influencers
topics.description: Recognise advertising on TV, websites, video platforms and in games, including labels such as "Anzeige" and "Werbung". Understand how influencers earn money through product placement and sponsored posts, and analyse persuasion tricks.
evidence: Identify advertising on TV, websites, YouTube and in games, including labels such as "Anzeige" or "Werbung"
Explain how influencers earn money with product placement and sponsored posts
Analyse the tricks an advert uses (music, famous people, promises) to persuade children
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} watches a video where someone shows off toys or snacks, can they tell whether it is advertising, and explain how the person earns money from it?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Binary Codes
topics.description: Encode and decode information using only two states (0/1, on/off, black/white), for example pixel pictures from grids of 0s and 1s. Design a small binary code yourself and discover that each extra bit doubles the number of things you can tell apart.
evidence: Encode and decode a message using only two symbols (e.g. 0/1, light on/off, black/white)
Colour a black-and-white pixel picture from a grid of 0s and 1s and encode their own picture
Design their own binary code for a small set of items (e.g. 4 animals with 2 bits) and say how many items 3 bits can distinguish
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets a grid of 0s and 1s, can they colour in the hidden picture, and make a code like that for a friend?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Children's Search Engines
topics.nameDe: Mit Kindersuchmaschinen suchen (fragFINN, Blinde Kuh, Helles Köpfchen)
topics.description: Search for information with German children's search engines and portals (fragFINN, Blinde Kuh, Helles Köpfchen, Klexikon), which show only checked, child-safe websites, and pick a suitable result.
evidence: Search for a topic in a children's search engine (fragFINN, Blinde Kuh, Helles Köpfchen) and open a suitable result
Explain why children's search engines show only checked, child-safe websites
Use a children's encyclopaedia site (e.g. Klexikon) to answer a question
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use a children's search engine like fragFINN or Blinde Kuh to find out something for school, and explain why it is safer than an ordinary search engine?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Hardware, Software and Computer Parts
topics.nameDe: Hardware, Software und Bestandteile eines Computers
topics.description: Name the main parts of informatics systems (input devices, output devices, processor, memory, storage) using technical terms, and distinguish hardware (the physical parts) from software (programs and apps).
evidence: Name input devices (keyboard, mouse, microphone, camera), output devices (screen, speaker, printer) and storage
Explain the difference between hardware (parts you can touch) and software (programs / apps)
Use technical terms (processor, memory, operating system) at an age-appropriate level
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} sort computer parts into "input" and "output" and explain the difference between hardware and software?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Ways of Communicating Digitally
topics.description: Know digital ways of communicating (messenger, e-mail, video call, learning platform), compare them with a letter or phone call, and choose a suitable channel for a purpose.
evidence: Name digital ways to communicate and compare them with a letter or phone call
Choose a suitable channel for a purpose (quick message, sending a file, video call)
Write a short e-mail with subject, greeting and closing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain when you would send a message, write an e-mail or make a video call, and write a short e-mail with a greeting?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Keyboard Skills
topics.description: Type short texts on the German QWERTZ keyboard: capitals with shift, the German special characters ä, ö, ü and ß, punctuation and correction keys, building towards using both hands with a basic finger position.
evidence: Type short sentences using shift for capitals, space and backspace
Find the German special characters (ä, ö, ü, ß) and punctuation on the QWERTZ keyboard
Use both hands with a basic finger position rather than single-finger hunting
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} type a short German sentence on a keyboard, including capital letters, umlauts and a full stop?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Healthy and Age-Appropriate Media Use
topics.description: Use media in a healthy, age-appropriate way: agree and keep screen-time rules, take offline breaks, know the effects on sleep, eyes and mood, and read the German age ratings for films (FSK) and games (USK).
evidence: Agree and keep screen-time rules (e.g. a family media agreement) and plan offline breaks
Explain effects of too much screen time on sleep, eyes and mood
Read FSK / USK age ratings and explain why a game or film is not suitable for their age
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} stick to agreed screen-time rules, and do they know what the USK or FSK number on a game or film means?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Passwords
topics.description: Keep passwords secret, create strong but memorable passwords (for example with the sentence method), log out on shared devices, and understand why different accounts need different passwords.
evidence: Explain why passwords must be secret, even from friends
Create a strong, memorable password using the sentence method
Log out on shared devices and explain why different accounts need different passwords
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} keep their school password secret, even from best friends, and log out when they finish on a shared computer?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Right to One's Own Image
topics.description: Understand the German "Recht am eigenen Bild": everyone may decide whether pictures or videos of them are taken and shared. Ask permission before photographing, filming or posting others, and respect a "no".
evidence: Ask for permission before photographing or filming someone and before sharing the picture
Explain that everyone may decide about pictures of themselves (Recht am eigenen Bild)
Delete or not post a photo when someone objects, and know the school rules for photos
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} ask friends before taking or sending a photo of them, and delete it if a friend says no?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: States and State Diagrams
topics.description: Describe an automaton in terms of its states and the transitions between them that inputs trigger (traffic light, door, ticket machine). Draw and read simple state diagrams.
evidence: Name the states of a traffic light or door and what causes each change
Draw a state diagram for a simple vending machine (states, inputs, transitions)
Use a given state diagram to predict what the machine does after a sequence of inputs
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} draw the states of a traffic light (red, red-amber, green, amber) with arrows showing what comes next?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: First Block-Based Programs
topics.description: Write and run first programs in a visual, block-based language (ScratchJr, Scratch, Open Roberta): an event starts a sequence of blocks that moves a character or robot. Programs need exact commands, unlike everyday language.
evidence: Build and run a program that starts on an event (green flag / button) and makes a character move, speak and change costume
Explain why the computer needs exact block commands rather than everyday language
Change the order of blocks and predict the effect before running the program
topics.assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} made a character move and talk in Scratch or ScratchJr, and can they say what happens if two blocks are swapped?
topics.laenderNotes: Separate compulsory Informatik in Kl. 5/6 exists only in some Länder. NRW has had it since 2021/22, with 2 lessons spread over Kl. 5–6 or given only in Kl. 6. Thüringen has "Medienbildung und Informatik" from Kl. 5, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern "Informatik und Medienbildung", and Baden-Württemberg is extending compulsory Informatik to Kl. 5/6. Elsewhere the content is covered within other subjects or later: Sachsen in "Technik/Computer", Bayern in "Natur und Technik" (Gymnasium Kl. 6/7), and most other Länder from Kl. 7 or later. Berlin, Brandenburg and Hessen have no compulsory Informatik in Sek I (Informatik-Monitor 2026/27).

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Programming the Calliope mini
topics.description: Program the Calliope mini, a microcontroller board developed in Germany for schools, with a block editor (MakeCode, Open Roberta). Use buttons and sensors as input and the LED matrix, sound and RGB LED as output.
evidence: Flash a program (MakeCode or Open Roberta) that shows an image or text on the LED matrix when button A is pressed
Use a sensor (light, temperature, shaking) as input and react with LEDs or sound
Explain the input–processing–output steps of their Calliope project
topics.assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} programmed a Calliope mini (or similar board) so that it shows a picture or plays a sound when a button is pressed or it is shaken?
topics.laenderNotes: The Calliope mini was launched in 2016 as a German counterpart to the BBC micro:bit and has been given to many Grundschulen through Land and foundation programmes. Coverage varies by Land and school.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Testing and Debugging
topics.description: Test programs systematically: predict the expected result, compare it with what happens, find the bug, and fix it one change at a time instead of starting over.
evidence: Predict the expected result before running a program and compare it with the actual result
Find and fix a bug in a given program (e.g. a wrong turn or a wrong loop count)
Explain the step-by-step strategy used to locate the bug
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}}'s program doesn't do what they want, do they test it step by step to find the mistake, rather than starting again from scratch?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Secret Writing: the Caesar Cipher
topics.description: Encrypt and decrypt messages with simple historical ciphers, especially the Caesar cipher (shifting letters by a key). Understand that encryption, unlike ordinary encoding, keeps a message secret from anyone without the key.
evidence: Encrypt and decrypt a short message with a Caesar wheel for a given key
Explain the difference between encoding (anyone who knows the code may read it) and encrypting (only those with the key)
Crack a Caesar message by trying keys or looking for frequent letters
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use a Caesar wheel to write a secret message that only a friend with the key can read, and crack one without the key?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Files and Folders
topics.nameDe: Dateien speichern und in Ordnern organisieren
topics.description: Save work as files with meaningful names, organise them in folders, find them again, and recognise common file types.
evidence: Save a file with a meaningful name in the right folder and open it again later
Create a folder structure for a project (e.g. by subject and topic)
Recognise common file types by their extension (.docx, .jpg, .mp3)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} save their work on the computer with a sensible name in the right folder and find it again next week?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Input, Processing, Output (EVA)
topics.description: Describe how informatics systems work using the EVA principle (Eingabe – Verarbeitung – Ausgabe, the German name for input–process–output). Data come in, are processed according to rules, and results go out.
evidence: Describe a device in terms of input, processing and output (e.g. a self-checkout scanner)
Act out the EVA principle in a role play (one child inputs, one processes by a rule, one outputs)
Assign hardware components to E, V or A
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain what goes in, what happens inside and what comes out when you scan a product at the supermarket checkout?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Cyberbullying
topics.description: Recognise cyberbullying (repeated, often public, round the clock), respond by not replying, saving evidence, blocking and reporting, get help from trusted adults or help services, and support others as an upstander.
evidence: Explain what cyberbullying is and how it differs from teasing (repeated, public, 24/7)
Describe what to do: don't reply, take screenshots, block, report, tell a trusted adult
Name help services (e.g. Nummer gegen Kummer 116 111, juuuport) and act as an upstander
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know what to do if someone is being bullied in a chat: not join in, save the messages, block and tell a trusted adult?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Netiquette
topics.description: Know and keep rules for respectful online communication (Netiquette). Messages without tone of voice or facial expression are easily misunderstood, so they have to be worded with care.
evidence: Agree class rules for online communication and follow them
Explain how messages without tone or facial expression can be misunderstood and how emojis can help or confuse
Rewrite a rude message politely
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} think about how a message might come across before sending it, and could they turn a rude message into a friendly one?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Word Processing
topics.description: Write, correct and format texts in a word processor: choose fonts and sizes, add headings and pictures, use the spell-checker, and save the document properly.
evidence: Write, correct and format a text (font, size, bold, alignment)
Insert and position a picture and a heading
Use the spell-checker and save the document in the right folder
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} type up a short text on the computer, give it a heading, add a picture and save it?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Copyright and Citing Sources
topics.description: Understand that pictures, music, videos and texts belong to their creators (Urheberrecht). Use only material you may use, such as freely licensed (Creative Commons) material, and always say where it comes from.
evidence: Explain that pictures, music and texts belong to their creators and cannot simply be reused
Find and use freely licensed material (e.g. Creative Commons, children's image databases) and follow the licence
Add a source line for every picture or text taken from others
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} uses a picture from the Internet for a school project, do they check whether they are allowed to use it and write down where it came from?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Making Short Videos
topics.description: Plan, film and edit short videos such as stop-motion clips or explainer videos: use a storyboard, choose camera shots and sound for effect, and cut and arrange the clips.
evidence: Plan a short film or stop-motion clip with a storyboard
Use camera shots (close-up, long shot) and sound deliberately for effect
Edit clips (cut, reorder, add a title or music) and present the result
topics.assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} made a short stop-motion or explainer video, planning it first and then cutting it together?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Unsafe Contacts Online
topics.description: Recognise warning signs of unsafe online contacts (cybergrooming): requests for photos, secrets, meetings or moving to a private chat. Never meet online contacts, block and report them, and tell a trusted adult.
evidence: Recognise warning signs of unsafe contacts (asking for photos, secrets, a meeting, moving to a private chat)
Never agree to meet online contacts and tell a trusted adult
Block and report a contact in a game or app
topics.assessmentPrompt: If someone {{name}} only knows from an online game asks for a photo or wants to meet, do they know to say no, block them and tell an adult?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: AI in Everyday Life
topics.description: Recognise applications of artificial intelligence in everyday life (voice assistants, recommendations, translation, face unlock, chatbots). Understand that AI systems learn patterns from many examples rather than only following hand-written rules.
evidence: Name AI applications they use (voice assistant, recommendations, translation, face unlock, chatbots)
Explain that AI systems learn patterns from many examples rather than only following hand-written rules
Distinguish an AI system from a simple automaton (e.g. traffic light vs voice assistant)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} name a few things that use AI, like a voice assistant or video recommendations, and explain how that is different from a traffic light?
topics.laenderNotes: Separate compulsory Informatik in Kl. 5/6 exists only in some Länder. NRW has had it since 2021/22, with 2 lessons spread over Kl. 5–6 or given only in Kl. 6. Thüringen has "Medienbildung und Informatik" from Kl. 5, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern "Informatik und Medienbildung", and Baden-Württemberg is extending compulsory Informatik to Kl. 5/6. Elsewhere the content is covered within other subjects or later: Sachsen in "Technik/Computer", Bayern in "Natur und Technik" (Gymnasium Kl. 6/7), and most other Länder from Kl. 7 or later. Berlin, Brandenburg and Hessen have no compulsory Informatik in Sek I (Informatik-Monitor 2026/27).

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Tracing and Comparing Algorithms
topics.description: Trace algorithms by hand to work out their result, and compare different algorithms for the same problem, for example sorting cards or the halving strategy in a guessing game (binary search). Notice that some need fewer steps than others.
evidence: Sort a set of cards using two different methods and count the comparisons each one needs
Find a number between 1 and 100 in at most 7 guesses by halving (binary search) and explain why it works
Trace a given algorithm by hand to work out its result
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a "guess my number between 1 and 100" game, does {{name}} use the halving strategy, and can they explain why it is faster than guessing at random?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Loops in Programs
topics.description: Use loop blocks (repeat n times, forever, repeat until) to shorten programs and repeat actions, and predict how often an action will run.
evidence: Replace repeated blocks with a "repeat n" loop (e.g. to draw a square)
Use "forever" and "repeat until" and explain the difference
Predict how often an action runs in a loop before running the program
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a coding app, can {{name}} use a "repeat" block to draw a square, instead of dragging the same blocks four times?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Conditions and Input in Programs
topics.description: Use if-then(-else) blocks with conditions so a program reacts to input such as a key press, a touch, a sensor value or a typed answer, and test both branches.
evidence: Use if-then(-else) so a program reacts to a key press, a touch or a sensor value
Write a quiz question that checks an answer and responds "Correct" or "Try again"
Explain the condition in a branch and test both paths
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} program a little quiz that says "Correct" or "Try again" depending on the answer?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Evaluating Websites and Sources
topics.description: Judge whether information and its source are trustworthy and suitable: who is behind a website (author, Impressum), why it was made, how up to date it is, and whether other sources agree.
evidence: Check who is behind a website (Impressum, author) and why it was made
Compare information from two sources and notice contradictions
Judge whether a source is suitable for children, up to date and trustworthy
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} check who made a website and compare it with another source before trusting what it says?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Search Strategies
topics.description: Plan a search: choose and combine precise keywords, refine them when the results are poor, read a result list critically (title, address, snippet, ads), and keep useful sources.
evidence: Choose and combine precise keywords and refine them when the results are poor
Read a result list: identify title, address, snippet and ads or sponsored results
Save and note useful sources (bookmark, link list)
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} searches online, do they choose good keywords, change them if the results don't fit, and skip the adverts at the top?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: How the Internet Works
topics.nameDe: Internet und Netzwerke: wie Daten übertragen werden
topics.description: Name the basic parts of networks and the Internet (devices, WLAN router, cables, servers). Understand that data travel in addressed packets according to agreed rules (protocols).
evidence: Name basic parts of the Internet (device, WLAN router, cable, server) and their roles
Explain in a role play that data are split into packets with addresses that travel separately
Explain that devices need agreed rules (protocols) to exchange messages
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain roughly how a photo gets from one phone to another: through the router, over the Internet in small packets?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Storage Locations and Backups
topics.description: Distinguish local storage (on the device, on a USB stick) from external or cloud storage, compare them by capacity, access and security, and make backups to prevent data loss.
evidence: Distinguish local storage (device, USB stick) from external / cloud storage
Compare storage options by capacity, access and security
Make a backup copy of important work and explain why
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know whether their schoolwork is saved on the tablet itself or in the cloud, and why it is good to keep a backup copy?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Messengers and Class Chats
topics.description: Use messenger groups such as the class chat responsibly: keep agreed rules, recognise chain letters (Kettenbriefe) and scary messages, and know the age rules and need for parental consent for messenger apps.
evidence: Follow class-chat rules (no late-night messages, no photos of others without consent, no insults)
Recognise chain letters (Kettenbriefe) and frightening messages, and do not forward them
Explain the age rules for messenger apps and why parental consent is needed
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a scary chain message arrives in the class chat saying "forward this or…", does {{name}} know not to forward it and to tell an adult?
topics.laenderNotes: The Klassenchat usually starts around Kl. 4–5 with the first smartphone. Schools and Länder often advise against official class groups on commercial messengers and prefer school messengers or learning platforms.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Collaborating Online
topics.description: Work together in shared documents, digital pinboards or a class blog: divide tasks, comment constructively, avoid overwriting others' work, and combine contributions into a joint product.
evidence: Work with classmates in a shared document or digital pinboard without overwriting others' work
Divide tasks and comment constructively on others' contributions
Combine contributions into a joint product (class newspaper, blog, presentation)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} worked with classmates on one shared digital document or pinboard, each adding their part without deleting others' work?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Digital Presentations
topics.description: Create clear digital slides with few words and suitable pictures, use them to support a talk rather than reading them out, and improve them with feedback.
evidence: Create slides with few words, pictures and a clear structure
Present using the slides as support rather than reading them out
Give and use feedback on readability and design
topics.assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} made a few slides for a school talk, with short keywords and pictures, and presented with them without reading everything out?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Cost Traps and In-App Purchases
topics.description: Recognise cost traps in "free" apps and games (in-app purchases, loot boxes, subscription traps), understand the business models behind them, and know that purchases by children need parental consent (Taschengeldparagraph §110 BGB).
evidence: Identify in-app purchases, loot boxes and subscription traps in "free" apps and games
Explain how free apps make money (ads, data, purchases)
Explain that children's purchases need parental consent and how purchase locks work
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} understand that a "free" game can still cost money through in-game purchases, and that they must ask before buying anything?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Phishing and Malware
topics.description: Recognise suspicious messages, links, pop-ups and downloads, know what malware can do, and behave safely: install apps only from official stores with permission, and close dubious pages.
evidence: Recognise suspicious messages (urgent, a prize, unknown sender, strange link)
Explain what malware can do and why apps should only be installed from official stores with permission
Show safe behaviour: not clicking pop-ups, closing the page, asking an adult
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets a message saying "You've won a new phone – click here!", do they know it is probably a trick and not click?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Decision Trees
topics.description: Experience a principle of machine learning hands-on. Build a decision tree of yes/no questions from training examples, use it to classify new examples, and see why few or one-sided examples lead to mistakes.
evidence: Act out classifying objects with a decision tree of yes/no questions
Build a decision tree from training examples (e.g. healthy / unhealthy snack) and test it on new examples
Explain why a tree learned from few or one-sided examples makes mistakes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} build a yes/no question tree that sorts pictures (e.g. of animals or snacks) into groups, and explain why it gets some new pictures wrong?
topics.laenderNotes: Explicit in the NRW Kernlehrplan 5/6. Elsewhere machine learning is mostly taught from Kl. 7 or in projects.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Limits and Risks of AI
topics.nameDe: Grenzen und Risiken von KI (Fehler, Bias, KI-generierte Inhalte)
topics.description: Recognise that AI systems make mistakes and can be biased by their training data. Know that AI can generate realistic fake images, voices and texts, and discuss fair rules for using AI tools, for example for homework.
evidence: Give examples of AI mistakes and explain how biased training data can cause them
Recognise that AI can generate realistic but fake images, voices or texts
Discuss rules for using AI tools (chatbots) honestly for homework
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that AI chatbots and image generators can be wrong or make fake pictures, and have they thought about when it is OK to use them for schoolwork?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Learning from Examples: Neural Networks
topics.description: Understand the basic idea of artificial neural networks: they are trained with many labelled examples and adjust their internal connections until they recognise patterns. Try this with a simple classifier tool.
evidence: Train a simple image or sound classifier (e.g. Teachable Machine) with example data and test it
Describe in simple terms that a neural network adjusts connections during training
Show how more varied training data changes the results
topics.assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} trained a computer to recognise pictures or sounds with examples, and can they explain why it needs lots of different examples?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Flowcharts and Structograms
topics.description: Represent algorithms in the two diagram forms used in German schools: the flowchart (Programmablaufplan, PAP) and the Nassi-Shneiderman structogram. Read such diagrams and execute them by hand.
evidence: Convert an everyday instruction into a Programmablaufplan (PAP) using the standard symbols
Read a Struktogramm with a loop and a branch and execute it by hand
Identify sequence, branch and loop in a given PAP or Struktogramm
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} draw a flowchart (PAP) of a simple everyday process, with a yes/no decision, and follow one that someone else drew?
topics.laenderNotes: PAP and Struktogramm are explicit in the NRW Kernlehrplan 5/6. In other Länder they usually appear from Kl. 7.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Recommendation Algorithms
topics.description: Understand that apps and platforms choose what to show next using algorithms based on what you watched, liked and how long you looked. Different people therefore see different feeds and can end up in a filter bubble.
evidence: Explain that apps choose what to show next based on what you watched, liked and how long you looked
Compare two people's feeds or recommendations and explain the differences
Describe how recommendations can trap people in a "filter bubble" and how to break out
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know why their video app keeps suggesting similar videos, and that a friend sees different suggestions?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Computing in Work and Society
topics.description: Describe how informatics systems have changed everyday life and work (checkouts, factories, medicine, communication), weigh up the advantages and disadvantages of automation, and understand that people decide how systems are designed and used.
evidence: Describe how computers have changed jobs (e.g. supermarket checkout, car factory, doctor's surgery)
Name advantages and disadvantages of automation for people
Explain that people decide how informatics systems are designed and used
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} give an example of a job that has changed because of computers, and say what is better and what is worse about it?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Binary Numbers, Bits and Bytes
topics.description: Convert small numbers between the decimal and binary systems using place values (16-8-4-2-1), explain bit and byte, and compare amounts of data (KB, MB, GB) with everyday examples.
evidence: Convert numbers 0–31 between decimal and binary using the place values 16-8-4-2-1
Explain bit and byte and put the data units in order (KB, MB, GB, TB)
Compare file sizes with everyday examples (a text vs a photo vs a film)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write the number 13 in binary (1101) and explain why a film needs much more storage than a text?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Information versus Data
topics.description: Distinguish data (stored signs and symbols) from information (the meaning people give them in a context). Represent information as data in a suitable form, and recognise codes in everyday life such as QR codes, barcodes, Morse and Braille.
evidence: Explain with examples that data only become information when interpreted in a context (e.g. "30" as temperature, age or price)
Represent a given piece of information as data in a suitable form (table, symbol, code)
Name everyday examples of encoded data (QR code, barcode, Morse code, Braille)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why the number "30" on its own means nothing until you know whether it is a temperature, a price or an age?
topics.laenderNotes: Separate compulsory Informatik in Kl. 5/6 exists only in some Länder. NRW has had it since 2021/22, with 2 lessons spread over Kl. 5–6 or given only in Kl. 6. Thüringen has "Medienbildung und Informatik" from Kl. 5, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern "Informatik und Medienbildung", and Baden-Württemberg is extending compulsory Informatik to Kl. 5/6. Elsewhere the content is covered within other subjects or later: Sachsen in "Technik/Computer", Bayern in "Natur und Technik" (Gymnasium Kl. 6/7), and most other Länder from Kl. 7 or later. Berlin, Brandenburg and Hessen have no compulsory Informatik in Sek I (Informatik-Monitor 2026/27).

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Comparing Encryption Methods
topics.description: Compare substitution ciphers (letters are replaced) with transposition ciphers (letters are rearranged, e.g. Skytale). Understand the role of the key, and judge how secure a method is.
evidence: Encrypt a message with a transposition method (e.g. Skytale) and explain how it differs from substitution
Explain the role of the key and why a short key can be cracked by trying every option
Compare two methods for security and explain why messengers use encryption
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why a Caesar code is easy to crack, and why apps like messengers encrypt messages?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Fake News and Manipulated Images
topics.description: Recognise misinformation and manipulated images or videos, understand why people spread them (attention, money, opinion), check suspicious content, and decide not to pass it on.
evidence: Explain why people spread false information (attention, money, opinion)
Check a suspicious message, image or video using reverse image search or a fact-check site
Decide not to forward unverified chain messages and explain why
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets a shocking message or picture in a chat, do they check whether it is true before forwarding it?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Data Protection and My Rights
topics.description: Understand how apps and websites collect and use personal data, check privacy settings and app permissions, and know the basic idea of data protection law (DSGVO): data belong to the person, consent is needed, and as little as possible should be collected (Datensparsamkeit).
evidence: Describe how apps and websites collect and use personal data (location, contacts, usage) and why it is valuable to companies
Check and change privacy settings and app permissions
Explain the basic idea of data protection: data belong to the person, consent is needed, collect as little as possible
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} check which permissions an app wants, like location or contacts, and turn off the ones it doesn't need?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Variables in Programs
topics.description: Create and use variables to store and change values while a program runs (score, lives, counter), use them in conditions, and trace their values.
evidence: Create a variable (e.g. score, lives) that starts at a value and changes during a game
Use a variable in a condition ("if lives = 0 then game over")
Trace the value of a variable step by step through a short program
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a game {{name}} made with block coding, is there a score that goes up and a game-over when the lives run out?
topics.laenderNotes: Not explicitly required by the NRW Kernlehrplan 5/6; common in Gymnasium school curricula and in Kl. 7+ elsewhere.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Raster and Vector Graphics
topics.description: Raster graphics store a colour value for every pixel; vector graphics store objects such as lines and circles with their attributes. Pupils compare scaling, file size and typical uses, and calculate the memory needed for an image from resolution and colour depth (RGB, 24 bit).
evidence: Explains why a photo becomes blocky when enlarged but a logo in SVG does not
Calculates the uncompressed file size of an image from resolution and colour depth
Chooses raster or vector format for given purposes and justifies the choice
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} must design a school logo that will be printed on both a pin and a banner, can they explain which kind of graphic to use and why?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern treats pixel and vector graphics in Natur und Technik 6; NRW in the Wahlpflichtfach 9/10.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Spreadsheets: Formulas and Cell References
topics.description: Pupils build spreadsheets in which cells contain values or formulas, copy formulas with relative references and fix them with absolute references ($), and understand the spreadsheet as a data-flow model in which results update automatically.
evidence: Writes formulas with cell references and basic functions (SUMME, MITTELWERT)
Explains the difference between relative and absolute references when copying a formula
Traces which cells change when an input value is altered
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} plans the budget for a class trip in a spreadsheet, can they set it up so that changing the number of pupils updates all costs?
topics.laenderNotes: Sachsen teaches spreadsheets in Kl. 7, Saarland in 8, Bayern in Informatik 9 (NTG), Niedersachsen in 10; often also in Mathematik.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Character Encoding: ASCII and Unicode
topics.description: Computers store text as numbers. Pupils encode and decode text with the ASCII table, explain why 7 or 8 bits are not enough for all the world's scripts and emojis, and how Unicode/UTF-8 solves this, including what goes wrong when encodings are mixed ("Mojibake" with ä, ö, ü).
evidence: Encodes a short word in ASCII as decimal and binary numbers and decodes it again
Explains how many different characters can be coded with 7, 8 and 16 bits
Explains why umlauts sometimes appear garbled in e-mails or files
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} receives a text where "Grüße" appears as "GrÃ¼ÃŸe", can they explain what went wrong with the encoding?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Sensors, Actuators and Microcontrollers
topics.description: Pupils build and program small embedded systems (e.g. Calliope mini, Arduino) that read sensors (light, temperature, distance) and control actuators (LEDs, motors, buzzers), using the input–processing–output principle and threshold values.
evidence: Connects a sensor and an actuator to a microcontroller and reads sensor values
Programs a reaction to a threshold value (e.g. switch on a light when it gets dark)
Explains the system with the input–processing–output (EVA) model
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants a plant to "call for water" when the soil is dry, can they plan and program a microcontroller with a sensor and an alarm?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Networks: Clients, Servers and IP Addresses
topics.nameDe: Rechnernetze: Client, Server, Router und IP-Adressen
topics.description: Pupils describe local networks and the internet as networks of networks, explain the roles of clients, servers, switches and routers, and how data packets with IP addresses are forwarded hop by hop. They read a URL and explain what happens when a web page is requested.
evidence: Explains the roles of client, server and router when loading a web page
Explains why data are split into addressed packets that may take different routes
Reads the parts of a URL and finds the IP address of a device
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} opens a website from their phone, can they explain which devices the request passes and how the reply finds its way back?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Natur und Technik 7, BW Kl. 7, Sachsen Kl. 8.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Objects, Classes, Attributes and Methods
topics.description: Pupils describe elements of documents and graphics (a text paragraph, a rectangle) as objects with attributes and values that belong to a class and can be changed by methods. They use object cards and class cards and dot notation such as rechteck1.füllfarbe = rot.
evidence: Describes a graphic object with its class, attributes and attribute values on an object card
Distinguishes a class (blueprint) from its objects (instances)
Uses dot notation to describe a method call that changes an attribute value
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a slide with several text boxes, can they describe each as an object of a class with attributes such as font size and colour?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern introduces the object-oriented view in Natur und Technik 6, Sachsen in Kl. 7; NRW starts object orientation in the Einführungsphase.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Building Web Pages with HTML and CSS
topics.nameDe: Webseiten mit HTML und CSS gestalten
topics.description: Pupils write web pages in HTML (headings, paragraphs, lists, links, images, tables), style them with CSS, and explain the separation of content and presentation and the hypertext structure of linked pages.
evidence: Writes a valid HTML page with headings, links and images
Changes the layout of several pages with one CSS file
Explains why content and presentation are kept separate
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} builds a small website for a school club, can they structure it in HTML and give all pages the same look with CSS?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern treats hypertext in Natur und Technik 7; NRW writes markup in the Wahlpflichtfach 9/10.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Securing Data and Accounts
topics.description: Pupils apply the protection goals confidentiality, integrity and availability to their own data: they plan backups (3-2-1 rule, versioning), use two-factor authentication and password managers, install updates and recognise social-engineering attacks.
evidence: Explains confidentiality, integrity and availability with examples
Plans a backup strategy for their own files
Sets up two-factor authentication and explains why it protects even if a password is stolen
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s laptop were stolen tomorrow, can they explain which of their data would be lost and how they could have protected them?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Data Types and Expressions
topics.description: Pupils use the basic data types integer, floating-point number, string and Boolean, evaluate arithmetic, comparison and logical expressions, convert between types and trace how assignments change variable values.
evidence: Chooses a suitable data type for a given value and explains the choice
Evaluates expressions with arithmetic, comparison and logical operators (and, or, not)
Traces the values of variables through a sequence of assignments
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s program prints "1010" instead of 20 when adding two inputs, can they explain the type error and fix it?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Conditionals and Loops in Code
topics.nameDe: Kontrollstrukturen: Verzweigung und Schleife im Quelltext
topics.description: Pupils implement algorithms with conditionals (if/elif/else), counting loops (for) and conditional loops (while), nest them, and represent them in structograms. They choose the right loop type and avoid endless loops.
evidence: Implements an algorithm with nested conditionals and loops
Chooses between a counting loop and a conditional loop and justifies the choice
Converts between a structogram and code
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} programs a number-guessing game, can they use a loop and conditions so that it gives hints until the number is found?

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: First Steps in Text-Based Programming
topics.description: Pupils move from block-based to text-based programming (typically Python, sometimes Java): they write, run and correct small programs with input and output, read error messages, and distinguish syntax errors from logical errors.
evidence: Writes and runs a small program that reads input and prints a result
Uses an error message to find and fix a syntax error
Distinguishes a syntax error from a program that runs but gives a wrong result
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} types a short Python program that asks for their age and prints the year they were born, can they fix the errors the computer reports?
topics.laenderNotes: BW starts text-based programming in the IMP profile Kl. 9; NRW in the Wahlpflichtfach 9/10 or the Einführungsphase; Bayern pupils outside the NTG start in Kl. 11.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Database Tables, Records and Keys
topics.description: A relational database stores data in tables whose rows are records and columns attributes with fixed data types. Pupils compare databases with spreadsheets, choose a primary key and explain why redundancy in one big table causes problems.
evidence: Identifies records, attributes, data types and the primary key in a given table
Explains why a primary key must be unique and chooses one
Explains with an example why storing the same data twice leads to inconsistencies
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at the school library's lending list, can they explain how it would be stored in a database and what the key is?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern (Informatik 9) and Sachsen (Kl. 9) introduce databases in Sek I; NRW, Niedersachsen and BW only in the Oberstufe.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Digitising Sound and Images
topics.description: Analogue signals such as sound are digitised by sampling at regular intervals and rounding each value to a fixed number of levels. Pupils explain sampling rate and bit depth, calculate data rates (e.g. CD audio) and judge the trade-off between quality and file size.
evidence: Explains sampling and quantisation with a sketch of an analogue signal
Calculates the data size of one minute of CD-quality audio
Explains how sampling rate and bit depth affect quality and file size
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} records a voice memo, can they explain how the sound becomes numbers and what a higher sampling rate changes?
