topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}}'s class prepares a song for the school festival, do they stick to the agreed signals, practise their part and give kind feedback to others?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Music from Around the World
topics.description: Sing songs and dance dances from various countries and regions — including classmates' heritage cultures — get to know instruments of the world (e.g. djembe, darbuka, sitar) and compare occasions for making music in different cultures.
evidence: Sing a song in another language and say where it comes from
Name and describe two instruments from other parts of the world
Compare how music is used at a celebration in two different cultures
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} sing you a song in another language from school and tell you which country it comes from or which instrument is typical there?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Songs for Seasons and Festivals
topics.nameDe: Lieder im Jahreskreis: Kinder-, Volks- und Festlieder
topics.description: Build a repertoire of children’s songs, German folk songs (Volkslieder) and songs for the seasons and festivals of the school year — spring songs, Laternen- and Martinslieder, Advent and Christmas songs, birthday songs, songs from other cultures — and sing them by heart.
evidence: Sing at least five songs from the school year by heart, one of them with all verses
Name the season or occasion a song belongs to
Sing a lantern song or Christmas song with the class at a school celebration
topics.assessmentPrompt: When St. Martin or Christmas comes around, can {{name}} sing a few of the traditional songs by heart, like 'Ich geh mit meiner Laterne'?
topics.laenderNotes: Repertoire is chosen by schools; regional and dialect songs (e.g. Plattdeutsch, bairisch) feature in some Länder, and religious festival songs are handled with care in mixed-belief classes.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Singing Back a Melody
topics.description: Use the singing voice (not the speaking voice) to echo short melodies and song phrases in tune, with good posture and breathing.
evidence: Echo a short sung phrase at the same pitch
Switch between speaking voice and singing voice on request
Sing a simple call such as 'Ku-ckuck' matching the teacher's pitch
topics.assessmentPrompt: When you sing a short tune like 'Kuckuck, Kuckuck' to {{name}}, can they sing it back at the same pitch rather than speaking it?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Note Values and Rests
topics.description: Read and clap whole, half, quarter and eighth notes (Ganze, Halbe, Viertel, Achtel) and the matching rests, often with rhythm syllables (ta, ti-ti), and understand that each value lasts half as long as the previous one.
evidence: Name and draw whole, half, quarter and eighth notes and their rests
Clap a written rhythm of quarters, eighths and half notes in time
Explain that two eighth notes last as long as one quarter note
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a written rhythm with quarter notes, eighth notes and a rest, can they clap it correctly and stay silent on the rest?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Musical Form: Repetition and Contrast
topics.description: Recognise repetition, variation and contrast as building principles of music: verse and chorus with intro and interlude in songs, and in Kl. 5–6 forms such as ABA and Rondo (ABACA), following them with form cards or movement.
evidence: Signal each return of the chorus (Refrain) while listening to a song
Lay out form cards (A, B) in the right order for an ABA piece
Identify a rondo by its recurring main theme and describe the contrasting episodes
topics.assessmentPrompt: While listening, can {{name}} raise a hand each time the main tune comes back and tell you whether the piece is built like A-B-A or A-B-A-C-A?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Reading Notes on the Staff
topics.description: Read the Stammtöne c'–c'' on the five-line staff (Notenlinien) with the treble clef (Violinschlüssel), on lines and in spaces, using the German note names c d e f g a h c — where German 'h' is English B.
evidence: Name the notes c' to c'' written on the staff, including the ledger-line c'
Draw a treble clef and place given notes correctly on lines or in spaces
Explain that the German note 'h' is called B in English
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a short melody written in the treble clef, can they name the notes — c, d, e, f, g, a, h — and show which one sits on a ledger line?
topics.laenderNotes: German note naming (h for B, b for B-flat) is used in all Länder; some schools introduce the staff already in Kl. 2.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Bars and Time Signatures
topics.description: Understand that beats are grouped into bars (Takte) separated by bar lines, hear and conduct 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 time and feel the stressed first beat (e.g. the 3/4 of a Walzer versus a march).
evidence: Count and conduct a simple pattern in 3/4 and in 4/4 time
Tell whether a piece heard swings in three or marches in two/four
Fill the bars of a given time signature correctly with note values
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you play a waltz and then a march, can {{name}} tell you which one goes in threes and count or conduct along?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Instrument Families and the Orchestra
topics.description: Recognise common instruments by sight and sound, group them into families (Streich-, Holzblas-, Blechblas-, Schlag- und Tasteninstrumente) by how they make sound, and know the groups and seating of the symphony orchestra as well as typical band instruments.
evidence: Identify at least six instruments by ear in a listening example
Sort instruments into families and explain how each family produces sound
Point out the instrument groups on an orchestra seating plan
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} hears a recording, can they pick out instruments like violin, flute, trumpet or timpani — and say which family each belongs to?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Opera, Ballet and Musical for Children
topics.description: Get to know music theatre — children's opera (e.g. Humperdinck's 'Hänsel und Gretel', children's versions of Mozart's 'Die Zauberflöte'), ballet (e.g. 'Der Nussknacker') and musicals — attend or stage a performance and understand the roles of singers, orchestra, dancers and conductor.
evidence: Explain the differences between opera, ballet and musical
Describe a scene from a children's opera or ballet and how the music supports it
Behave as an attentive audience member at a live performance
topics.assessmentPrompt: After a visit to a children's opera or ballet, can {{name}} explain what happened on stage and how the music, singing or dancing told the story?
topics.laenderNotes: Live visits depend on local opera houses and Kinderoper/Jugendkonzert programmes, which are dense in Germany but unevenly spread between cities and rural areas.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Programme Music
topics.nameDe: Programmmusik (z. B. Peter und der Wolf, Karneval der Tiere)
topics.description: Understand that instrumental music can tell a story or paint a picture: follow how instruments and themes represent characters in Prokofiev's 'Peter und der Wolf' or animals in Saint-Saëns' 'Karneval der Tiere', and in Kl. 5–6 longer works such as Smetana's 'Die Moldau' or Mussorgsky's 'Bilder einer Ausstellung'.
evidence: Match the characters of 'Peter und der Wolf' to their instruments
Explain how a piece depicts an animal or scene through tempo, pitch and timbre
Retell or act out the story of a programme piece while it plays
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} listens to 'Peter und der Wolf', can they tell you which instrument plays the bird, the cat and the wolf — and why those instruments fit?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Playing the Recorder
topics.description: Play simple melodies on the soprano recorder (Sopranblockflöte) — starting with the left-hand notes h, a, g — with gentle breath and tonguing ('dü'), increasingly from staff notation.
evidence: Cover the holes correctly to play h, a and g with a clear tone
Tongue notes separately with 'dü' instead of blowing hard
Play a short song from staff notation using at least five notes
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a recorder, can they play a simple tune like 'Hänschen klein' with a clean tone and no squeaks?
topics.laenderNotes: Not compulsory anywhere; offered as class instrument or AG in many Grundschulen. NRW funds JeKits (instruments, dance or singing, Kl. 1–4); many Kl. 5–6 offer Bläser-, Streicher- or Bandklassen instead.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Accompanying Songs with Ostinato and Drone
topics.description: Accompany a song with a repeated rhythmic or melodic pattern (Ostinato) or a drone fifth (Bordun, e.g. c–g) on percussion or barred instruments, keeping the tempo together with the singers.
evidence: Play a two-bar ostinato steadily through a whole song
Play a drone (e.g. c + g) on the beat on a barred instrument
Keep their accompaniment going when the singers move to the next verse
topics.assessmentPrompt: While others sing, can {{name}} keep playing a short repeated pattern on a drum or xylophone without speeding up or stopping?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Composers and Musical Eras
topics.nameDe: Komponistinnen und Komponisten, Epochen der Musikgeschichte
topics.description: Know lives and selected works of important composers — e.g. Johann Sebastian Bach, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Ludwig van Beethoven, Clara Schumann — and in Kl. 5–6 place music in eras such as Baroque, Classical and Romantic.
evidence: Tell two facts about the life of a composer such as Mozart or Beethoven and name one of their works
Recognise a famous excerpt (e.g. 'Eine kleine Nachtmusik', 'Ode an die Freude')
Place three composers on a simple timeline of musical eras
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears 'Eine kleine Nachtmusik' or Beethoven's 'Ode an die Freude', can they tell you who wrote it and something about that composer's life?
topics.laenderNotes: The German-speaking canon (Bach, Händel, Mozart, Beethoven, Schumann) dominates; Beethoven's 'Ode an die Freude' doubles as the European anthem, and the Nationalhymne is a Kl. 5–6 topic (Hymnen).

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Music, Media and Healthy Listening
topics.nameDe: Musik und Medien: Hörgewohnheiten, Lautstärke, Urheberrecht
topics.description: Reflect on where and how they hear music (radio, streaming, headphones), choose a volume that protects their hearing, and in Kl. 5–6 know the basics of copyright and personal rights when downloading, sharing or uploading music and videos.
evidence: Explain why loud music through headphones can damage hearing and set a safe volume
Describe their own and their family's listening habits
Explain why you may not freely upload someone else's song or a video of classmates
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} listens on headphones, do they keep the volume at a safe level — and can they explain why they shouldn't post someone else's song or a video of friends online without permission?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Singing in Parts: Rounds and Two-Part Songs
topics.description: Hold one's own part while others sing something different — first in a round (Kanon, e.g. 'Bruder Jakob'), later in simple two-part songs and choir arrangements.
evidence: Keep their own line in a three-part round without drifting into another group
Sing an ostinato or second voice against a melody
Explain how a round works (same melody, staggered entries)
topics.assessmentPrompt: When the family sings 'Bruder Jakob' as a round, can {{name}} keep singing their own part while the others start at different times?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Composing with Rhythm Building Blocks
topics.description: Compose a short piece by combining rhythm building blocks (Rhythmusbausteine) and simple melodic ideas, write it down in graphic or traditional notation, then rehearse and perform it with a group.
evidence: Combine at least four rhythm blocks into an 8-bar piece in 4/4 time
Notate their composition so another group can play it
Explain one choice they made to create repetition or contrast
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a set of rhythm cards, can they put together their own short piece, write it down and teach it to friends to play?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Scales, Half Steps and Accidentals
topics.description: Understand the major scale as a fixed pattern of whole and half steps (Ganz- und Halbtonschritte, e.g. e–f and h–c), and read sharps and flats (Kreuz, b) with German names such as fis, cis, b and es.
evidence: Locate the half steps of the C major scale on a keyboard picture
Name notes with sharps and flats using German names (fis, cis, es, b)
Build a major scale on G or F by applying the whole/half-step pattern
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a keyboard, can they show where the half steps are in C major and explain why G major needs an F sharp (fis)?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Class Ensemble Playing
topics.description: Play one’s own part reliably in a class ensemble (band, Bläserklasse, percussion group) from a part or play instructions, following conductor cues and performance markings (p, mf, f, crescendo, ritardando).
evidence: Play their part in a class arrangement from start to finish without stopping
Respond to conductor cues for entries, stops, dynamics and tempo changes
Explain markings such as mf, crescendo and ritardando in their part
topics.assessmentPrompt: In the school band or class ensemble, can {{name}} play their part all the way through, coming in on cue and following the loud/soft markings?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Songwriting
topics.nameDe: Songwriting: Text vertonen, Melodie und Akkordfolge
topics.description: Write a short song: choose or write lyrics, set them to a melody that follows the speech rhythm, build verse and chorus over a chord progression, and notate or record the result.
evidence: Write a verse and chorus with a singable melody that fits the text stresses
Put the melody over a chord progression and write the chord symbols
Present the song and explain one musical decision
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes a chorus about a school topic, can they make the important words fall on strong beats and put fitting chords under it?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Overview of Musical Eras
topics.description: Order the main eras of Western music (Middle Ages, Renaissance, Baroque, Classical, Romantic, 20th/21st century) on a timeline with dates, typical genres and composers, and assign listening examples to eras by their style features.
evidence: Put the eras in order with approximate dates
Name one typical genre and one composer for each era
Assign an unknown example to an era and justify it with two features
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears a harpsichord concerto and a Romantic symphony, can they place both in their eras and explain why?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Musical Acoustics and Overtones
topics.description: Explain musical sound physically: pitch as frequency, loudness as amplitude and timbre as the mix of overtones (Naturtonreihe). Relate the overtone series to brass instruments and to octave and fifth, and connect sound levels to protecting one's hearing.
evidence: Relate higher pitch to higher frequency and an octave to a doubled frequency
Explain with a spectrum or sound picture why a flute and a violin playing the same note sound different
Show how a brass player gets different natural notes without valves
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears a trumpet and a clarinet play the same note, can they explain why the two still sound different?
topics.laenderNotes: In Bayern the overtone series is Musisches-Gymnasium content in Kl. 8; Physik usually treats acoustics in Kl. 7–8 as well.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Bass Clef and Score Reading
topics.description: Read notes in the bass clef, follow a part in an orchestral or band score while listening (Mitlesen), and understand score layout: order of instrument groups, braces, transposing instruments and common performance markings.
evidence: Name notes in the bass clef across two octaves
Follow one instrument through a printed score while the recording plays and point to the current bar
Explain the order of instrument groups in an orchestral score
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} listens to a symphony excerpt with the score, can they show where the cellos have the melody?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Triads and Inversions
topics.nameDe: Dreiklänge (Dur, Moll, vermindert, übermäßig) und Umkehrungen
topics.description: Build triads by stacking thirds, tell major, minor, diminished and augmented triads apart on paper and by ear, and recognise root position, first and second inversion (Sextakkord, Quartsextakkord).
evidence: Build major and minor triads on any note and name their thirds
Identify a written triad as major, minor, diminished or augmented
Recognise and write the inversions of a triad
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the notes E–G–C, can they say which triad it is and in which position?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Major and Minor Keys
topics.description: Build major and natural minor scales on any note from the pattern of whole and half steps, find the key of a melody from its key signature and final note, and relate each major key to its relative minor (Paralleltonart) a minor third below.
evidence: Write a major and a natural minor scale on a given note with correct accidentals
Name the relative minor of a major key and explain why they share a key signature
Decide whether a short melody is in major or minor from its sound and last note
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets a melody in A minor without sharps or flats, can they explain why it is not in C major?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Naming and Hearing Intervals
topics.nameDe: Intervalle bestimmen und hören (Prime bis Oktave)
topics.description: Name intervals from the unison to the octave by counting steps and semitones (kleine/große Terz, reine Quinte …), write them on the staff and recognise characteristic ones by ear. Intervals are the building block for scales, chords and harmony.
evidence: Name the size and quality of intervals up to the octave written on the staff (e.g. große Terz, reine Quarte)
Write a given interval above or below a note, including accidentals
Recognise by ear at least the octave, fifth, major and minor third in short examples
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees C–E and C–E♭ on the staff, can they name both intervals and sing or play the difference?
topics.laenderNotes: Some Länder (e.g. Bayern) start interval work in Kl. 5–6; Berlin-Brandenburg lists intervals among the possible contents for Kl. 7–10.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Primary Chords and the Cadence
topics.nameDe: Hauptstufen und Kadenz: Tonika, Subdominante, Dominante
topics.description: Identify chords I, IV and V of a key as Tonika, Subdominante and Dominante, hear the tension and release of the cadence T–S–D–T, add the dominant seventh chord, and label chords with function symbols and pop chord symbols.
evidence: Play or write T, S, D and D7 in a given major key
Label the chords of a simple song with function symbols or chord symbols
Tell by ear whether a phrase ends with a full close (Ganzschluss) or a half close (Halbschluss)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} plays C, F, G7 and C, can they explain which chord creates the tension and why the last chord sounds like an ending?
topics.laenderNotes: Function theory (Funktionstheorie, T–S–D) is the usual German way of naming chords; step numbers (I–IV–V) and pop chord symbols are taught alongside, depending on Land and textbook.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: The Circle of Fifths
topics.description: Use the circle of fifths to find the key signature of any major or minor key, see how each step adds a sharp or flat, and identify closely related keys. It is the standard classroom tool for Tonartenbestimmung.
evidence: Draw the circle of fifths with major keys and their relative minors
State the number and order of sharps or flats for a named key
Name the neighbouring keys of a key on the circle and explain why they are closely related
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked for the key signature of E major, can they work it out with the circle of fifths?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Syncopation, Off-Beat and Swing
topics.description: Perform and notate syncopations and off-beat accents, feel the backbeat in rock and pop, and tell straight (binär) from swung (ternär) eighth notes, including the gap between notation and performance practice in popular music.
evidence: Clap or play a notated syncopated rhythm against a steady beat
Mark the syncopations in the score of a pop song
Play the same eighth-note line straight and swung and describe the difference
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears a pop song with a strong backbeat, can they clap the off-beat and then write down a syncopated rhythm from the chorus?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Motif, Theme and Variation
topics.description: Identify a motif and a theme in a piece, follow how composers develop them (repetition, sequence, inversion, augmentation, fragmentation) and how a theme is varied in rhythm, harmony or character.
evidence: Point out the main motif of a well-known piece and where it returns
Name at least three techniques of motivic development in a listening example or score
Describe how a variation differs from its theme
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears the opening of Beethoven's Fifth Symphony, can they show how the four-note motif keeps coming back in changed forms?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Playing in the Class Band
topics.nameDe: Klassenmusizieren mit Bandinstrumenten: Groove und Akkordbegleitung
topics.description: Play a rock or pop song in a class band on keyboard, guitar, bass, drums or percussion: keep a groove, change chords from chord symbols (e.g. I–V–vi–IV) and follow the song form.
evidence: Play a simple drum groove or bass line in time with the group
Change between at least three chords on keyboard or guitar from chord symbols
Follow the form (intro, verse, chorus) and come in at the right place
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s class plays a pop song, can they keep their part going through verse and chorus without stopping when the chords change?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: History of Popular Music and Youth Cultures
topics.description: Trace the main styles of popular music from blues and rock 'n' roll via beat, punk and disco to hip-hop and electronic music, relate them to youth cultures and social change, and name their musical features (instrumentation, rhythm, sound).
evidence: Place five popular music styles on a timeline with one example each
Describe the typical instrumentation and rhythm of two styles
Explain how one style expressed the attitude of a youth culture
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears a punk song and a disco song, can they describe the differences and name the youth cultures linked to them?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Copyright and the Music Business
topics.nameDe: Urheberrecht, GEMA und Streaming: Musik als Ware
topics.description: Understand who earns money from music: copyright and performing rights (GEMA in Germany), labels, streaming payouts and platform terms, and what is allowed when downloading, sampling or uploading music and videos.
evidence: Explain what copyright protects and that it expires after a fixed period
Describe how money from a stream is split between artists, labels and the collecting society
Decide whether a given upload (cover, sample, remix) needs permission
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to post a video with a chart song, can they explain whether that is allowed and who holds the rights?
topics.laenderNotes: GEMA is the German collecting society; the legal frame is the German Urheberrechtsgesetz within EU law.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: The Voice and Voice Change
topics.description: Understand how the voice works (breath, vocal folds, resonance), what happens during voice change in puberty, which voice types and registers exist and how to sing healthily, and use the changing voice creatively, e.g. in rap or rhythmic speech.
evidence: Describe the roles of breathing, vocal folds and resonance in a sung tone
Explain how voices change in puberty and how to sing safely during the change
Name soprano, alto, tenor and bass and find their own current range
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s voice is breaking, can they explain what is happening and choose a comfortable part or a rap part instead of straining?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Producing Music with a DAW
topics.nameDe: Musikproduktion mit DAW: Aufnahme, Loops, Effekte
topics.description: Use a digital audio workstation or music app to record, arrange loops and samples, edit (cut, quantise, mix) and add effects, producing a short track or remix and documenting the steps.
evidence: Record or import audio and MIDI tracks and arrange them on a timeline
Use quantising, volume and panning and at least one effect deliberately
Export a finished track and explain how it was built
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked to make a 30-second jingle on a tablet, can they layer drums, bass and melody and balance the mix?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Film Music: Functions and Techniques
topics.nameDe: Filmmusik: Funktionen und Techniken (Paraphrasierung, Kontrapunktierung, Leitmotiv)
topics.description: Analyse how film music works: underscoring, paraphrasing (Paraphrasierung), polarising and counterpointing (Kontrapunktierung), leitmotifs, diegetic and non-diegetic music, mickey-mousing, and how music steers the viewer's emotions.
evidence: Name the function of the music in a film scene, e.g. paraphrasing or counterpointing
Identify a leitmotif and explain which character or idea it stands for
Put different music under a short clip and describe how the effect of the scene changes
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches a scene twice with different music, can they explain with technical terms how the music changes what we feel?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern: Kl. 8; Berlin-Brandenburg lists film music under 'Funktionale Musik' for Kl. 7–10; it often returns in the Oberstufe under music and media.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Word and Music in Song
topics.description: Examine how composers set words to music: syllabic and melismatic setting, word painting, rhythm following the speech stresses, and strophic versus through-composed form, in art songs (Kunstlied) and pop songs alike.
evidence: Find examples of word painting in a song and explain them
Tell a strophic from a through-composed song and explain the choice
Describe how melody and rhythm follow the stresses of the text
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} listens to Schubert's 'Erlkönig', can they show how the music tells narrator, father, child and Erlkönig apart?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Music of a Non-European Culture
topics.nameDe: Musik einer außereuropäischen Kultur (z. B. Westafrika, Indien)
topics.description: Study one non-European musical culture in depth, e.g. West African drumming, Indian raga, Indonesian gamelan or Arabic maqam: its tone system, rhythm, instruments, forms and social or ritual functions, compared with European music.
evidence: Describe the tone system or rhythmic principle of the chosen music (e.g. polyrhythm, raga, maqam)
Explain the social or ritual function of the music in its culture
Play or sing a short pattern from the tradition and compare it with European music
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears West African drumming, can they explain polyrhythm and play one layer of the pattern?
topics.laenderNotes: The KMK EPA require knowledge of one non-European musical culture for the Abitur; many Länder return to it in the Oberstufe under globalisation and world music.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Judging Music: Facts and Values
topics.description: Distinguish factual statements about music (Sachurteil) from value judgements (Werturteil), judge pieces and performances with criteria such as originality, craft, effect, function and context, and respect differing tastes.
evidence: Sort statements about a song into factual statements and value judgements
Judge a piece or performance with at least three named criteria
Explain why two people can judge the same piece differently
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} says a song is 'bad', can they turn this into a judgement with criteria and separate it from facts about the music?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Arranging for the Class Ensemble
topics.description: Arrange a melody or song for the class instruments: choose a texture (melody with accompaniment, bass line, rhythm), write parts within each instrument's range, and test and revise the arrangement in rehearsal.
evidence: Write an accompaniment pattern and bass line for a given melody
Give the parts to instruments with suitable ranges
Rehearse the arrangement and revise a passage that did not work
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets a simple tune, can they write parts for keyboard, bass and percussion that the class can play?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Romantic Music
topics.nameDe: Musik der Romantik: Lied, Charakterstück, Programmmusik, sinfonische Dichtung
topics.description: Characterise Romantic music: expression of feeling, nature and longing, national styles, the virtuoso, small forms (Lied, character piece) and large forms (programme symphony, symphonic poem), with composers such as Schubert, Robert and Clara Schumann, Chopin, Liszt and Wagner.
evidence: Name typical subjects and forms of Romantic music
Show in an example how harmony, dynamics or orchestration express feeling
Explain the difference between programme music and absolute music
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears Smetana's 'Moldau', can they explain how it tells a story and why it is typically Romantic?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Viennese Classicism
topics.description: Describe the Viennese Classical style (balanced phrases, clear harmony, contrast and balance), its main genres (symphony, sonata, string quartet, concerto), the composers' path from court musician to free artist, and Beethoven as a bridge to Romanticism.
evidence: Name style features of Classical music and show them in an example
Explain how Haydn's and Beethoven's working conditions differed
Name the movements of a classical symphony and their usual characters
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares Haydn's position at court with Beethoven's in Vienna, can they explain what changed for composers?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern: Kl. 9 (with a Beethoven or Schubert portrait already in Kl. 7).

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Opera and Musical
topics.nameDe: Oper und Musical: Rezitativ, Arie, Ensemble, Song
topics.description: Compare the forms of music theatre: recitative and aria, ensemble and chorus in opera, song and dance numbers in the musical. Analyse how music characterises figures and drives the drama, e.g. in Mozart or in Bernstein's 'West Side Story'.
evidence: Tell a recitative from an aria and explain their dramatic functions
Describe how the music characterises two figures in one scene
Compare an opera and a musical in form, use of voice and audience
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches a scene from 'West Side Story', can they explain how the music shows the conflict between the two gangs?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Sonata Form
topics.description: Follow the sections of sonata form (exposition with two contrasting themes and key areas, development, recapitulation, coda) by ear and in the score, and explain how the form builds drama through contrast and return.
evidence: Draw a form diagram of a sonata movement with themes and keys
Identify the start of the development and the recapitulation by ear
Explain how the second theme's key changes between exposition and recapitulation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} listens to the first movement of a Mozart symphony, can they say when the development begins and what happens to the themes there?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Singing in Multi-Part Arrangements
topics.description: Hold an independent part in a three- or four-part vocal arrangement (choir piece or pop song), tune to the other voices, follow a conductor and shape dynamics and phrasing together.
evidence: Sing their own part securely while other parts sound
Read their part from a choral score and find their entries
Adjust volume and intonation to blend with the group
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s class rehearses a three-part arrangement, can they keep their part when the other voices come in?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Improvising over the Blues
topics.description: Improvise short melodic phrases over a 12-bar blues with the blues scale, call-and-response and motifs, keeping the form and the swing feel.
evidence: Play the 12-bar blues progression or follow it while others play
Improvise two- and four-bar phrases with the blues scale
Answer a phrase played by someone else (call and response)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s class jams a 12-bar blues, can they take a four-bar solo with the blues scale and come back in on time?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Baroque Music
topics.nameDe: Musik des Barock: Generalbass, Concerto, Oratorium
topics.description: Describe Baroque music (about 1600–1750): basso continuo (Generalbass), terraced dynamics and the doctrine of affects, the concerto principle (concerto grosso, solo concerto), suite, cantata and oratorio, and the role of court and church, with Bach, Händel and Vivaldi.
evidence: Explain the basso continuo and realise a few figured-bass chords
Show the alternation of tutti and soli in a concerto grosso
Relate a Baroque genre to its function at court or in church
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears a Vivaldi concerto, can they show where soloist and tutti alternate and explain what the continuo does?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern treats the Baroque in Kl. 10 and returns to figured bass in Mu13 (gA); elsewhere Baroque music often comes earlier, e.g. in Kl. 7–8.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Music 1890–1950: Impressionism to Twelve-Tone
topics.description: Explain how composers broke with major-minor tonality around 1900: Debussy's Impressionism (whole-tone scale, sound colour), Expressionism and free atonality, Schoenberg's twelve-tone technique, and Stravinsky's rhythm and Neoclassicism.
evidence: Describe features of Impressionist music in a listening example
Build a simple twelve-tone row and its inversion
Explain why atonal music sounds unfamiliar and how composers organised it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears Debussy and then Schoenberg, can they describe how each moves away from traditional tonality?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Polyphony and Fugue
topics.description: Distinguish homophonic and polyphonic textures and follow the structure of a fugue (subject, answer, countersubject, exposition, episodes, stretto), mainly in the music of Johann Sebastian Bach.
evidence: Describe a passage as homophonic or polyphonic and justify it
Mark the entries of the subject in a short fugue score
Explain subject, answer and episode with an example
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears a Bach fugue, can they count the voices as they enter with the subject?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Jazz: Roots, Styles and Features
topics.description: Explain jazz as a synthesis of African American and European traditions: the blues (12-bar form, blue notes), swing, improvisation and the main styles (New Orleans, Swing, Bebop, Cool Jazz, Jazzrock) with typical line-ups and musicians.
evidence: Describe the 12-bar blues form and the blue notes
Recognise two jazz styles by ear and name their typical features
Explain the social background of jazz in the USA
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears a swing big band and a bebop combo, can they tell them apart and explain what changed?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern: Kl. 10; Berlin-Brandenburg lists jazz among instrumental music for Kl. 7–10.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Music and Politics
topics.nameDe: Musik und Politik: Protestlied, Propaganda, NS-Musikpolitik
topics.description: Analyse how music is used politically: protest and freedom songs, anthems, propaganda music in dictatorships, the Nazi persecution of 'entartete Musik' and censorship in the GDR, and which musical means make music mobilising or manipulative.
evidence: Analyse the musical and textual means of a protest song
Explain with examples how the Nazi regime used and banned music
Discuss whether instrumental music can carry a political message
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares a Nazi march with a 1960s protest song, can they explain how each tries to influence listeners?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern makes 'Musik politisch' a Lernbereich of Kl. 11; Berlin-Brandenburg lists 'Musik und Herrschaft, Musik als Protest' for Kl. 7–10.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Comparing Interpretations
topics.description: Compare different recordings or arrangements of the same work (tempo, dynamics, articulation, instrumentation, historically informed or modern performance) and reach a reasoned judgement on each interpretive approach.
evidence: Describe measurable differences between two recordings, e.g. tempo and instrumentation
Relate the differences to interpretive intentions such as historical performance practice
Write a reasoned evaluation of which interpretation suits the work better
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears a Bach piece on harpsichord and on a modern piano, can they compare the recordings and justify which convinces them more?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Discussing Texts about Music
topics.description: Analyse texts about music such as reviews, composers' statements and aesthetic essays, reconstruct their claims, test them against listening examples and write a reasoned discussion, an Abitur task type in Musik.
evidence: Summarise the main claim and arguments of a text about music
Test a claim of the text against a musical example
Write a reasoned statement agreeing or disagreeing with the author
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads a critic's review of a concert, can they check the claims against the recording and argue for their own view?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Composing to a Brief with Commentary
topics.description: Compose or arrange music to set requirements (e.g. variations on a theme, a song setting, a piece in a given style) and explain and justify the compositional means in writing, an Abitur task type in Musik.
evidence: Compose a short piece that meets all given requirements
Explain in writing which musical means they used and why
Evaluate the result against the brief and suggest an improvement
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has to set a short poem in Romantic style, can they compose it and explain their harmonic choices in writing?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Extended Harmony
topics.nameDe: Erweiterte Harmonik: Nebenstufen, Septakkorde, Zwischendominante, Modulation
topics.description: Analyse harmony beyond the primary chords: secondary chords (Nebenstufen, Parallelen), seventh and diminished chords, secondary dominants and modulation to related keys, with function or step symbols.
evidence: Label the chords of a short chorale or song including secondary chords
Find a secondary dominant and the chord it resolves to
Show where and how a piece modulates
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} analyses a Bach chorale, can they spot the secondary dominant before the half close and name the new key?
topics.laenderNotes: At the Musisches Gymnasium in Bayern secondary dominants and modulation come in Kl. 9.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Methods of Music Analysis
topics.nameDe: Methoden der Werkanalyse: Hören, Notentext, Formübersicht
topics.description: Analyse a longer work systematically: listen with and without the score, describe the parameters (melody, harmony, rhythm, texture, instrumentation, form) in technical language with bar references, draw form charts, and combine the findings into an interpretation. This is the core of the written Abitur task 'Untersuchung, Analyse und Interpretation'.
evidence: Write a structured analysis of an excerpt covering several parameters with bar references
Draw a form chart or listening protocol of a movement
Link analytical findings to an interpretation of the work's meaning or effect
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets an unknown score excerpt in the Abitur, can they describe its structure with bar numbers and explain what the composer achieves?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Performing a Prepared Piece in Style
topics.description: Rehearse a piece from a chosen era independently, perform it vocally or instrumentally with a personal interpretation, and justify interpretive choices with knowledge of style and structure. This is the practical part of the Musik Abitur in Länder that test it.
evidence: Prepare and perform a piece with secure notes, rhythm and expression
Explain how their tempo, dynamics and articulation fit the style of the era
Demonstrate a passage vocally or instrumentally to illustrate an analysis
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} performs a Baroque piece in the practical exam, can they explain why they chose a light articulation and terraced dynamics?
topics.laenderNotes: Practical exam parts (musikpraktische Prüfung) exist only in some Länder; others examine Musik in writing or orally without a performance.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Music Aesthetics
topics.description: Discuss basic positions of music aesthetics: music as expression of feeling versus 'tönend bewegte Formen' (Hanslick), autonomy versus function, beauty and the concept of the work, and what music psychology says about why music moves us.
evidence: Explain Hanslick's position and an expression-aesthetic position
Apply one position to a piece they know
Discuss findings of music psychology on music and emotion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads Hanslick's claim that music expresses only itself, can they test it on a film score and on a Bach fugue?
topics.laenderNotes: Leistungskurs topic in most Länder; the KMK EPA name music-aesthetic and music-psychological questions as Leistungskurs extension.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Four-Part Choral Writing
topics.description: Arrange a melody with chord symbols or figured bass for mixed choir (SATB) following voice-leading rules: ranges, no parallel fifths or octaves, resolution of leading notes and sevenths.
evidence: Write a four-part harmonisation of a short melody
Check the setting for parallel fifths and octaves and correct them
Resolve the leading note and the dominant seventh correctly
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} harmonises a chorale phrase for SATB, can they avoid parallel fifths and lead the leading note upwards?
topics.laenderNotes: Choral arranging is eA content in Bayern (Mu12); in other Länder Tonsatz exercises appear in the Leistungskurs or not at all.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Gregorian Chant and Renaissance Polyphony
topics.nameDe: Gregorianik, Kirchentonarten und Vokalpolyphonie der Renaissance
topics.description: Describe Gregorian chant (psalmody, melisma, neumes and square notation, church modes) and Renaissance vocal polyphony (motet, mass, madrigal; cantus firmus and parody technique; imitation and word painting).
evidence: Transcribe a short chant from square notation and name its mode
Explain cantus firmus or parody technique with an example
Describe imitation and word painting in a Renaissance motet or madrigal
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a chant in square notation, can they transcribe it and say which church mode it uses?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: History of Western Vocal Music
topics.nameDe: Entwicklungen der abendländischen Vokalmusik: Kantate, Oper, Kunstlied
topics.description: Trace vocal music through the eras: word-music relations in Baroque cantata and oratorio (affects, musical-rhetorical figures), characterisation in Classical opera, and text interpretation in the Romantic Lied, each in its historical and social setting.
evidence: Analyse word-music relations in a Baroque aria or chorus
Explain how a Classical opera scene characterises its figures
Interpret a Romantic Lied with reference to the poem and the ideas of its time
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares a Bach aria with a Schubert song, can they explain how each composer interprets the text?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Music and Technology
topics.nameDe: Musik und Technik: elektronische Klangerzeugung, Sampling, Streaming
topics.description: Explain how technology has changed music since the 20th century: electronic instruments and synthesis, recording and sampling, electronic art music (e.g. Stockhausen, Reich), digital distribution and streaming, and their effects on creativity, the music economy and copyright.
evidence: Explain how a synthesizer or sampler produces or changes sound
Describe a work of electronic art music and a technology-based pop style
Discuss how streaming changes what musicians earn and how music is made
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears a track built from samples, can they explain the technique and discuss whether it counts as original work?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Development of Instrumental Music
topics.nameDe: Entwicklungen der Instrumentalmusik vom Barock bis zur Romantik
topics.description: Compare instrumental music across eras: Baroque concerto and fugue, Classical sonata and symphony, Romantic piano music between salon and virtuosity, programme and absolute music, and how public concerts and audiences changed.
evidence: Compare a Baroque, a Classical and a Romantic instrumental work in texture, form and harmony
Explain the debate between programme music and absolute music
Describe how the public concert changed the role of music
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets three short instrumental excerpts, can they order them by era and justify the order with analysis?

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: New Music after 1945
topics.nameDe: Neue Musik nach 1945: Serialismus, Aleatorik, Klangflächen, Minimal Music
topics.description: Explain main currents of art music since 1945 (serialism, aleatory and chance with Cage, sound-mass composition with Ligeti and Penderecki, minimal music with Reich and Pärt, current trends), their compositional means and notation, and their links to political and social developments.
evidence: Describe the compositional principle of two currents with examples
Read a graphic or aleatoric score and explain what is fixed and what is free
Take a reasoned position on an aesthetic statement about New Music
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears Ligeti's 'Atmosphères' and a piece by Steve Reich, can they explain the different principles behind them?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Magnets and Magnetic Materials
topics.description: Pupils explore attraction and repulsion between north and south poles, identify ferromagnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt), magnetise and demagnetise a nail, and explain this with the model of Elementarmagnete, including why poles cannot be separated.
evidence: Predicts attraction or repulsion between given poles
Sorts materials into magnetic and non-magnetic
Explains magnetising a nail and breaking a magnet in two with the Elementarmagnet model
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} broke a bar magnet in half, could they predict whether they get a separate north and south pole and explain why with a model?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Circuit Symbols and Diagrams
topics.description: Pupils use the standard circuit symbols (cell/battery, lamp, switch, motor, buzzer, wire) to draw circuit diagrams with straight lines and build circuits from given diagrams.
evidence: Draws a correct circuit diagram for a built circuit using standard symbols
Builds a circuit from a given diagram
Finds the fault in a diagram that cannot work
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were given a circuit diagram with a battery, two lamps and a switch, could they build it and say what happens when the switch is opened?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Closed Circuits, Conductors and Insulators
topics.nameDe: Der elektrische Stromkreis: Leiter und Nichtleiter
topics.description: Pupils build closed circuits with a source, consumers and switches, test which materials conduct, and explain current with a simple model of freely moving electrons in metals.
evidence: Builds a working circuit with battery, lamp and switch and explains why it must be closed
Tests materials and classifies them as conductors or insulators
Explains with the electron model why current flows only in a closed loop
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} had a battery, a bulb, wires and a set of objects, could they find out which objects let current through and explain the result?
topics.laenderNotes: NRW Physik and BB Naturwissenschaften 5/6 (Themenfeld 3.9 Technik) treat circuits in Kl. 5/6; BW BNT 5/6 has no circuit standard, electricity follows in Physik from Kl. 7.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Characteristics of Living Things
topics.description: Pupils use a fixed list of criteria (Bewegung, Reizbarkeit, Stoffwechsel, Wachstum, Entwicklung, Fortpflanzung, Aufbau aus Zellen) to decide whether something is alive. Only things showing all criteria count as living; borderline cases like a candle flame or a car are discussed.
evidence: Lists the characteristics of living things
Applies all criteria to decide whether a plant, a flame and a robot are alive
Explains why one criterion alone (e.g. movement) is not enough
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked whether a candle flame is alive because it 'grows' and 'needs air', could they use the full list of criteria to explain why it is not?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Using a Light Microscope
topics.description: Pupils name the parts of a light microscope, prepare a wet mount (Frischpräparat) such as onion epidermis, focus from low to high magnification, calculate total magnification and make a scientific drawing (Zeichnung nach Vorgaben).
evidence: Names the main parts (ocular, objective, stage, coarse and fine focus, light source) and their function
Prepares an onion-skin wet mount and focuses it starting with the lowest magnification
Calculates total magnification and produces a labelled pencil drawing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Given an onion and a microscope, could {{name}} prepare a slide, find the cells and draw what they see with labels and the magnification?
topics.laenderNotes: NRW and Berlin/Brandenburg place light microscopy in Kl. 5/6; BW BNT 5/6 only requires magnifier/stereo magnifier, so microscopy often starts with Biologie in Kl. 7.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Plant and Animal Cells
topics.description: Pupils learn that all living things are built of cells, name the light-microscope structures (Zellmembran, Zellplasma, Zellkern; in plants also Zellwand, Vakuole, Chloroplasten) and order the system levels Zelle – Gewebe – Organ – Organismus.
evidence: Labels the visible structures of plant and animal cells
States two differences between plant and animal cells and links chloroplasts to plants' way of feeding
Orders cell, tissue, organ and organism with one example each
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a drawing of an unknown cell with a cell wall and green chloroplasts, could they say whether it came from a plant or an animal and why?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Skeleton, Joints and Muscles
topics.description: Pupils name the main sections of the skeleton and their functions (support, protection, movement), distinguish joint types (ball-and-socket, hinge), explain the double-S-shaped spine and the antagonist principle (Gegenspielerprinzip) of biceps and triceps, and discuss posture damage from heavy school bags.
evidence: Labels skull, spine, rib cage, shoulder and pelvic girdle and limbs
Explains with a model how biceps and triceps move the forearm
Matches joint types to examples and their range of movement
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} bent and stretched their arm while holding the other hand on the upper arm, could they explain which muscle works when and why muscles always work in pairs?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Nutrients and a Balanced Diet
topics.description: Pupils name carbohydrates, fats and proteins plus vitamins, minerals, fibre and water and their roles, test foods with simple Nährstoffnachweise (iodine for starch, grease-spot test for fat), and assess a day's meals against the DGE nutrition circle or food pyramid and energy needs.
evidence: Carries out and documents the iodine starch test and the fat spot test
Names the main function of each nutrient group
Evaluates a given daily menu and suggests improvements for a balanced diet
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wrote down everything they ate in a day, could they check it against the food pyramid and suggest one concrete improvement?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: The Scientific Method Cycle
topics.description: Pupils learn the German 'Erkenntnisweg' as a fixed sequence: observe a phenomenon, ask a question, state a testable Vermutung (hypothesis), plan and run an experiment, and check whether the result supports the hypothesis. Observation (Beobachtung) and interpretation (Deutung) are written separately.
evidence: Formulates a testable hypothesis ('Ich vermute, dass …, weil …') for an observed phenomenon such as a sinking candle
Keeps observation and explanation apart when describing an experiment
States whether a result confirms or refutes the hypothesis and suggests what to test next
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} noticed that ice cubes melt faster in salt water than in tap water, could they turn this into a question, a hypothesis and a simple experiment that tests it?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Using a Gas Burner
topics.description: Pupils light, regulate and switch off a Teclu or Bunsen burner in the correct order, distinguish the luminous yellow flame from the hot non-luminous blue flame, and heat a test tube safely (angled, never pointing at people). It is the first 'Führerschein' style skill in German science lessons.
evidence: Lights and extinguishes the burner in the correct sequence (gas tap, lighter, air supply)
Explains the difference between the luminous and the non-luminous flame and where the flame is hottest
Heats a liquid in a test tube safely using a holder and correct angle
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} light a gas burner on their own, turn it into a hot blue flame and safely warm water in a test tube?
topics.laenderNotes: The Teclu burner is standard in German, Austrian and Swiss schools; many schools issue a 'Brennerführerschein' in Kl. 5/6.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Measuring and Graphing Results
topics.description: Pupils measure physical quantities as Maßzahl plus Einheit with suitable instruments, record repeated readings in tables, and present them as bar or line graphs (e.g. a temperature-time curve). They recognise reading errors and why measurements beat subjective senses.
evidence: Records measurements with number and unit in a prepared table
Draws a line graph with labelled axes and a sensible scale from a measurement series
Names one source of measurement or reading error and how to reduce it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measured the temperature of cooling tea every two minutes, could they put the values in a table and draw a correctly labelled line graph?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Lab Safety Rules
topics.description: Pupils learn the rules of the science room (Fachraum): safety goggles, tied-back hair, no eating, emergency stop switch, fire blanket and eye shower, and the meaning of GHS hazard pictograms. The rules follow the KMK safety guideline for teaching (RiSU) and are often signed by pupils.
evidence: Explains the purpose of at least five lab rules and points out the emergency switch, eye shower and fire blanket
Matches common GHS pictograms (flammable, corrosive, harmful) to their meaning
Behaves according to the rules during a practical without reminders
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a bottle with a red-bordered flame pictogram in the science room, could they say what it means and which precautions to take?
topics.laenderNotes: Safety instruction (Sicherheitsbelehrung) at the start of each school year is required by the KMK 'Richtlinie zur Sicherheit im Unterricht' (RiSU) in all Länder.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Controlling Variables
topics.description: Pupils plan experiments in which only one factor is changed while all others are kept constant, and they use a control set-up (Kontrollansatz). The classic Kl. 5/6 context is germination: water, warmth, light and air are varied one at a time.
evidence: Names the changed, measured and constant factors in a planned experiment
Designs a control set-up for comparison
Explains why a test that changes two factors at once gives no clear answer
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wanted to find out whether cress seeds need light to germinate, could they set up dishes that change only the light and keep water, warmth and seed number the same?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Writing a Lab Report
topics.description: Pupils write a standard German Versuchsprotokoll with the headings Fragestellung, Vermutung, Material, Durchführung (incl. labelled sketch of the set-up), Beobachtung and Auswertung/Deutung. The protocol is a recurring assessed format from Kl. 5 onwards.
evidence: Writes a complete protocol with all standard headings for an experiment they carried out
Draws a labelled cross-section sketch of the apparatus
Writes observations in the past tense without interpretation and puts the explanation under Auswertung
topics.assessmentPrompt: After filtering muddy water in class, could {{name}} write a protocol with question, hypothesis, materials, procedure sketch, observation and explanation in the right sections?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Exploring a Local Habitat
topics.nameDe: Lebensraum erkunden: Hecke, Wald oder Wiese
topics.description: Pupils investigate a habitat near school (hedge, forest edge, meadow, pond), identify typical organisms with simple keys, collect and examine invertebrates gently, and record seasonal changes over the year in a field protocol.
evidence: Identifies at least five organisms of a local habitat with a key or app
Records observations at the same site in two seasons and compares them
Describes how the structure of the habitat (layers of a forest or hedge) offers niches to different animals
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} visited the hedge behind the school in autumn and in spring, could they record and explain what had changed for plants and animals?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Waste Separation and Recycling
topics.description: Pupils sort household waste into the German fractions (Wertstoff/Gelber Sack, paper, glass, organic, residual, hazardous waste such as batteries), separate a drinks carton into its layers, try a recycling process such as making paper, and evaluate their own waste avoidance.
evidence: Assigns typical household items to the correct bin and explains the material property behind it
Separates a composite drinks carton into paper, plastic and aluminium
Suggests two ways to avoid waste in their own daily life
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} had an empty yoghurt pot, a juice carton, a dead battery and apple peel, could they put each in the right bin and explain why?
topics.laenderNotes: Context is the German dual system (Gelber Sack/Wertstofftonne, deposit 'Pfand'); bin colours vary by municipality.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Identifying Plants with a Key
topics.description: Pupils use a dichotomous identification key (printed or app) to identify native flowering plants and trees, recognise families such as Kreuzblütler, Lippenblütler or Rosengewächse by flower structure, and press and label specimens in a herbarium.
evidence: Identifies an unknown native plant by working step by step through a dichotomous key
Assigns plants to a family using flower features
Names and recognises two or three native deciduous and coniferous trees
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} collected a flowering plant on a school walk, could they identify it with a key and say which family it belongs to?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Pollination and Fertilisation
topics.description: Pupils distinguish pollination (transfer of pollen by insects or wind) from fertilisation (fusion of pollen and egg cell after the pollen tube grows), describe how the ovary becomes a fruit and the ovule a seed, and contrast this with vegetative propagation (runners, tubers).
evidence: Explains the difference between pollination and fertilisation
Describes how a cherry fruit develops from the flower
Gives one example each of insect pollination, wind pollination and vegetative propagation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that a cherry tree gives no fruit after a cold, bee-less spring, could they explain the chain from pollination to fruit?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Flower Structure
topics.description: Pupils dissect a flower (e.g. cherry or rapeseed) from outside in and lay out a Legebild of sepals, petals, stamens (anther, filament) and pistil (stigma, style, ovary), naming the male and female parts.
evidence: Dissects a flower and arranges a correctly labelled Legebild
Identifies stamens as male and pistil as female parts
Counts and records the number of each flower part
topics.assessmentPrompt: Given a fresh tulip or cherry blossom, could {{name}} take it apart, lay out the parts in order and name the male and female parts?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Seed Structure and Germination
topics.description: Pupils describe the structure of a bean seed (seed coat, cotyledons with stored food, embryo) and find out by controlled experiments that germination needs water, warmth and air but not light, distinguishing germination from later growth.
evidence: Labels seed coat, cotyledons and embryo on a soaked bean
Plans a germination experiment with a control set-up for one condition
States the germination conditions and explains why light is not needed at first
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} set up cress seeds on dry cotton, wet cotton, in the fridge and in a dark cupboard, could they predict and explain which ones would germinate?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Organs of a Flowering Plant
topics.description: Pupils name root, shoot axis (Sprossachse), leaf and flower and explain how they work together: roots anchor and take up water and minerals, the stem transports, leaves produce food, and flowers serve reproduction.
evidence: Labels the organs on a whole plant
Explains the function of each organ
Describes the path of water from the soil to the leaves
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} put a white flower in coloured water, could they predict what happens and explain which plant organs are involved?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Seed and Fruit Dispersal
topics.description: Pupils classify dispersal by wind (dandelion, maple 'Propeller'), animals (burrs, berries eaten), water and self-dispersal, relate fruit structure to dispersal, and test this with simple functional models such as paper helicopters.
evidence: Assigns given fruits to a dispersal type based on their structure
Builds and tests a model of a wind-dispersed fruit, changing one variable
Explains why dispersal is an advantage for the plant
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} found a maple seed spinning to the ground, could they explain how its shape helps the tree and design a paper model to test it?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Changes in Puberty
topics.description: Pupils describe physical changes in puberty (growth spurt, body hair, breasts, voice change, first period and first ejaculation) and emotional changes, understand that timing varies, and learn body care and hygiene.
evidence: Names physical changes in girls and boys during puberty
Describes emotional changes and that timing differs between individuals
Explains suitable hygiene measures for puberty
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s friend worried about being the only one in class whose voice had not changed yet, could they explain why puberty starts at different times?
topics.laenderNotes: Sexualerziehung is a cross-curricular legal mandate in all Länder (parents must be informed in advance); the biological part sits in Biologie/NaWi Kl. 5/6 and is revisited in Kl. 8/9.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: States of Matter and Changes of State
topics.description: Pupils name the three states and the six transitions (schmelzen, erstarren, verdampfen, kondensieren, sublimieren, resublimieren), record the heating curve of water and determine melting and boiling temperatures as substance properties.
evidence: Names all state transitions with the correct terms in a diagram
Records and interprets the temperature curve of heating water, including the boiling plateau
Uses melting and boiling points to predict the state of a substance at a given temperature
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heated ice until the water boiled while measuring the temperature, could they sketch the curve and explain why it stays flat at 0 °C and 100 °C?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Mass, Volume and Floating
topics.nameDe: Masse, Volumen und Dichte: Schwimmen, Schweben, Sinken
topics.description: Pupils measure mass with a balance and volume with a measuring cylinder or overflow method, and use a qualitative idea of density (heavy for its size) to explain why objects float, hover or sink in water.
evidence: Determines the volume of an irregular object by displacement
Explains why a large wooden block floats while a small iron nail sinks
Predicts and explains floating, hovering or sinking for given objects
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a huge steel ship float but a steel coin sink, could they explain the difference using mass, volume and density?
topics.laenderNotes: Floating/sinking is a BW BNT core topic (3.1.3); in NRW density appears in Physik later (Druck und Auftrieb).

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Mixtures and Solutions
topics.description: Pupils distinguish pure substances from mixtures (Gemenge, Lösung, Suspension, Emulsion), investigate water as a solvent (salt, sugar, mineral water) and recognise a saturated solution.
evidence: Classifies everyday products (orange juice, salad dressing, salt water, granite) as types of mixture
Shows experimentally that dissolved salt is still present
Explains what a saturated solution is
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} kept stirring salt into a glass of water until some stayed at the bottom, could they explain what happened and whether the salt has disappeared?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Properties of Substances
topics.description: Pupils distinguish an object (Körper) from the substance (Stoff) it is made of and identify substances by properties such as colour, smell, hardness, deformability, solubility, electrical conductivity, magnetism and melting temperature, summarised in a Steckbrief.
evidence: Explains the difference between object and substance with examples
Tests at least four properties of an unknown substance and records them
Uses a property profile (Steckbrief) to identify a substance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were given three white powders (sugar, salt, flour), could they plan tests based on properties to tell them apart?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Separating Mixtures
topics.description: Pupils choose and carry out separation methods based on differing properties: sorting, sieving, magnetic separation, sedimenting and decanting, filtering, evaporating; and relate them to technical uses such as salt production or a sewage plant.
evidence: Separates a mixture of sand, salt and iron filings in a sensible order
Justifies each method by the property it exploits
Describes one technical application (water treatment or salt works)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were given a mixture of sand, salt and iron filings, could they plan and carry out steps to get all three back separately?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Combustion and Fire Extinguishing
topics.description: Pupils investigate the conditions for burning (fuel, oxygen from the air, ignition temperature – the Verbrennungsdreieck) with candles and the burner, explain that combustion releases energy, and derive extinguishing methods by removing one condition.
evidence: Names the three conditions for combustion and shows each in a candle experiment
Explains why a candle under a glass goes out
Matches extinguishing methods (water, blanket, removing fuel) to the condition they remove
topics.assessmentPrompt: If oil in a pan caught fire, could {{name}} explain why a lid is the right choice and why water would be dangerous?
topics.laenderNotes: Combustion is BW BNT 3.1.4 (Kl. 5/6); NRW treats it in Chemie from Kl. 7.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Fish Adapted to Water
topics.nameDe: Fische: Angepasstheit an das Leben im Wasser
topics.description: Pupils describe fish features (streamlined body, scales and mucus, fins, gills, swim bladder, lateral line, external fertilisation via Laich) as adaptations to life in water, explaining breathing and hovering (Schweben) in water.
evidence: Explains how gills take oxygen from water
Explains the function of the swim bladder for hovering at a depth
Relates body shape and fins to energy-efficient swimming
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watched a goldfish hovering still in the middle of a tank, could they explain how it stays at that depth and how it breathes?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Teeth Types and Diet
topics.description: Pupils compare the Raubtiergebiss (dog: Fangzähne, Reißzähne), the Pflanzenfressergebiss (cattle: no upper incisors, broad grinding molars) and the Allesfressergebiss (pig, human), and explain the cow as a Wiederkäuer with a four-chambered stomach.
evidence: Identifies a carnivore, herbivore and omnivore skull from its teeth
Explains the function of canines, carnassials and grinding molars
Describes the path of food through the ruminant stomach in the right order
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were shown the skull of a dog and of a cow, could they say which is which and explain how the teeth fit the food?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Dog and Cat as Mammals
topics.nameDe: Hund und Katze – Säugetiere als Haustiere
topics.description: Using the dog (Hetzjäger, descended from the wolf) and the cat (Schleichjäger, Zehengänger with retractable claws) pupils learn the typical mammal features (fur, lungs, constant body temperature, live birth, suckling) and how body build fits hunting style. Domestication and breeding explain why dogs differ from wolves.
evidence: Lists five features that make dog and cat mammals
Compares how dog and cat hunt and relates this to their senses, legs and claws
Explains that dog breeds arose from wolves through breeding by humans
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watched a cat stalk a bird and a dog chase a ball, could they explain how each animal's body and senses fit its way of hunting?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Livestock Farming and Animal Welfare
topics.description: Pupils compare forms of keeping farm animals (e.g. laying hens in Boden-, Freiland- and Biohaltung, read via the EU egg code 0–3; pigs, cattle), relate them to the animals' natural needs, and form a reasoned judgement about artgerechte Haltung and consumer choices.
evidence: Decodes the first digit of an egg stamp and describes the matching husbandry form
Compares two husbandry forms against the animal's natural behaviour
Gives a reasoned personal judgement weighing animal welfare, price and environment
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} found the code '0-DE-…' and '3-DE-…' on two egg boxes, could they explain what the numbers mean for the hens and argue which eggs they would buy?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Birds Adapted for Flight
topics.description: Pupils explain how birds are built for flight: lightweight hollow bones, feathers (Konturfeder, Daunenfeder), strong breast muscles and a streamlined body; they distinguish gliding and flapping flight and compare Nesthocker and Nestflüchter.
evidence: Explains three features of the bird body that save weight or provide lift
Compares a bird bone with a mammal bone and interprets the difference
Distinguishes altricial and precocial chicks with one example each
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} held a cut chicken bone and a beef bone, could they explain what the difference tells us about how birds can fly?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Measuring Temperature
topics.description: Pupils learn why the sense of warmth is unreliable, how a liquid thermometer works (thermal expansion), how the Celsius scale is defined by the fixed points 0 °C and 100 °C, and read analogue and digital thermometers correctly, including negative values.
evidence: Shows with three water bowls that the hand misjudges temperature
Reads analogue thermometers correctly at eye level, including below zero
Explains how the Celsius scale is defined
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} put one hand in cold and one in warm water and then both in lukewarm water, could they explain the strange feeling and why we use thermometers?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Magnetic Fields and the Compass
topics.description: Pupils make magnetic fields visible with iron filings and small compasses, draw field-line patterns, and explain the compass needle as a small magnet aligning with Earth's magnetic field.
evidence: Draws the field-line pattern of a bar magnet from an iron-filings experiment
Explains why a compass needle points north
Builds a simple compass from a magnetised needle
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} magnetised a sewing needle and floated it on a cork in water, could they explain why it turns to point north?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Series and Parallel Circuits
topics.description: Pupils compare series and parallel circuits (what happens when one lamp is removed, brightness), explain why household devices are connected in parallel, and build AND and OR switch circuits for practical tasks such as a two-switch alarm.
evidence: Predicts and tests what happens in series and parallel circuits when one lamp is unscrewed
Explains why devices at home are wired in parallel
Designs an AND or an OR circuit for a given task
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked to wire a bell that rings when either the front or the back door button is pressed, could they draw and build the right circuit?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Effects of Current and Electrical Safety
topics.nameDe: Wirkungen des Stroms und Sicherheit im Umgang mit Elektrizität
topics.description: Pupils describe the heating, lighting and magnetic effects of current with device examples, explain short circuits and how fuses and circuit breakers protect, and know why mains electricity (230 V) and overhead railway lines are life-threatening.
evidence: Names a device for each effect of electric current
Explains what a short circuit is and how a fuse protects the circuit
States rules for safe use of electrical devices and checks a device for visible damage
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} found a lamp with a damaged cable, could they explain the danger and what a fuse in the fuse box would do if the wires touched?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: How Light Travels and How We See
topics.description: Pupils distinguish luminous and illuminated objects, show that light travels in straight lines (Lichtstrahl model), explain seeing with the sender–receiver model (light must enter the eye), and explain images in a pinhole camera.
evidence: Classifies objects as light sources or illuminated bodies
Explains with a ray diagram why we see a book in a lit room but not in total darkness
Explains why a pinhole camera image is upside down
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} claimed 'we see because our eyes send out rays', could they explain with a diagram what really happens when we see a tree?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Reflection, Scattering and Absorption
topics.nameDe: Reflexion, Streuung und Absorption von Licht
topics.description: Pupils explain the appearance of objects by directed reflection (mirror), scattering (white paper) and absorption (black cloth), and justify why reflectors and light clothing protect pedestrians and cyclists in the dark.
evidence: Distinguishes directed reflection and scattering with examples
Explains why black objects look black
Justifies why a reflector makes a cyclist visible to drivers
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} cycled home in the dark in November, could they explain why reflectors and a light jacket make them visible to a car driver?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Sound, Pitch and Loudness
topics.description: Pupils explain sound as vibration, relate pitch to frequency (Hz) and loudness to amplitude, change both on string and wind instruments, and distinguish audible sound, ultrasound (bats, medicine) and infrasound.
evidence: Shows that every sound source vibrates
Changes pitch and loudness on an instrument and explains the cause
Gives examples of ultrasound in nature and medicine
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} shortened a vibrating guitar string or plucked it harder, could they explain what changes in the sound and why?
topics.laenderNotes: Sound and light are NRW Physik Erprobungsstufe content; BW teaches acoustics and optics in Physik from Kl. 7.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Sound Transmission and Noise Protection
topics.description: Pupils explain with the particle model that sound needs a medium, describe reflection (echo) and absorption of sound, measure sound levels in decibels with a smartphone app, and evaluate noise-protection measures for health.
evidence: Explains why there is no sound in a vacuum
Measures sound levels at school and relates them to health risks
Proposes and justifies noise-protection measures for a classroom or street
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measured the noise in the school canteen with a phone app, could they judge whether it is harmful and suggest ways to make it quieter?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Shadows
topics.description: Pupils construct shadows with straight light rays, predict how shadow size changes with distance, and explain core shadow (Kernschatten) and half shadow (Halbschatten) with two light sources.
evidence: Constructs a shadow with rays and predicts its size when the object moves
Explains core and half shadow with two lamps
Explains why shadows have the shape of the object
