topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} stood between two lamps on a stage, could they draw why they see one dark and two lighter shadows?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Breathing and Gas Exchange
topics.description: Pupils describe the airways and lungs, explain chest and abdominal breathing with a lung model (bell jar), and explain gas exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the alveoli as another case of surface enlargement.
evidence: Labels trachea, bronchi, lungs and alveoli
Explains inhalation using the diaphragm model
Describes the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between alveoli and blood
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} played with a bell-jar lung model, could they explain what the rubber sheet stands for and why the balloons fill with air?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Heart, Blood and Circulation
topics.description: Pupils explain the heart as a double pump with atria, ventricles and valves, trace the body and lung circulation through arteries, capillaries and veins, describe blood components and their tasks, and measure pulse and breathing rate at rest and after exercise.
evidence: Traces the path of a red blood cell through lung and body circulation on a diagram
Names blood components and the task of each
Collects and graphs pulse data before and after exercise and explains the increase
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measured their pulse before and after running up the stairs, could they explain why it rises and what the blood is transporting faster?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Smoking and Addiction Prevention
topics.description: Pupils explain how nicotine, tar and carbon monoxide damage lungs, heart and blood vessels (including e-cigarettes), what addiction means, and develop strategies to say no under peer pressure; legal age limits come from the Jugendschutzgesetz.
evidence: Names three harmful substances in cigarette smoke and their effects
Explains what makes nicotine addictive
Role-plays or writes a convincing refusal strategy for a peer-pressure situation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If an older pupil offered {{name}} a vape at the bus stop, could they explain what it does to the body and how to say no without losing face?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Digestion
topics.description: Pupils follow food through mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine, explain the division of labour between organs, model enzymes as 'scissors' that break nutrients into small building blocks, and explain the villi as surface enlargement for absorption into the blood.
evidence: Orders the digestive organs and states what happens in each
Explains with a simple model how enzymes break down starch
Explains why the folded small intestine absorbs nutrients efficiently
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} chewed a piece of bread for a long time and noticed it tasting sweet, could they explain what is happening and what happens to the bread afterwards?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Food Chains, Webs and Decomposers
topics.description: Pupils build food chains and webs for a native habitat with producers, consumers and decomposers (earthworm, fungi, bacteria), and explain leaf-litter decomposition as nature's recycling that closes the cycle of materials.
evidence: Draws a food chain and a food web for a forest with correct arrow direction
Assigns organisms to producers, consumers and decomposers
Explains what happens to fallen leaves and why this matters for the forest
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wondered why the forest floor does not pile up metres high with leaves, could they explain who breaks them down and what happens to the nutrients?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Introduction to Photosynthesis
topics.description: Pupils state photosynthesis as a word equation (water + carbon dioxide → glucose + oxygen, using light energy in chloroplasts) and explain why it is the basis of food and oxygen for animals and humans.
evidence: Writes the word equation of photosynthesis with light energy and chlorophyll
Explains where the plant's substances come from (air and water, not soil)
Explains why animals depend on plants for food and oxygen
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked where the wood of a huge oak tree comes from, could they explain that it is built mostly from air and water using sunlight?
topics.laenderNotes: NRW requires the word equation in Kl. 5/6; BW BNT 5/6 only covers the energy chain Sun → plant → human, formal photosynthesis follows in Biologie from Kl. 7.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Fertilisation, Pregnancy and Birth
topics.description: Pupils compare egg and sperm, describe fertilisation, the development of embryo and foetus, birth, risks to the unborn child (alcohol, smoking), and basic methods of contraception for responsible life planning.
evidence: Describes fertilisation and implantation in the right order
Describes key stages of embryo and foetus development and of birth
Explains why a pregnant woman should avoid alcohol and smoking, and names two contraceptive methods
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw ultrasound pictures from different months of a pregnancy, could they describe what is developing and why the mother avoids alcohol?
topics.laenderNotes: Contraception is explicit in NRW Kl. 5/6 (IF3) but not in BW BNT 5/6 (3.1.6), where it follows in later grades.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Sex Organs and the Menstrual Cycle
topics.description: Pupils name the male and female sex organs with correct terms and functions, explain egg and sperm cell production, describe the menstrual cycle (ovulation, menstruation) in outline, and reflect on respectful language about sexuality.
evidence: Labels the male and female sex organs on diagrams and states their functions
Describes the phases of the menstrual cycle and when ovulation happens
Uses correct terms instead of slang and explains why respectful language matters
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked by a younger sibling what a 'period' is, could they explain it correctly and respectfully in simple words?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Simple Particle Model
topics.description: Pupils learn that substances consist of tiny moving particles and use this model to explain the three states, changes of state, dissolving and diffusion; they discuss where the model differs from reality (particles are not small balls of the substance).
evidence: Draws particle diagrams for solid, liquid and gas and explains the differences
Explains dissolving of sugar in tea with the particle model
Names one limitation of the particle model
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} noticed that a drop of ink spreads faster in hot water than in cold water, could they explain this with the particle model?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Amphibians and Their Protection
topics.description: Using frog and toad, pupils describe the metamorphosis from spawn to tadpole (gills) to frog (lungs and skin breathing), explain why amphibians depend on water and moist habitats, and discuss threats and protection such as toad-crossing fences (Krötenzäune) during spring migration.
evidence: Orders and describes the stages of frog development, including the change in breathing
Explains why amphibians need both water and land habitats
Names two threats to native amphibians and a protection measure
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw volunteers setting up a low fence along a road in March, could they explain what it is for and why toads are at risk?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Insects: Body Plan and Metamorphosis
topics.description: Using bee or May beetle, pupils describe the insect body plan (head, thorax, abdomen; six legs; exoskeleton; tracheae), compare it with vertebrates, and distinguish complete (egg–larva–pupa–adult) and incomplete metamorphosis.
evidence: Labels the three body sections and states two differences to a vertebrate
Orders the stages of complete metamorphosis for a butterfly or beetle
Distinguishes complete and incomplete metamorphosis with an example each
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} found a caterpillar and a grasshopper nymph, could they explain how each develops into an adult and which one has a pupa stage?
topics.laenderNotes: Invertebrates are a BW BNT section (3.1.7); NRW Biologie 5/6 focuses on vertebrates and seed plants.

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Reptiles Adapted to Land
topics.description: Using native examples (Zauneidechse, Ringelnatter) pupils explain how reptiles are independent of water: dry horny scales, lung breathing, internal fertilisation and shelled eggs. As cold-blooded animals they warm up in the sun.
evidence: Names three reptile features that allow life away from water
Compares reptile and amphibian skin, breathing and eggs
Explains why a lizard basks in the sun in the morning
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} found a lizard sunning itself on a warm wall, could they explain why it does this and why, unlike a frog, it can live in a dry place?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: How Animals Survive Winter
topics.description: Pupils distinguish the German triad Winterschlaf (hedgehog, dormouse: body temperature drops sharply), Winterruhe (squirrel, badger: wakes to feed) and Winterstarre/Kältestarre (frog, lizard: cold-blooded, body temperature follows surroundings), plus winter fur, fat reserves and bird migration.
evidence: Assigns hedgehog, squirrel and frog to the correct overwintering strategy
Explains each strategy in terms of body temperature and energy use
Explains why only warm-blooded animals can hibernate in the strict sense
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} found a hedgehog asleep under leaves in January and a squirrel digging up nuts, could they explain the difference between how the two animals survive winter?
topics.laenderNotes: The three-way Winterschlaf/Winterruhe/Winterstarre distinction is a standard German textbook topic (BW BNT 3.1.4(12); BB Naturwissenschaften 5/6 Themenfeld 3.3 'Die Sonne als Energiequelle').

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Comparing the Vertebrate Classes
topics.description: Pupils compare fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals by skin covering, breathing, body temperature (wechselwarm/gleichwarm) and reproduction, assign unknown species to a class by criteria and see the order as a hint of evolutionary relationship.
evidence: Completes a comparison table of the five classes for skin, breathing, body temperature and reproduction
Assigns borderline animals (whale, bat, penguin, salamander) to the correct class with reasons
Distinguishes cold-blooded and warm-blooded animals
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were told that whales live in the sea and look like fish, could they use the class criteria to prove that whales are mammals?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Energy Forms and Conversion Chains
topics.description: Pupils describe energy chains in nature (Sun → plant → human) and technology (power station → household), distinguish fossil and renewable energy carriers, understand that energy is converted rather than used up, and derive energy-saving rules such as Stoßlüften and switching off devices.
evidence: Draws an energy conversion chain for a given device or food chain
Classifies energy carriers as fossil or renewable
Derives and justifies three energy-saving rules for school or home
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} ate a bowl of muesli and then cycled to school, could they trace the energy back to the Sun in a chain of conversions?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Temperature versus Heat
topics.description: Pupils distinguish temperature (how hot a body is, measured in °C) from heat (energy transferred from a hotter to a colder body) and describe temperature equalisation until thermal equilibrium, using everyday technical language precisely.
evidence: Uses 'temperature' and 'heat' correctly in explanations
Predicts the final temperature trend when hot and cold water are mixed
Explains why a metal spoon in hot tea gets warm
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} left a cup of hot cocoa on the table, could they explain where the heat goes and when the cooling stops?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Thermal Expansion
topics.description: Pupils observe that solids, liquids and gases expand when heated, explain this with the particle model, give technical examples (expansion joints on bridges, bimetal strip) and describe the anomaly of water (densest at 4 °C) and why lakes freeze from the top.
evidence: Explains thermal expansion with the particle model
Gives two technical examples where expansion must be considered
Explains why fish survive the winter at the bottom of a frozen lake
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw gaps between sections of a railway bridge, could they explain why engineers build them and what would happen without them?

topics.subject: Naturwissenschaften
topics.name: Heat Transfer and Insulation
topics.description: Pupils distinguish the three ways heat travels – Wärmeleitung (conduction), Wärmemitführung (convection) and Wärmestrahlung (radiation) – and explain insulation in houses, thermos flasks, clothing and animal fur or feathers.
evidence: Assigns everyday situations (radiator, sunbathing, hot pan handle) to the correct type of heat transfer
Tests materials for insulation in a fair comparison
Explains how a thermos flask or a bird's plumage reduces heat loss
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared a woolly hat and a thin cap on a cold day, could they explain which type of heat transfer the hat reduces and why trapped air helps?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Moon Phases and Eclipses
topics.description: Using straight-line propagation of light and a Sun–Earth–Moon model, pupils explain the lunar phases as changing views of the half-lit Moon and explain solar and lunar eclipses as shadows, including why eclipses are rare.
evidence: Explains a phase (e.g. waxing crescent) with a sketch of Sun, Earth and Moon positions
Explains solar and lunar eclipses with umbra and penumbra
Explains why there is not an eclipse every month (tilted lunar orbit)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a half moon in the evening sky, can they show with a ball and a lamp where Sun, Earth and Moon are?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Solar System and Gravity
topics.description: Pupils describe the structure of the solar system (Sun, planets, moons, comets, asteroid belt), explain that gravity holds it together and keeps planets on their orbits, and explain weightlessness in the ISS as free fall rather than missing gravity.
evidence: Orders the planets and describes differences between rocky planets and gas giants
Explains that gravity between masses keeps moons and planets on their orbits
Explains why astronauts in the ISS float although gravity there is almost as strong as on the ground
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told that "there is no gravity in space", can they correct this using the example of the ISS and the Moon?
topics.laenderNotes: An obligatory Inhaltsfeld in NRW (IF6 Sterne und Weltall); in most other Länder astronomy is optional or part of Erdkunde.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Stars, Light-Years and Stellar Evolution
topics.description: Stars are suns at enormous distances measured in light-years. Pupils describe the main stages of a star's life (from gas cloud via main sequence to red giant and white dwarf, or supernova for massive stars) and how spectra and parallax tell us about stars.
evidence: Explains the light-year as a distance and compares distances to the Moon, the Sun and the nearest star
Describes the life cycle of a Sun-like star and of a massive star
Names spectra and parallax as ways astronomers learn about composition and distance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that the light of a star took 600 years to reach us, can they explain what this means and that the star might have changed since?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Electric Charge and the Electron Model
topics.description: Bodies become charged when electrons are transferred by rubbing; like charges repel, unlike charges attract. Pupils explain the electroscope, describe the forces between charges with an electric field, and use the electron–ion-core model (Elektronen-Atomrumpf-Modell) to explain charging and why metals conduct.
evidence: Explains charging by rubbing as a transfer of electrons and predicts attraction or repulsion
Explains how an electroscope shows charge
Explains with the electron–ion-core model why metals conduct and insulators do not
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} rubs a balloon on their hair and it then sticks to the wall, can they explain what happened with electrons?
topics.laenderNotes: Berlin-Brandenburg (7/8) and Bayern (NuT 7, Kl. 9 elementary charge) teach electrostatics early; NRW places it in IF9 Elektrizität.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Mechanical Energy and Its Conservation
topics.description: Pupils identify potential (Lageenergie), kinetic (Bewegungsenergie) and elastic energy (Spannenergie) in processes such as a swing, a trampoline or a roller coaster, draw energy-flow diagrams, and explain that the total energy is conserved while some is converted into thermal energy.
evidence: Names the energy forms at each point of a pendulum swing or trampoline jump
Draws an energy-flow diagram for a bouncing ball including thermal energy
Explains with energy conservation why a ball never bounces back to its starting height
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches a roller coaster, can they explain where it has most potential and most kinetic energy and why the second hill must be lower than the first?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Density
topics.description: Density is mass per volume (ρ = m/V, in g/cm³ or kg/m³) and characterises a substance. Pupils determine densities of regular and irregular bodies (displacement method), identify materials from a density table and convert units.
evidence: Calculates the density of a body from measured mass and volume
Determines the volume of an irregular stone by displacement and then its density
Uses a density table to identify a material and converts g/cm³ into kg/m³
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a shiny ring, can they find out by measuring whether it could be made of gold?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern places density in Natur und Technik 7 and Berlin-Brandenburg in 7/8; BW teaches it in BNT 5/6.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Simple Machines and the Golden Rule
topics.nameDe: Einfache Maschinen und Goldene Regel der Mechanik
topics.description: Levers, fixed and loose pulleys, block and tackle and the inclined plane reduce the force needed but increase the distance: force × distance stays the same (Goldene Regel der Mechanik). Pupils apply the lever law F₁·a₁ = F₂·a₂ and justify the golden rule with energy conservation.
evidence: Calculates a missing force or lever arm with the lever law
Explains for a block and tackle with four rope sections why the force is quartered and the rope distance quadrupled
Justifies the golden rule with conservation of energy
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to lift a heavy stone with a crowbar, can they explain where to place the pivot and calculate the force needed?
topics.laenderNotes: Required in NRW (IF7), BW (3.2.7) and Berlin-Brandenburg (7/8); not a separate topic in Bayern or Niedersachsen.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Speed and Uniform Motion
topics.description: Speed is distance per time (v = s/t). Pupils calculate speeds, convert between m/s and km/h, distinguish average from instantaneous speed, and read and draw position–time graphs for uniform motion, where the slope is the speed.
evidence: Calculates speed, distance or time with v = s/t and converts km/h into m/s (factor 3.6)
Distinguishes the average speed of a journey from the speed shown on a speedometer
Reads speeds from the slope of a position–time graph and draws the graph for a described journey
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} cycles 6 km to school in 20 minutes, can they work out their average speed in km/h and m/s and sketch the position–time graph?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Forces, Deformation and Hooke's Law
topics.description: Forces are recognised by their effects: they deform bodies or change their motion. Force is measured in newton with a spring balance (Federkraftmesser), which works because the extension of a spring is proportional to the force (Hooke's law, F = D·s) within its elastic range. Forces are drawn as arrows with point of application, direction and length.
evidence: Names the two kinds of effects of forces with examples (deformation, change of speed or direction)
Draws a force as an arrow to scale and measures forces with a spring balance
Measures the extension of a spring and decides whether Hooke's law holds, including its limit
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hangs more and more weights on a rubber band and on a steel spring, can they explain which one follows Hooke's law and how a spring balance uses this?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Mass and Weight
topics.description: Mass (kg) is a property of a body that measures its inertia and does not depend on location; weight (N) is the gravitational force on it, F_G = m·g, with the local gravitational field strength (Ortsfaktor) g ≈ 9.81 N/kg on Earth and 1.62 N/kg on the Moon.
evidence: Explains why an astronaut's mass stays the same on the Moon while the weight changes
Calculates weights with F_G = m·g for Earth and other celestial bodies
Measures mass with a balance and weight with a spring balance and relates the two
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that a rover "weighs 900 kg", can they explain what is wrong with the wording and calculate its weight on Earth and on Mars?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Inertia: Newton's First Law
topics.description: A body stays at rest or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed unless a net force acts on it. Pupils use the principle of inertia to explain everyday situations such as seat belts, a tablecloth trick or why a spacecraft needs no engine to keep moving.
evidence: States the principle of inertia and corrects the idea that motion needs a force
Explains with inertia why passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes
Identifies whether the forces on a body are balanced from its state of motion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} says "the ball stops because its force is used up", can they explain with the principle of inertia what really slows it down?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Action–Reaction and Balanced Forces
topics.description: Forces always come in pairs: if A pushes B, B pushes A with an equal and opposite force (actio = reactio). Pupils distinguish such interaction pairs, which act on two different bodies, from two balanced forces acting on the same body.
evidence: Names the partner force for a given force (e.g. foot pushes ground – ground pushes foot)
Explains why interaction forces do not cancel each other out
Distinguishes the equilibrium of weight and table force on a book from the interaction pair book–Earth
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} jumps off a small boat onto the jetty, can they explain why the boat moves backwards?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Law of Reflection and Mirror Images
topics.nameDe: Reflexionsgesetz und Bild am ebenen Spiegel
topics.description: At a mirror the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal (Einfallslot). With this law and straight-line propagation pupils construct where the virtual mirror image lies and explain its properties (same size, same distance, left–right swapped).
evidence: Measures angles of incidence and reflection from the normal and states the law
Constructs the mirror image of a point and of a simple object with rays
Explains why the image is virtual and appears as far behind the mirror as the object is in front
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} stands 2 m in front of a mirror, can they draw where their image appears and explain with the law of reflection why it is there?
topics.laenderNotes: Taught in Kl. 8 in Bayern, 7/8 in BW, already in Kl. 5/6 in Niedersachsen and in Kl. 9/10 in Berlin-Brandenburg (Themenfeld Optische Instrumente).

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Analysing Measurement Series
topics.description: Evaluate a measurement series by plotting it with axis labels and units, drawing a line of best fit (Ausgleichsgerade) and checking proportionality via constant quotients (Quotientengleichheit). From the slope the pupil reads off a physical constant such as a spring constant or a resistance.
evidence: Plots a measurement table as a graph with the dependent variable on the y-axis, labelled axes and units
Checks proportionality both by constant quotients and by a straight line through the origin
Determines a constant (e.g. D in F = D·s) from the slope of the line of best fit and states it with its unit
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures how far a spring stretches for five different weights, can they draw the graph, decide whether stretch is proportional to force and work out the spring constant from it?
topics.laenderNotes: Spreadsheet evaluation of data is explicitly required in NRW (IF7) and in the KMK 2024 standards (digital tools).

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Magnetic Fields of Currents and Electromagnets
topics.description: A current produces a magnetic field (Oersted). Pupils draw the field lines around a straight wire and a coil using the right-hand rule, explain why an iron core strengthens a coil, and describe applications of electromagnets such as relays, door openers and scrap cranes.
evidence: Draws the circular field lines around a wire and determines their direction
Explains the field of a coil as the superposition of the fields of its windings and compares it with a bar magnet
Explains how a relay uses an electromagnet to switch a second circuit
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} winds a wire around a nail and connects a battery, can they explain why the nail now picks up paper clips and how to make it stronger?
topics.laenderNotes: BW (3.2.4) and Niedersachsen teach electromagnets in 7/8; Bayern in Kl. 10 (Elektromagnetismus).

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Electrical Power and Energy Costs
topics.description: Electrical power is P = U·I and the energy transferred is E = P·t, usually given in kilowatt-hours. Pupils read rating plates, calculate the energy use and running costs of appliances from a tariff, and compare devices for a purchase decision.
evidence: Calculates power from voltage and current and reads it from a rating plate
Calculates the yearly energy use in kWh and the cost of an appliance
Compares two appliances (e.g. fridges of different energy-label classes) with physical and other criteria
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s games console uses 150 W for 3 hours a day, can they work out what it costs per year?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Household Wiring and Electrical Safety
topics.description: Pupils describe how a home circuit is built (phase, neutral and protective earth conductor, Schuko socket, fuses and circuit breakers, residual-current device/FI-Schutzschalter) and explain how these protect people and wiring. They relate the danger of current to its size and path through the body.
evidence: Explains the role of the protective earth conductor in a device with a metal case
Explains how a circuit breaker and a residual-current device (FI) protect against different dangers
Explains why the current through the body, not the voltage alone, determines the danger
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees that the bathroom has an FI switch, can they explain what it does and why it is required there?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Calculating Series and Parallel Circuits
topics.description: In series circuits the current is the same and voltages add (R = R₁ + R₂); in parallel circuits the voltage is the same and currents add (1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂). Pupils calculate total resistance, currents and voltages for circuits with two or three resistors and explain household circuits as parallel connections.
evidence: Calculates the total resistance of two resistors in series and in parallel
Determines all currents and voltages in a circuit with three resistors
Explains why household appliances are connected in parallel
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} connects two identical lamps once in series and once in parallel to the same battery, can they predict and explain which are brighter?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Voltage
topics.description: Voltage (unit volt) describes how much energy each unit of charge transfers: it is the "drive" of the current, produced by separating charges in a battery or generator. Pupils measure voltage with a voltmeter connected in parallel and use the loop rule for series circuits.
evidence: Connects a voltmeter in parallel to a component and reads the voltage
Explains voltage as energy per charge, e.g. why a 9 V battery transfers more energy per charge than a 1.5 V cell
Applies the loop rule to the voltages across components in a series circuit
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} connects two 1.5 V batteries in series to a torch, can they predict and measure the voltage across the lamp?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Electric Current
topics.description: Electric current is the flow of charge per time (I = Q/t, unit ampere). Pupils measure current with an ammeter connected in series and explain that current is the same everywhere in an unbranched circuit and splits at junctions (junction rule).
evidence: Connects an ammeter in series and reads the current with the correct range
Explains with the charge-flow model that no current is "used up" in a lamp
Applies the junction rule to find an unknown current in a parallel circuit
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} thinks that the current is weaker after the lamp than before it, can they test and correct this idea with two ammeters?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Resistance and Ohm's Law
topics.description: The resistance of a component is defined as R = U/I (unit ohm). Ohm's law states that for metal wires at constant temperature the current is proportional to the voltage, so R is constant. Pupils record U–I characteristics and distinguish ohmic resistors from lamps whose resistance rises when they heat up.
evidence: Calculates resistance, voltage or current with R = U/I
Records the U–I characteristic of a resistor and of a lamp and interprets both
Explains the difference between the definition of resistance and Ohm's law
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures the current through a bulb at different voltages, can they decide whether it obeys Ohm's law and explain the result?
topics.laenderNotes: Kl. 8 in Bayern, 7/8 in Niedersachsen and Berlin-Brandenburg; BW is qualitative in 7/8 and quantitative in 9/10.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: What Resistance Depends On
topics.description: The resistance of a wire grows with its length, falls with its cross-section and depends on the material: R = ρ·l/A, and for metals it rises with temperature. Pupils plan experiments with controlled variables to find these dependencies and explain why cables are thick and heating wires thin.
evidence: Plans an experiment that varies only the length (or cross-section) of a wire
Uses R = ρ·l/A to compare wires of different materials
Explains why extension cables for high power must have a large cross-section
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to choose between a thin and a thick extension cable for a heater, can they justify the choice with resistance?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Mechanical Work
topics.description: Work is done when a force moves a body along its direction: W = F·s, measured in joule (1 J = 1 N·m). Work is energy transferred mechanically. Pupils distinguish lifting work, acceleration work and friction work and recognise that no work is done when carrying a bag horizontally.
evidence: Calculates the lifting work to carry a bag up stairs
Explains that work transfers energy and equals the change of energy
Explains why holding a heavy box still is tiring but no physical work is done
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} carries a 10 kg crate up to the third floor, can they calculate the work done and say into which energy form it went?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Power
topics.description: Power is energy transferred per time (P = E/t = W/t, unit watt). Pupils calculate the power of people climbing stairs, of motors and of appliances, compare them, and distinguish power (kW) from energy (kWh).
evidence: Measures their own power when running up stairs
Calculates power, energy or time with P = E/t
Explains the difference between kW and kWh with an example
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} and a friend run up the same stairs, can they find out who has the greater power and explain why it is not simply the faster one?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Efficiency and Energy Degradation
topics.description: In every real energy converter part of the energy ends up as thermal energy that can hardly be used any more (Energieentwertung). The efficiency η = useful energy / supplied energy describes the quality of a converter. Pupils compare LED and incandescent lamps, electric and combustion engines, and draw Sankey diagrams.
evidence: Calculates the efficiency of a device from supplied and useful energy or power
Draws a Sankey diagram for a car engine or a power station
Explains why energy is conserved yet we still speak of "energy loss"
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares a 60 W bulb and a 7 W LED that are equally bright, can they explain the difference with efficiency?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Buoyancy and Archimedes' Principle
topics.description: A body in a fluid experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the displaced fluid (Archimedes). Pupils derive buoyancy from the pressure difference between top and bottom, calculate it, and decide from buoyancy and weight (or densities) whether a body sinks, floats or hovers, e.g. a ship, a submarine or a hot-air balloon.
evidence: Calculates the buoyant force with F_A = ρ_fluid·g·V
Explains buoyancy as the difference of hydrostatic pressure forces on top and bottom
Predicts whether a body sinks, hovers or rises by comparing buoyant force and weight
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wonders why a steel ship floats while a steel nail sinks, can they explain it with Archimedes' principle?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Acceleration and Free Fall
topics.description: Acceleration is the change of velocity per time (a = Δv/Δt). Pupils describe uniformly accelerated motion with velocity–time graphs, use v = a·t and s = ½·a·t², and explain free fall as motion with g ≈ 9.81 m/s² that is independent of mass when air resistance is negligible.
evidence: Calculates an acceleration from a change of speed and the time taken
Reads acceleration as the slope and distance as the area in a velocity–time graph
Explains with the vacuum tube experiment why a feather and a coin fall equally fast without air
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} drops a stone into a well and hears it hit the water after 2 s, can they estimate how deep the well is and what assumptions they made?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern and Niedersachsen introduce acceleration in Kl. 7/8; BW (3.3.5) fixes it in Kl. 10, Berlin-Brandenburg in 9/10; NRW and NI deepen it in the Einführungsphase.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Pressure and Hydraulics
topics.description: Pressure is force per area (p = F/A, unit pascal; 1 bar = 100 000 Pa). Pupils explain why snowshoes or sharp knives work, use the particle model for pressure in gases and liquids, and explain how a hydraulic press or brake multiplies force because the pressure spreads evenly.
evidence: Calculates pressures in Pa and bar and compares a stiletto heel with a flat shoe
Explains gas pressure with particles hitting the walls of a container
Calculates the output force of a hydraulic lift from the two piston areas
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a car being lifted in a garage by a small pump, can they explain with pressure how such a small force can lift it?
topics.laenderNotes: Obligatory in NRW (IF8 Druck und Auftrieb); Berlin-Brandenburg covers gas pressure in 7/8; not in the BW and Niedersachsen Gymnasium plans; optional NTG profile in Bayern.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Adding and Resolving Forces
topics.description: Forces are vectors. Pupils add forces acting along a line and at an angle with a scale drawing (Kräfteparallelogramm) to find the resultant, and resolve a force into components, e.g. the weight on an inclined plane into a downhill and a normal component.
evidence: Adds two forces in the same and opposite directions and states the resultant
Constructs the resultant of two forces at an angle with a force parallelogram to scale
Resolves the weight of a sledge on a slope into components parallel and perpendicular to the slope
topics.assessmentPrompt: If two friends pull a boat with ropes at an angle, can {{name}} construct the total force on the boat with a scale drawing?
topics.laenderNotes: BW treats forces at an angle only in Kl. 10 (3.3.5); Bayern adds velocity arrows in Kl. 8.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Hydrostatic and Air Pressure
topics.description: The weight of liquid or air above a point causes pressure that increases with depth: in water p = ρ·g·h (about 1 bar per 10 m). Air pressure is about 1 bar at sea level and falls non-linearly with height. Pupils explain diving, ear pressure, drinking straws and barometers.
evidence: Calculates the hydrostatic pressure at a given depth with p = ρ·g·h
Explains why air pressure decreases non-linearly with height using the particle model
Explains why a dam wall is thicker at the bottom
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} dives to the bottom of a 4 m deep pool and feels pressure in their ears, can they explain where it comes from and how big it is?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Eye and Vision Defects
topics.description: The eye forms a real, inverted image on the retina; the lens changes its focal length to focus (Akkommodation). Pupils explain short-sightedness and long-sightedness and why diverging or converging spectacle lenses correct them.
evidence: Labels the optical parts of the eye and explains where the image is formed
Explains accommodation as a change of the lens's focal length
Draws why a short-sighted eye needs a diverging lens and a long-sighted eye a converging lens
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s friend can read but not see the board clearly, can they explain what is wrong with the image in the eye and which glasses help?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Refraction of Light
topics.description: When light passes from air into water or glass it changes direction at the boundary: towards the normal when entering the optically denser medium, away from it when leaving. Pupils measure the angles and explain everyday effects such as the "broken" straw or a pool looking shallower.
evidence: Draws the refracted ray at an air–glass boundary bending towards the normal and at glass–air away from it
Measures pairs of angles of incidence and refraction and describes the qualitative relation
Explains with a ray diagram why a straw in water looks bent
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a coin at the bottom of a glass of water, can they draw why it seems higher than it really is?
topics.laenderNotes: Snell's law (Brechungsgesetz with sine) is quantitative in some Länder (e.g. BW Kl. 7/8 optional, Bayern Oberstufe); most Sek I plans keep refraction qualitative.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Colour: Spectrum and Colour Mixing
topics.description: A prism splits white light into the spectrum because each colour is refracted differently (Dispersion); infrared and ultraviolet lie beyond the visible ends. Coloured objects absorb part of the spectrum. Pupils distinguish additive colour mixing of light (RGB, screens) from subtractive mixing of pigments (CMYK, printing).
evidence: Explains the spectrum behind a prism and places infrared and ultraviolet next to it
Explains the colour of a red T-shirt in white and in green light by absorption and reflection
Predicts additive mixtures (red + green = yellow) and explains why screens use RGB but printers CMYK
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} zooms into a phone screen showing yellow, can they explain why they only see red and green dots?
topics.laenderNotes: Colours and colour mixing appear already in Natur und Technik 7 in Bayern; BW places the prism in 7/8.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Optical Instruments
topics.description: Pupils explain how a camera, magnifying glass, microscope and telescope use one or two lenses to form images, and judge what these instruments made possible in research and everyday life.
evidence: Explains how a camera or projector produces a sharp real image on a sensor or screen
Describes the magnifying glass as a lens used inside its focal length
Explains the two-lens principle of microscope or telescope (objective and eyepiece)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks through a telescope, can they explain why two lenses are needed and what each does?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Image Formation by Converging Lenses
topics.description: Converging lenses focus parallel light in the focal point (Brennpunkt); diverging lenses spread it. Pupils construct images with the three principal rays (Parallel-, Mittelpunkt-, Brennpunktstrahl), describe how image size and position change with object distance, and use the lens equation 1/f = 1/g + 1/b where the Land requires it.
evidence: Identifies converging and diverging lenses by shape and by their effect on parallel light
Constructs the image of an object with the principal rays and states whether it is real, inverted, enlarged or reduced
Predicts how the image changes when the object moves towards the focal point and checks this on the optical bench
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} moves a candle closer to a magnifying lens, can they predict with a ray diagram what happens to the image on the screen?
topics.laenderNotes: BW treats lenses qualitatively; Berlin-Brandenburg uses the lens equation in Kl. 9/10; Niedersachsen introduces lenses already in Kl. 5/6. NRW stresses construction and simulation.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Total Internal Reflection
topics.description: Light going from glass or water into air is fully reflected above the critical angle (Grenzwinkel). Pupils explain how optical fibres (Glasfaserkabel), endoscopes and reflecting prisms use this effect.
evidence: States that total internal reflection only occurs from the optically denser into the less dense medium
Demonstrates the critical angle with a semicircular glass body and a light ray
Explains how light is guided through a bent optical fibre
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that the internet travels "as light through glass", can they explain why the light does not escape from the fibre?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Measurement Uncertainty
topics.description: Every measurement has an uncertainty: pupils distinguish random scatter from systematic errors, repeat measurements and use the mean, estimate the reading uncertainty of an instrument, and give results with a sensible number of significant digits.
evidence: Distinguishes random errors (scatter of repeated readings) from systematic errors (e.g. zero offset of a scale)
Calculates the mean of repeated measurements and states a range such as t = (2,4 ± 0,1) s
Rounds a calculated result to a number of digits that matches the precision of the input values
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} times a falling ball five times and gets slightly different values, can they explain why, give a mean with an uncertainty and suggest how to measure more precisely?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Uses of Ionising Radiation
topics.nameDe: Medizinische und technische Anwendungen ionisierender Strahlung
topics.description: Pupils explain how X-ray imaging, CT, radioactive tracers (e.g. PET, thyroid scans), radiotherapy and sterilisation of food or instruments use ionising radiation, and weigh benefits and risks for patients and staff.
evidence: Explains how an X-ray image is formed by different absorption in tissues and bones
Explains why tracers for medical diagnosis need a short half-life
Weighs benefits and risks of an application with physical and medical arguments
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a broken arm X-rayed, can they explain why bones show up white and why the staff leave the room?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Atomic Nuclei and Isotopes
topics.description: The atomic nucleus consists of protons and neutrons (nucleons) and is tiny compared with the atom (Rutherford's scattering experiment). Pupils read nuclide notation, explain isotopes as nuclei with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, and use the chart of nuclides (Nuklidkarte).
evidence: Explains what Rutherford's gold-foil experiment showed about the atom
Reads mass number, atomic number and neutron number from nuclide notation such as ¹⁴C
Explains what isotopes are and finds them on the chart of nuclides
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads about "carbon-12" and "carbon-14", can they explain what is the same and what is different about these atoms?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Radioactive Decay and Half-Life
topics.description: Radioactive decay is random for a single nucleus but statistically predictable for many: after each half-life half of the remaining nuclei have decayed. Pupils model decay with dice, read half-lives from decay curves and apply them to radiocarbon dating and to the storage time of radioactive waste.
evidence: Explains why the decay of a single nucleus cannot be predicted but that of many nuclei can
Determines the half-life from a measured or simulated decay curve
Calculates the remaining fraction after several half-lives and applies it to C-14 dating
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that a substance has a half-life of 30 years, can they explain how much of it is left after 90 years and whether it is then "gone"?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Nuclear Fusion and the Sun
topics.description: Light nuclei such as hydrogen isotopes fuse into helium and release energy; this powers the Sun and other stars. Pupils explain why fusion needs extremely high temperatures and describe the idea and challenges of fusion reactors (e.g. ITER, Wendelstein 7-X).
evidence: Describes the fusion of hydrogen to helium in the Sun
Explains why fusion requires temperatures of millions of degrees
Compares fusion and fission as energy sources by fuel, waste and technical maturity
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that fusion is "the energy of the stars", can they explain what happens in the Sun and why we cannot simply copy it yet?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Nuclear Fission and Nuclear Power
topics.description: Heavy nuclei such as U-235 can split after absorbing a neutron, releasing energy and further neutrons. Pupils explain the controlled chain reaction in a reactor (moderator, control rods, cooling), its risks and the problem of long-term storage of waste, and assess information from different interest groups, including the German nuclear phase-out (2023) and the search for a repository.
evidence: Describes a fission reaction and explains why a chain reaction can occur
Explains the roles of moderator, control rods and coolant in a reactor
Compares arguments of different groups on nuclear power and waste storage and states a reasoned position
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that Germany switched off its last nuclear plants in 2023 while other countries build new ones, can they explain how a reactor works and weigh the arguments?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Detecting Radiation and Activity
topics.description: Ionising radiation can be detected with a Geiger–Müller counter, a cloud chamber or a film badge. Pupils measure count rates, subtract the natural background (Nullrate), and explain the activity of a source in becquerel (decays per second).
evidence: Explains how a Geiger–Müller counter detects radiation
Measures the background count and corrects a measured count rate for it
Explains the unit becquerel and why activity is not the same as danger
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} switches on a Geiger counter in the classroom and it ticks without any source, can they explain why and how to deal with it in a measurement?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Quarks and Leptons
topics.description: Protons and neutrons are made of up and down quarks; electrons and neutrinos are leptons. Pupils describe matter as built from a few elementary particles and explain beta decay as a quark changing its type.
evidence: Explains the quark composition of proton (uud) and neutron (udd) and checks the charges
Names electron and neutrino as leptons
Explains β⁻ decay as the change of a down quark into an up quark
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked what a proton is made of, can they answer with quarks and show that the charges add up?
topics.laenderNotes: Quarks are part of Sek I in Bayern (Kl. 10) and BW (9/10); NRW introduces them in the Grundkurs; other Länder do not require them.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Radiation Dose and Protection
topics.description: Ionising radiation can damage cells and DNA. Pupils compare the effective dose (sievert) from natural sources, medical imaging and flights, judge limits critically, and apply the protection rules distance, shielding, short exposure time and avoiding incorporation.
evidence: Explains how ionising radiation can damage living cells
Compares typical doses (natural background in Germany, X-ray, CT, flight) in mSv
Applies the rules of radiation protection to a concrete situation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs a CT scan and is worried about radiation, can they compare its dose with the natural yearly dose and weigh benefit against risk?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Alpha, Beta and Gamma Radiation
topics.description: Unstable nuclei decay and emit alpha particles (helium nuclei), beta particles (electrons) or gamma radiation (high-energy photons). Pupils compare range, penetrating power, ionising effect and deflection in fields, write simple decay equations, and compare them with X-rays.
evidence: Describes what each type of radiation consists of and how it is produced in the nucleus
Compares the penetrating power of α, β and γ radiation (paper, aluminium, lead)
Writes a decay equation for an α or β decay and checks mass and charge numbers
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} must choose a shield for an alpha and for a gamma source, can they explain what material and thickness are needed?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Force on a Current and the Electric Motor
topics.description: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force (Lorentz force) perpendicular to current and field. Pupils determine its direction with a hand rule (e.g. conductor swing), and explain how a DC motor uses this force with a commutator to keep rotating.
evidence: Predicts the direction of the force on a conductor swing with a hand rule
Explains the role of the commutator in a DC motor
Names ways to make a motor turn faster or reverse its direction
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} takes apart a small toy motor, can they point out magnet, coil and commutator and explain why it turns?
topics.laenderNotes: BW teaches the motor in 7/8, Bayern in Kl. 10, Berlin-Brandenburg in 9/10.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Generator and Alternating Voltage
topics.description: A generator turns a coil in a magnetic field (or a magnet in a coil), which continuously changes the field and induces an alternating voltage. Pupils describe the sine-shaped voltage, its period and frequency (50 Hz in the European grid) and compare generator and motor as reverse processes.
evidence: Explains why a rotating coil produces a voltage that changes direction
Reads period, frequency and peak voltage from an oscilloscope or data-logger graph
Compares the energy conversion in a generator with that in a motor
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} turns the crank of a hand generator connected to a lamp, can they explain why it gets harder to turn when the lamp lights up?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Semiconductors: Diode, LED and Solar Cell
topics.description: Semiconductors conduct better when warm or illuminated and can be doped. Pupils describe the diode as a one-way valve for current, record its characteristic curve, and explain LEDs and solar cells as semiconductor devices that convert between electrical energy and light.
evidence: Shows that a diode conducts in one direction only and draws its characteristic curve
Explains why an LED needs a series resistor
Explains the energy conversion in a solar cell and how its power depends on the light
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} connects an LED the wrong way round and it stays dark, can they explain why?
topics.laenderNotes: Part of BW 3.3.2 and Niedersachsen Elektrik II (9/10); NTG profile in Bayern Kl. 10; not required in NRW.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Electromagnetic Induction
topics.description: A voltage is induced in a coil whenever the magnetic field through it changes, e.g. by moving a magnet or switching a current. The induced voltage is larger for faster changes, more windings and stronger fields. Pupils name applications such as induction hobs, wireless charging and bicycle dynamos.
evidence: Shows with a coil, magnet and voltmeter that only a change of the field induces a voltage
Names the factors that increase the induced voltage
Explains an everyday application such as wireless phone charging with induction
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} pushes a magnet into a coil and holds it still, can they explain when the meter shows a voltage and when not?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Transformer and Power Transmission
topics.description: A transformer changes alternating voltages: U₁/U₂ ≈ N₁/N₂ for an ideal transformer. Pupils explain why it only works with AC and why electrical energy is transmitted at high voltage: for the same power the current is smaller and the energy lost as heat in the lines (P = I²·R) drops.
evidence: Calculates output voltage or number of windings with the transformer equation
Explains why a transformer does not work with direct current
Explains with P = U·I and P_loss = I²·R why transmission lines use 380 kV
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees high-voltage power lines, can they explain why the electricity is not simply sent at 230 V?
topics.laenderNotes: Niedersachsen treats motor, generator and transformer only as "black boxes" in Sek I.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Energy Storage
topics.description: Wind and solar energy fluctuate, so a sustainable supply needs storage and flexible grids. Pupils compare pumped-storage plants, batteries, hydrogen (power-to-gas) and heat storage by capacity, efficiency and time scale and calculate simple storage examples.
evidence: Explains why the supply of solar and wind energy fluctuates over a day and a year
Calculates the energy stored in a pumped-storage reservoir with E = m·g·h
Compares two storage technologies by capacity, efficiency and time scale
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that "we need storage for the dark doldrums (Dunkelflaute)", can they explain the problem and compare two ways to store energy?
topics.laenderNotes: Emphasised by the KMK 2024 standards (nachhaltige Energieversorgung, insbesondere Energiespeicherung).

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Power Stations and Energy Sources
topics.description: Pupils explain how thermal, hydro, wind and solar power stations provide electrical energy, compare conventional and renewable sources by efficiency, CO₂ emissions, availability and cost, and discuss the German Energiewende (coal and nuclear phase-out) with physics arguments.
evidence: Describes the energy conversion chain in a coal or gas power station and in a wind turbine
Compares at least three energy sources by criteria such as efficiency, CO₂ and availability
Takes a reasoned position on a local energy question (e.g. a wind farm) and separates facts from values
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s town debates a new wind farm, can they explain how it produces electricity and argue for or against it with physics facts?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern treats energy supply as project work in Kl. 11; NRW IF11 and BW 3.3.2 in Kl. 9/10.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Calculating Mechanical Energy
topics.description: Pupils calculate potential energy E = m·g·h, kinetic energy E = ½·m·v² and elastic energy E = ½·D·s², and solve problems with energy balances, e.g. the speed at the bottom of a slide or the height a ball reaches when thrown upwards.
evidence: Calculates E_pot and E_kin with correct units
Uses an energy balance to find the speed at the bottom of a slide without friction
Explains why doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy and the braking distance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} goes down a 5 m water slide, can they use energy conservation to estimate their speed at the bottom and explain why the real value is lower?
topics.laenderNotes: Quantitative in Kl. 9 in Bayern, Kl. 7/8 (E_pot) and 10 in BW, Kl. 9/10 in Niedersachsen.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Newton's Second Law
topics.description: A net force accelerates a body: F = m·a. Pupils calculate accelerations, forces and braking distances, explain why heavier vehicles need more force for the same acceleration, and connect the law to the change of momentum F·Δt = m·Δv.
evidence: Calculates the acceleration of a body from net force and mass
Determines the net force from all forces on a body before applying F = m·a
Explains with F = m·a why a fully loaded lorry brakes less quickly than an empty one
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a car of 1 200 kg brakes with a force of 6 000 N, can {{name}} work out the deceleration and how long it takes to stop from 50 km/h?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern introduces it in Kl. 8 as F·Δt = m·Δv; BW places it in Kl. 10; NRW and Niedersachsen formalise it in the Einführungsphase (Kl. 11).

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Friction
topics.description: Friction opposes relative motion. Pupils distinguish static, sliding and rolling friction, use F_R = μ·F_N with tabulated coefficients, and discuss where friction is wanted (tyres, brakes) and where it is reduced (bearings, lubrication).
evidence: Distinguishes static, sliding and rolling friction with examples
Measures the sliding friction of a block with a spring balance and calculates μ
Explains why ABS keeps tyres rolling instead of sliding to shorten the braking distance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} pulls a box across a floor, can they explain why it is harder to start it moving than to keep it moving?
topics.laenderNotes: Berlin-Brandenburg teaches friction in 9/10 (Themenfeld Newton); NRW in the Einführungsphase; Bayern only mentions it in Kl. 8; Niedersachsen has no separate friction content.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
topics.description: Visible light is a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum, which ranges from radio and mobile-phone radiation via microwaves, infrared, visible and ultraviolet to X-rays and gamma rays. Pupils order the ranges by wavelength and energy, name uses and risks, and know that sensors (thermal cameras, UV meters) detect what our senses cannot.
evidence: Orders radio, microwave, infrared, visible, UV and X-ray radiation by wavelength
Names a use and a health consideration for at least four ranges (e.g. Wi-Fi, IR camera, sunburn, X-ray)
Explains that thermal cameras show infrared radiation emitted by warm bodies
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that mobile-phone radiation and X-rays are "both radiation", can they place both in the spectrum and explain why only one is ionising?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Earth's Radiation Budget and Greenhouse Effect
topics.description: Earth absorbs short-wave solar radiation and emits long-wave infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit part of the infrared, which raises the surface temperature (natural greenhouse effect); more CO₂ strengthens this (anthropogenic effect). Pupils also discuss albedo (Rückstrahlvermögen) and tipping elements.
evidence: Draws a simple radiation balance with incoming solar and outgoing infrared radiation
Explains the difference between the natural and the anthropogenic greenhouse effect
Explains with albedo why melting sea ice amplifies warming (feedback)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears someone say "the greenhouse effect is bad", can they explain why without any greenhouse effect Earth would be frozen, and what changes when CO₂ increases?
topics.laenderNotes: New binding content in the KMK 2024 standards (Klimaphysik); older Länder plans place it in Erdkunde or as an optional physics context.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Evaluating Technology with Criteria
topics.description: Pupils follow a structured evaluation procedure for a physics-related decision (e.g. heat pump or gas boiler, a phone charger, radiation protection): collect physics and non-physics criteria, weigh them, separate the factual judgement (Sachurteil) from the value judgement (Werturteil) and reflect on the decision.
evidence: Lists physical criteria (efficiency, power, risk) and non-physical criteria (cost, environment, comfort) for a decision
Weighs the criteria explicitly and justifies a decision
Separates statements of fact from value judgements in a discussion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has to advise their family whether a balcony solar module is worth it, can they list criteria, weigh them and explain which parts of their advice are facts and which are opinions?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Physical Models and Their Limits
topics.description: Physics explains with models (light ray, particle model, electron–ion-core model, field lines) that are made for a purpose. Pupils say which aspect of reality a model represents, use it to predict, and name where it fails, e.g. the ray model cannot explain diffraction.
evidence: Names for a given model (e.g. light ray) what it represents and what it leaves out
Uses a model to make a prediction and compares it with an experiment
Gives an example where a model fails and a better model is needed
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked whether light "really consists of rays", can they explain that the ray is a model, what it is good for and where it reaches its limits?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Changing Internal Energy: Work and Heat
topics.nameDe: Erster Hauptsatz: Änderung der inneren Energie
topics.description: The internal energy of a body can be changed by heat transfer or by work: ΔU = Q + W. Pupils explain heating by friction or compression (bicycle pump, air pump) and cooling by expansion (spray can), and recognise this as energy conservation for thermal processes.
evidence: Explains why a bicycle pump gets warm when compressing air
States the first law and applies it to compression and expansion examples
Explains why a spray can gets cold when used
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} rubs their hands together and later uses a deodorant spray, can they explain both temperature changes with internal energy?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Gas Pressure and the Gas Laws
topics.description: For a fixed amount of gas pressure, volume and absolute temperature are linked: p·V = const at constant temperature (Boyle–Mariotte), V/T = const at constant pressure and p/T = const at constant volume. Pupils explain these relations with the particle model and apply them to tyres, balloons and syringes.
evidence: Explains with the particle model why pressure rises when a gas is compressed or heated
Calculates a new pressure or volume with p·V = const or p/T = const
Explains why the absolute temperature must be used in the gas laws
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} pumps up bike tyres in a cold garage and then rides in the sun, can they explain what happens to the tyre pressure?
topics.laenderNotes: Niedersachsen (9/10) and Bayern (gas pressure, Kl. 9) treat gas laws; Berlin-Brandenburg covers gas pressure in 7/8; NRW and BW do not require them.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Internal Energy and Absolute Temperature
topics.description: In the particle model, temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles and internal energy is the total energy of all particles. Pupils explain the absolute zero, use the Kelvin scale and distinguish temperature, internal energy and heat (Wärme) as transferred energy.
evidence: Explains temperature with the motion of particles and why there is a lowest possible temperature
Converts between °C and K
Distinguishes temperature, internal energy and heat in an example (bathtub vs cup of tea)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares a cup of hot tea with a lukewarm bathtub, can they explain which has the higher temperature and which more internal energy?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Specific Heat Capacity
topics.description: The energy needed to heat a substance depends on mass, temperature change and the material: ΔE = c·m·ΔT. Pupils measure c for water with an immersion heater, calculate heating energies and costs, and explain why water is a good heat store and moderates the climate.
evidence: Calculates the energy needed to heat water for a shower
Determines the specific heat capacity of water from a heating experiment and discusses losses
Explains with the high c of water why coastal climates are milder
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} boils 1 litre of water in a 2 kW kettle, can they estimate how long it takes and why it actually takes a bit longer?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Heat Engines and Heat Pumps
topics.description: Heat engines (petrol engine, steam turbine, Stirling engine) convert part of the internal energy of a hot gas into mechanical work; the rest must be released at lower temperature, which limits the efficiency. A heat pump works the other way round and moves energy from cold outside air into a warm house using electrical work.
evidence: Describes the cycle of a four-stroke engine or Stirling engine with energy flows
Explains why no heat engine can have an efficiency of 100 %
Explains why a heat pump can deliver more heat than the electrical energy it uses
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s family considers a heat pump, can they explain how it "pumps" heat from cold air into the house?
topics.laenderNotes: Niedersachsen uses the Stirling engine and cycles in 9/10; in most Länder heat engines are a context for energy degradation rather than a separate unit. Not part of the Oberstufe in the five Länder checked.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Momentum and Its Conservation
topics.description: Momentum p = m·v is a vector quantity; in a closed system the total momentum is conserved. Pupils explain recoil and rocket propulsion, use F·Δt = Δp for impacts, and apply conservation in one and two dimensions.
evidence: Calculates momentum and states its direction
Uses conservation of momentum to calculate the recoil speed of a cannon or skater
Explains with F·Δt = Δp why airbags and crumple zones reduce forces
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} throws a heavy ball while standing on a skateboard, can they predict how fast they roll backwards?
topics.laenderNotes: Kl. 10 in Bayern and BW, Einführungsphase in NRW; not in the Niedersachsen and Berlin-Brandenburg Gymnasium plans.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions
topics.description: In collisions momentum is always conserved, kinetic energy only in elastic ones. Pupils calculate final velocities for perfectly inelastic collisions, analyse elastic collisions on an air track, and determine how much kinetic energy is converted.
evidence: Calculates the common velocity after a perfectly inelastic collision
Checks with measured data whether a collision on an air track was elastic
Calculates the kinetic energy converted into other forms in an inelastic collision
topics.assessmentPrompt: If two bumper cars collide and stick together, can {{name}} work out how fast they move afterwards and how much energy went into deformation?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Horizontal Projectile Motion
topics.description: A horizontal throw is the superposition of a uniform horizontal motion and free fall (Unabhängigkeitsprinzip). Pupils derive the parabolic path, calculate range, flight time and impact velocity, and analyse throws with video analysis.
evidence: Splits the motion into independent x- and y-components and writes the equations x(t) and y(t)
Calculates flight time and range for a ball rolling off a table
Evaluates a video recording of a throw and compares it with the model
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} kicks a ball horizontally off a 1.25 m high wall at 8 m/s, can they work out where it lands?
topics.laenderNotes: Kl. 10 in Bayern, BW and Berlin-Brandenburg (9/10); Einführungsphase (Kl. 11) in NRW and Niedersachsen. The oblique throw is optional in most Länder.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Newton's Law of Gravitation
topics.description: Any two masses attract each other with F = G·m₁·m₂/r². Pupils explain weight as a special case, calculate the field strength g at different heights, and describe the gravitational field with field lines as a model for action at a distance.
evidence: Calculates the gravitational force between Earth and Moon with the law of gravitation
Derives the local value of g at the Earth's surface and at the height of the ISS
Draws the field lines of the Earth's gravitational field and explains the field model
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that the ISS orbits at 400 km height, can they calculate how much weaker gravity is there and explain why astronauts still float?
topics.laenderNotes: Einführungsphase in NRW and Bayern (Kl. 11), Q1 in Berlin-Brandenburg; not in the BW and Niedersachsen plans.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Kepler's Laws and Satellite Orbits
topics.description: Planets move on ellipses with the Sun at one focus, sweep out equal areas in equal times and obey T²/a³ = constant. Pupils derive the third law for circular orbits from gravitation, calculate orbital periods of satellites (e.g. geostationary orbit) and trace the change from the geocentric to the heliocentric world view.
evidence: States Kepler's three laws and explains why planets are faster near the Sun
Derives T²/r³ = const for circular orbits from gravitation as centripetal force
Calculates the radius of a geostationary orbit
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wonders why a TV satellite seems to hang still in the sky, can they calculate how high it must be?
topics.laenderNotes: NRW Einführungsphase and Bayern 11 (as independent project work); Berlin-Brandenburg only in the Leistungskurs; not in BW and Niedersachsen.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Circular Motion and Centripetal Force
topics.description: In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the direction changes, so a centripetal force F_Z = m·v²/r = m·ω²·r towards the centre is needed. Pupils describe the motion with period, frequency and angular velocity and identify which force acts as centripetal force (rope, friction, gravity).
evidence: Calculates period, frequency, angular velocity and orbital speed of a circular motion
Identifies the force providing the centripetal force in a car in a bend or a chain carousel
Calculates the centripetal force and explains why "centrifugal force" is an inertial effect
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} swings a bucket of water in a vertical circle, can they explain why the water stays in and how fast the bucket must go?
topics.laenderNotes: BW (3.3.5) and Berlin-Brandenburg teach it in Kl. 10; NRW, Niedersachsen and Bayern in Kl. 11 (Einführungsphase). Not part of the KMK Abitur standards, which start with fields.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Planning Experiments and Error Analysis
topics.description: Plan an experiment from a theory-based hypothesis, choose measuring methods (incl. digital data logging and video analysis), linearise non-linear relations for evaluation and analyse how measurement uncertainties affect the result. This is the Oberstufe form of experimental work required for the Abitur.
evidence: Derives a testable hypothesis from theory and plans which quantities to vary, measure and keep constant
Linearises a relation (e.g. plots T² against l) to determine a constant from the slope with a regression tool
Estimates the uncertainty of a result from the input uncertainties and discusses whether the hypothesis is supported
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to find g with a pendulum, can they plan the measurement, evaluate it with a suitable linear plot and say how precise their value is?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Postulates of Special Relativity
topics.description: Einstein's two postulates state that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames and that the speed of light is the same for all observers. Pupils explain how the Michelson–Morley result supports the constancy of c and why simultaneity becomes relative.
evidence: States the two postulates of special relativity
Explains why adding velocities "classically" fails for light
Explains with a thought experiment (train and lightning) why simultaneity depends on the observer
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} imagines shining a torch forward from a very fast rocket, can they explain why the light is not faster than c?
topics.laenderNotes: Only a suggested extension in the KMK standards. NRW (Einführungsphase) and Bayern (Kl. 11 project work) treat it for all; Berlin-Brandenburg only in the Leistungskurs; BW as an elective topic; absent in Niedersachsen.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Time Dilation and Length Contraction
topics.description: Using a light clock and Pythagoras, pupils derive that moving clocks run slow by the factor γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) and that moving lengths contract. They apply this to muons from cosmic rays and to the corrections needed for GPS satellites.
evidence: Derives the time dilation factor with a light clock
Explains why cosmic-ray muons reach the ground despite their short lifetime
Calculates time dilation for a satellite or particle and judges when it matters
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that GPS would be wrong by kilometres without relativity, can they explain which effect is responsible?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Harmonic Oscillations
topics.description: An oscillation is harmonic when the restoring force is proportional to the displacement; then the displacement follows a sine function y(t) = ŷ·sin(ω·t). Pupils describe amplitude, period, frequency and phase, record oscillations with sensors and link the motion to the projection of a circular motion.
evidence: Reads amplitude, period and frequency from a recorded oscillation graph
Explains why a linear restoring force leads to a harmonic oscillation
Writes the equation y(t) for a given oscillation and relates ω to the frequency
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} records the motion of a mass on a spring with a phone sensor, can they read off its period and write down the equation of motion?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern starts oscillations and waves in Kl. 11; NRW and Niedersachsen in the Qualifikationsphase.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Huygens' Principle and Interference
topics.description: Every point of a wavefront is the source of an elementary wave (Huygens). Pupils explain diffraction at gaps and obstacles, and interference of two coherent sources with path differences: constructive for Δs = k·λ and destructive for Δs = (2k+1)·λ/2, demonstrated in a ripple tank and with sound.
evidence: Explains diffraction behind a narrow gap with Huygens' principle
Determines constructive and destructive interference from the path difference
Explains the interference pattern of two loudspeakers or two ripple-tank sources
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} walks between two loudspeakers playing the same tone, can they explain why it gets quieter and louder at certain places?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Spring and Simple Pendulums
topics.description: The period of a spring pendulum is T = 2π·√(m/D), that of a simple pendulum for small angles T = 2π·√(l/g). Pupils test the formulas experimentally, explain why the period of a simple pendulum does not depend on the mass, and analyse the energy changes during the oscillation.
evidence: Calculates the period of a spring or simple pendulum
Checks experimentally how the period depends on mass, spring constant or length
Describes the conversion between kinetic and potential (or elastic) energy during one period
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants a pendulum clock to tick once per second, can they calculate how long the pendulum must be?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Standing Waves
topics.description: Two waves of equal frequency travelling in opposite directions form a standing wave with nodes and antinodes. Pupils explain the possible wavelengths on a string fixed at both ends and in air columns (L = k·λ/2) and apply this to musical instruments and microwave ovens.
evidence: Explains how a standing wave forms by reflection and superposition
Calculates the possible frequencies of a guitar string from its length and wave speed
Measures the wavelength of a standing wave (e.g. microwave or sound tube) from node distances
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} presses a guitar string at half its length, can they explain why the tone is one octave higher?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Mechanical Waves
topics.nameDe: Mechanische Wellen: Kenngrößen, Transversal- und Longitudinalwellen
topics.description: A wave transports energy but not matter by coupled oscillators. Pupils use wavelength, frequency and propagation speed (c = λ·f), distinguish transverse from longitudinal waves and explain that only transverse waves can be polarised, with examples from ropes, sound and light (polarising filters).
evidence: Calculates wavelength, frequency or speed with c = λ·f
Distinguishes transverse and longitudinal waves and gives an example of each
Explains polarisation with two polarising filters and why sound cannot be polarised
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at an LCD screen through polarising sunglasses and turns their head, can they explain what they see?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Mass Defect and Binding Energy
topics.description: A nucleus has less mass than its separate nucleons; the mass defect corresponds to the binding energy via E = m·c². The binding energy per nucleon curve explains why fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei both release energy.
evidence: Calculates the mass defect and binding energy of a nucleus from tabulated masses
Explains the shape of the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve and its maximum near iron
Explains with the curve why both fission and fusion release energy
