topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at the binding-energy curve, can they explain why uranium is split but hydrogen is fused to gain energy?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Kl. 13 at both levels; NRW Leistungskurs (E = mc² also in the Grundkurs); not in Niedersachsen and Berlin-Brandenburg.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Standard Model of Particle Physics
topics.description: All known matter consists of six quarks and six leptons; three fundamental interactions (strong, weak, electromagnetic) are mediated by exchange particles (gluons, W/Z bosons, photons), and the Higgs field gives particles mass. Pupils describe beta decay with the weak interaction and know how particle accelerators such as those at CERN test the model.
evidence: Sorts elementary particles into quarks, leptons and exchange bosons
Assigns the four interactions to their exchange particles and examples
Describes β⁻ decay as a weak process with a W⁻ boson in a simple diagram
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears about the discovery of the Higgs boson at CERN, can they explain where it fits into the Standard Model?
topics.laenderNotes: Not binding in the KMK standards; Bayern treats it with beta decay in Kl. 13, BW as an elective deepening topic in the Leistungsfach, NRW touches quarks in the Grundkurs.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Law of Radioactive Decay
topics.description: The number of undecayed nuclei falls exponentially: N(t) = N₀·e^(−λt), with decay constant λ = ln 2 / T½, and the activity is A = λ·N. Pupils fit measured decay data, determine half-lives (e.g. radon or a protactinium generator), and use the law for dating.
evidence: Derives the relation λ = ln 2 / T½ and converts between them
Determines the half-life from measured count rates with a logarithmic plot or regression
Calculates the age of a sample from its remaining activity
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures the count rate of a short-lived source every 20 s, can they determine its half-life with the decay law?
topics.laenderNotes: Only a suggested extension in the KMK standards. Taught at both levels in Bayern (13) and Niedersachsen; in NRW only in the Leistungskurs; not in the Berlin-Brandenburg Q-phase.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Trajectories of Charged Particles
topics.nameDe: Bahnen geladener Teilchen: e/m, Wien-Filter, Massenspektrometer
topics.description: Pupils calculate the paths of charged particles in homogeneous fields: parabolas in transverse electric fields and circles in magnetic fields with r = m·v/(q·B). They determine the specific charge e/m with the fine-beam tube (Fadenstrahlrohr) and explain velocity filters and mass spectrometers as applications.
evidence: Derives the radius of the circular path from Lorentz force = centripetal force
Determines e/m of the electron from fine-beam tube data
Explains how a Wien filter selects one speed and how a mass spectrometer separates isotopes
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures the radius of the glowing electron circle in a fine-beam tube, can they calculate the specific charge of the electron?
topics.laenderNotes: The KMK standards put quantitative trajectories at eA. NRW (Grundkurs) and Bayern (both levels) nevertheless determine e/m with the fine-beam tube, and Bayern and Niedersachsen teach the Wien filter at both levels.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Coulomb's Law and Electric Potential
topics.description: The force between two point charges is F = q₁·q₂/(4π·ε₀·r²). Pupils describe the radial field of a point charge, define the electric potential as energy per charge relative to a zero level, and interpret voltage as a potential difference, including equipotential lines.
evidence: Calculates the force between two charges with Coulomb's law and compares it with gravity
Defines the potential and draws equipotential lines for a point charge and a plate capacitor
Explains voltage as a potential difference and calculates the work on a charge moved in the field
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares the electric and gravitational force between two electrons, can they calculate both and explain the result?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Electric Field Strength
topics.description: The electric field strength is the force per charge on a test charge, E = F/q, in N/C = V/m. In the homogeneous field of a plate capacitor E = U/d. Pupils measure forces on charged bodies and use the Millikan experiment to show that charge is quantised in multiples of the elementary charge e.
evidence: Calculates field strength, force or charge with E = F/q
Uses E = U/d for a plate capacitor and explains why the field inside is homogeneous
Explains how the Millikan experiment shows that charge comes in multiples of e = 1.6·10⁻¹⁹ C
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sets up a plate capacitor with 2 000 V across 4 cm, can they calculate the field strength and the force on a charged oil droplet?
topics.laenderNotes: The Millikan experiment is part of the NRW Grundkurs and the Berlin-Brandenburg Q1; Bayern introduces the elementary charge already in Kl. 9.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Field Concept
topics.description: A field describes how space around a charge, magnet or mass is changed so that forces act at a distance. Pupils compare electric, magnetic and gravitational fields, use field lines as a model (direction, density, sources) and discuss what the model can and cannot show.
evidence: Draws the field lines of a point charge, a dipole, a plate capacitor and a bar magnet
Explains what direction and density of field lines mean
Compares the electric, magnetic and gravitational field by sources and kind of force
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked how the Sun "knows" where the Earth is, can they explain the field idea and its limits?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Magnetic Flux Density
topics.description: The strength of a magnetic field is described by the flux density B, defined by the force on a current-carrying conductor, F = I·l·B (unit tesla). Pupils measure B with a current balance or a Hall probe and investigate the field of a long coil, B = μ₀·μ_r·N·I/l.
evidence: Determines B from the force on a conductor in a current balance
Investigates how the field inside a long coil depends on current, number of turns and length
Uses a Hall probe or app sensor to measure magnetic flux density
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} uses the magnetometer in a phone near a coil, can they explain what B measures and how it depends on the current?
topics.laenderNotes: The Hall effect itself is eA/Leistungskurs content in NRW, Niedersachsen, Berlin-Brandenburg and BW; Bayern treats it at both levels.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Faraday's Law and Lenz's Rule
topics.description: The induced voltage equals the rate of change of the magnetic flux Φ = B·A through the coil times the number of turns: U = −N·ΔΦ/Δt (eA: −N·dΦ/dt). The minus sign expresses Lenz's rule: the induced current opposes its cause, as in eddy-current brakes and the jumping ring.
evidence: Calculates the induced voltage for a changing B-field and for a changing area
Explains with Lenz's rule why a magnet falls slowly through a copper tube
Interprets a measured U(t) graph as the derivative of a Φ(t) graph
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} drops a magnet through a copper pipe and it falls slowly, can they explain why with Lenz's rule?
topics.laenderNotes: The KMK standards require the differential form only at eA; gA courses work with difference quotients.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Capacitor and Capacitance
topics.description: A capacitor stores charge and electrical energy. Its capacitance is C = Q/U; for a plate capacitor C = ε₀·ε_r·A/d. The stored energy is E = ½·C·U². Pupils measure the charge with a charge amplifier or by integrating a discharge current and discuss capacitors as short-term energy stores (camera flash, supercaps).
evidence: Calculates capacitance, charge or voltage with C = Q/U and for a plate capacitor
Explains how a dielectric and the plate geometry change the capacitance
Calculates the energy stored in a capacitor and compares it with a battery
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at the capacitor in a camera flash, can they work out how much energy it stores and why the flash is so bright for such a short time?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Charging and Discharging a Capacitor
topics.description: When a capacitor discharges through a resistor, current and voltage fall exponentially: U(t) = U₀·e^(−t/RC). Pupils record charging and discharging curves with a data logger, determine the time constant τ = R·C, and get the charge as the area under the I–t curve.
evidence: Records a discharge curve and determines the time constant τ = R·C
Describes the charging and discharging curves with exponential functions
Determines the stored charge from the area under the current–time graph
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures how the voltage of a discharging capacitor falls over time, can they find R·C from the graph and predict when only 1 % is left?
topics.laenderNotes: Grundkurs content in NRW, Bayern and Niedersachsen; only Leistungsfach/Leistungskurs in BW and Berlin-Brandenburg.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Lorentz Force on Moving Charges
topics.description: A charge moving through a magnetic field experiences the Lorentz force F = q·v·B, perpendicular to velocity and field. Pupils explain qualitatively why charged particles move on circular or helical paths (fine-beam tube, aurora, Earth's magnetic shield) and determine directions with a hand rule.
evidence: Calculates the Lorentz force on an electron moving perpendicular to B
Determines the direction of deflection of electrons and positive ions with a hand rule
Explains qualitatively why the path in a homogeneous B-field is a circle and how the aurora forms
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a picture of the northern lights, can they explain with the Lorentz force why they appear near the poles?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Self-Induction and Inductance
topics.description: A coil opposes changes of its own current because the changing field induces a voltage in it: U = −L·dI/dt. Pupils explain delayed switching-on and voltage spikes when switching off, calculate the inductance of a long coil and the energy stored in its magnetic field.
evidence: Explains why a lamp in series with a coil lights up with a delay
Explains the high voltage when switching off a coil (e.g. in an ignition coil)
Calculates the inductance of a long coil and the energy E = ½·L·I²
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a spark when unplugging a motor, can they explain it with self-induction?
topics.laenderNotes: eA/Leistungskurs in NRW and Niedersachsen; Bayern teaches it at both levels; BW has one example in the Basisfach.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Accelerating Charges in Electric Fields
topics.description: A charge accelerated through a voltage U gains kinetic energy q·U = ½·m·v². Pupils calculate electron speeds in an electron gun, use the electron-volt as energy unit, and describe qualitatively the parabolic path in a transverse field.
evidence: Calculates the final speed of an electron after acceleration through a given voltage
Converts energies between joule and electron-volt
Explains qualitatively the path of an electron entering a transverse electric field
topics.assessmentPrompt: If an electron in an old TV tube is accelerated by 20 kV, can {{name}} calculate its speed and check whether it is still well below the speed of light?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Photoelectric Effect
topics.description: Light can release electrons from a metal only above a threshold frequency, however bright it is; the electrons' maximum energy grows linearly with frequency. Pupils explain why the wave model fails here and how Einstein's photon idea, h·f = W_A + E_kin, explains the observations.
evidence: Describes the Hallwachs experiment and the key observations of the photoelectric effect
Explains which observations contradict the wave model of light
Uses Einstein's equation to calculate the work function or the maximum electron energy
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that red light cannot discharge a zinc plate however bright it is, but weak UV light can, can they explain why?
topics.laenderNotes: Grundkurs content in NRW, BW and Berlin-Brandenburg; Bayern and Niedersachsen treat the photoelectric effect only at eA and determine h at gA with LEDs or the X-ray spectrum.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Photons and Planck's Constant
topics.description: Light energy is transferred in quanta (photons) with E = h·f and momentum p = h/λ. Pupils determine h, for example from the onset voltages of LEDs of different colours or with the counter-field method, and calculate photon energies and numbers for lasers and lamps.
evidence: Calculates the energy of a photon of given wavelength in J and eV
Determines Planck's constant from LED onset voltages or counter-field data
Estimates how many photons per second a 1 mW laser pointer emits
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures at which voltage red, green and blue LEDs start to glow, can they use the data to determine Planck's constant?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: X-Ray Spectra
topics.description: An X-ray tube produces a continuous bremsstrahlung spectrum with a sharp short-wavelength limit (Duane–Hunt law, λ_min = h·c/(e·U)) and characteristic lines of the anode material. Pupils explain both parts and determine h from the cut-off; eA courses add Bragg reflection on crystals.
evidence: Explains how bremsstrahlung and characteristic lines are produced in an X-ray tube
Uses the Duane–Hunt law to calculate the limiting wavelength or Planck's constant
Explains why the characteristic lines identify the anode material
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} increases the voltage of an X-ray tube, can they predict how the spectrum changes and why?
topics.laenderNotes: Not named in the KMK standards; Grundkurs in NRW, both levels in Bayern, eA/Leistungskurs in Niedersachsen and Berlin-Brandenburg, absent in BW.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Relativistic Momentum and E = mc²
topics.description: At speeds close to c, momentum and energy grow without limit: p = γ·m·v and E = γ·m·c², so no massive particle reaches c. Pupils use the rest energy E₀ = m·c² and the relativistic energy of electrons in accelerators, and explain why a cyclotron fails for very fast particles.
evidence: Explains why the speed of light cannot be reached by accelerating a particle
Calculates the speed of an electron accelerated through 1 MV relativistically and classically and compares
Uses E₀ = m·c² to relate rest mass and energy
topics.assessmentPrompt: If an electron gains 1 MeV in an accelerator, can {{name}} show that the classical formula would give a speed faster than light, and correct it?
topics.laenderNotes: Leistungskurs in NRW (cyclotron) and Berlin-Brandenburg; Bayern treats relativistic momentum at both levels in Kl. 12.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Damped and Forced Oscillations, Resonance
topics.description: Real oscillations lose energy (damping). A periodically driven oscillator responds most strongly when the driving frequency matches its natural frequency (resonance). Pupils compare mechanical and electrical oscillators energetically, record resonance curves and discuss wanted and dangerous resonance (radio tuning, bridges, buildings in earthquakes).
evidence: Describes the exponential decay of amplitude in a damped oscillation
Records a resonance curve and explains how damping changes it
Explains a case of resonance catastrophe and how engineers prevent it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches a video of the Tacoma Narrows bridge, can they explain resonance and why soldiers break step on bridges?
topics.laenderNotes: Berlin-Brandenburg treats damping and resonance qualitatively already in Kl. 9/10.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Double Slit and Diffraction Grating
topics.description: Light passing a double slit or a grating produces interference maxima at sin α = k·λ/g. Pupils measure the wavelength of laser light, explain the spectra of white light behind a grating, and use a grating spectrometer to compare light sources; this shows the wave nature of light.
evidence: Derives the condition for maxima at a double slit or grating from the path difference
Determines the wavelength of a laser from measured maxima positions
Explains the spectrum of white light behind a grating and why red is diffracted most
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} shines a laser pointer through a CD acting as a grating, can they measure the pattern and calculate the laser's wavelength?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern starts double-slit interference in Kl. 11; the grating and X-ray diffraction follow in Kl. 12.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Single-Slit Diffraction
topics.description: Light passing a single slit produces a broad central maximum and minima at sin α = k·λ/b. Pupils derive the minima by dividing the slit into zones, explain the narrowing of the pattern for wider slits, and relate it to the resolution limit of optical instruments.
evidence: Derives the condition for minima at a single slit
Determines a slit width from the measured pattern
Explains why the double-slit pattern is modulated by the single-slit envelope
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a laser beam through a narrowing slit, can they explain why the light spreads out more instead of less?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Electromagnetic Waves
topics.description: An oscillating circuit opened up into an antenna (Hertzian dipole) emits electromagnetic waves: coupled electric and magnetic fields travelling at the speed of light. Pupils explain how radio, mobile phones and microwaves use them, place them in the spectrum and show reflection, polarisation and interference with microwaves.
evidence: Describes the dipole as an open oscillating circuit and the fields it emits
Calculates the wavelength of a radio or Wi-Fi signal from its frequency
Demonstrates polarisation or interference of microwaves and explains the result
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a Wi-Fi router's antennas, can they estimate the wavelength used and explain how the signal is produced?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern treats electromagnetic waves at both levels in Kl. 12; the Hertzian dipole is Leistungskurs/Leistungsfach content in NRW and BW.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Interferometers
topics.description: An interferometer splits a light beam, sends the parts along different paths and recombines them; tiny path changes shift the interference pattern. Pupils explain the Michelson interferometer, measure small lengths or refractive indices, and know its role in the Michelson–Morley experiment and gravitational-wave detectors.
evidence: Explains the beam paths in a Michelson interferometer
Calculates a length change from the number of shifted fringes
Explains how LIGO uses an interferometer to detect gravitational waves
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that LIGO measures length changes smaller than a proton, can they explain the principle of the interferometer?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The LC Oscillating Circuit
topics.description: In a circuit of capacitor and coil, energy swings between the electric field of the capacitor and the magnetic field of the coil. Pupils describe the analogy with a spring pendulum, use Thomson's formula T = 2π·√(L·C), and explain why real circuits are damped.
evidence: Describes the energy exchange between capacitor and coil over one period
Calculates the frequency of an LC circuit with Thomson's formula
Draws the analogy between LC circuit and spring pendulum quantity by quantity
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} tunes an old radio, can they explain that they are changing the frequency of an oscillating circuit?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: A Quantum Model of the Atom
topics.description: Pupils explain why Bohr's model of fixed orbits fails and describe the atom with a quantum model in which electrons occupy states with certain energies and probability distributions (orbitals). They relate the model to line spectra and to the structure of the periodic table (eA: Pauli principle).
evidence: Names successes and failures of Bohr's atomic model
Describes an orbital as a region of high probability density, not an orbit
Explains qualitatively how the quantum model explains discrete energy levels
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s chemistry book shows electron shells and the physics book shows orbitals, can they explain how the two pictures are related?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Electron Diffraction and the de Broglie Wavelength
topics.description: Electrons passing through a graphite foil produce diffraction rings like waves. Their de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/p. Pupils determine the wavelength from the ring diameters, check λ ∝ 1/√U, and explain why electron microscopes resolve smaller details than light microscopes.
evidence: Explains the rings in the electron diffraction tube as wave interference
Calculates the de Broglie wavelength of electrons for a given accelerating voltage
Explains why the resolution of an electron microscope is better than that of a light microscope
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} raises the accelerating voltage in an electron diffraction tube, can they predict and explain how the rings change?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Franck–Hertz Experiment
topics.description: In the Franck–Hertz experiment electrons collide with mercury or neon atoms; the current drops at regular voltage intervals because atoms only absorb fixed energy portions. Pupils interpret the characteristic curve and relate the 4.9 V spacing to the light emitted.
evidence: Describes the setup and explains the periodic drops in the current
Determines the excitation energy from the measured curve
Relates the excitation energy to the wavelength of the emitted UV or visible light
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown a Franck–Hertz curve with minima every 4.9 V, can they explain what this says about mercury atoms?
topics.laenderNotes: Leistungskurs only in Berlin-Brandenburg.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Line Spectra and Energy Levels
topics.description: Atoms emit and absorb light only at specific wavelengths because their electrons can only have discrete energies. Pupils explain emission and absorption spectra (including Fraunhofer lines), draw energy-level diagrams, and calculate wavelengths of transitions, e.g. the Balmer series of hydrogen.
evidence: Explains emission and absorption lines with transitions between energy levels
Calculates the wavelength of a transition from an energy-level diagram
Explains how the Fraunhofer lines reveal the elements in the Sun
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a street lamp through a grating and sees only a few coloured lines, can they explain why?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern introduces photons, spectra and energy levels already in Kl. 9 (Atome); in BW energy levels appear only in the Basisfach with astro focus.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The One-Dimensional Potential Well
topics.description: An electron confined between infinitely high walls can only form standing de Broglie waves, so its energy is quantised: E_n = n²·h²/(8·m·L²). Pupils derive the energy levels, sketch the wave functions and probability densities, apply the model to dye molecules and discuss its limits for real atoms.
evidence: Derives the allowed energies from the standing-wave condition
Sketches ψ and |ψ|² for the first three states
Uses the model to estimate the colour of a dye molecule and names its limits
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} models an electron in a molecule as a particle in a box, can they explain why its energy can only take certain values?
topics.laenderNotes: eA in the KMK standards, NRW and Berlin-Brandenburg; Bayern and Niedersachsen teach it at both levels; absent in BW.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Quantum Objects at the Double Slit
topics.description: Single photons or electrons arrive at random points on a screen, yet many of them build up an interference pattern. Pupils explain the basic features of quantum objects: stochastic predictability, superposition, the determined probability distribution, and complementarity (which-path information destroys interference), e.g. with a Mach–Zehnder interferometer.
evidence: Describes how an interference pattern builds up from single detection events
Explains why the place where a single photon is detected cannot be predicted while the pattern can
Explains with a which-path experiment that path information and interference exclude each other
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches a simulation where single electrons hit a screen behind a double slit, can they explain what is random and what is predictable?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Uncertainty Principle
topics.description: Position and momentum of a quantum object cannot both be sharply defined: Δx·Δp ≥ h/(4π). Pupils derive the relation qualitatively from single-slit diffraction, estimate its consequences for electrons in atoms, and distinguish it from measurement error.
evidence: Derives Δx·Δp ≈ h from single-slit diffraction of electrons
Estimates the minimum momentum uncertainty of an electron confined to an atom
Explains why the relation is a property of quantum objects, not of imperfect instruments
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that "Heisenberg says we disturb things when we measure", can they explain what the uncertainty principle really states?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Probability Interpretation of the Wave Function
topics.description: In quantum mechanics a wave function ψ describes the state; the square of its absolute value gives the probability density of finding the object at a place (Born's interpretation). Pupils interpret |ψ|² qualitatively for the double slit and simple bound states.
evidence: States that |ψ|² gives a probability density, not a "smeared-out" particle
Relates the brightness of an interference pattern to |ψ|²
Sketches |ψ|² for a simple situation and reads off where the object is likely found
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a graph of |ψ|² for an electron, can they explain what it tells us and what it does not?

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Quantum Worldview
topics.description: Pupils reflect on how quantum physics changes the concepts of reality, locality, causality and determinism (Copenhagen interpretation, entanglement) and how modern quantum technologies (quantum cryptography, quantum computers) use these features. In eA courses the coincidence method shows that single photons exist.
evidence: Explains in what sense quantum physics is not deterministic for single events
Describes entanglement in simple terms and why it does not allow faster-than-light messages
Discusses an application of quantum technology and its significance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked whether "the Moon is there when nobody looks", can they discuss what quantum physics says about reality?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Running a Class Council
topics.description: Pupils run a regular class council with defined roles (chair, minute-taker, timekeeper), an agenda collected beforehand, discussion rules and decisions by vote or consensus, and follow up on agreed actions.
evidence: Takes on a Klassenrat role and fulfils it
Distinguishes decisions by majority and by consensus and when each fits
Keeps minutes of decisions and checks them at the next meeting
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} chaired the next class council, could they lead the class through the agenda, a vote and recording the decision?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Electing a Class Representative
topics.description: Pupils discuss the tasks and qualities of a class representative (Klassensprecher/in), run a democratic election with candidates, secret ballot and counting, and understand majority vote and acceptance of the result.
evidence: Lists tasks of a class representative and qualities needed
Organises a secret ballot and counts it correctly
Explains why the losing side should accept the result
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s new class had to elect a class representative, could they explain how a fair election works and what the winner's job will be?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Student Council and School Bodies
topics.description: Pupils describe the Schülervertretung (Schülerrat of all class representatives, Schülersprecher, SV liaison teacher) and the school conference (Schulkonferenz) where pupils, parents and teachers decide together, and judge the value of pupil participation.
evidence: Draws the structure of the SV from class to school level
Explains which decisions the Schulkonferenz takes and who sits on it
Judges with an example how pupils can influence school life
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wanted water fountains installed at school, could they explain which way through the SV and school bodies the idea would have to go?
topics.laenderNotes: The legal name and composition of SV bodies and the Schulkonferenz are set by each Land's school law.

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Media Use and Social Networks
topics.description: Pupils record and reflect on their own media use (media diary, screen time), describe the influence of social networks on communication and self-presentation, and know basic rules such as the right to one's own image and how to respond to cyberbullying.
evidence: Keeps and evaluates a one-week media diary
Explains two ways social networks influence how young people see themselves
Explains the right to one's own image and what to do in a case of cyberbullying
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s friend posted an embarrassing photo of a classmate in the class chat, could they explain why this is a problem and what the classmate can do?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Children's Rights
topics.description: Pupils describe the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989, valid in Germany since 1992) with its protection, provision and participation rights, find examples where these rights are respected or violated in Germany and worldwide (child labour, child soldiers), and name organisations that protect them.
evidence: Names at least five children's rights and groups them
Identifies the violated right in a given case
Names an organisation or institution that protects children's rights
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read about children working in a quarry instead of going to school, could they say which children's rights are being violated?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Needs, Wants and Goods
topics.description: Pupils distinguish basic, cultural and luxury needs (Existenz-, Kultur-, Luxusbedürfnisse), explain that needs backed by purchasing power become demand (Bedarf), distinguish goods and services, and understand scarcity as the reason for economising.
evidence: Sorts given needs into basic, cultural and luxury needs and explains that this depends on context
Explains the difference between Bedürfnis and Bedarf
Explains why scarcity forces choices
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wished for a new smartphone, could they explain whether this is a need or a want and when it becomes 'Bedarf'?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Functions of Money
topics.description: Pupils explain the problems of barter, and the three functions of money – medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account – with cash and digital payment as examples.
evidence: Explains a disadvantage of barter with an example
Names and illustrates the three functions of money
Compares paying with cash and with card or smartphone
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} imagined a world without money where they had to trade their bike for food, could they explain the problems and the jobs money does for us?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Managing Pocket Money
topics.description: Pupils plan their pocket money with a simple budget or household book (Haushaltsbuch), distinguish fixed and variable spending, save for a goal and evaluate consumer wishes against available means.
evidence: Keeps a pocket-money book for several weeks
Plans how long it takes to save for a goal
Evaluates a spontaneous purchase against their savings plan
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} got 25 euros a month and wanted a 60-euro game, could they make a realistic saving plan and keep track of their spending?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Minors and Contracts
topics.description: Pupils learn the age levels of legal capacity (under 7 no capacity, 7–17 limited capacity, 18 full), that a purchase is a contract, and that minors' purchases are valid if paid with pocket money given for free use (§ 110 BGB), with consequences for in-app purchases and subscriptions.
evidence: States the three levels of legal capacity
Decides in given cases whether a minor's purchase is valid
Explains why a phone subscription signed by a 12-year-old is not valid without parents' consent
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} bought a 40-euro game with saved pocket money and their parents wanted to return it, could they explain whether the purchase is valid?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Advertising and Sales Strategies
topics.description: Pupils analyse adverts with the AIDA model, recognise digital strategies (influencer marketing, labelled 'Anzeige/Werbung', in-game offers) and supermarket tricks (shelf height, checkout zone), and judge their influence on their own buying.
evidence: Analyses an advert using the AIDA steps
Identifies advertising in a social-media post by its labelling and features
Names three supermarket sales strategies and how to resist them
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watched an influencer praising new sneakers, could they tell whether it is advertising and explain how it tries to make them buy?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.domainEn: Living Together in Family and School
topics.name: Family Roles and Changing Family Forms
topics.nameDe: Familie: Rollen und Lebensformen im Wandel
topics.description: Pupils describe different family forms (two-parent, single-parent, patchwork, same-sex parents, multi-generation), the needs and roles of family members, how gender roles and household tasks have changed, and the consequences of role expectations.
evidence: Names and describes at least four family forms without judging them
Compares the division of household tasks in a 1960s family and today
Evaluates a situation where role expectations cause conflict in a family
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared a 1960s advert showing a housewife with families today, could they describe how family roles have changed and why?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.domainEn: Living Together in Family and School
topics.name: Resolving Conflicts through Mediation
topics.description: Pupils analyse conflicts by feelings, interests and needs of those involved, use I-messages, and follow the steps of peer mediation (Streitschlichtung) to reach a fair agreement or compromise.
evidence: Describes the interests and feelings of both sides in a conflict case
Rewrites an accusation as an I-message
Leads or takes part in a role-played mediation following the fixed steps
topics.assessmentPrompt: If two classmates argued over a broken pencil case, could {{name}} guide them through the steps of a Streitschlichtung to an agreement?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.domainEn: Living Together in Family and School
topics.name: Rules, Rights and Duties at School
topics.nameDe: Regeln, Rechte und Pflichten in der Schule
topics.description: Pupils explain why communities need rules, distinguish class rules, the school's Schulordnung and the Land's Schulgesetz (e.g. compulsory schooling, right to participate), and justify rights and duties of pupils.
evidence: Explains the purpose of rules with a school example
Distinguishes a class rule, the school rules and the school law
Names two rights and two duties of pupils
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s class wanted to ban phones at break time, could they explain who can decide this rule and which rights and duties are involved?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Tasks of the Municipality
topics.description: Pupils describe the municipality's mandatory tasks (school buildings, waste collection, water, roads) and voluntary tasks (swimming pool, library, youth centre), its bodies (elected council, mayor, administration) and how it is financed by taxes and fees (kommunale Selbstverwaltung).
evidence: Sorts municipal tasks into mandatory and voluntary
Explains the roles of council, mayor and administration
Names sources of municipal income and why money must be prioritised
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s town wanted to close the swimming pool to save money, could they explain who decides this and why the town cannot simply stop collecting rubbish instead?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Youth Participation in Local Decisions
topics.nameDe: Mitbestimmung in der Gemeinde: Kinder- und Jugendparlament
topics.description: Pupils analyse a local controversy (e.g. a skate park versus parking spaces), identify the positions and interests of different groups, and describe ways for children and young people to participate: youth parliaments, citizens' petitions, public council sessions.
evidence: Identifies at least three positions and their interests in a local conflict
Describes two ways young people can influence local decisions
Writes or presents a reasoned proposal to the youth parliament or council
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s town planned to build a car park on the only football field, could they identify who wants what and suggest how young people could make their voice heard?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Media, Information and Opinion
topics.description: Pupils distinguish news, opinion and advertising, use children's news (e.g. logo!, Kindernachrichten) as sources, check information for reliability (who, source, date, evidence) and recognise that media select and frame topics according to interests.
evidence: Classifies media texts as news report, comment or advertising
Checks a viral claim with at least two independent sources
Explains with an example how a headline can steer opinion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a shocking video claim shared in the class chat, could they check whether it is true and explain how they decided?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Federalism: Bund, Länder and Gemeinden
topics.description: Pupils distinguish the three levels of the German state (federation, Länder, municipalities) with their parliaments and responsibilities, and explain consequences such as different school systems in each Land (Kulturhoheit der Länder).
evidence: Assigns tasks (army, schools, waste collection) to the correct level
Names the parliament of each level (Bundestag, Landtag, Gemeinderat)
Explains why school holidays and school types differ between Länder
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s cousin in another Land had different school holidays and subjects, could they explain why using the idea of federalism?
topics.laenderNotes: Not an explicit Kl. 5/6 standard in NRW Wirtschaft-Politik (end of Sek I); taught as an outlook in some Gesellschaftslehre/Politik courses – placement uncertain.

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Basic Rights in the Grundgesetz
topics.description: Pupils get to know Germany's constitution (Grundgesetz, 1949) and selected basic rights – human dignity (Art. 1), free development of personality, equality (Art. 3), freedom of religion, opinion and assembly – and see that rights find limits where they affect the rights of others.
evidence: Quotes Article 1 and explains what human dignity means in a school situation
Matches everyday cases to the affected basic right
Explains with an example why a basic right can be limited
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard someone say 'I can say anything I want – freedom of opinion!', could they explain what Article 5 protects and where its limits are?
topics.laenderNotes: Only introductory in Kl. 5/6 (BB 'Merkmale unserer Demokratie'); systematic study of the Grundgesetz follows in Kl. 7–10 in all Länder.

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Youth Protection Law
topics.description: Pupils explain the purpose of the Jugendschutzgesetz and its age limits (going out at night, alcohol and tobacco, films and games with FSK/USK ratings), and know that criminal responsibility starts at 14.
evidence: Reads FSK/USK ratings and explains what they mean
States age limits for staying out, alcohol and tobacco
Explains why the law protects rather than punishes young people
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wanted to watch a film rated 'FSK 16' at the cinema with friends, could they explain the rule and why it exists?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Elections and Voting Principles
topics.description: Pupils explain why democracies hold elections, the five principles of German elections (allgemein, unmittelbar, frei, gleich, geheim), the role of parties in simple terms, and voting ages (e.g. 16 in local elections in several Länder).
evidence: Names and explains the five voting principles
Identifies which principle is violated in a given case
Explains the difference between direct democracy in Athens and representative democracy today
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a parent filling in a postal ballot for an adult child, could they say which voting principle is violated?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Child Poverty and the SDGs
topics.description: Pupils compare children's living situations in differently developed regions, explain the UN Sustainable Development Goals 'No poverty' and 'Quality education', and describe approaches against child poverty in Germany and worldwide.
evidence: Compares the daily life of children in two regions of the world
Explains SDG 1 and SDG 4 and why they are linked
Describes two approaches to fighting child poverty and judges them
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read that many children worldwide cannot go to school because they must work, could they explain how poverty and education are linked and what could help?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Market and Price
topics.description: Pupils describe a market as a meeting of supply and demand (weekly market, online shop) and explain in simple terms why prices rise when demand exceeds supply and fall when supply is high (e.g. seasonal strawberries), including the role of competition.
evidence: Identifies suppliers and buyers on a given market
Predicts the price change for a seasonal product in and out of season
Explains how competition between sellers affects prices
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} noticed that strawberries are cheap in June but expensive in December, could they explain why using supply and demand?
topics.laenderNotes: NRW Wirtschaft-Politik places market and price formation at the end of Sek I; some Gesellschaftslehre and Politik/Wirtschaft courses introduce a simple supply–demand model in Kl. 6 – placement uncertain.

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Sustainable Consumption
topics.nameDe: Nachhaltiger Konsum: Siegel und Fairer Handel
topics.description: Pupils explain sustainability with its ecological, economic and social dimensions, follow the production chain of a T-shirt or chocolate, recognise labels (Fairtrade, EU-Bio, Blauer Engel), and evaluate individual and political measures for saving resources.
evidence: Explains the three dimensions of sustainability with a product example
Explains what two labels guarantee
Evaluates one personal and one political measure for resource saving
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} had to choose between a cheap T-shirt and a more expensive Fairtrade one, could they weigh the social, ecological and economic aspects?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Career Choice and Vocational Training
topics.description: Pupils explore their interests and strengths, gather information on occupations, the dual vocational training system, university and other paths, and plan next steps such as an internship (Betriebspraktikum).
evidence: Describes their own strengths and interests with a test or portfolio
Explains how dual vocational training works
Plans and reflects on a work-experience placement
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked what they could do after school, could they explain the difference between an apprenticeship and a degree and how to find out what suits them?
topics.laenderNotes: Systematic career orientation: NRW "Kein Abschluss ohne Anschluss" from Kl. 8; BW subject "Wirtschaft / Berufs- und Studienorientierung" (WBS) from Kl. 8 (G8).

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Civic Participation
topics.description: Pupils describe forms of participation beyond elections – citizens' initiatives, petitions (incl. online), demonstrations, referendums in Länder and municipalities, voluntary work – and judge their opportunities and limits.
evidence: Names forms of participation with examples
Plans a simple participation action on a local issue
Judges opportunities and limits of a petition or demonstration
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wanted a safer cycle path to school, could they explain which ways of political participation they could use?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Disinformation and Algorithms
topics.description: Pupils recognise disinformation and manipulated content, explain how recommendation algorithms and filter bubbles shape what people see on social media, and apply fact-checking strategies.
evidence: Checks a viral post with fact-checking strategies (source, date, reverse image search)
Explains how algorithms personalise feeds
Discusses risks of filter bubbles for democratic debate
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a shocking video shared in a class chat, could they check whether it is genuine before passing it on?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Media in a Democracy
topics.nameDe: Funktionen der Medien in der Demokratie
topics.description: Pupils explain the functions of media in a democracy (information, opinion forming, criticism and control – "fourth estate"), press freedom, the public-service broadcasting system and the difference between news and commentary.
evidence: Names the functions of media in a democracy
Distinguishes news, report and commentary
Explains why press freedom matters with an example
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared a news report and a commentary on the same topic, could they explain the difference and why both matter?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Constitutional Principles of the Grundgesetz
topics.description: Pupils explain the five structural principles of the Basic Law in Article 20 – democracy, rule of law, social state, federal state, republic – and the "eternity clause" (Art. 79(3)) as a lesson from Weimar.
evidence: Names and explains the five principles of Article 20 with examples
Explains why Art. 1 and 20 cannot be changed
Links the eternity clause to the experience of the Weimar Republic
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read Article 20 of the Grundgesetz, could they explain each principle with an everyday example?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Basic Rights and Their Limits
topics.description: Pupils distinguish human and citizens' rights, explain basic rights as defensive rights against the state, and solve simple cases where basic rights collide (e.g. freedom of expression vs. personal honour, freedom of assembly vs. traffic).
evidence: Distinguishes human rights and citizens' rights in the Grundgesetz
Explains basic rights as protection against the state
Solves a simple case of conflicting basic rights with arguments
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard about a demonstration that blocks a motorway, could they explain which basic rights collide and how a court might weigh them?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Youth Crime and Juvenile Criminal Law
topics.description: Pupils describe forms of youth crime (incl. cyberbullying), the age limits of criminal responsibility (14, 18, 21), the educational principle of the Juvenile Courts Act and its measures, and discuss prevention and punishment.
evidence: Names the age limits of criminal responsibility in Germany
Explains the educational principle of juvenile criminal law with its measures
Discusses preventive and repressive measures against youth crime
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read about a 15-year-old caught shoplifting, could they explain what happens under juvenile criminal law and why?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: The Rule of Law
topics.description: Pupils explain the elements of the rule of law – separation of powers, government bound by law, independent courts, legal recourse, legal certainty – and contrast it with a dictatorship.
evidence: Explains horizontal separation of powers in Germany
Explains why judges must be independent
Contrasts the rule of law with arbitrary rule using an example
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that a government ignored a court ruling, could they explain why this violates the rule of law?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Household Budget and Debt
topics.description: Pupils plan a household or personal budget, explain causes of debt among young people (mobile contracts, buy now pay later, overdraft) and strategies to avoid over-indebtedness.
evidence: Draws up a monthly budget with income and fixed and variable costs
Explains the costs of credit, overdraft and buy-now-pay-later
Names ways out of debt including debt counselling
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wanted to buy a phone on instalments, could they calculate the real cost and judge whether they can afford it?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Contracts and Consumer Rights
topics.description: Pupils explain how a purchase contract is formed, the rights and duties of buyer and seller, warranty rights for defects, the right of withdrawal for online purchases, general terms and conditions, and where consumers can get help (consumer advice centres).
evidence: Explains offer and acceptance as the basis of a contract
Explains warranty and the 14-day right of withdrawal online
Names institutions that help consumers enforce their rights
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s new headphones broke after two weeks, could they explain what rights they have against the shop?
topics.laenderNotes: In Bayern this is part of Wirtschaft und Recht (Kl. 9); in NRW of Wirtschaft-Politik (IF 8).

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Online Shopping, Data and Algorithms
topics.description: Pupils describe how online shops and platforms use personal data and algorithms (personalised prices and ads, recommendations), explain the economic value of data and judge opportunities and risks of online trade for consumers.
evidence: Explains how personal data are used for targeted advertising
Names rights under data protection law (e.g. information, deletion)
Judges opportunities and risks of online shopping
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} noticed that ads for trainers follow them everywhere online, could they explain how this works and what rights they have?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: The Circular Flow of the Economy
topics.description: Pupils use the circular flow model to show the flows of money and goods between households, firms, the state, banks and other countries, and explain how a change in one sector affects others.
evidence: Draws the simple circular flow between households and firms
Extends the model with state, banks and foreign countries
Explains the effects of a tax increase using the model
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that people are saving more and spending less, could they use the circular flow model to explain the effects on firms?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Co-Determination at Work
topics.description: Pupils explain co-determination in German firms: the works council (Betriebsrat), youth and trainee representation, and employee seats on supervisory boards, and discuss its benefits for employees and firms.
evidence: Explains the tasks and rights of a works council
Explains employee representation on the supervisory board
Discusses advantages and disadvantages of co-determination
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} started an apprenticeship, could they explain who represents their interests in the company?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Collective Bargaining and Unions
topics.description: Pupils describe the role of unions and employers' associations, the free collective bargaining guaranteed by Art. 9(3) GG, the course of a wage dispute (negotiation, strike, arbitration) and the statutory minimum wage.
evidence: Describes the steps of a collective bargaining round
Explains the right to strike and its limits
Judges the effects of a strike on different groups
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s train was cancelled because of a strike, could they explain how wage disputes work in Germany and who decides?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Firms and Starting a Business
topics.description: Pupils explain the goals and functions of firms (procurement, production, sales, value chain), the elements of a business model (idea, market, price, location, legal form, financing) and judge opportunities and risks of self-employment.
evidence: Describes a firm's value chain
Develops a simple business model for a product idea
Judges opportunities and risks of self-employment
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wanted to start selling their own designed T-shirts, could they set out a simple business plan and name the main risks?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Extremism and Militant Democracy
topics.description: Pupils explain causes and forms of right-wing, left-wing and religious extremism, antisemitism and group-focused enmity, and the instruments of "militant democracy" (party bans, protection of the constitution, forfeiture of basic rights).
evidence: Distinguishes extremist from radical or populist positions
Explains instruments of militant democracy
Judges threats to the free democratic basic order with examples
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw extremist stickers in their neighbourhood, could they explain why the Grundgesetz allows defending democracy against its enemies?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Interest Groups and Lobbying
topics.description: Pupils describe interest groups (business associations, unions, environmental and social organisations, NGOs), their ways of influence (lobbying, campaigns, expertise) and discuss the line between legitimate representation and undue influence (lobby register).
evidence: Names interest groups and their aims
Describes ways of influencing politics
Discusses whether lobbying strengthens or weakens democracy
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read that a car industry association met ministers before a law on emissions, could they discuss whether this is legitimate?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Political Parties
topics.description: Pupils explain the constitutional role of parties (Art. 21), their functions (representing interests, recruiting personnel, forming opinions), place parties on the political spectrum and compare their positions on an issue.
evidence: Explains the functions of parties in a democracy
Places parties on a left-right and a liberal-authoritarian axis
Compares party positions on a current issue using programmes
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} used a voting advice app, could they explain how parties differ and what parties do between elections?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: The Bundestag Electoral System
topics.description: Pupils explain the personalised proportional representation for the Bundestag: first and second vote, constituencies, the 5 % threshold and the 2023 electoral reform, and compare majority and proportional voting.
evidence: Explains the functions of the first and second vote
Calculates seat distribution from a simple result
Compares majority and proportional representation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a ballot paper for the Bundestag election, could they explain what each of the two votes decides?
topics.laenderNotes: The voting age is 18 for the Bundestag but 16 for European elections (since 2024) and, in several Länder, for Land or municipal elections (e.g. Brandenburg, Hamburg, Baden-Württemberg).

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: The Single Market
topics.description: Pupils explain the four freedoms of the single market (goods, services, capital, persons), and discuss opportunities and challenges for consumers, companies and workers.
evidence: Names the four freedoms with everyday examples
Explains advantages of the single market for consumers
Discusses challenges such as wage competition
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wanted to do an apprenticeship in Austria, could they explain which EU freedom allows this and what else the single market changes?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: European Integration: Motives and Stages
topics.description: Pupils describe the motives (peace, reconciliation, prosperity) and stages of European integration from the European Coal and Steel Community (1951) and Treaties of Rome (1957) to Maastricht (1992) and Lisbon (2009), and the EU as a community of values.
evidence: Names motives of European integration after 1945
Puts the main treaties on a timeline
Explains what makes the EU a community of values
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard the EU called a "peace project", could they explain where the idea comes from?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: EU Institutions and Law-Making
topics.description: Pupils describe the tasks of the European Parliament, the Council of the EU, the European Commission, the European Council and the Court of Justice, and outline the ordinary legislative procedure and the difference between regulations and directives.
evidence: Names the main EU institutions and their tasks
Outlines the ordinary legislative procedure
Distinguishes regulations from directives with an example
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that a new EU rule requires the same charger for all phones, could they explain which institutions decided it and how?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Analysing International Conflicts
topics.description: Pupils analyse an international conflict, crisis or war with a fixed scheme – actors, causes, interests, course, options for resolution – and distinguish types of conflicts (interstate war, civil war, terrorism, hybrid war).
evidence: Applies a conflict analysis scheme to a current conflict
Distinguishes types of armed conflict
Develops and evaluates options for conflict resolution
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} followed a war in the news, could they analyse the actors, causes and interests involved?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Universal Human Rights
topics.description: Pupils explain the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), the idea of universality and indivisibility, the European Convention on Human Rights, and assess human rights violations and the ways to protect rights.
evidence: Explains the universality of human rights
Names institutions protecting human rights (UN, European Court of Human Rights)
Assesses a current human rights violation and possible responses
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read a report by Amnesty International, could they explain which human rights are violated and how they could be protected?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: The United Nations
topics.description: Pupils describe the aims and main organs of the UN (General Assembly, Security Council with veto, Secretary-General, International Court of Justice), peacekeeping missions, and judge possibilities and limits of the UN.
evidence: Names the aims of the UN Charter
Explains the role of the Security Council and the veto
Judges why the UN often fails to stop wars
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that the Security Council could not agree on a war, could they explain how the veto works and why this matters?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: The Federal Constitutional Court
topics.description: Pupils explain the Federal Constitutional Court as guardian of the Basic Law: constitutional complaint, judicial review of laws, disputes between organs, and discuss its role with landmark rulings (e.g. climate ruling 2021).
evidence: Explains how a citizen can file a constitutional complaint
Describes a landmark ruling and its consequences
Discusses the court's role in controlling politics
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that Karlsruhe struck down a law, could they explain who can go to the court and why its rulings bind parliament?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: How a Federal Law Is Made
topics.description: Pupils trace the federal legislative process from initiative to promulgation, explain the role of the Bundesrat (consent and objection laws, mediation committee) and of the Federal President.
evidence: Draws the legislative process as a flow chart
Distinguishes laws requiring consent from objection laws
Explains the role of the mediation committee
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} followed a new law in the news, could they explain the steps it must pass before it applies?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: The Parliamentary System
topics.description: Pupils explain the functions of the Bundestag (legislation, electing the chancellor, control of government), the role of government and opposition, the chancellor principle and the constructive vote of no confidence.
evidence: Names the functions of the Bundestag
Explains how the chancellor is elected and can be removed
Explains why government and majority form a unit in a parliamentary system
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watched a Bundestag debate, could they explain who governs, who controls and how the chancellor got into office?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Poverty, Wealth and Basic Income Support
topics.description: Pupils describe the extent and development of poverty and wealth in Germany (relative poverty line, child poverty, income gaps incl. gender pay gap), basic income support for jobseekers (Grundsicherung, called Bürgergeld from 2023) and discuss measures to secure the minimum subsistence.
evidence: Explains relative and absolute poverty
Analyses statistics on income differences between groups
Discusses a measure against child poverty
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read that one in five children in Germany is at risk of poverty, could they explain how poverty is measured here?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Migration, Asylum and Integration
topics.nameDe: Migration, Asyl und Integration in Deutschland
topics.description: Pupils describe immigration to Germany (labour migration, refugees), the right of asylum (Art. 16a GG, Geneva Refugee Convention), citizenship and naturalisation, and discuss conditions for successful integration.
evidence: Distinguishes refugees, asylum seekers and labour migrants
Explains the asylum procedure in outline
Discusses conditions and responsibilities for integration
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} had a new classmate who fled from Afghanistan, could they explain the legal situation of refugees and what helps integration?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Social Insurance in Germany
topics.description: Pupils explain the five branches of statutory social insurance (health, long-term care, pension, unemployment, accident), the principles of insurance, provision and welfare, the solidarity principle and the pay-as-you-go pension system and its demographic challenge.
evidence: Names the five branches and who pays for them
Explains the solidarity principle and the generational contract
Explains why demographic change puts pressure on pensions
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a payslip, could they explain what the social contributions are for and why pensions are under pressure?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Saving, Investing and Interest
topics.description: Pupils compare forms of saving and investing (savings account, fixed deposit, funds, shares) by return, risk and liquidity (magic triangle of investment), and explain compound interest and inflation's effect on savings.
evidence: Explains the magic triangle of return, risk and liquidity
Calculates the growth of savings with compound interest
Explains how inflation reduces the real value of savings
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} received 1,000 euros for their birthday, could they compare investment options and explain the risks?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: The Social Market Economy
topics.description: Pupils explain the principles of Germany's social market economy (market freedom with social balance, competition policy, social security; Erhard, Müller-Armack), compare it with a free market economy and a planned economy, and judge its strengths and problems.
evidence: Names the principles of the social market economy
Compares free market, social market and planned economy
Explains why the state protects competition (Bundeskartellamt)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that the Bundeskartellamt blocked a merger, could they explain why the state intervenes in a market economy?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Taxes and the Public Budget
topics.description: Pupils distinguish taxes, fees and contributions, direct and indirect taxes, explain the main items of the federal budget and discuss the fairness of taxation (progressive income tax).
evidence: Distinguishes direct and indirect taxes with examples
Interprets a diagram of the federal budget
Explains the principle of progressive income tax
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at their first payslip, could they explain which taxes and contributions are deducted and what the state does with them?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: The Euro and Monetary Union
topics.description: Pupils describe the features of the Economic and Monetary Union – the euro, the European Central Bank, convergence criteria and the Stability and Growth Pact – and discuss its advantages and the experience of the euro crisis.
evidence: Names advantages of a common currency
Explains the convergence criteria
Describes the euro crisis and its causes in outline
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} travelled from Germany to Italy and Croatia, could they explain why they can pay with the same money and what holds the euro together?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Free Trade and Protectionism
topics.description: Pupils describe the growing interconnection of world trade, the aims of actors (WTO, states, companies, NGOs), the features of free trade and protectionism (tariffs, quotas, subsidies) and judge free-trade agreements.
evidence: Explains tariffs and other protectionist measures
Describes the role of the WTO
Judges the effects of a free-trade agreement on different groups
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that a country raised tariffs on imported cars, could they explain who wins and who loses?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: NATO, the Bundeswehr and German Security
topics.description: Pupils describe NATO's tasks and the alliance case (Art. 5), the role of the Bundeswehr as a "parliamentary army" (deployment needs the Bundestag), compulsory military service debates and Germany's security policy after 2022.
evidence: Explains collective defence under Article 5
Explains why Bundeswehr deployments abroad need the Bundestag's approval
Discusses current debates on security and military service
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard a debate about bringing back compulsory military service, could they explain the role of the Bundeswehr and NATO?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Inflation and Price Stability
topics.description: Pupils explain how inflation is measured (consumer price index, basket of goods), its causes (demand, costs, money supply) and effects on savers, borrowers and people on low incomes, using recent inflation (2022/23).
evidence: Explains the consumer price index and basket of goods
Names causes of inflation with the example of 2022
Explains who loses and who gains from inflation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} noticed that their favourite snack costs 30 % more than two years ago, could they explain what inflation is and how it is measured?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Populism and Threats to Democracy
topics.description: Students analyse threats to liberal democracy – populism (people vs. elite), polarisation, social disintegration, disinformation and illiberal tendencies – and evaluate democratic responses.
evidence: Defines populism with its core features
Analyses a populist statement
Evaluates measures to strengthen democratic resilience
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard a politician claim to speak for "the real people" against "the elites", could they analyse this as a populist pattern?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Representative versus Direct Democracy
topics.description: Students compare representative and direct (plebiscitary) democracy, analyse referendums at Land and municipal level and in other countries (Switzerland, Brexit), and discuss more direct democracy at federal level.
evidence: Compares advantages and risks of both forms
Analyses a referendum case using criteria
Argues a reasoned position on federal referendums
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked whether Germany should have national referendums like Switzerland, could they argue both sides and reach a judgement?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Media Logic and Political Staging
topics.description: Students analyse the logic of mass and social media (news values, agenda setting, framing, personalisation, scandalisation) and how politics is staged for the media, and evaluate the influence of media on political decision-making.
evidence: Explains agenda setting and framing with a current example
Analyses a staged political media event
Evaluates the influence of media on politics
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watched a politician's carefully staged visit to a flood area, could they analyse what the media logic behind it is?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Separation of Powers
topics.description: Students explain Montesquieu's theory of separation of powers and analyse its horizontal, vertical (federalism) and temporal forms as well as the "interlocking" of government and parliamentary majority in Germany.
evidence: Explains Montesquieu's argument for separating powers
Distinguishes horizontal, vertical and temporal separation
Analyses where powers interlock in the German parliamentary system
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that ministers are also members of the Bundestag, could they discuss whether this contradicts the separation of powers?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Social Contract Theories
topics.description: Students compare the social contract theories of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau – state of nature, image of humans, purpose and form of the state – and trace their influence on modern constitutions.
evidence: Compares the state of nature and image of humans in Hobbes and Locke
Explains Rousseau's idea of the general will
Traces an element of the Grundgesetz back to a contract theory
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked why people should obey a state at all, could they compare the answers of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Social Roles and Identity
topics.description: Students compare the structural-functional role model (Dahrendorf's homo sociologicus: role expectations, sanctions) with interactionist theory (Mead, Krappmann: role-taking, balancing identity), and use them to analyse role conflicts and identity formation, also in digital networks.
evidence: Explains the homo sociologicus with role expectations and sanctions
Explains balancing identity according to the interactionist view
Analyses a role conflict and evaluates solutions
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were captain of the football team and also a friend of a player who was dropped, could they analyse this role conflict with role theory?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Socialisation
topics.description: Students explain socialisation as the process by which individuals become members of society, compare the influence of agents (family, peers, school, media, work) and the role of norms, values and sanctions.
evidence: Distinguishes primary, secondary and tertiary socialisation
Compares the influence of family and peers
Explains the role of norms and sanctions with examples
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked who influenced their values most – parents, friends or social media – could they answer using the concept of socialisation agents?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Supply, Demand and Market Equilibrium
topics.description: Students use the supply-and-demand model to explain price formation and equilibrium, shifts of the curves, market forms (polypoly, oligopoly, monopoly) and the assumptions of the model, including the homo oeconomicus.
evidence: Draws supply and demand curves and finds the equilibrium
Explains shifts of a curve and their effect on price and quantity
Criticises the assumptions of the model and the homo oeconomicus
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that a bad harvest made coffee more expensive, could they show this with shifting curves in the market model?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Market Failure and Environmental Policy
topics.description: Students explain forms of market failure – external effects, public goods, market power, information asymmetry – and evaluate instruments to correct them, especially CO₂ pricing and emissions trading.
evidence: Explains external costs with the example of CO₂ emissions
Explains why public goods are underprovided by markets
Evaluates emissions trading and a CO₂ tax
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked why a flight is cheaper than a train ticket although it harms the climate more, could they explain this as market failure?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Democratic Legitimacy of the EU
topics.nameDe: Demokratische Legitimation und Zukunft der EU
topics.description: Students evaluate the decision-making powers of EU institutions with regard to democratic legitimacy ("democratic deficit"), the effect of EU law on national legislation, and discuss future models of integration (federation, intergovernmental cooperation, differentiated integration).
evidence: Explains the debate on the democratic deficit
Explains the primacy of EU law with a case
Discusses future models of integration
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard someone say "Brussels decides everything and nobody elected them", could they evaluate this claim?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Theories of International Trade
topics.description: Students explain theories of international trade – absolute and comparative advantage (Smith, Ricardo), arguments for protection (infant industry, security) – and analyse current trade conflicts and the limits of national economic policy.
evidence: Explains comparative advantage with a numerical example
Explains arguments for protectionism
Discusses the limits of national economic policy under globalisation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked why a country that can produce everything more cheaply still gains from trade, could they explain comparative advantage?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Concepts of Peace and Conflict Research
topics.description: Students explain concepts of peace and conflict research – negative and positive peace, structural violence (Galtung), causes of war – and discuss how different ideas of peace can be implemented.
evidence: Distinguishes negative and positive peace
Explains structural violence with an example
Discusses strategies of peacebuilding
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked whether a ceasefire means peace, could they answer with Galtung's concepts?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Theories of International Relations
topics.nameDe: Theorien internationaler Beziehungen: Realismus und Institutionalismus
topics.description: Students explain realism (states, power, security dilemma) and institutionalism (cooperation, international institutions, interdependence), and use them to analyse international politics and the role of the UN.
evidence: Explains the core assumptions of realism and institutionalism
Explains the security dilemma
Analyses a current conflict with both theories
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} analysed NATO enlargement, could they explain how a realist and an institutionalist would interpret it differently?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Deliberative Democracy
topics.description: Students explain the theory of deliberative democracy (Habermas: public discourse, the "unforced force of the better argument") and evaluate deliberative formats such as citizens' assemblies.
evidence: Explains the ideal of deliberation
Compares deliberative with pluralist democracy
Evaluates a citizens' assembly as a deliberative format
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read about a citizens' assembly on climate policy, could they evaluate it with the theory of deliberative democracy?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Pluralist and Identitarian Democracy
topics.description: Students compare the pluralist theory of democracy (Fraenkel: competition of interests, consensus on rules, common good a posteriori) with identitarian concepts (Rousseau, common good a priori), and judge which theory underlies the Grundgesetz.
evidence: Explains the core ideas of pluralist theory
Contrasts it with the identitarian concept of the common good
Judges risks of the identitarian model with historical examples
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard a politician claim to know "the will of the people", could they analyse this with the contrast between pluralist and identitarian democracy?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Rawls' Theory of Justice
topics.description: Students explain Rawls' theory of justice – original position, veil of ignorance, principle of equal liberty and difference principle – and use it to evaluate social-policy measures, comparing it with libertarian criticism.
