evidence: Explains the veil of ignorance and the two principles
Applies the difference principle to a social-policy measure
Compares Rawls with a libertarian position
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} had to design a tax system without knowing whether they would be rich or poor, could they explain what Rawls would expect them to choose?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Individualisation and Social Change
topics.description: Students explain theories of social change and the "de-structuring" of society – Beck's individualisation thesis and risk society, value change (Inglehart) – and discuss whether class and strata still shape life chances.
evidence: Explains Beck's individualisation thesis
Explains Inglehart's theory of value change
Discusses whether social origin still determines life chances
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked whether people today are freer to choose their lives than their grandparents, could they discuss this with Beck's theory?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Dimensions of Social Inequality
topics.description: Students describe dimensions, indicators and causes of social inequality (income, wealth, education, health; Gini coefficient) and evaluate inequalities against principles of justice (performance, need, equal opportunities).
evidence: Names dimensions and indicators of social inequality
Interprets a Lorenz curve or Gini coefficient
Evaluates an inequality against different principles of justice
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learned that the richest 10 % own more than half of Germany's wealth, could they evaluate this with different ideas of justice?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Models of Social Structure
topics.description: Students compare models of vertical and horizontal inequality – class (Marx), strata (Geißler's house), social situations and milieus (Sinus) – in their historical context and judge how well they describe today's society.
evidence: Explains Marx's class model and a strata model
Explains the Sinus milieus with value orientation and social position
Judges which model best describes society today
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared Marx's two-class model with the Sinus milieu map, could they explain what each captures and misses?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Models of the Welfare State
topics.description: Students compare welfare-state models (liberal, conservative, social-democratic after Esping-Andersen), explain financing options of social benefits and evaluate distribution effects and the future of the German welfare state.
evidence: Compares three welfare-state models with country examples
Explains contribution- and tax-financed social benefits
Evaluates a reform proposal for the German welfare state
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared the welfare systems of Germany, Sweden and the USA, could they assign them to models and evaluate them?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Monetary Policy of the ECB
topics.description: Students explain the goal (price stability around 2 %), strategy and instruments of the European Central Bank (key interest rates, open-market operations, bond purchases) and discuss conflicts between a single interest rate and different national situations.
evidence: Explains the ECB's mandate and independence
Explains how a rise in key interest rates is meant to reduce inflation
Discusses why one interest rate can suit some euro countries but not others
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that the ECB raised interest rates, could they explain the intended effect on prices and the side-effects for borrowers?
topics.laenderNotes: NRW's new Kernlehrplan (from 2027) puts ECB monetary policy in the Leistungskurs only; the KMK EPA Sozialkunde/Politik lists economic policy as content for both course levels, so it is marked gA here.

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: The Business Cycle
topics.description: Students describe the model of the business cycle (upswing, boom, downturn, recession), interpret leading, coincident and lagging indicators (e.g. ifo index, GDP, unemployment) and explain causes of economic fluctuations.
evidence: Draws and labels the phases of the business cycle
Assigns indicators to leading, coincident and lagging
Interprets current data to determine the phase of the cycle
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read that the ifo business climate index fell for the third time, could they explain what this says about the economy?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Demand-Side versus Supply-Side Policy
topics.description: Students compare demand-side (Keynesian: deficit spending, anticyclical policy) and supply-side (monetarist: deregulation, tax cuts, stable money) economic policy with their assumptions, instruments and historical contexts, and discuss public debt.
evidence: Explains the assumptions and instruments of Keynesian policy
Explains the assumptions and instruments of supply-side policy
Assigns a current measure to a concept and discusses public debt
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard a government plan a big investment programme in a recession, could they explain which economic theory stands behind it?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: Goals of Economic Policy
topics.nameDe: Ziele der Wirtschaftspolitik: Magisches Viereck und Wohlstand
topics.description: Students explain the goals of the Stability and Growth Act (1967) – price stability, high employment, external balance, steady growth – with indicators, goal conflicts, and extended goals (fair distribution, environment) and alternative measures of prosperity beyond GDP.
evidence: Names the four goals and their indicators
Explains a goal conflict (e.g. inflation vs. employment)
Compares GDP with alternative measures of prosperity
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that the economy grew but emissions rose too, could they discuss whether GDP is a good measure of prosperity?

topics.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
topics.name: German Foreign and Security Policy
topics.nameDe: Deutsche Außen- und Sicherheitspolitik in NATO und EU
topics.description: Students evaluate goals, possibilities and limits of German foreign and security policy within NATO and the EU's Common Foreign and Security Policy, including the "Zeitenwende" after 2022 and the debate on Germany's international responsibility.
evidence: Explains the instruments of the EU's Common Foreign and Security Policy
Describes the shift in German security policy after 2022
Evaluates Germany's international role with criteria
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard the term "Zeitenwende", could they explain what changed in German security policy and evaluate the change?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Advent and Christmas
topics.description: Know German Advent and Christmas customs and their meaning — Advent wreath and calendar counting down, St. Nicholas on 6 December, Christmas Eve (Heiligabend) with the nativity story — and that families celebrate in different ways or not at all.
evidence: Explain the meaning of the four Advent candles and the Advent calendar
Retell the Christmas story (birth of Jesus) in simple words
Describe how their own or other families celebrate (or do not celebrate) Christmas
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why a new candle is lit on the Advent wreath each Sunday and tell you what Christians celebrate at Christmas?
topics.laenderNotes: Customs vary regionally (Christkind in the south and west vs. Weihnachtsmann in the north and east; Knecht Ruprecht or Krampus with St. Nikolaus).

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: St. Martin and the Lantern Procession
topics.description: Know the legend of St. Martin sharing his cloak with a beggar and the customs of 11 November — lantern processions with Martinslieder, Martinsfeuer, Weckmann or Martinsgans — and discuss what sharing means today.
evidence: Retell the legend of St. Martin and the beggar
Describe the customs of Martinstag (lanterns, songs, procession)
Give an example of sharing in their own life inspired by the story
topics.assessmentPrompt: When the lantern procession comes up in November, can {{name}} tell you the story of St. Martin and why sharing is at its heart?
topics.laenderNotes: Strongest in the Rhineland and other catholic regions (processions led by a rider as St. Martin); in Protestant areas sometimes linked to Martin Luther (born 10 Nov); many Kitas and schools celebrate it as a secular festival of sharing.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Friendship
topics.description: Think about what makes a good friend (trust, loyalty, helpfulness, honesty), how friendships begin, change and end, and how to repair a friendship after a quarrel.
evidence: Name three qualities of a good friend and explain why they matter
Describe how a friendship can change over time
Suggest how to make up after a quarrel with a friend
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain what makes someone a really good friend — and what they would do to make up after a falling-out?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Wishes, Needs and Happiness
topics.description: Name their wishes and check whether they can be fulfilled, distinguish basic needs from wishes and important from less important things, and think about what makes a good, happy life.
evidence: Sort wishes into basic needs and nice-to-haves
Explain why some wishes cannot or should not be fulfilled
Describe what makes them truly happy and compare with others
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} could wish for three things, can they tell you which they really need, which are just nice to have — and what actually makes them happy?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Valuing and Protecting Nature
topics.description: Experience and marvel at nature with all senses, recognise humans as part of and dependent on nature, notice harmful human interventions (litter, noise, pollution, cruelty to animals) and practise protective behaviour — waste separation, saving resources, caring for animals and plants.
evidence: Describe a nature experience using at least three senses
Explain how a specific human behaviour harms animals or plants
Carry out a protective action at school (e.g. sorting waste, a clean-up) and explain why it matters
topics.assessmentPrompt: On a walk, does {{name}} notice litter or damaged plants, and can they explain why protecting nature matters and what they themselves can do?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Asking Big Questions
topics.description: Wonder about the world and ask philosophical questions that have no simple factual answer — 'What is a friend?', 'Do animals think?', 'Is it ever okay to lie?' — and tell them apart from questions that can be looked up.
evidence: Ask at least one 'big question' about a picture book or everyday experience
Sort questions into those you can look up and those you have to think about
Share and explain their own first answer to a big question
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} asks something like 'Why is there anything at all?' or 'Is it ever okay to lie?', can they tell that this is a different kind of question from 'How tall is a giraffe?'

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Philosophical Conversation
topics.description: Take part in a philosophical conversation (Philosophierkreis): listen to others, refer to what they said ('I agree with X because…'), stay on the question and accept that people can hold different, well-founded views.
evidence: Follow conversation rules (one speaker at a time, talking object)
Refer explicitly to a classmate's contribution when speaking
Accept a different view without mocking it
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a family discussion — say, whether it's fair that siblings get the same pocket money — does {{name}} listen to others and respond to what they actually said?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Religion Around Us
topics.nameDe: Religion im Alltag und in unserer Klasse
topics.description: Notice where religion appears in everyday life (church bells, crosses, headscarves, kippa, prayer, baptism or naming ceremonies) and in their own class — where classmates may attend evangelical, catholic or Islamic Religionsunterricht and others Ethik — and match common symbols (cross, Star of David, crescent) to religions, respecting religious and non-religious views.
evidence: Match the cross, Star of David and crescent moon to Christianity, Judaism and Islam
Name situations in which religion plays a role for people (festivals, prayer, baptism, funerals)
Explain respectfully that some classmates belong to a religion and others don't
topics.assessmentPrompt: On a walk through town, can {{name}} recognise a church, a cross or a Star of David and say which religion it belongs to — and accept that some families are not religious at all?
topics.laenderNotes: RU is an ordinary subject under Art. 7 Abs. 3 GG, except where the Bremer Klausel (Art. 141 GG) applies (Bremen, Berlin); Hamburg teaches dialogical Religionsunterricht für alle; Brandenburg has LER from Kl. 5. In the eastern Länder most pupils have no religious affiliation, in Bayern and the Saarland most do.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Recognising and Handling Feelings
topics.nameDe: Gefühle wahrnehmen, benennen und mit ihnen umgehen
topics.description: Name feelings in themselves and others from facial expression, gesture and language, distinguish pleasant and unpleasant feelings, reflect on how feelings influence actions and use strategies for strong feelings (pause, breathe, leave the situation, talk about it).
evidence: Name at least six feelings and recognise them in pictures or situations
Describe how a feeling influenced something they did
Use one strategy to calm down when angry and explain it
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is furious about losing a game, can they name the feeling and use a strategy — like taking a breath or stepping away — before reacting?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Helping Others and Social Engagement
topics.nameDe: Anderen helfen und sich sozial engagieren
topics.description: Recognise situations in which others need help (loneliness, illness, poverty, disability), practise mutual help in class, learn from people who committed themselves to others (e.g. Mother Teresa, Hermann Gmeiner of SOS-Kinderdorf) and carry out a small aid project such as a donation or sponsorship.
evidence: Recognise a situation in which someone needs help and offer it appropriately
Describe the motives of a person known for helping others
Plan and carry out a small helping or donation project with the class
topics.assessmentPrompt: When a classmate is left out or struggling, does {{name}} notice and offer help — and can they tell you about someone known for helping others?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Myself: Strengths, Limits and Mistakes
topics.nameDe: Ich bin einmalig: Stärken, Grenzen, aus Fehlern lernen
topics.description: Describe what makes them unique (appearance, preferences, abilities), assess strengths and weaknesses honestly, accept help, and learn that patience, practice and learning from failure help to overcome limits — without judging people by their abilities.
evidence: Describe three personal strengths and one thing they find hard
Ask for and accept help politely when they reach a limit
Tell about a time they learned from a mistake or failure
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you what they're good at and what they find hard — and how they deal with it when something doesn't work the first time?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Resolving Conflicts Peacefully
topics.description: Recognise causes of conflicts (misunderstandings, envy, competition), weigh possible solutions and use non-violent strategies — talking it out, I-messages (Ich-Botschaften), apology, compromise, or asking a mediator (Streitschlichter).
evidence: Identify the cause of a conflict in a story or role play
Use an I-message to say what bothered them
Propose a compromise both sides can accept
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} argues with a friend over a toy, can they say what bothers them without insults and suggest a solution that works for both?
topics.laenderNotes: Many Grundschulen train pupils as Streitschlichter (peer mediators); social learning is also anchored in Sachunterricht and school-wide programmes.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Why We Need Rules
topics.description: Explain why groups need rules (classroom, playground, traffic), formulate good rules, judge rules by criteria (order, fairness, consideration) and consider fair consequences when rules are broken, such as making amends (Wiedergutmachung) or a second chance.
evidence: Explain what could happen in a situation without rules
Formulate a class rule and give its purpose
Suggest a fair, appropriate consequence for a broken rule
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} could make one new rule for the playground, can they explain why it is needed and what should happen if someone breaks it?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Islamic Festivals
topics.description: Know the fasting month of Ramadan and its meaning, the Festival of Breaking the Fast (Ramadanfest/Zuckerfest, Eid al-Fitr) and the Festival of Sacrifice (Opferfest, Eid al-Adha) with their customs, and how Muslim classmates and families in Germany celebrate them.
evidence: Explain why Muslims fast during Ramadan and what fasting involves
Describe how the Zuckerfest (Eid al-Fitr) is celebrated
Compare one Islamic festival with a festival of another religion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain what Ramadan is and how Muslim classmates might celebrate the Zuckerfest at its end?
topics.laenderNotes: Several Länder (e.g. NRW, Niedersachsen, Hessen, Bayern as Islamunterricht/Islamischer Unterricht) offer Islamic religious education, so Muslim pupils may learn about these festivals in RU rather than Ethik.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Jewish Festivals
topics.nameDe: Jüdische Feste: Schabbat, Pessach, Chanukka, Sukkot
topics.description: Know the weekly Shabbat and major Jewish festivals — Pesach (exodus from Egypt, Seder meal), Chanukka (festival of lights with the eight-branched Chanukkia), Sukkot (Laubhüttenfest) — with their stories, rituals and symbols, and Jewish life in Germany today.
evidence: Explain what is remembered at Pesach and name an element of the Seder meal
Describe Chanukka and the meaning of the Chanukkia
Explain why Shabbat is a day of rest and how it is celebrated
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you what Jewish families remember at Pesach or Chanukka and describe one ritual or symbol of the festival?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: The Church Year and Public Holidays
topics.nameDe: Kirchenjahr und Feiertage: Ostern, Pfingsten, Erntedank
topics.description: Place the main Christian festivals in the church year — Advent, Christmas, Lent and Easter (Karfreitag, Ostern: death and resurrection of Jesus), Ascension, Pentecost, Erntedank (harvest thanksgiving) — tell religious meanings apart from customs (Easter bunny, eggs), and know that Germany’s public holidays follow this calendar but differ between Länder.
evidence: Order the main Christian festivals through the year
Explain the religious meaning of Easter and how it differs from the egg-and-bunny customs
Name a public holiday that exists only in some Länder
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you what Christians remember at Easter — beyond chocolate eggs — and put Easter, Pentecost and Christmas in the right order through the year?
topics.laenderNotes: Public holidays differ: Fronleichnam (e.g. BW, BY, HE, NW, RP, SL), Allerheiligen (BW, BY, NW, RP, SL), Reformationstag (eastern and northern Länder), Buß- und Bettag (Sachsen), Weltkindertag (Thüringen), Internationaler Frauentag (Berlin, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern).

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Death, Grief and Comfort
topics.description: Talk about experiences of birth and death, understand grief as a natural reaction and ways of comforting (Trost), and know different ideas of what comes after death in religions and worldviews (resurrection, paradise, rebirth, nothing).
evidence: Describe ways to comfort someone who is grieving
Name two different ideas about what happens after death from religions or worldviews
Express their own thoughts about life and death in words, pictures or writing
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a pet or grandparent dies, can {{name}} talk about their feelings, think of ways to comfort others — and tell you what different people believe happens after death?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Giving Reasons and Judging
topics.description: Distinguish an opinion from a reasoned judgement, give reasons and counter-reasons (pro and contra) on a moral question, test claims with examples and thought experiments ('What if everyone did that?') and form a justified position of their own.
evidence: Give at least two reasons for their opinion on a moral question
State a counter-argument to their own view
Use a thought experiment or example to test a claim
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} says 'homework should be banned', can they give reasons, think of a good argument against their own view, and then decide what they really think?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Places of Worship
topics.description: Describe the main features of a church (altar, cross, font, organ, tower), a synagogue (Torah ark, bimah, eternal light) and a mosque (mihrab, minbar, minaret, prayer rugs, washing area), how people behave there and — ideally after a visit — compare them.
evidence: Name two typical features each of a church, a synagogue and a mosque
Explain respectful behaviour when visiting a place of worship (e.g. shoes off in a mosque, head covering in a synagogue)
Compare what the three buildings have in common
topics.assessmentPrompt: After visiting a church or mosque, can {{name}} name special objects inside — like the altar or the prayer niche — and explain how visitors are expected to behave?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Sacred Texts and Commandments
topics.description: Know that Judaism has the Tanakh with the Torah, Christianity the Bible (Old and New Testament) and Islam the Koran, how these texts are treated and used, and central commandments and stories — e.g. the Ten Commandments, the double commandment of love, the Good Samaritan.
evidence: Match Torah, Bible and Koran to their religions and describe how they are handled with respect
Retell one story or commandment from a sacred text and its moral message
Compare a religious commandment with a rule from everyday life
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you which holy book belongs to which religion, and retell a story like the Good Samaritan and what it teaches?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Creation Stories and Science
topics.nameDe: Woher kommt die Welt? Schöpfungserzählungen und Naturwissenschaft
topics.description: Compare mythological and religious creation stories (e.g. the biblical seven days) with scientific explanations (Big Bang, evolution) and understand that they answer different kinds of questions.
evidence: Retell a creation story from one religion or culture
Describe in simple terms the scientific account of how the Earth and life developed
Explain one way the religious and scientific accounts answer different questions
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears both the creation story from the Bible and the Big Bang explanation, can they explain how the two differ and what each is trying to answer?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Fairness, Justice and the Golden Rule
topics.description: Think about what is fair — equal shares versus sharing by need, equal minimum rights for all children (UN-Kinderrechtskonvention) — and the Golden Rule ('Treat others as you want to be treated') as a principle shared by many religions and philosophies.
evidence: Explain the Golden Rule and apply it to a conflict situation
Compare equal sharing with sharing by need in an example and judge which is fairer
Name two children’s rights and explain why every child should have them
topics.assessmentPrompt: If there are three slices of cake and one child hasn't eaten all day, can {{name}} discuss whether equal shares or sharing by need is fairer — and connect it to 'treat others as you'd like to be treated'?
topics.laenderNotes: Kinderrechte are also a Sachunterricht topic in most Länder (UN-Kinderrechtskonvention, ratified by Germany in 1992).

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Motives and Consequences of Actions
topics.nameDe: Über das eigene Handeln nachdenken: Beweggründe und Folgen
topics.description: Reflect on why they act (feelings, wishes, attitudes) and on the consequences of their actions for themselves and others, take responsibility, and weigh alternatives such as giving in or standing firm, honesty or lying.
evidence: Name the motive behind a character’s action in a story
Predict short- and long-term consequences of a choice for different people
Discuss with reasons whether a lie can ever be justified
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} broke something and nobody saw, can they think through what might happen if they tell the truth or keep quiet — and what a responsible choice would be?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Respect, Diversity and Prejudice
topics.description: Value the diversity of ways of living, beliefs and opinions, distinguish opinion, criticism and prejudice (Vorurteil, Stereotyp), understand that perception is subjective and can deceive, and use respectful language towards others, especially outsiders.
evidence: Explain the difference between a prejudice and an opinion with an example
Describe how two people can perceive the same situation differently
Show respectful behaviour towards someone excluded, e.g. inviting them to join
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears a classmate say 'All boys are…' or 'People from there are…', can they explain why that is a prejudice and respond respectfully?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Responsible Consumption
topics.description: See through attempts by advertising and peers to influence what they buy (brands as status symbols), distinguish needs from wants, and evaluate consequences of consumption for people elsewhere (working conditions, cheap products), animals and the environment (ecological footprint), finding concrete alternatives.
evidence: Distinguish a need from a want in their own purchases
Explain how a cheap product can have hidden costs for workers or the environment
Analyse an advert or brand and explain how it tries to persuade
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} wants a particular brand of trainers, can they explain why — and think about who made them and under what conditions?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Judaism, Christianity and Islam Compared
topics.nameDe: Judentum, Christentum und Islam: Gemeinsamkeiten und Unterschiede
topics.description: Explain central beliefs and practices of the three Abrahamic religions — one God, Abraham as common ancestor, Shabbat / Sunday / Friday prayer, Jesus' death and resurrection in Christianity, the Five Pillars of Islam — and identify shared values such as charity (Nächstenliebe, Barmherzigkeit).
evidence: Explain why Judaism, Christianity and Islam are called 'Abrahamic' religions
Name a central belief or practice specific to each of the three
Identify a value the three share and give an example of it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain what Judaism, Christianity and Islam have in common — like belief in one God and Abraham — and one thing that is different in each?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern's Gymnasium Ethik treats Judaism and Christianity in Kl. 6 and Islam in a later year; other plans (e.g. LER Brandenburg) include Islam, Buddhism and Hinduism already in Kl. 5–6.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Religious and Non-Religious Worldviews
topics.description: Understand that people orient their lives by different worldviews — religions (including Buddhism and Hinduism) and non-religious views such as humanism, atheism or agnosticism — and that freedom of religion and belief (Art. 4 GG) protects all of them.
evidence: Explain the difference between believing in God, not believing in God and being unsure
Name a non-religious source of values (e.g. humanism, human rights)
Explain what religious freedom in Germany's Basic Law means
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that some people believe in God, some don't and some aren't sure — and that in Germany everyone is free to choose?
topics.laenderNotes: LER (Brandenburg) and Ethik (Berlin) explicitly include non-religious worldviews; Humanistische Lebenskunde (HVD) is a voluntary subject in Berlin and Brandenburg.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Arguing Rationally
topics.description: Build and test arguments: state a thesis, give reasons and examples, draw valid conclusions, check consistency, truthfulness and testability, and respond to counter-arguments in a debate.
evidence: Write an argument with thesis, reason, example and conclusion
Find the contradiction or missing premise in a weak argument
Answer a counter-argument in a debate without personal attacks
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} claims that a school rule is unfair, can they give a reason and an example and answer a counter-argument?
topics.laenderNotes: In NRW this belongs to Praktische Philosophie (Sek I), in Niedersachsen to Werte und Normen, in Brandenburg to LER and in most other Länder to Ethik.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Islam: Beliefs, Practice and Branches
topics.nameDe: Islam: Mohammed, Koran, Fünf Säulen; Sunniten, Schiiten, Aleviten
topics.description: Explain the foundations of Islam (Muhammad, the Qur'an as revelation, the five pillars, mosque and community), its main branches (Sunni, Shia, Alevi) and its ethical teachings, and compare them with Judaism and Christianity.
evidence: Explain the five pillars and what they mean for believers
Describe the significance of the Qur'an and of Muhammad
Name shared ethical ideas of Judaism, Christianity and Islam
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} visits a mosque, can they explain what happens at Friday prayer and why the Qur'an is central?
topics.laenderNotes: Islamic religious education exists in several Länder (e.g. NRW, Niedersachsen), and Bayern offers 'Islamischer Unterricht' as a subject choice. In ev./kath. RU Islam is studied in interreligious units, usually in Kl. 7–8.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Muslim Life in Germany; Islam and Islamism
topics.nameDe: Muslime in Deutschland; Islam und Islamismus
topics.description: Gain a differentiated picture of Muslim everyday life in Germany (prayer, food rules, headscarf debate, mosque communities, discrimination) and distinguish the religion of Islam from political Islamism and extremism.
evidence: Describe everyday religious practice of Muslims in Germany
Explain the difference between Muslims and Islamists
Discuss a current debate such as the headscarf from several perspectives
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears someone equate Muslims with terrorists, can they explain why that is wrong and what Islamism means?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Growing Up: Identity and Peer Pressure
topics.nameDe: Erwachsen werden: Identität, Selbstbild und Gruppendruck
topics.description: Reflect on the changes of puberty in body, relationships and goals, on how identity forms through self-image and the views of others, and on the tension between belonging to a peer group and acting on one's own convictions, including resisting group pressure.
evidence: Compare their self-image with how others see them and draw a conclusion
Explain how a peer group can support and pressure its members
Show in a role play how to say no to group pressure respectfully
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s friends push them to do something they think is wrong, can they explain what is going on and refuse without losing face?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Constructive Communication in Conflicts
topics.nameDe: Konflikte konstruktiv lösen: Sach- und Beziehungsebene, Ich-Botschaften, Feedback
topics.description: Analyse the causes of conflicts (interests, perceptions, prejudices, communication problems), distinguish the content and the relationship level of a message, and use active listening, mirroring, I-messages and feedback rules to solve conflicts without false solutions such as violence or giving in.
evidence: Identify the interests behind each side's position in a conflict scene
Rephrase an accusation as an I-message and mirror the other person's feelings
Apply a conflict-resolution model to reach a compromise in a role play
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} argues with a friend about a group task, can they say what bothers them without blaming, listen to the other side and find a fair agreement?
topics.laenderNotes: Taught in all Ersatzfächer, under different names: Ethik (e.g. Bayern Eth7), Praktische Philosophie (NRW), Werte und Normen (Niedersachsen), LER (Brandenburg). Ev./kath. RU frame conflict and reconciliation with Christian ethics.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Bullying, Cyberbullying and Bystanders
topics.description: Understand how bullying and cyberbullying work (repetition, imbalance of power, roles of perpetrator, victim, assistants and bystanders), take the victim's perspective, and know ways to stop bullying, from getting help to showing civil courage.
evidence: Describe the roles in a bullying situation and how the group keeps it going
Explain the special features of cyberbullying and how to secure evidence
Propose concrete steps a bystander can take without endangering themselves
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a classmate being mocked in the class chat, can they explain what they could do and whom they could ask for help?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Rights and Duties of Young People
topics.nameDe: Rechte und Pflichten im Jugendalter: Jugendschutz, Strafmündigkeit
topics.description: Know the rights and duties that grow with age in Germany (Jugendschutzgesetz on alcohol, going out and media; criminal responsibility from 14; religious majority) and reflect on how freedom and moral responsibility grow together.
evidence: Name three rules of the Jugendschutzgesetz and the reasons for them
Explain what criminal responsibility from age 14 means
Discuss which new freedom brings which responsibility
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} turns 14, can they explain which new rights and responsibilities they now have?
topics.laenderNotes: In most Länder pupils may decide themselves about attending Religionsunterricht from age 14 (Religionsmündigkeit); Bayern and Saarland set this at 18.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Love, Friendship and Sexuality
topics.description: Distinguish acquaintance, friendship and partnership, infatuation and love (e.g. Aristotle's three kinds of friendship, Fromm's art of loving), reflect on expectations, consent and responsibility in relationships, and respect different sexual orientations.
evidence: Explain Aristotle's three kinds of friendship with examples
Discuss which expectations in a relationship are legitimate
Explain why consent and respect are preconditions of sexuality
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} discusses a friendship that is only useful, can they relate it to Aristotle's kinds of friendship?
topics.laenderNotes: Sex education is cross-curricular (Biologie, Ethik/RU); in ev./kath. RU the topic is framed by the Christian understanding of love and partnership.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: The Search for Meaning
topics.nameDe: Sinnsuche: Quellen von Sinn und Grenzsituationen
topics.description: Explore what can give life meaning (relationships, achievement, helping, creativity, nature, religion), weigh fun and pleasure against deeper sources of meaning, and reflect on crises such as illness, failure and death as challenges and chances to grow.
evidence: Name and compare different sources of meaning with examples
Discuss a thought experiment such as Nozick's experience machine
Explain how a crisis can change what someone finds meaningful
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked whether a life of constant fun would be a good life, can they argue with Nozick's experience machine?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Animal Ethics
topics.description: Discuss the moral status of animals (sentience, reason, language), problem areas such as factory farming, animal experiments and keeping pets, and the consequences of one's own consumption for animals.
evidence: Explain criteria for moral status and apply them to humans and animals
Weigh arguments for and against animal experiments
Judge their own diet or consumption with regard to animal welfare
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} discusses whether eating meat is wrong, can they use the criterion of sentience in their argument?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Environmental Ethics
topics.nameDe: Umweltethik: Begründungen des Naturschutzes und Nachhaltigkeit
topics.description: Compare reasons for protecting nature (anthropocentric, pathocentric, biocentric, ecocentric) and the concept of sustainability, analyse links between modern lifestyles and environmental problems with a case-analysis method, and judge their own behaviour.
evidence: Explain two different justifications for protecting nature
Analyse an environmental case (plastic, diet or energy) with a case-analysis method
Derive a reasoned rule for their own behaviour
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} argues about cutting down a forest for a road, can they bring in different reasons for protecting nature?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Social Engagement and Volunteering
topics.description: Understand social engagement as a pillar of a humane society, explore ways to get involved at school (pupil council, peer mediation, tutoring), locally (clubs, rescue services, welfare organisations) and globally (NGOs), and plan or carry out a small project.
evidence: Describe three forms of volunteering and what they contribute
Explain what volunteers gain, e.g. the experience of self-efficacy
Plan a small engagement project for their class or neighbourhood
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s class wants to help in their neighbourhood, can they plan a project and say what it would achieve for others and for themselves?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Buddhism
topics.nameDe: Buddhismus: Vier Edle Wahrheiten, Achtfacher Pfad, Meditation
topics.description: Explain Buddhism as a reform of Hinduism (the life of the Buddha, the Four Noble Truths, the Middle Way and the Eightfold Path, meditation), and compare its ethics and its mystical path with the revealed religions.
evidence: Explain the Four Noble Truths
Describe the Eightfold Path and its ethical part
Compare meditation in Buddhism with prayer in an Abrahamic religion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that Buddhism has no creator god, can they explain how it still guides how people live?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Hinduism
topics.description: Explain core ideas of Hinduism (Brahman and Atman, samsara, karma, dharma, moksha and the three paths to liberation, the caste system and its critique) and its influence on everyday life in India.
evidence: Explain the cycle of rebirth and the role of karma
Describe the three paths to moksha
Discuss the caste system and how it is criticised today
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears someone say 'that's karma', can they explain what karma means in Hinduism?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Peace Ethics: Just War and Pacifism
topics.description: Compare just-war theory and its misuse with pacifism (e.g. Gandhi, King), analyse a current armed conflict and the situation of those affected, and apply nonviolent communication and de-escalation to personal conflicts.
evidence: Explain the criteria of a just war and a pacifist objection
Analyse a current conflict from the perspective of those affected
Use nonviolent communication (observation, feeling, need, request) in a role play
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} discusses whether military help for a country under attack is right, can they use just-war criteria and a pacifist argument?
topics.laenderNotes: Peace ethics is also part of ev./kath. RU (Christian ethics of peace) and of Politik; in the Oberstufe it returns with Kant's 'Zum ewigen Frieden' and a global peace order.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Conscience
topics.nameDe: Gewissen: Entstehung und Deutungen (Thomas von Aquin, Kant, Freud)
topics.description: Reflect on experiences of conscience before and after actions, compare interpretations of conscience (reason and natural law in Thomas Aquinas, the inner court in Kant, the super-ego in Freud, socialisation), and recognise how conscience can be shaped or silenced, e.g. by rationalisation or repression.
evidence: Compare two interpretations of conscience
Analyse a dilemma in which conscience conflicts with loyalty or rules
Explain one defence mechanism that silences conscience
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} feels guilty after lying to a friend, can they explain what their conscience is according to two different thinkers?
topics.laenderNotes: In ev./kath. RU conscience is also discussed in the light of Christian ethics, in kath. RU including the Church's teaching on the formation of conscience.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Responsibility
topics.nameDe: Verantwortung: Absicht, Mittel, Umstände und Folgen einer Handlung
topics.description: Analyse the structure of responsibility (who is responsible for what, to whom and before which authority) and judge actions by intention, means, circumstances and consequences, for oneself, for others and for society.
evidence: Describe the dimensions of responsibility in a case
Judge an action separately by intention, means and consequences
Explain why good intentions alone do not justify an action
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} shares a video that hurts a classmate 'as a joke', can they analyse their responsibility by intention and consequences?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Media Ethics
topics.nameDe: Medienethik: Information und Meinung, Wahrheit, Verantwortung, Daten
topics.description: Distinguish information from opinion, judge the credibility of sources with simple criteria and theories of truth, recognise staged reality and manipulation in social networks, and discuss the responsibility of journalists, platforms and users, including the press code and data protection.
evidence: Separate facts from opinions in a news item
Check a viral claim with criteria of credibility
Discuss who is responsible for a harmful post: author, platform or users
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a shocking post that is shared thousands of times, can they check whether it is true and explain who is responsible?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Scepticism and the Limits of Knowledge
topics.nameDe: Skeptizismus: Gorgias, Descartes, Gehirn im Tank
topics.description: Discuss sceptical arguments (Gorgias' three theses, Descartes' methodical doubt, the brain-in-a-vat thought experiment) and answers to them, and their consequences for how we see ourselves and live together.
evidence: Explain Descartes' methodical doubt and the cogito
Use the brain-in-a-vat thought experiment to state the sceptical problem
Discuss whether radical scepticism can be refuted
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked how they know they are not dreaming right now, can they explain Descartes' answer?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Philosophical Questions and the Origins of Philosophy
topics.nameDe: Ursprünge des Philosophierens: Staunen, Zweifel, Mythos und Logos
topics.description: Recognise wonder and doubt as starting points of philosophy, distinguish philosophical from everyday and scientific questions (Kant's four questions), and see how the Presocratics moved from myth to rational explanation (logos).
evidence: Formulate a philosophical question and explain why it is philosophical
Assign questions to Kant's four questions
Explain the difference between a mythical and a Presocratic explanation of the world
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} asks 'Why is there something rather than nothing?', can they explain why this is a philosophical question?
topics.laenderNotes: Where Philosophie starts only in the Oberstufe, this introduction comes at the beginning of the Einführungsphase.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Socrates and the Socratic Dialogue
topics.description: Explain Socrates' method of questioning (testing definitions, 'I know that I know nothing') in contrast to the sophists, e.g. Protagoras' homo-mensura sentence, and conduct a Socratic conversation that examines a concept such as justice or courage.
evidence: Explain Socrates' method and its aim
Contrast Socrates with the sophists
Lead or take part in a Socratic dialogue that tests a definition
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a classmate defines courage as 'not being afraid', can {{name}} ask Socratic questions that test the definition?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Analysing Philosophical Texts
topics.nameDe: Philosophische Texte erschließen: Argumentationsrekonstruktion und Strukturbild
topics.description: Read a philosophical text methodically: identify thesis, premises, conclusion and key terms, reconstruct the argument in standard form or as a structure diagram, and test it for validity and plausibility.
evidence: Reconstruct an argument from a short text in premise-conclusion form
Draw a structure diagram of a text's line of thought
Check one premise for plausibility and the conclusion for validity
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads an excerpt from Plato, can they write the argument down as premises and conclusion?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Fundamentalism and Religious Extremism
topics.description: Recognise fundamentalism and extremism in different religions (features, recruitment, dangers), distinguish them from devout faith, and discuss how a free society should respond.
evidence: Name features of religious extremism with examples from more than one religion
Explain how extremist groups recruit young people online
Distinguish strong faith from extremism with criteria
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} comes across an extremist video online, can they recognise its manipulative features and explain why it is not normal religious practice?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Critique of Religion
topics.description: Explain major modern critiques of religion (Feuerbach's projection theory, Marx's 'opium of the people', Nietzsche's 'death of God', Freud's illusion) and possible replies, and distinguish atheism from agnosticism.
evidence: Explain Feuerbach's projection thesis
Compare two critiques of religion
Formulate a reply to one critique from a religious perspective
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads Feuerbach's claim that God is a projection of human wishes, can they explain it and give a possible reply?
topics.laenderNotes: In ev./kath. RU the critique of religion is usually treated in Kl. 10 or the Oberstufe under the question of God.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Proofs of God and the Problem of Evil
topics.description: Examine an argument for the existence of God (e.g. cosmological or ontological) and its critique, and the theodicy problem, i.e. how a good and almighty God can allow suffering, with several answers.
evidence: Reconstruct one proof of God and a critique of it
State the theodicy problem as a logical trilemma
Compare two answers to the theodicy problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} asks why God allows earthquakes, can they state the theodicy problem and compare two answers?
topics.laenderNotes: Also core content of ev./kath. RU, usually in Kl. 9–10 or the Oberstufe.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Medical Ethics and Assisted Dying
topics.description: Apply the four principles of medical ethics (autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence, justice) and the concepts of person and moral status to cases, especially assisted dying (passive, indirect and active euthanasia, assisted suicide) in the context of German law.
evidence: Apply the four principles to a medical case
Distinguish forms of assisted dying and the German legal situation
Evaluate an argument such as the slippery-slope argument in the debate
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} discusses whether doctors should help a terminally ill patient to die, can they use the four principles and the different forms of assisted dying?
topics.laenderNotes: The legal frame (Federal Constitutional Court ruling of 2020 on § 217 StGB) is German. In kath. RU the Church's position on the protection of life is a required perspective.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Human Beings as Natural and Cultural Beings
topics.nameDe: Der Mensch als Natur- und Kulturwesen
topics.description: Discuss what makes humans special: evolutionary origins and behaviour (cooperation, aggression), the human as a 'deficient being' that needs culture (Gehlen), as spirit open to the world (Scheler), language and education, and why any definition of human nature is problematic.
evidence: Explain one anthropological position in its main steps
Compare a biological and a cultural explanation of a behaviour
Discuss why any definition of 'human nature' is problematic
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that aggression is 'just human nature', can they discuss this with biological and cultural arguments?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Human Dignity and Personhood
topics.description: Explain what human dignity means and how it is justified (theologically through the image of God, by Kant through persons as ends in themselves, in Art. 1 of the Grundgesetz), and discuss the concept of the person (Locke, Singer) and its ethical consequences.
evidence: Compare a religious and a Kantian justification of human dignity
Explain why Art. 1 GG makes dignity inviolable
Discuss a case in which the concept of person is contested
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads Art. 1 of the Grundgesetz, can they explain two ways to justify why human dignity is inviolable?
topics.laenderNotes: In ev./kath. RU the theological justification (Gottebenbildlichkeit) is required; Ethik and Philosophie start from Kant and the Grundgesetz.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Cultural Relativism and Universalism
topics.nameDe: Werte und Normen zwischen Kulturrelativismus und Universalismus
topics.description: Compare cultural relativism (moral norms are valid only within a culture) with universalist positions (some norms bind all humans), test both on cases such as human rights or traditional practices, and evaluate their consequences for tolerance.
evidence: Explain a culturally relativist and a universalist position in their argumentative steps
Apply both to a concrete case
Judge which position better supports tolerance and human rights
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears 'that is just their culture' about a practice that harms children, can they discuss relativism and universalism?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Kant's Ethics of Duty
topics.nameDe: Pflichtethik Kants: guter Wille und kategorischer Imperativ
topics.description: Explain Kant's deontological ethics: the good will, acting from duty versus in accordance with duty, the categorical imperative in its formula of universal law and its formula of humanity, and autonomy; test the imperative on cases and against objections.
evidence: Test a maxim with the formula of universal law
Explain the formula of humanity and its link to human dignity
Compare Kant's ethics with utilitarianism on one case
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wonders whether a lie to protect a friend is allowed, can they test the maxim with the categorical imperative?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Aristotle's Virtue Ethics
topics.nameDe: Tugendethik des Aristoteles: Mesoteslehre und Eudaimonie
topics.description: Explain Aristotle's virtue ethics: the good life (eudaimonia) as goal, ethical and intellectual virtues acquired by habit, the doctrine of the mean (courage between cowardice and recklessness) and practical wisdom, and compare it with rule-based ethics.
evidence: Explain the doctrine of the mean with two virtues
Explain why virtues are acquired by practice
Discuss strengths and weaknesses of virtue ethics compared with Kant
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked whether being extremely honest can be a fault, can they answer with Aristotle's doctrine of the mean?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Utilitarianism
topics.nameDe: Utilitarismus: Bentham, Mill; Handlungs-, Regel- und Präferenzutilitarismus
topics.description: Explain the utilitarian principle of the greatest happiness of the greatest number, Bentham's hedonic calculus and Mill's higher pleasures, act, rule and preference utilitarianism (Singer), apply them to cases and discuss objections concerning justice and minority rights.
evidence: Apply the utilitarian calculation to a moral dilemma
Explain the difference between act and rule utilitarianism
Discuss an objection, e.g. sacrificing one person for many
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} considers the trolley dilemma, can they explain what a utilitarian would do and why critics object?
topics.laenderNotes: Core Oberstufe content of Ethik and Philosophie in all Länder; ev./kath. RU treat it among models of ethical judgement (Leitfrage 'Was soll ich tun?').

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Fallacies and Unfair Argument
topics.description: Recognise fallacies and unfair techniques (ad hominem, appeal to the majority, straw man, slippery slope, is-ought fallacy) in debates and online, and respond to them fairly.
evidence: Identify three fallacies in a debate transcript or comment thread
Explain why an inference from 'is' to 'ought' is invalid
Rephrase a fallacious argument into a fair one
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads 'If we allow this, soon everything will be allowed', can they name the type of argument and test it?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Philosophical Problem Reflection
topics.description: Carry out a full philosophical problem reflection on a text, picture or case: identify the problem and place it in context, work on it by analysing and comparing positions, and take and justify a position of one's own. This is the standard structure of Abitur tasks in Philosophie and Ethik.
evidence: Formulate the philosophical problem in a given material
Compare two positions on it with arguments
Write a reasoned own position that weighs the arguments
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets an excerpt from Berkeley in the exam, can they state the problem, compare it with another position and take a reasoned stand?
topics.laenderNotes: The task format is used by Philosophie (e.g. NRW, Berlin, Brandenburg in Sek II), Ethik (e.g. Bayern, Baden-Württemberg, Sachsen) and Werte und Normen (Niedersachsen). Ev./kath. Religionslehre use the related operators of the religion EPA. In G8 Länder such as Berlin and Brandenburg the Oberstufe starts one year earlier.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: The Question of God
topics.nameDe: Die Gottesfrage: Gottesbilder, Theismus, Atheismus, Agnostizismus
topics.description: Discuss ways of speaking about God (personal God, images and metaphors, negative theology, the Trinity), arguments of theism, atheism and agnosticism, and what believing in God means for a person's life.
evidence: Compare two images of God and their function
Reconstruct an atheist and a theist argument
Explain why many theologians call talk about God analogical or metaphorical
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} says they cannot imagine an old man in the sky, can they explain other ways in which religions speak about God?
topics.laenderNotes: Ev. RU focuses on the Christian talk of God (e.g. Luther, Bonhoeffer), kath. RU adds the teaching of the Church; in Ethik and Philosophie the topic appears as philosophy of religion.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Religion and State in Germany
topics.nameDe: Religion und Staat in Deutschland: Religionsfreiheit, Religionsunterricht, Kirchensteuer
topics.description: Explain the German model of state and religion: freedom of religion (Art. 4 GG), religious neutrality combined with cooperation (Art. 7 Abs. 3 GG on religious education, Art. 140 GG on church tax and the legal status of religious communities), positive and negative freedom of religion, and current debates such as crucifix, headscarf and Islamic religious education.
evidence: Explain positive and negative freedom of religion with a case
Describe the legal basis of religious education and of church tax
Discuss a court case such as the crucifix or headscarf ruling
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wonders why a state school offers religious education, can they explain the constitutional basis and the alternatives?
topics.laenderNotes: Special arrangements exist in Berlin and Bremen (Art. 141 GG, 'Bremer Klausel'), in Brandenburg (LER as ordinary subject) and in Hamburg ('Religionsunterricht für alle').

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Religion and Science
topics.nameDe: Religion und Naturwissenschaft: Schöpfung, Evolution und Modelle ihres Verhältnisses
topics.description: Compare models of the relationship between religion and science (conflict, independence, dialogue, integration), read creation texts and the theory of evolution each in their own kind of language, and discuss truth claims, creationism and the limits of scientific explanation.
evidence: Explain two models of the relationship between faith and science
Compare the kind of statement made in Genesis 1 with that of evolution theory
Discuss why creationism is criticised by scientists and theologians alike
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that evolution disproves God, can they explain the different kinds of statements and the models of their relationship?
topics.laenderNotes: Core Oberstufe topic of ev./kath. RU (Leitfrage 'Was ist wahr?'); in Ethik and Philosophie it belongs to truth and knowledge.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Human Rights: Justification and Universality
topics.nameDe: Menschenrechte: Begründung, universeller Geltungsanspruch und Durchsetzung
topics.description: Explain the justification of human rights (natural law, human dignity, contract), the Universal Declaration of 1948, objections from cultural relativism and problems of enforcement, and develop their own position on universal validity.
evidence: Explain two justifications of human rights
Discuss an objection to their universality
Analyse a case where human rights are violated and how they could be enforced
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that human rights are a Western idea, can they discuss the objection and give a reasoned answer?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Social Contract Theories
topics.nameDe: Staatsphilosophie: Gesellschaftsvertrag bei Hobbes, Locke und Rousseau
topics.description: Explain why state power needs legitimation and how contract theories justify it (Hobbes' state of nature and Leviathan, Locke's natural rights and right of resistance, Rousseau's general will), and assess them in view of democracy and its endangerment by populism.
evidence: Compare the state of nature in Hobbes and Locke
Explain how each theory legitimises state power
Assess a populist claim with the idea of the general will or of rights
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} imagines a world without government, can they explain what Hobbes and Locke would expect and what follows for the state?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Bioethics at the Beginning of Life
topics.nameDe: Bioethik am Lebensanfang: Pränataldiagnostik, PID, Genomeditierung, Schwangerschaftsabbruch
topics.description: Discuss ethical questions at the beginning of life (prenatal and preimplantation diagnosis, genome editing with CRISPR, abortion) using the concepts of person, dignity and moral status of the embryo (the SKIP arguments) and different ethical theories.
evidence: Explain the SKIP arguments for the moral status of the embryo
Compare two positions on preimplantation diagnosis
Take a reasoned position on genome editing of embryos
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads about 'designer babies', can they discuss genome editing with the arguments about the moral status of the embryo?
topics.laenderNotes: Germany's Embryonenschutzgesetz is stricter than the law in many other countries; ev. and kath. RU also discuss the churches' positions.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Ethics of Technology and Artificial Intelligence
topics.nameDe: Technik- und KI-Ethik: Verantwortung, Autonomie, Diskriminierung
topics.description: Discuss ethical problems of technology and AI: responsibility for decisions of autonomous systems such as self-driving cars, bias and discrimination in algorithms, surveillance and data, generative AI and authorship, and whether machines can be moral agents.
evidence: Apply two ethical theories to a dilemma of an autonomous car
Explain how bias in training data leads to discrimination
Take a reasoned position on who is responsible for an AI decision
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that an AI tool rejected job applicants unfairly, can they explain how this happens and who is responsible?
topics.laenderNotes: The new NRW Sek II plan for Philosophie (in force from 2027) makes artificial intelligence a compulsory applied-ethics and epistemology topic.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Free Will and Determinism
topics.description: Discuss whether the will is free: determinist and indeterminist positions, findings of neuroscience (Libet experiment, Roth, Singer) and their critique ('reasons are not causes'), compatibilism (Bieri), and the consequences for responsibility and punishment.
evidence: Explain a determinist and an indeterminist position
Explain the Libet experiment and two objections to its interpretation
Discuss what follows for moral responsibility if the will is not free
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that brain research proves we have no free will, can they explain the Libet experiment and why philosophers doubt the conclusion?
topics.laenderNotes: NRW: the Grundkurs treats a determinist and an indeterminist position, the Leistungskurs adds compatibilism; Bayern adds Kant, Sartre and Bieri on freedom.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Discourse Ethics
topics.description: Explain Habermas' discourse ethics: a norm is valid if all those affected could agree to it in a free, rational discourse; the rules of discourse and the ideal speech situation, their use for solving conflicts, and objections.
evidence: State the discourse principle and two rules of discourse
Apply discourse ethics to a conflict between stakeholders
Discuss an objection, e.g. the problem of those who cannot take part, like future generations
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s school must decide on a mobile-phone ban, can they explain how a discourse-ethical process would reach a fair rule?
topics.laenderNotes: NRW: Leistungskurs only; Bayern already teaches Habermas at grundlegendem Anforderungsniveau (Eth12).

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Ethical Judgement in Steps
topics.description: Form a well-founded moral judgement on a case in steps: describe the situation and those affected, name the conflicting values and norms, apply ethical theories, weigh the arguments and justify a decision. The method is shared by Ethik, Philosophie and ev./kath. Religionslehre.
evidence: Analyse a case with a step model of ethical judgement
Apply at least two ethical theories and compare their results
Write a reasoned judgement that addresses counter-arguments
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets a case about organ donation, can they work through the steps and reach a reasoned judgement?
topics.laenderNotes: In ev./kath. RU the step models (e.g. after Tödt) also weigh biblical and theological arguments and church positions.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Nietzsche's Critique of Morality
topics.nameDe: Moralkritik Nietzsches: Herren- und Sklavenmoral, Nihilismus
topics.description: Explain Nietzsche's genealogy of morals (master and slave morality, 'herd morality', resentment), his diagnosis of nihilism and his ideal of self-determination, and discuss what follows for the possibility of justifying morality.
evidence: Explain the distinction between master and slave morality
Relate Nietzsche's critique to Christian or Kantian ethics
Assess whether the critique undermines all morality
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads Nietzsche on 'herd morality', can they explain his claim and argue whether he is right?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern: eA plan (Eth12); elsewhere an optional author in the Leistungskurs.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Kant's Theory of Knowledge
topics.nameDe: Kants Erkenntnistheorie: a priori, a posteriori, synthetische Urteile
topics.description: Explain Kant's synthesis of rationalism and empiricism: judgements a priori and a posteriori, analytic and synthetic, forms of intuition and categories, the 'Copernican turn' and the limits of knowledge (things in themselves).
evidence: Classify judgements as analytic or synthetic and as a priori or a posteriori
Explain the Copernican turn in Kant's epistemology
Explain why for Kant we cannot know things in themselves
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked whether '7 + 5 = 12' tells us something new, can they explain Kant's idea of synthetic judgements a priori?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: The Mind–Body Problem
topics.description: Compare dualist positions (Descartes, interactionist dualism) and materialist-monist positions (identity theory, functionalism) on how mind and body relate, discuss the problem of consciousness (qualia), and ask whether AI systems could have minds.
evidence: Reconstruct a dualist and a materialist position
Explain the qualia problem with a thought experiment such as Mary's room
Discuss whether a computer could have consciousness
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} asks whether a chatbot really understands, can they discuss it with dualist and materialist positions?
topics.laenderNotes: Compulsory in the NRW Qualifikationsphase; in other Länder philosophy of mind is often an elective topic.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Rationalism and Empiricism
topics.nameDe: Erkenntnistheorie: Rationalismus und Empirismus (Descartes, Locke, Hume)
topics.description: Compare rationalist (Descartes: innate ideas, reason as the source of knowledge) and empiricist theories of knowledge (Locke's tabula rasa, Hume's impressions and ideas and the problem of induction), and judge their strengths and weaknesses.
evidence: Reconstruct Descartes' and Locke's views on the origin of knowledge
Explain Hume's problem of induction
Assess which position better explains mathematical and scientific knowledge
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked whether we know that the sun will rise tomorrow, can they explain Hume's problem of induction?
topics.laenderNotes: The KMK EPA Philosophie illustrate an Abitur task with Berkeley's empiricism; Bayern teaches epistemology mainly in the eA plan.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Philosophy of Science
topics.description: Discuss how science gains knowledge and how far it can be trusted: induction and its problem, Popper's falsificationism, Kuhn's paradigm shifts, criteria that separate science from pseudoscience, and the reliability of knowledge generated by AI.
evidence: Explain Popper's principle of falsification with an example
Apply criteria to decide whether a claim is scientific or pseudoscientific
Discuss how reliable knowledge generated by AI systems is
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that astrology is 'confirmed by experience', can they use Popper's criterion to test the claim?
topics.laenderNotes: Bayern: Popper in the eA plan; NRW: validity claims of the sciences in Grund- and Leistungskurs.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Jonas' Ethics of Responsibility
topics.nameDe: Verantwortungsethik nach Hans Jonas: Fernethik und Heuristik der Furcht
topics.description: Explain Hans Jonas' imperative of responsibility for future generations and for nature (the new categorical imperative, ethics of distance, heuristics of fear), apply it to climate change and technological risks, and discuss intergenerational justice.
evidence: State Jonas' new categorical imperative and how it differs from Kant's
Apply the heuristics of fear to a technological risk
Discuss obligations to future generations in climate policy
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} discusses whether we owe anything to people born in 100 years, can they use Jonas' argument?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Hope in the Face of Death
topics.nameDe: Was darf ich hoffen? Tod und Jenseitsvorstellungen der Religionen
topics.description: Compare religious and secular answers to death and suffering: resurrection in Christianity, the hereafter in Judaism and Islam, rebirth and liberation in Hinduism and Buddhism, and secular views such as Epicurus', and reflect on what hope means for living.
evidence: Compare the ideas of the hereafter of three religions
Explain a secular position on death, e.g. Epicurus'
Discuss how ideas about death shape how people live
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked what religions say happens after death, can they compare three answers and a secular view?
topics.laenderNotes: Leitfrage 'Was darf ich hoffen?' of the ev./kath. EPA, where Christian eschatology is the focus; Ethik treats it comparatively.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Interreligious Dialogue and Truth Claims
topics.description: Compare models of how religions relate to each other's truth claims (exclusivism, inclusivism, pluralism), know criteria for constructive dialogue, and take part in or plan a dialogue encounter.
evidence: Explain the three models with an example each
Name criteria for respectful interreligious dialogue
Plan or reflect on a dialogue encounter, e.g. a visit to a synagogue or mosque
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears 'only my religion is true', can they place the statement among the models and discuss how dialogue is still possible?
topics.laenderNotes: Dialogue competence is a required competence of ev. and kath. RU in the KMK EPA; in Ethik interreligious content appears as comparative study of religions.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Ideas of the Good Life
topics.nameDe: Glück und gelingendes Leben: Aristoteles, Epikur, Stoa, Frankl
topics.description: Compare ancient answers to the question of the good life (Aristotle's eudaimonia, Epicurus' pleasure and freedom from pain, the Stoic life according to reason) with modern ones (Frankl's meaning through self-transcendence, empirical happiness research such as flow), and develop their own idea of a good life.
evidence: Compare the ideas of happiness of Aristotle, Epicurus and the Stoics
Explain Frankl's idea that meaning is found through self-transcendence
Assess a finding of happiness research for their own life
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked whether a rich, comfortable life is automatically a happy one, can they answer with Epicurus and Aristotle?
topics.laenderNotes: NRW places 'Entwürfe eines gelingenden Lebens' in the Einführungsphase (Kl. 11), Bayern in Kl. 13.

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Theories of Justice: Aristotle and Rawls
topics.description: Explain Aristotle's distinction between distributive and corrective (commutative) justice and Rawls' justice as fairness (original position, veil of ignorance, two principles, difference principle), and apply them to questions of social justice such as fair wages or equal opportunities in education.
evidence: Distinguish distributive and commutative justice with examples
Explain the veil of ignorance and the difference principle
Apply Rawls to a current question of social justice
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} discusses whether managers should earn 100 times more than workers, can they argue with Rawls' difference principle?

topics.subject: Religion & Ethik
topics.name: Arendt: Power, Violence and the Banality of Evil
topics.nameDe: Hannah Arendt: Macht und Gewalt; Eichmann-Prozess
topics.description: Explain Hannah Arendt's distinction between power (people acting together) and violence, and her report on the Eichmann trial with the thesis of the 'banality of evil', and discuss the tension between law and justice in the prosecution of Nazi crimes.
evidence: Explain Arendt's distinction between power and violence
Explain the thesis of the banality of evil and the criticism of it
Discuss the Eichmann trial as a case of law and justice
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads about Eichmann as a 'desk perpetrator', can they explain what Arendt meant by the banality of evil?

topics.subject: Sachunterricht
topics.subjectEn: General Studies (integrated science and social studies)
topics.name: Observing and Describing
topics.description: Look closely and over time at a plant, animal, object or event, notice details with several senses and describe them in words or a simple drawing, separating what was seen from what is guessed.
evidence: Describe at least four observable features of an object or living thing (colour, shape, size, texture, movement)
Produce a labelled observation drawing of something seen directly
Say what changed when observing the same thing on two occasions (e.g. a bean seedling on Monday and Friday)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches a snail on a leaf for a few minutes, can they describe exactly what they saw and draw it with labels?

topics.subject: Sachunterricht
topics.subjectEn: General Studies (integrated science and social studies)
topics.name: Living and Non-Living Things
topics.description: Tell living things from non-living things using signs of life: they feed, grow, breathe, reproduce, move or react, and they die.
evidence: Sort pictures into living and non-living
Name at least three signs of life
Explain why a plant counts as living even though it does not walk
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why a tree is alive but a stone is not?

topics.subject: Sachunterricht
topics.subjectEn: General Studies (integrated science and social studies)
topics.name: Me and My Identity
topics.nameDe: Ich bin ich: Stärken und Interessen
topics.description: Describe oneself — appearance, likes, strengths, things still being learned — and recognise that every person is unique and valuable.
evidence: Present a "Steckbrief" about themselves
Name at least two own strengths
Name something that makes a classmate special
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you three things they are good at and one thing they are still learning?

topics.subject: Sachunterricht
topics.subjectEn: General Studies (integrated science and social studies)
topics.name: Recognising Feelings
topics.description: Name basic feelings (joy, anger, fear, sadness), recognise them in oneself and others through facial expression and body signals, and express them appropriately.
evidence: Name at least four feelings and show them through facial expression
Describe how a feeling shows in the body (e.g. heart beating when scared)
Express a feeling in an "I" sentence
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is angry, can they say what they feel and where they feel it in their body?

topics.subject: Sachunterricht
topics.subjectEn: General Studies (integrated science and social studies)
topics.name: Naming Body Parts
topics.description: Name the main external parts of the body (head, trunk, arms, legs, hands, feet) including the correct terms for the genitals (Scheide/Vulva, Penis), as German curricula require.
evidence: Point to and name at least ten body parts
Use correct terms for the external genitals without embarrassment
Group body parts into head, trunk and limbs (Kopf, Rumpf, Gliedmaßen)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} name the parts of the body on a body outline, including the private parts, with the correct words?

topics.subject: Sachunterricht
topics.subjectEn: General Studies (integrated science and social studies)
topics.name: Crossing the Road Safely
topics.description: Cross the road safely as a pedestrian: stop at the kerb (Bordsteinkante), look left–right–left (right-hand traffic), use traffic lights, zebra crossings and crossing guards (Schülerlotsen), and never run out between parked cars.
evidence: Stop at the kerb and look left–right–left before crossing
Explain the meaning of the pedestrian light colours and the zebra crossing
Explain why crossing between parked cars is dangerous
topics.assessmentPrompt: On a walk, does {{name}} stop at the kerb, look both ways in the right order and cross only when it is safe?
topics.laenderNotes: Verkehrserziehung starts in Kita and Kl. 1 with police support in all Länder.

topics.subject: Sachunterricht
topics.subjectEn: General Studies (integrated science and social studies)
topics.name: The Four Seasons
topics.description: Name the four seasons in order and describe typical changes in weather, daylight, plants and animals during each one in Germany.
evidence: Name the four seasons in order
Describe one weather and one nature feature typical of each season
Sort pictures (e.g. a tree in blossom, bare tree) into seasons
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a picture of a bare tree with snow, can they name the season and say what comes next?

topics.subject: Sachunterricht
topics.subjectEn: General Studies (integrated science and social studies)
topics.name: Time Words and Daily Routine
topics.description: Use time words (gestern, heute, morgen, vorher, nachher, morgens, mittags, abends) correctly and put events of the daily routine in order.
evidence: Order pictures of a daily routine and narrate it
Use gestern/heute/morgen correctly in sentences
Answer "what happens before / after ..." questions about the school day
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you what they did yesterday, what they do today and what will happen tomorrow, using the right words?

topics.subject: Sachunterricht
topics.subjectEn: General Studies (integrated science and social studies)
topics.name: Asking Investigable Questions
topics.description: Turn curiosity about everyday phenomena into questions that can be answered by observing, trying out, asking someone or looking it up — the GDSU aim of meeting things with interest.
evidence: Formulate at least two own questions about a phenomenon shown in class
Say for a question whether it can be answered by trying it out, by asking someone or by looking it up
Pick one question and suggest a first way to find the answer
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} notices that puddles disappear after rain, can they ask a question about it that they could actually find out?
